M. Drouyn de Lhuys to Count Wulewski.—(Communicated to the Earl of 
Clarendon by Count Walewski, June 27, 1853.) 


M. le Comte, Paris, le 25 Juin, 1853, 

LE Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg, en livrant a la publicite la dépéche 
circulaire que M. le Comte de Nesselrode vient, par ordre de Sa Majesté 
Empereur Nicolas, d’envoyer a toutes les Légations de Russie a l'étranger, & 
donné A ce document Ja valeur d’un manifeste adressé a l'Europe elle-méme ; 
aussi ai-je pensé qu'il était nécessaire de vous faire part des réflexions générales 
que sa lecture m’a suggerées. 

Je remarquerai, tout d’abord, que de l'exposé méme du différend de la 
Russie avec la Porte, tel que le représente M. de Nesselrode, il résulte que la 
mission de M. le Prince Menchikoff & Constantinople n’avait qu'un but—le 
réglement des difficultés relatives au partage des Saints Lieux de Jérusalem 
entre les diverses communions Chrétiennes—et que ce but a été rempli a la 
satisfaction du Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg. La question qui se débat 
aujourd'hui est done toute nouvelle; elle ne se rattache, par aucun cdté, A celle 
de Jérusalem, et elle touche par tous 4 l’indépendance et a la souveraineté du 
Sultan. O’est le jugement qu’en ont deja porté, a Constantinople méme, les 
enn de la France, de l’Autriche, de la Grande Bretagne, et de la 

russe. 

Comment prétendre, en effet, que pour garantir aux Chrétiens du rit 
Oriental la possession de quelques sanctuatres déterminés, il faille les couvrir 
dans toute l’étendue de Empire Ottoman d’une protection officielle qui substi- 
tuerait l'autorité morale de l’ Empereur de Russie 4 celle qui revient légitimement 
au Grand Seigneur? Quelle corrélation existe-t-il entre deux faits si différens, et 
en quoi le plus important pourrait-il étre considéré comme wn appendice, comme 
une conséquence nécessaire de celui qui Vest le moins? 

A l’appui de ses prétentions, le Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg invoque ses 
anciens Traités avec la Porte, rappelle des analogies historiques, et fait valoir des 
griefs. Ce sont, M. le Comte, ces trois ordres d’arguments que je me propose 
de passer en revue aussi succinctement que posable | 

Quand on examine les Traités que la Russie a conclus avec la Turquie, on 
voit que, si elle a quelque fois stipulé pour des sujets du Sultan, ces derniers 
appartenaient soit 4 des provinces que les chances de la guerre avaient 
momentanément fait perdre 4 la Porte et 4 la rétrocession desquelles des 
conditions pouvaient étre posées, soit & des provinces qui, pendant la durée des 
hostilités, sétaient compromises envers le Gouvernement Ottoman et que la 
politique et humanité commandaient de protéger contre son ressentiment, 

Aucune de ces stipulations n'a le caractére de généralité quon essaye 
aujourd'hui de leur attribuer, et le Traité de Koutehouk Kainardji, notamment, ne 
confére & la Russie qu’un droit de protection limité et défini sur une église 
desservie par des prétres Russes, qu’il était question de fonder dans le faubourg 
de Galata, Cela ne veut pas dire assurément que dans la pratique et par la 
force des choses, le Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg n’ait été naturellement ameneé 4 
s'intévesser pour les Chrétiens du rit Grec qui forment dans la Turquie d'Europe 
la majorité de la population. Mais si a Porte, de son cété, a du tenir compte 


[ 240} 


2 


des sympathies de la Russie pour l'Eclise d’Orient, elle n'a pas jusqu’a présent 
souscrit d’engagement qui lui otft le mérite de sa tolérance, et lui imposat, au 
lieu de devoirs librement remplis & I’égard de ses propres sujets, des obligations 
envers tine Puissance Etrangére. Cest la que reside toute la question, et en 
énoncer simplement les termes, ¢’est en démontrer déja toute l'importance, 

Les analogies auxquelles se référe la circulaire de M. le Comte de Nessel- 
rode, s'appliquent-elles mieux a la situation présente ? 

S'il est survenu entre les Princes du Saint Empire, 4 l’époque de la 
réforme, des pactes relatifs a lexercice du culte nouveau dans leurs possessions, 
faut-il rappeler d’abord que cet Empire était une association d’etats régie par 
un méme chef, et ensuite que les transactions dont on parle ont été le résultat 
de longues guerres intestines ou de combinaisons politiques dans lesquelles le 
caractore électif de la dignité Impériale exergait nécessairement une grande 
influence ? ; 

~ Quant & nos capitulations avec la Turquie, M. le Comte, vous savez 
qu’elles. ne nous ont jamais donné le droit de protection sur les sujets 
Catholiques du Sultan. Si la France a pu rendre 4 cette fraction minime de la 
population Ottomane des services du genre de ceux que la Russie s‘honore elle- 
meme d'avoir rendas ses coréligionnaires, sa protection directe et officielle ne 
s'est jamais exercée que sur des établissements Ctrangers desservis par des pretres 
également étrangers et dont le chef spiritucl réside a Rome. La protection de 
la Russie, au contraire, s'appliquerait i un clergé composé de sujets du Sultan 
et soumis hitrarchiquement 4 un patriarche qui dépend aussi de la Porte. i 
n'y aurait done aucune assimilation possible entre la position des deux Puis- 
sances. 

Je consigne ici du reste un important passage d'un memoire de M. le Comte 
de Saint Priest, Ambassadeur du Roi Louis XVI a Constantinople de 1768 & 
1785, et qui détermine nettement le earactére de notre Protectorat. Voici 
comment s'exprime M, le Comte de Saint Priest : 

“(Op a decore le zéle de nos rois de l'expression de protection de la religion 
Catholique en Levant; mais elle est illusoire et servait & egarer ceux ui 
n'approfondissent pas la chose, Jamais les Sultans wont eu seulement Vidée 
que les monarques Frangais se crussent autorisés 4 simmiscer de la religion des 
sujets dela Porte. Il n'y a point de Prince, dit fort sagement un de mes predé- 
ceaseurs, M. le Marquis de Bonnat, dans un mémoire sur cette matiére, quelque 
étroite union qu'il ait avee un autre Souverain, qui lui permette de se méler de 
la religion de ses sujets. Les ‘Tures sont aussi délicats que d'autres lii-dessus, 

I] est aisé de comprendre que la France, n’ayant jamais traité avec Ta 
Porte qu’a titre @amitié, n'a pu lui imposer des obligations otieuses de leur 
nature. Aussi le premier point de mes instructions me prescrivait d/éviter tout 
ce qui pourrait causer de Vombrage & la Porte en donnant trop d’extension aux 
capitulations en matiére de religion,” 

Cette citation me dispense de toute autre explication sur un point qu'elle 
éclaire avec une si incontestable autorite. 

Ainsi donc, M. le Comte, ni les anciens ‘Traités, ni les analogies que l'on 
invoque, ne peuvent servir de bases ausst solides qu'on le pense aux pretentions 
du Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg. 

Reste la question des griefs. Ce que la Russie reproche 4 la Porte, c'est 
un manque de procédés. Chaque Gouvernement, sans deute, est le seul juge 
des exigences de sa dignité; mais il faut, eependant, que la réparation demeure 
toujours proportionnée a l’offense. Or des excuses ou des regrets constituent 
ordinuirement la réparation d’un tort de forme, C'est pour la premiére fois que 
l'on voit exiger d'un Souverain, dans un cas semblable, abandon de son influence 
morale sur la plus notable partie de ses sujets. 

Jojouterai que, si la Russie fait a la Porte un griet de ses tergiversations 
dana l'affuire des Licux Saints, la France ne serait pas moins fondée & lui ailresser 
les _mémes reproches, et que si elle s'en est abstenue, c'est qu'elle a pris en 
considération les embarras d'une Puissance qui, entrainée par deux couranta 
contraires et d'une force égale, ne croyait pouvoir garder son équilibre qu’en 
contructant tour & tour des obligutions contradictoires, 

Le méme caprit de modération a porté le Gouvernement ile Sa Majesté 
Impériale 4 tenir compte de Ia difference des temps, des changements operés, 
depuis un sitcle, dans les rapports des diverses Puissanees, et de la Russie en 
particulier, uvee Empire Ottoman; ct, bien que nous puissions alléguer, a 


3 


Vappui des réclamations des péres de Terre Sainte, les clauses d'un Traité formel, 


nous n’avons rien demande qui dit priver les Grecs des avantages que les 
‘événements avaient places entre leurs mains ; loin de 1A, nous avons consent a ce 
qu’on leur ouvrit un sanctuaire, celui de la Mosquée de l’Ascension, dont 
aces leur était interdit, et que les efforts tout récens dun Ambassadeur 
de France, M. lAmiral Roussin, ayaient en partie restitue au culte 
Chrétien. Quant a cette clef de la grande porte de l'Eglise de Beth- 
iéeom dont on @ tant parlé, on a seulement oublié de dire que les Grees en 
posséJaient une toute semblable, et que celle des Latins, loin de leur assurer la 
propricte d'un temple toujours reserve 4 Yautre communion, ne leur aecordait 
qu'un simple droit de passage. On n’a pas rappelé non plus qu’en réparation. 
el'oubli d’une promesse donné 4 la Légation de Russie par le Divan, quand 
l'Ambassade de France en recevait une differente, l'un des deux firmans destinés 
A régler la question des Lieux Saints a coneédé, sur la demande de M. le Prince 
Menchikoff, au Patriarche Gree de Jerusalem la surveillance exclusive de 
travaux de reconstruction qu’exige V'etat de la grande coupole de I’Eglise du 
Saint Sépulere. Tous ces fhits, AM. le Comte, s’ils ne peuvent pas plus invalider 
nos titres, sous peine du renversement des principes généralement reconnus: du 
droit public, que ne le ferait méme un Traité conclu sang notre participation, 
constituent néanmoins autant de derogations plus ou moins importantes, st 
non aux récents engagements de In Porte cnvers nous, que notre digmite 
nous imposaib le devoir de faire respecter intégralement, du moins au texte 
précis de nos Capitulations de 1740. Si, done, ses intentions cussent ete 
imoins conciliantes, s'il n’eut él¢ pénétré de cette idée qu'aucune des Parties 
Gontractantes de la Convention du 13 Juillet, 1841, ne pouvait user de tous ses 
droits antérieurs i cette transaction Europecenne sans courir le risque de 
comprometire le repos que la garantie collective des Puissances a eu pour but. 
d'assurer 4 l’Empire Ottoman, le Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Impeériale auratt 
eu la pleine faculté non seulement dopposer des réserves qui sont d'un usage 
constant en diplomatie, mais de faire, 4 son tour, entendre des menaces. 

C'est une autre ligne de conduite que la France a suivie, et la modération 
dont elle a fait preuve, outre qu'elle lui ote toute part de responsabilité dans In 
crise actuelle, lui donne également le droit d'espérer que les sacrifices quelle a 
faits pour le maintien de la tranquillité en Orient, ne seront pas perdus, et que 
le Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg, mu par des considerations analogues, saura 
enfin trouver un moyen de concilier ses prétentions avec les prerogatives de la 
gouveraineté du Sultan, et trancher autrement que par la foree un différend 
dont tant d'intéréts attendent aujourd hui la solution. 

Je vous autorise, M. le Comte, 4 communiquer cette dépéche 4 Lord 
Clarendon, 

Agréez, &e.

HIS Imperial Majesty the Sultan, in order to afford a fresh proof of his 
Royal benevolence towards all elasses of his subjects, has issued Imperial orders 
adorned with the Royal cypher, addressed to the Greek, Armenian, and Catholic 
Patriarchs, to the Protestant Agent, and to the Chief Priest of the Jews, con- 
firming their rcligious privileges, aud the rights and immunities belonging to their 
churches and other places appertaining to them. 

Copies of these firmans are inclosed for your Excellency’s perusal,

Inclosure 2 in No. 7. 


Imperial Firman addressed to the Agent of the Protestants. 


(Translation.) 
TO the Agent of the Protestants, Stephen; may his honours increase | 
Decreed :— 

God, the dispenser of mercies, i placing my august person, in pursuance 
of his eternal will, upon the glorious and exalter throne of the Imperial 
Caliphate, having confided to tny Royal hands und Sovereign rule as a suered 
and special deposit—to him be the thanks and glory !—numerous countries arid 
cities and many people of all classes and nations, ever sinee the glorious day on 
which | isoendel the throne, according to the Imperial duties imposed upon the 
Caliphate, my Government has never ceased (by the Divine Grace), conformably 
with my Royal will and sincere and benevolent intentions, to give practically 
their constant and careful attention that all classes of my Imperial subjects 
should enjoy full protection, and that they should be move especially one and 
all at perfect ease with regard to their religious and spiritual affnirs. 

The beneficial effects and advantages aceruing thereby have been at all times 
manifest, and it is my ardent and Imperial desire that no abuses whatever should 
arise outof negligence or carelessness. therefore wish and require that the 
special concessions granted by me in favour of my faithful Protestant subjects, 
concerning their worship and religious affairs and all other concerns relatin 
thereto, should be at all times preserved inviolate ; and my peremptory Imperia 
orders have been issued, to wit, that no contravention whatever thine concer 
sions should take place, and that any persons acting in contravention thereto 
should know that they will thereby incur my Royal displeasure, 

In order to remove all grounds of excuse on the part of those who. should 


6 


be guilty of negligence in these matters, communication hereof has been made to 
the necessary authorities ; and this high decree has been issued from my 
Imperial Divan in public confirmation of my Royal intentions for the complete 
and truthful execution hereof. 3 

You, the aforesaid agent, shall on receipt of these presents act always in 
conformity with this Imperial order, and be careful in abstaining from any con- 
travention thereof. On the occurrence of anything inconsistent with this 
peremptory decision you will hasten to make immediate representation thereof 
to our Sublime Porte. . 

Be it therefore thus made known unto you, giving full credence to my 
Imperial cypher. : 

Given in the third decade of the illustrious Moon of Shaban in the 
year 1269 (beginning of June, 1553).

_ NOTHING has yet come to my knowledge in confirmation of the intel- 
ligence transmitted to the Porte a few days ago by the agent of Prince Ghika, 
and purporting that the Russian army had already crossed the frontier of 
Moldavia, and were within two hours’ march of Jassy.. 3 

This deficiency in our advices from the scene of action is the less important 
as T learn from the correspondence received with your Lordship's instructions 
to the 8th instant by Queen's messenger Capel, that the Hussian Government 
hud declured its intentions of passing the frontier and occupying one or both of 
the Danubian Principalities the moment an unfavourable answer to Count 
Nesselrode’s letter of the 49 ultimo should be received at Odessa. 

Of this intention | have admonished Reshid Pasha, and I have also com- 
munieated on the same subject with M. de la Cour, | | 

I find them both disposed to act on my opinion, such as I have alread 
announced to your Lordship in the antici vation of that very measure which 
Russia has now declared ils resolution to adopt. : 

The military occupation of any part of the Ottoman Empire without the 
consent of the Porte would, no doubt, justify a recourse to hostilities, But the 
preservation of peace, so long as it is possible to preserve it with a chance 


af settling by negotiation the existing difference, is of such deep importance that 
I have not hesitated to advise forbearance on the approaching invasion of the 
Ottoman territory, It is notorious that the Principalities are placed under 
circumstances of # special character with reference to the neighbouring Powers 
and the consequences of @ foreign military oceupation within their limits are in 
practice by no means 60 likely to disturb the interests of the Porte as if a similar 
act of aggression were committed against those parts of the Empire which ‘are 
direetly administered by this Government. It may be added that, in a milita 
point of view, resistance could not be offered to Russia in that quarter sind 
present circumstances with any prospect of success, 

Reasoning from the ubove distinction the Porte, | conceive, may defer the 
moment of actual and reciprocal hostilities without diseredit ‘or inercase of 
risk, until an opportunity 1s afforded for learning the sentiments entertained by 
Her Majesty's Government as well as by that of France. : 

Agreeably to the same course of policy, | have advised Reshid Pasha not 
to withdraw the Hospodars immediately on the entrance of the Russian forces ; 
and [have prepared an instruction for the guidance of Her Majesty's Consuls 
ut Josey and Bucharest, Meee 

OF this instruction | inclose herewith a copy, and solicit your Lordship's 
attention to its contents, as offering a more complete account of the motives 
and basal under which I have framed it, in the hope of your Lordghip's 
approval. )

Inclosure in No. 8. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Consul Gardner. 


Sir Therapia, June 20, 1853. 


| 

NOTWITHSTANDING the delusive appearances of quiet mentioned in 
the last report which 1 have received from you, there is no longer room for 
doubt as to the intentions of the Russian Government with respect to the two 
Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. An occupation of one or of both 
those provinces by the armics of Russia will take place with very little, if any 
delay; not, as on a former occasion with the consent and participation of 
Turkey, but for purposes adverse, if not hostile, to the views and interests of the 
Porte. 

T have reason to presume that the Sultan’s Government will not take full 
advantage of their right to resist such an invasion, and that, ma spirit of peace 
and conciliation, they will rather be disposed to learn the opinion, of friendly 
Powers before they commit themselves to any act of defensive hostility. 

It is natural to expect asa result of this principle, that the Hospodars of 
Moldavia and Wallachia will not be ‘nstructed to retire so long ts they are 
allowed to keep up an unrestrained intercourse with the Porte, and so long a8 
the existing institutions of each province are respected. — ee 

It appears to me that m the supposed case you will have no difficulty m

les priviléges religieux when afterwards it is stated that the note proposed 
to Prince Menchikolf * eontenait toutes les assurances demandées,” and again 
where it is said, “la Sublime Porte n'hésitera jamais A maintenir et & donner 
leg uesurances contenues et promises dans le projet de note.” Count Buol 
ays, that assurances given in i diplomatic note betweeen two Ministers charged 
with the Foreign Affairs of their respective States, constitute an engagement, and 
therefore that there need have been to difficulty in giving those assurance: 
and in transmitting the late firmans, and in stating that what was therein

towards his own subjecte, he would in the strongest manner recommend to the

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Recetved July 3.) 


(No. 260.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 30, 1853. 

THE Emperor of Russia, some time ago, requested His Imperial Majesty 
the Emperor of Austria to depute a General officer to be present at the military 
inspections and reviews which are about to take place at St. Petersburgh, and 
in conformity with this desire Lieutenant-General Giulay, the Governor of 
Milan, has been designated for that mission, and he has this day left Vienna to 
fulfil its duties. 

This officer is charged with an autograph letter from his Sovereign to the 
Emperor of Russia, strongly recommending him as possessing his entire 
confidence. 

Although General Giulay has no political character, yet he has been made 
acquainted with the tenor of the despatches of which he is the bearer to the 
Austrian Chargé d'Affaires, M. de Lebzeltern, and he will use whatever oppor- 
tunity may be afforded him to recommend to the Emperor the views of his 
Government, and to bring before him the dangerous complications which would 
undoubtedly arise from the occupation of the Principalities upon the refusal of 
the Porte to conform to the ultimatum transmitted by the note of Count 
Nesselrode of the 3lst of May, and the hope that, by the mediation of the Allies 
of His Imperial Majesty and of the Sultan, such an arrangement, may be 
arrived at as shall be satisfactory to both Parties. 

In case these anxious desires of this Government should not be obtained, 
and General Giulay should find the occupation of the Principalities already 
accomplished or decided upon, he is then instructed to seek an opportunity 
strongly to urge the Emperor of Russia not to enter those provinces with any 
force which would create an upprehension that his views surpassed the object of 
obtaining a guarantee for the reparation he desired ; an object which would as 
completely be fulfilled by a small body of troops as by an army. 

As General Giulay is one of the most Aietinguished officers in the Imperial 
army, it is hoped that his influence may be beneticially exerted to promote the 
objects of his Government, 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

My Lord, Berlin, July 1, 1853. 


BARON MANTEUFFEL went to the country some days ago, and I have 
consequently been unable to hold any communication with his Excellency since 
the arrival of your Lordship’s last despatches. 

lseaw M. de le Coq, the Under Secretary of State, this morning, but he 
assured me that no intelligence of importance connected with Eastern affairs had 
reached the Foreign Department, except a copy of the answer returned on the 
16th ultimo by Reshid Pasha to Count Nesselrode’s letter of the 3ist May. 
He read this communication to me, observing that it appeared to him to bea 
dignified, well-reasoned paper, and that although he had no hope it would be 
received as it ought to be at St. Petersburgh, he must consider that it contained 
assurances that should satisty the Russian Government, if they were disposed to 
accept anything short of ther demands. 

We had some conversation on the possible occupation of the Princtpalities, 
and it appears to be the impression here that there ts no question at present of 
any other warlike demonstration being attempted, but that Russia will quietly 
hold these ‘l'urkish provinces, and refuse to evacuate them until the Porte shall 
be induced to yield to her demands, 

We conversed about the feeling that would be excited in Austria by this 
occupation, and he said that he thought that in one way it would haye a salutary 
effect, as. it could not fail to be hurtful to her interests, and must impress on her 
the necessity of uniting with the Western Powers in endeavouring to arrest the 
further advance of Russian predominance in the East, 

Baron Budberg, whom I saw yesterday, and questioned as to whether 
orders had been sent from St. Petersburgh to occupy the Principalities, said that 
he had no positive information on the subject, but he gave me to understand 
that he believed they had been dispatched on the 24th ultimo, He was not, 
however, at all certain on the subject, though he appeared not to entertain the 
least doubt, if they had not been already sent, that there would be no delay in 
forwarding them, observing that the presence of the combined squadron at the 
Dardanelles was looked upon as a menace, before which the Emperor could not 
have the appearance of vielding. 

The Russian Minister said further that he had just heard from Baron 
Mevendorff, from Vienna, that Count Buol had expressed his disapprobation of 
the Porte’s having rejected the note as altered by Prince Menchikoff, at Odessa, 
for he considered the terms of it were nearly those which the Porte had at one 
time agreed to accept. 

_- L think it right to report this to your Lordship, as it may possibly be the 
impression which Baron Meyendorff has described to his Government as having 
been produced by this ducument at Vienna, 


I have, &e.

COUNT COLLOREDO on the 28th ultimo read to me a despatch from

heen desired by M. Drouyn de Lhuys to inform him of the combined action of 
France and England upon Turkish affairs, and to point out the advantages that 
would ensue from a combined action between the Four Powers, having for its 
hasis the Treaty of 1841, which in the opinion of M, Drouyn de Lhuys imposes 
upon the Powers who signed it an obligation to make identical efforts for the 
maintenance of the Ottoman Empire. 

Upon this Count Buol observes that the Treaty of July 13, 1841, strictly 
imposes upon the Five Powers no other obligation than that of conforming to 
the ancient rule of the Ottoman Empire for closing the Dardanelles and the 
Bosphorus to foreign ships of war so longas the Porte remains at pence; but 
that the Treaty originated in the unanimous desire of the Great Powers to 
eatablish by a solemn act their union and the entire identity of their intentions 
for the establishment of Kurepean pence, 

Count Buol adds that the Austrian Government fully admit that the main 
tenance of the integrity and independence of the Ottoman Empire is an essential 
condition of general peace, and that they will zealously aid in maintaining that 
Empire in the present moment of difficulty, although they cannot ive to 
the Treaty of 1541 an interpretation more extended than the one above 
mentioned, 

It follows, however, Count Buol says, that if the actual complication shorted 
unfortunately end in war, Austria would claim for herself and would retoynize 
‘n other Powers who signed the Treaty of 1841 an entire liberty of action; and 
that if she did not act conjointly with the Three Powers, it was becaure she 
holieved that acting singly was likely to lead to more useful results, Never- 
theless, in eventually using this liberty of action for the re-establishment ef peace 
and the maintenance of the Ottoman Empire as on clement of Lurepenn equi 
librium, all the efforts of Austria in the present phases of the question must tend 
to prevent things from coming to this extremity. 

With this object Count Buol informs Count Colloredo, that on the 16th

native, in case the united efforts of the Cabinets should unfortunately fail in

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 5.) 


(No. 05, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, July 4, 185. 

1 HAVE the honour to inclose herewith an article from the “ Moniteur,” 
by which your Lordship will see that 40,000 stand of arms have been ceded by 
the French to the Turkish Government. 

This article has been written in consequence of a demand made by 
AI. de Kisseleff of M. Drouyn de Lhuys as to the truth of the statement which 
he had seen in the “Constitutionnel,” to the effect that arms had been furnished 
by the French Government to Turkey, and French officers sent into the service 
of the Porte. M. de Kisseleff added, that these facts, if true, constituted an act 
of war on the part of France. : 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, ‘That he could not at the moment reply as 
to the question of facts, but that he had at once a word to say on the assump- 
tion of M. de Kisseleff, that, should they prove true, they were acts of war. 
France had constantly supplied States in alliance with her with arms on their 
demand, and French officers had for many years been in the Turkish service. 
Besides, Russia had no right to treat the Onental question to-day as a question 
of peace, to-morrow as one of war. Russia had herself declared, that in 
oceupying the Principalities she was not at war with Turkey. Why then was 
France to show hostile intentions if she supplied ‘Turkey with a certain quantity 
of arms?” 

“ But’ said M. Drouyn de Lhuys to M. Kisseleff, “1 will answer your 
question by another. Why have you bought such enormous quantities of 
quinine in Franee? It can only be in preparation for a campaign in the marshy 
regions of the Danube. Answer my question, and I will answer yours.” 

L have, &c. 
*(Siened) COWLEY.

Inclosure 2 in No. 24. 


Sir G. H. Seymour to Count Nesselrode. 


(Confidential. ) 


My dear Count Nesselrode, St. Petersburgh, June 3}, 1853. 

1 BEG to acknowledge the receipt of the confidential letter of this 
date, which you have done me the honour of addressing to me. 

The object upon which, at this moment, my thoughts are the most 
intent being, that any misunderstanding between our two Governments 
should be removed by frank explanations and assurances, [ abstain from 
offering you several observations which are suggested by your com- 
munication. 

Were it necessary, | might demonstrate the great difference which 
exists between a de jure Protectorate exercised by one Sovereign over i 
few thousand of Catholics, and that which it is proposed should be 
granted to another Sovereign by whom it would be exercised over several 
millions of his co-religionists. 

This point, however, | only allude to; and passing over others tn 
complete silence, | will only dwell upon one which, in your Excellency's 
opinion, appears to affect the consistency of Her Majesty's Government. 

The English Government, aoe very correctly observe, were a party to 
the transfer from the Crown of France to that of Greece, of a portion of 
that protection exercised during centuries by the French Sovereigns over 
a certain number of the subjects of the Porte. You give to be under- 
stood, that it would be little reasonable were objections to be now raised 
to attributing to the Emperor of Russia a similar right of protection with 
regard to those subjects of the Sultan who profess the Greek creed. 

Tam hardly qualified to give an opinion upon the subject of the 
extent of the Protectorate rights enjoyed by France in virtue of her 
ancient capitulations ; but a more important consideration presents itself 
forcibly to my mind. 

If the independence of Turkey has been ever held to be an object of 
such European importance, that even a fraction of a privilege obtained 
from the Porte could not be transferred from a mighty Nronatch like him 
af France, to a Sovereign of new ereation and of such inferior power 
as the King of Greece, without the concurrence of Russia and Great 
Britain-—a coneurrence obtained by previous nerotiation, how, I would 
ask, could it be otherwise but that the ate sudden and unexpected attempt 
of one of the Great Powers to obtain for itself the immediate possession 
of a privilege of great magnitude, should give rise to surprise and hesita- 
tion on the part of Governments interested in, and pledged to the support 
of the Ottoman Empire ? 

It appears to me, that only one answer can be returned to the inquiry, 
and that the answer is of a nature to satisly every impartial person that 
the difficulties which exist between the Crown of Russia and the Porte, 
ought to be settled by peaceable means, and not by violence; and that the 
questions pending are such as should be examined by the Great Powers, 
the Allies of Russia and the co-supporters of ‘Turkish independence, as 
well as by Russia herself. 

This inference is, | think, clear and unexceptionable; while, as 
regards the Queen's Government, the entire confidence which has been 
reposed in the assurances of the Imperial Cabinet may be taken as the 
surest pledge of the desire felt by Her Majesty's Ministers, that every just 


21 


demand which can be made by the Emperor, should be fully acquiesced 
in by Turkey and by the Powers which have undertaken to support her 
independent existence. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 28, 1855. 
ONE of my colleagues who, from the circumstances of his having 
passed many years here, and having married a Russian, is considered as 
almost belonging to the country, has remurked to me in strict conlidence, 
that having ba the greatest admiration for the Emperor's character, 
and the utmost confidence in the prudence of the Chancellor, he is lost in 
astonishment at the sudden adoption of a line of policy which at once 
puts His Majesty in contradiction with the professed objects of his whole 
olitical career. He has arrived at the conclusion of the Emperor being 
impelled by some motives which have not yet transpired, and a knowledge 
of which he is endeavouring by every means to arrive at. 
My colleague, who lives more 1m Russian society than in that of his 
brother diplomatists, further acquaints me that the only clue which he has 
been able to obtain is this,—that the Emperor, by what means he coes 


not know, has been possessed with the idea of Her Majesty's Government

enjoy at Constantinople; and that in secking to resist these attempts, 
His Imperial Majesty’s policy is naturally directed rather against

Sir G. H. Seymowr to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July ¢.) 
(No. 326.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 28, 1853. 


UPON calling upon the Chancellor yesterday, I learnt froin him that 
orders for the occupation of the Principalities had been sent off on the 
27th instant. According to a report which prevails here, these orders 
had been despatched some days previously ; this, however, can hardly be 
the case after the written assurance given to me by Count Nesselrode on 
the ~yth instant. 

‘he Chancellor placed in my hands the inclosed copy of the answer 
returned to his letter by Reschid Pasha. He had, he said, no objection 
to urge against its style, still, however, it was a refusal of the Imperial 
propositions, and as such involved a resort by the Emperor to those 
tyeasures which had been announced. At the same time his Excellency 
clung to the hope of matters being settled peaceably. He had tittle 
doubt that this result would be obtained if the occupation of the Prin- 
cipalities should not be regarded by Great Britain and France as a 
easus belli. 

[lis Excellency proceeded to speak: of the plan of reconciliation (it 
might probably with more propriety be called of submission) devised by 
M. de Bourqueney, He expressed his warm satisfaction at the idea, 
and observed that it was one which would be accepted willingly (4 deux 
mains) by the Imperial Government. 

He next adverted to the manifesto which had just been published. 

This paper, a translated copy of which was forwarded to your 
Lordship by post yesterday, was intended for the Russian people; the 
circular which was about to be made public, was directed in some 
measure to foreign States, and would be found to contain the most 
positive assurances as to the Emperor's intention of not seeking any 
territorial aggrandizement. 

This may he so—but some degree of incredulity may be exeused in 
those who having followed the late proceedings of the Russian Govern- 
ment have had the opportunity of seeing how impossible it is to reconcile 
professions with acts. | 

Of this difficulty fresh proof was offered me yesterday, when once 
more the Chancellor stated that. the concessions on the part of the Porte 
insisted upon by the Emperor, were to he considered solely with reference 
to the question of the Holy Places, and to the precautions which it was 
necessary to take, to avoid a repetition of causes of complaint like those 
whieh had been given by the Porte. 

This statement appears to be hardly reconcileable with the terms of 
the Russian manifesto, from which it might be inferred that the very 
existence of the Greek Church was in danger from the fanaticism of the 
Turks, If it is desired, however, to contrast the language of the Russian 
Cabinet with its acts, the materials are certainly not winiting:. 

Nothing can be more striking than to listen, as 1 Irequently have 
occasion to do, to the ardent wishes for the preservation of peace expressed 
by the Chancellor, and to observe that these are accompanied, first, by the 
sublication of the circular already in your Lordship’s hands, next by the 
fasue of orders for the occupation of the Principalities, then again by the 
issue of an appeal (and that upon false rounds) to the religious feelings 


23 


of a people eminently sensible to any danger with which their Chureh is 
threatened, and then by the preparation of a fresh circular destined for 
publication. . 

Mee impartial persons who witness what is passing here have 
remarked, that whilst it is given to be understood that Russia has been 
foreed into an unfortunate conflict from which she has every desire to 
escape before it assumes a more serious form, provided only that the con- 
ciliatory disposition of her Allies allow her to doso with credit, every step 
ahe takes tends only to render the task assigned to the friends of peace the 
more difficult. 

It now is given to be understood (for | cannot say that it is directly 
staterl) that the occupation of the Danubian Provinces will afford a fresh 
and favourable opportunity for negotiation. 

May this prove to be the case, but f must confess that it strikes me 
that were the wishes of the Imperial Cabinet intent upon peace, occuy ation 
would not have been actually undertaken until sufficient time had been 
given for the deliberations of friendly Governments; nor again am | by 
any means satisfied that when the occupation has been effected it will be 
found that the Russian Councils have become more reasonable than they 
are at present. 

| am compelled, however, much against my will, to pay but slight 
attention to words, and am led to doubt whether this very occupation may 
not hereafter be put forward as a fresh obstacle between the Imperial 
Government and concession, 

To return to the conversation which I held with the Chancellor, it 
remains only for me to state that his Exectleney in-alluding to the firman 
which it was in contemplation to issue in favour of the Greek Church, 
observed that, as must be known to me, the Emperors Government could 
not accept of any firman in the light of an adequate reparation ; that what 
one firman granted another, as had been seen, could overthrow ; and, con- 
sequently, that the Emperor desired that the concessions made by the 


Porte should be sanctioned by some instrument having the force of an 


international engagement, 
I have, &e.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received July 7.) 


(No. 510. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, July 6, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS in speaking on the Oriental question to 
some of my colleagues has expressed himself in the following sense, 

The position of Russia is such that she must either accept or refuse 
the right of the Five Powers to interfere under the Treaty of 1841 for the 
defence and protection of the integrity and independence of ‘Turkey. 

If Russia accepts our interpretation of our rights under that Treaty, 
a valuable result will have been obtained. If aha refuses it, a warning 
will be given to Europe of the necessity of insisting on some more 
obligatory act. ‘This might consist of a Treaty by which the Five Powers 
would bind themselves to respect and maintain the integrity of the 
Ottoman Empire and the independence of its Government, to refer all 
points of difference which may arise between them and ‘Turkey to the 
arbitration of a conference, and, in the event of the dissolution of the 
Turkish Empire from internal canses, to abjure all schemes of individual 
benelit. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys has also ere the opinion that if Russia 
should refuse to be a party to such a Treaty the remaining Pour Powers 
should sign it without her. 

I have, &e.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 8.) 


(No. 117.) 
My Lord, Therapia, June 24, 1855. 

WE are still without any positive information of the entrance of the 
Russian army into Moldavia, though eee Ene indicates the approaching 
execution of that measure, and we are in daily expectation of hearing that 
it has actually taken place. 

Meanwhile a new incident has occurred, ‘The Internuncio, actin 
under instructions, has presented to Reshid Pasha an extract of adespateh 
addressed to him by Count Buol. The purport of the communication is 
an overture or proposal tending eventually towards a mediation by 
Austria. Reshid Pasha lost no time in sending it to me; and, sub- 
sequently, he extended the communication to my colleagues of France and 
Prussia. Baron de Bruck also made a similar comm unication successively 
to each of us. The extract of Count Buol’s instruction is inclosed here- 
with in copy. | 

My first object was to ascertain the impression made on Reshid Pasha 
by this overture, and I found that he was no more disposed than before to 
recede from the principle hitherto maintained by the Porte. I learnt, 
moreover, that although Baror de Bruck had pressed him for an immediate 
answer, his Highness had declined giving one, until he should have con- 
ferred with his colleagues, and taken the Sultan’s pleasure. 

My second object was to obtain from Baron de Bruck some explanation 
of the ground on which Count Buol had placed his hope of a successful 
mediation. 1 could learn nothing beyond an anxiety to prevent war, anc 
an impression that the Emperor of Russia was embarrassed, and would be 
glad to find some means of extrication. Could we hope by a prompt 


acceptance of the Austrian idea to afford Prince Menchikolf a motive for’ 


delaying the occupation of the Danubian Principalities? Nothing appeared 
to warrant any such hope. 

In spite of these unpromising circumstances—of the recollection that 
neither Prince Menchikoff nor Count Nesselrode would hear of the 
slightest variation in the terms of that draft of a note which constituted 
the last Russian ultimatum, and of the certainty that neither could the 
Porte recede, nor could we advise her to recede, from the point at issue 
—| conceived that, independently of any prospect of success, no incon- 
siderable advantage might be made to accrue by proper management 
from the Austrian suggestion. 

Far, therefore, from making any difficulties, proposed a meeting of 
the four Representatives, which accordingly took place at my house this 
morning, 

It is unnecessary to trouble your Lordship with the particulars: of 
what occurred during our conference, which, being unauthorized by any 
special instructions, was carried on rather in the spirit of a desultory 
eonversation than in thatofa regular discussion. For my own part, I felt 
deeply the importance of keeping every chance of necommodation open as 


27 


long as possible, of having it clearly understood at the same time that 
there could be no question of ceding the diplomatic engagement required 
by Russia, of keeping fairly in view the position of the Sultan’s Govern- 
ment with respect to its allies and to its people, of not giving to such 
communication as we might agree in adopting any charaeter but that of a 
mere suggestion proceeding from the four Representatives, and, finally, of 
bringing simultaneously before the Porte a strong expression of our belief 
that real and comprehensive improvement of the condition of the Sultan's 
non-Mussulman subjects could be no longer deferred. 

It is but justice to state that T found the French Ambassador, the 
Austrian Internuncio, and the Prossian Envoy, animated as to these 
several points with sentiments of the most satisfactory description, and | 
‘afer from the harmony which prevailed among us, that whatever difference 
of opinion arising from difference of position may exist as to the ulterior 
means of supporting the Sultan in his strugele with Russia, your 
Lordship will find little difficulty in directing the joint moral action of the 
four Powers towards the adjustment of the present question, if it be 
capable of adjustment by diplomatic means, and to the establishment of a 
more complete understanding and coneurrence between them and the 
Porte in that broad Kuropean sense and Christian spirit which Ter 
Majesty's Government have never ceased to promote and to recommend, 
L found them at the same time most reasonably alive to the ex pediency of 
keeping open a door for Russia's accession to the same system of policy 
hereafter, and of our being, as much as possible, careful not to give 
umbrage in that quarter by any premature display of our concurrent 
understanding in contrast with the insulated position of Russia. 

The immediate results of our meeting are consigned to a memorandum 
without signature, which | inclose herewith for your Lordship’s informa- 
tion, though Lam not at liberty to represent it as invested with any formal 
character. In fact, it is a simple unofficial record of the purpose of our 
meeting, and of certain points on which our opinions agreed. 

Since we separated I have received from Mr. Pisani a report, which I 
inclose, in copy, herewith, and | have seen a Russian circular, dated from 
St. Petersburgh the 30th ultimo, o,s., and published as a supplement to 
the “Qdessa Gazette.’ Both these papers show that the Porte on its 
side, and Russia on hers, persist in maintaining respectively the one 
essential point in dispute, and the latter removes w jatever doubt might by 

ossibility have remained of the Emperor's determination to send his army 
into the Principalities. 

Linder these circumstances, I repeat that the object of entertaining 
the Austrian suggestion, so far as to place it under the notice of the Porte 
as an idea proceeding, by adoption, from the Representatives of the four 
Powers at Constantinople, is not with a view to any immediate result, but 
to afford an opportunity for diplematte action ina form at once the most 
affective and the least unpalatable to Russia, It would seem, if solemn 
declarations are still to be trusted, that the Emperor of Russia, if not 
resisted by force, will confine his: military aggressions on Turkey to the 
oveupation of the two Principalities, and as it is all but certain that the 
Porte will not offer resistance to that measure, we may safely conclude 
that, barring accidents, no nearer approach to hostilities will take place 
for the present, It is obvious, at the same time, that the occupation itself 
is not only an aggressive act, constituting a case of war, and justly 
entitling the Porte to act at onee on that principle, but that it has the 
effect of placing the Porte in a state of embarrassing and hazardous 
apprehension, imposing heavy burthens on the Empire, and unsettling: its 
most important relations at home and abroad. So painful and exhausting 
‘« the attitude thus forecd upon the ‘Torkish Government, that if not 
relieved by more successful negotiations, or assisted without reserve by 
their allies, they can hardly be expected to hold out for any great length 
of time, and they will finally be reduced to the necessity of either 
snrrendering what they conceive to be essential to the Sultan's indepens 
dence and Sovereign righi, or acquiescing in an act of spoliation wholly 
at variance with the declared principles of 1841, and, in fact, decisive of 
that great question which the live fading Powers of Christendom then

hedged round with the most solemn pledges of their honour and good

| venture, therefore, to submit that the course which Iam now taking 
in concert with my colleagues of Austria, France, and Prussia, is the one 
best calculated to anticipate the views of Her Majesty's Government, and 
to meet the exigencies of the case, by affording Russia an opening for 
reconsideration, in so far as her own precipitancy admits of it, without 
that additional delay which would be incurred by a reference to our 
respective Courts. | | 

If this last effort for a peaceful solution fail, it is difficult to foresee 
any issue of the struggle, aceeptable either to the Porte or to Europe, but 
that which is to be obtained by the active cooperation of England and 
France, with a general concurrence from other Powers, and ao lon 
uncertain perspective of dangers and sacrifices, not indeed to be avoided, 
but not the less to he deplored. 

I have to remark, in conelusion, that Baron de Bruck has made

proceeding from the Four Powers, | do not propos? to anticipate in any

Inclosure 3 in No. 80. 
M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord. Therapia, June 23, 1855. 

RESHID PASHA informs me that M. de Steindl called to-day to 
urge his Highness to give him an answer whether the Porte was inclined 
to try the proposed experiment for the renewal of negotiations with 
Russia, as contained in the extract of the despatch communicated yester- 
day by Baron de Bruck. 

_ "The Pasha replied to M. de Steindl, that his answer was already 
pies to Baron de Bruck himself, namely, that he could not take upon 
limself cither to reject or to adopt the proposal, without previously taking 
the advice of his colleagues, and submitting the same to the Sultan. But 
in his opinion, he was led to believe that this experiment would not 
answer the purpose of Russia; that the Porte had already offered official 
and formal assurances, which have not been considered as containing 
sufficient guarantees, Consequently the only thing which could satisfy 
the Emperor of Russia would be a treaty enga ement; to this the Porte, 
added he, cannot yield, for the reasons repeatedly stated. 

Subsequently, M. de Steind! communicated another despatch, which 
Baron de Bruck had just received, approving the line pursued by the 
Porte until now in the question at issue; an stating, at the same time, 
that Russia does not entertain any hostile views against Turkey, but 
would enter the Principalities as a material guaranty until she could 
obtain some moral one. 

Despatches arrived from the Princes of Moldavia and Wallachia 
contain nearly the same information, that Russia has no intention to go 
to war, but only to occupy the Principalities until she could compel fie 
Porte to offer the guarantees required by the Emperor. :

(No. 118.) 
My Lord, Therapia, June 24, 1853. 

HAVING. observed in Count Nesselrode’s despatch to Baron Brunnow 
of June 1, as communicated by the latter to your Lordship, a passage which, 
more tangibly than others of the same cast, conveys a very erroneous impression 
of my conduct during the late negotiations between Prince Menchikoff and 
Reshid Pasha, and one scarcely less malevolent of Reshid Pasha’s opinions at 
the same juncture, I thought it due to the cause of truth and fair-dealing to put 
the matter at rest on the most obvious and indisputable authority, 

1 applied for a statement of the real facts to Reshid Pasha himself; and 
his Highness having mentioned Mr. Alison as also cognizant of the truth, I 
applied to that gentleman likewise for the same purpose, 

I have now the honour to inclose the correspondence, which is, fortunately, 
as short as it is decisive. 

I have to request that it may be submitted to Her Majesty the Queen, and 
also to the members of Her Majesty's Government. 

Your Lordship knows how heavy a responsibility weighs on me at the 
present important and delicate juncture. T am earnestly desirous of meriting 
the confidence it implies; and I should despise the calumny propagated by 
Count Nesselrode, were it not purposely intended to deprive me of that 
confidence, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Upon the whole, I conclude that the Russian Cabinet, not knowing 
exactly how the occupation of the Principalities will be taken, is preparing 
‘n some measure for the worst. On this point, however, [am happy to 
say, that there is every appearance of the Porte’s intending, in pursuance 
of my suggestion, to forego its right of war for the present; and, protest- 
ing against the occupation, to appeal to the Four Powers, who, together 
with Russia, concluded the Treaty of 1841.

upon me in order to dissuade the Protestant converts from using disre-

No. 36. 
Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received July 8.) 


(No, 434.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 1, 1853. 

IN the course of a conversation which I held with the Chancellor on 
the 29th ultimo, he observed that the hopes of a peaceable solution of 
difficulties which he still entertained, were founded upon the resolution 
taken by England and France, of not considering the occupation of the 
Principalities as constituting a casue belli, and upon the interpretation 
which he understood Her Majesty’s Government to give to the provisions’ 
of the Convention of July 1641. 

His Excellency stated to me twice over, and with considerable 
emphasis, that the position of Russia was this: that her armies were 
entering the Prineipalities, and that she then waited for the overtures 
which miglt be made to her. “ And,’ 1 added, “she is of course disposed 
to receive them favourably.” 

After some little hesitation, the Chancellor corrected my phrase by 
saying. “She remains in the hope that any overture which may be made, 
may be such as can be entertained.” We proceeded to speak of the 
possibility of some middle course being taken, which might satisfy the 
demands of Russia without wounding the dignity or injuring the inde- 
pendence of Turkey; and as the Chancellor's language upon the subject 
was very guarded, I observed that what I was driven to conclude was, 
that the settlement of the question would be found in some arrangement 
which should reconcile the terms of the non-accepted note of Prince 
Menchikoff with those of the note of the Porte which the Prince had not 
felt at liberty to aceept. By manner, but not in actual words, Count 
Nesrelrode appeared to assent to this remark. 

I bezged Count Nesselrode to inform me whether it was true, as it 
had been stated to me, that the Emperor's Government had applied to 
that of Austria for its good offices? His Fxcellency replied, that he 
hardly knew how to answer the inquiry; that the thing had been done of 
itself, as it were spontaneously (“Cela s'est fait de soi-méme et pour ainsi 
dire spontanément,”) 

The inference which I am disposed to draw from the conversation 
of which 1 have reported the most essential points are: Ist, That the 
Emperor has given up finally his original intention of not allowing the 
alteration of a word, or a “comma,” in the note presented by his Ambas- 
sador. 2ndly, That although the Russian Government will hardly be 
brought to propose any modification in the substance or form of its pro- 
positions to the Porte, they would not be sorry that some slightly modified 
conditions should be prepared by a friendly Court; and, 3rdly, That though 
they feel the disadvantage of the position in which they have placed them- 
selves, they will be more disposed to persevere in a very evil course, than 
by quitting it, to depart widely from the conditions laid down by Prince 
Menchikof 

The Chancellor spoke much of the distracted state of Turkey, and of 
the great probability that the discontent of the Greeks, that is, of the 
great majority of the Sultan’s subjects, may lead to some revolutionary 
movement which may bring on a sudden crisis fatal for the Sultan’s 
authority. He expressed his doubts as to this contingency being suffi- 
ciently contemplated by Her Majesty's Government. 

‘To these observations | returned no answer; and indeed, | could have 
made none but such as would have given offence. I could only have 
remarked, that under the treatment which the Sultan has experienced 
successively at the hands of both hia Imperial neighbours, the wonder was, 
not that there was a danger of an ouvbreak of his subjects, but that they 
were not already engaged in revolution, ( 

In alluding to what is passing at Constantinople, I took an oppor- 
tunity of remarking that nothing could be more pacific and judicious than 


————~ = = 


ou 


the advice which had been constantly given to the Porte by Lord Strat- 
ford, and that his Lordship’s conciliatory conduct had opposed the most 
dignified answer to the calumnies by which he had been assailed, 
IT have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 8.) 


(No. 336. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 1, 1853. 

T LEARN that the Greek Minister has been speaking to several 
persons here of the disorganized state of Turkey, and of the dreadful 
outrages which have been committed of late upon Christians by bands of 
armed Albanians and others. 

These statements, brought forward simultaneously and at such a 
moment. of crisis by Greek and Russian authorities, give me some uneasi- 
ness, and lead me to suspect that there may be better reasons than those 
we are acquainted with for these anticipations of a revolutionary move- 
ment in Turkey which have been expressed, | 

The ery of “'The Orthodox Greek Faith in danger,” which has been 
raised here, is indeed of itself sufficient to induce the Christian subjects of 
the Porte to rise in rebellion; but I should be glad to feel convinced 
that no more direct appeals had been made to their fanaticism and dis- 
content. 

Supposing a revolutionary movement to take place in Turkey, it 
would hardly surprise me if, even now, at the eleventh hour, the Emperor 
were seen to undertake the protection of the remains of the Sultan’s 
authority. ‘This policy | take to be directed rather against Turkish inde- 
penser: than against the existence of Turkey, and till very lately I 

elieve His Majesty to have been prepared alike to show himself in frowns 
or in smiles, so that he were but definitively recognized as the invincible 
opponent or the pretended protector of the Sultan. 
~ In w conversation which I held two or three days ago with the Greek 
Envoy, | pointed out to him again that the best interests of his country 
uired that peace should be preserved in his neighbourhood, 

I begged of him to see things in their true light, and to feel convinced 
that if Turkey were to be destroyed and dismembered by a violent pro- 
cess, not one acre of territory would fall to the lot of Greece. 

Upon this point I found M, Zographo, is Ta ee reasonable.

No. 39. 


Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clorendon.—(Received July 8.) 


(No, 339.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 1, 1855. 

A'T a moment when such general attention is bestowed upon the plan 
to be devised for reconciling the demands made upon the Porte by Russia 
with the concessions which she can accept without the loss of independence 
and dignity, | would venture to submit the following very simple idea to 
your Lordship’s consideration. 

First, that the Turkish Government should, in a letter from Reshid 
Pasha to the Chancellor or in a khatti-cheriff, announce the confirmation of 
all the privileges and immunities enjoyed either in virtue of treaties or from 
ancient usage by the Greeks; specific mention being made of the fresh 
sanction thus given being applicable to the arrangements lately made 
with regard to the Holy Places. 

Second, that this letter or khatti-cheriff should be brought to St. 
Petersburgh by a special Ambassador from the Sultan, to whom its 
delivery, accompanied if thought necessary by an official note, should be 
entrusted. 

Third, that upon the receipt of the letter or khatti-cheriff by the 
Emperor’s Government, official copies of the same should be communicated 
by the Porte to the Representatives of the Great Powers at Constantinople 
in an official note in which the Sultan’s firm intention of respecting the 
privileges thus afresh and collectively secured to the Greeks, and notified 
to the Mmperor, might be repeated, 

T have no means of knowing whether this humble suggestion may be 
approved of by Her Majesty's Government, whether even, if so approved, 
it would meet the views of Austria, nor again whether even in this 
hypothesis the offer would be considered as acceptable by the Kimperor, 
I would only venture to remark that whilst the acceptance by Russia of 
good aud honourable terms would be a point of great importance, even 
the rejection of such conditions would tend to strengthen a good cause, 

I have, Re. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 8.) 


(No. 271. Confidential.) 
My Lord Berlin, July 5, 1853. 

WHEN I saw Baron Manteuffel yesterday | found him a good deal 
agitated, and I discovered that he had just had an interview with the 
Russian Minister, who had held strong language to him on the subject of 
the independent policy which Prussian desired to follow in the Eastern 
Question, and had ele remarks on the erroneous views which his Excel- 
leney had taken as to the bearing of the Treaty of 1841 on the present 
atate of this affair. Baron Budberg, after making some observations In 
support of this statement, complained of the conduct of both Chevalier 
Bunsen and M, de Wildenbruch, remarking that they had acted as 
enemies of Russia, and were not to be trusted. Baron Manteuflel replied 
that the King could not change his Ministry to please the Emperor, an 
that he was prepared to defend their conMuct, 

I understand also that Baron Budberg has been pressing Baron 
Manteuffel to declare what the future policy of Prussia will be in case 
more serious events should occur, and has said that a mere neutrality 
would not satisfy the Emperor, as that would be all to the disadvantage 
of Russia, and that he has gone as far as to threaten that unless a diffe- 
rent line of policy were announced, Prussia might look in vain to Russia 
for assistance in ease of any future difficulties with France, 

I have not been able to discover whether Baron Budberg held this 
language by instructions from his Government or not, but it is clear, an 
I hold the information from the best authority, that the Russian Minister 
has been endeavouring to intimidate Baron Manteuffel, and to urge 
him to change a policy which may be hereafter detrimental to Prussian 
interests, 

Baron Manteuffel is, lam assured, resolved not to swerve from the 
line which he has taken, and unless some foreign influence 1s exercised, 
over the King, there is no present reason to apprehend that any change 
will come over the policy of the Prussian Government.

HER. Majesty's Government having, after mature deliberation, seen reason 
to advise the Sultan not to exercise his unquestionable right of declaring war 
against Russia upon the occupation of the Principalities, it was highly satisfactory 
to them to find that, before the receipt of my despateh, No. 81, of the 15th ultimo, 
your Excellency had tendered similar advice to His Highness, who had deter- 
mined to act upon it; but if Russian aggression were to be carried farther, and 
if any other portion of Turkish territory were to be invaded, active operations 
on the part of Turkey would seem to be inevitable, and eventually the English 
and French fleets might be called upon to protect Constantinople. 

Before, however, the time for adopting a policy of resistance shall arrive, it 
is alike our duty and our interest to exert our utmost efforts, in conjunction 
with Her Majesty's allies, to preserve peace on terms that shall be safe and 
honourable to the Sultan, and shall satisfy every claim that ltussia can with 
justice put forward, 

The Emperor of Russia throughout these painful negotiations has declared, 
and he lias recently, upon more than one occasion, renewed the declaration, that 
he seeks no increase of power or influence over the Greek subjcets of the Porte ; 
and desires only the maintenance of the status quo in religious matters, and the 
fulfilment of ¢xisting Treaties. Her Majesty’s Government therefore recom- 
mend the Turkish Government to take this declaration as the basis of a fresh 


48 


agreement, and to embody in one separate Convention the stipulations with 
respect to religious matters in the ‘Treaties of Kainardji and Adrianople, by 
which Turkey is now bound to Russia. 3 5 Aes 

I accordingly inclose the Project of a Convention which Her Majesty's 
Government are of opinion that the Sultan, without loss of power, might 

sropose, and the Emperor might, without loss of dignity, accept. Her Majesty's 

beaiaatict consider this form of ugreement preferable to that of a_ note, 
because, as the Kmperor has demanded the adoption of Prince Menchikoif’s 
note, sans variante, and the Porte has rejected the demand, it can hardly be 
expected that any mode of settling the question by a note should be devised ; 
while, on the ether hand, a Convention is more precise and less liable to miscon- 
struction than a note, followed, as the latter might be, by an answer giving 
to it a different meaning than that understood by the party signmg tt, which 
must either be admitted by silence, or the whole matter must again be reopened 
and diseussecl. 

The first Article of the Convention commences by reciting the words of the 
seventh Article of the Treaty of Kainardji; it then adverts to the recent firmans, 
as showing how the obligation has been carried out by the Sultan, and concludes 
by renewing and confirming the Treaties of Kainardji and Adrianople. 

This project has been proposed to the French Government, and has 
received its cordial assent. 

Your Exeelleney is accordingly instructed to bring this Convention under 
the consideration of the Porte, and to state that Her Majesty's Government 
would further recommend that it should be sent to St. Petersburgh by a special 
Ambassador, who should have power to sign, but not to alter it without refer- 
ence to the Porte. He should lay before the Emperor the recent firman in 
favour of the Greek Church, together with the firmans respecting the holy 
places, and be empowered to give a written assurance as to their fulfilment, 
taking care, however, that such assurance should in no way infringe upon the 
rights acquired by the Latin Church, nor militate against a simular guarantee 
being given to France and to other Powers; and lastly, the Ambassador should 
by Convention or note assign to the Russians at Jerusalem a hospital, or such 
other buildings as may be required. 

If the Porte should think proper to act upon this advice, and if a proposal 
so fair and honourable be rejected, Her Majesty's Government must consider 
that it will be manifest to the world that the claim of religious rights covers 
ulterior designs on the part of Nussia, hostile to the independence of Turkey, 
and the Sultan may then justly claim the sympathy and support of every 
Government in Europe.

Draft of Convention between Russia und the Porte. 


HIS Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias having expressed to His 
Highness the Sultan his desire, that at this particular juncture no doubt or 
uncertainty should exist as to the right of the members of the Orthodox 
Eastern Church fully to. participate in the privileges, imnyunities, and other 
advantages which, by the Treaty between Russia and the Sublime Porte, 
concluded at Koutehouk-Kainardji on July 49, 1774, and by the further Treaty 
between the same Powers, concluded at Adrianople on the 7g se aan 1829, 
were secured to that Church in various parts of the Ottoman dominions; and 
His Hizhness the Sultan being anxious to comply with the desire of His 
Imperial Majesty in this respect; it has seemed good to His Majesty the 
Emperor of all the Russias, and to His Highness the Sultan, that a special and 
separate Act should be concluded between them for that purpose, and they have 
accord ngly named as their Plenipotentiaries, that is to say, His Majesty the 
Emperor of all the Russias 


and His Highness the Sultan 


49 


who, having communicated their respective full powers, found in due and proper 
form, have agreed upon and concluded the following Articles: 


ARTICLE I, 


The Sublime Porte having in times past promised constantly to protect the 
Christian religion in all its churches within the Ottoman dominions, and His 
Highness the Sultan, in fulfilment of that promise, having since his accession to 
the Throne studied to insure to all classses of his subjects full and entire security 
for the exercise of their religion, and His Highness having in these latter days 
more specifically declared his sovereign will that the special paviene and 
immunities in regard to matters pertaining to their religion granted of old to the 
Christian clergy, subjects of the Sublime Porte, to their churches, convents, and 
other properties dependent on those establishments, to their shrines and 
oratories, should be hereafter and for ever maintained within His Highness’ 
dominions, His Highness renews and confirms by the present instrument in 
favour of the ceclesiastics and other members of the Orthodox Eastern Church 
all the promises, engagements, and stipulations, in their favour contained in the 
Treaties concluded at Koutchouk-Kainardji on July }7, 1774, and at Adrianople 
on September yy, 1829, between Russia and the Sublime Porte. And His 
Highness the Sultan further engages that any privileges or immunities in regard 
to matters pertaining to their religion, which the Sublime Porte may hereafter 
grant to the clergy of other Christian sects, subjects of the Sublime Porte, 
within the Ottoman dominions, shall be equally granted to and enjoyed by the 
elergy of the Orthodox Eastern Church in the said dominions. 


ARTICLE IL. 


The present Convention shall be ratified, and the ratifications exchanged,

ON the Tth instant Count Colloredo read me a despatch from Count 
Buol, stating that Baron Meyendorll had communicated to him several 
despatches of June 23, from Count Nesselrode, which showed the earnest 
desire of Russia for a peaceful solution of the question now pending with 
the Porte. Count Nesselrode affirms that Prince Menchikofl’s note con- 
tains no other engagement than that which the Porte in its last note was 
ready to give, and he eannot conceive why modifications shoulil be sought 
for unless it is to eflace every vestige of guarantee for the immunities 
enjoved ab antiquo by the Greek religion in ‘Turkey. ‘Besides, Russia has 
au announced the occupation of the Principalities as an eventual 
measure, whereas the two naval Powers have already put in exectition an 
effective and immediate measure in taking up a position within the ports 
and maritime dominions of the Porte, and to this naval possession Russia 
can only oppose a military possession. ry ‘i 

By thus compromising the dignity of Russia and giving encourage. 
ment to the Porte, the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh has been placed im a 
position to render all negotiation impossible, whatever modifications 
might be proposed to the Russian note, \ . 

in another despatch Count Nesselrode expresses his satisfaction at 
the desire manifested by the French and English Representatives at 
Vienna to endeavour with the Austrian Government to find a satisfactory 
solution. He alludes particularly to the project of sending an Ambas- 
aador from the Porte with the note of Prince Menchikoff, and leaving to 
the Emperor to give in return to the Sultan the assurance that His 
Imperial Majesty in no way intended to encroach upon his sovereign 
rights. Count Nesselrade declares that this entirely meets the views of 
the Emperor, and that the Russian troops, if they have entered the Prin- 
cipatities, would be immediately withdrawn, if the note signed is sent by 
an Ambassador to St. Petersburgh, and the foreign fleets quit their 

resent anchorage, ‘The note once delivered, the Cabinet of St, Peters- 

Fieen will be ready to explain its meaning (i en préciser le sens), by 
giving to the Ottoman Government all the assurances best caleulated to 
tranquillize it upon the use and the extent of the guarantees demanded by 
Russia: these guarantees, Count Nessclrode attirms, being absolutely 
nothing more than the strict maintenance of the status quo founded in 
custom and Treaties. Paes 

Russia asks nothing new, nothing that implies an intervention im the 
internal affairs of ‘Turkey, nothing that shall go bree the rights of 
superintendence (surveillance) over the orthodox creed and its churches 
resulting from the Treaty of Kainardji, Count Buol then says that 
whatever may be the value of the arguments adduced by Russia, he 
cannot disguise from himself the grave and pressing reasons that should 


ol 


weigh with the Porte for effecting a reconciliation with its powerful 
neighbour as quickly as possible, provided that the honour and indepen- 
dence of the Sultan are guarded ; and he dwells upon all the financial and 

litical evils that a prolongation of the present crisis must entail upon 

urkey. He adds that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, although it 
persists in obtaining Prince Menchikoff’s note without alteration, yet 
offers at the same time to give the Porte all the assurances necessary for 
dissipating the doubts and calming the apprehensions that had led to her 
resistance, and Count Buol strongly recommends the Ottoman Govern- 
ment to accept the formal contradiction which Russia is ready to give 
beforchand to the alarm that the text of the Russian note had created, 
and to get rid of its present embarrassments, if not by signing Prince 
Menchikolf’s note without alteration, at least by endeavouring to frame 
one ad nearly as possible approaching to it, and of a nature to satisfy the 
Emperor of Russia within the limits traced by his Cabinet. 

[tis in this sense, Count Buol says, that Baron Bruck will be directed 
to advise the Porte, and he earnestly hopes that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, whose interests are entirely identical with’ those of Austria on the 
question, may instruct Lord Stratford to support the conciliatory efforts 
that will be made by the Internuncio. 

My first remark to Count Colloredo had reference to the astounding 
statement of Count Nesselrode, that the oceupation of the Principalities 
had been imposed upon Russia in consequence of the naval possession of 
the maritime dominions of the Porte by the fleets of England and France, 
which was a fiction so palpable that Count Nesselrode could not seriously 
expect that in any quarter it should be believed, 

With respect to the project attributed to the French Minister at 
Vienna, [ said that it might furnish the means of arriving at a peaceful 
solution of the difficulty, provided that the objectionable parts of Prince 
Menchikoff’s note were entirely neutralized by the assurances that Count 
Nesselrode now seemed prepared to give; but ,that after all that had 
passed it was impossible to leave the Russian part of the transaction in

communicated beforehand, and be satisfactory to the Porte. 

{ said Her Majesty's Government was happy to think that the 
interest of England and Austria were entirely identical upon the Eastern 
question, and that Lord Stratford de Redelifle had already supported the 
recommendations of the Internuncio to the Porte, but that we could give 
no advice inconsistent with the dignity and independence of the Sultan, 
which Austria as well as England desired to uphold. 

Count Colloredo earnestly requested me to permit his Government toa 
give an assurance at St. Petersburgh, that simultaneously with the eva- 
cuation of the Principatities, the British and French fleets would quit the 
Turkish waters, ; 

I replied, that when all differences were settled between Russia and 
the Porte, and that the Principalities were evacuated, it might easily be 
supposed that the Bay of Besiea was not a place where it was desirable 
that the combined fleets should long remain; but that Her Majesty’s 
Government would give no assurance upon the subject, because the pre- 
sence of the fleets in the Turkish waters was neither a violation of 
Treaties nor an infraction of international law, and could not therefore be 
considered in the same light as the occupation of the Principalities, which 
was a violation of Treaty and of the Law of Nations, and constituted an 
act of war against ‘Turkey,

ON the 7th instant, Count Colloredo read to me a despatch from 
Count Buol, containing the views of the Austrian Government upon the 
answers addressed by Reshid Pasha to the note of Count Nesselrode, 

Count Buol anticipates that this answer will not he well received at 
St. Petersburgh, because Reshid Pasha although affirming that the Porte is 
ready to repeat the assurances given in the note communicated to Prince 
Menchikolf shortly before his departure, yet at the same time declares that 
the Sultan finds it really impossible to enter upon any diplomatic engage- 
ments for that object. ¥ 

If by that, Count Buol remarks, Reshid Pasha understands a synal- 
lagmatic contract or « bilateral Act, his disinclination to agree to it 1s 
natural, because, in fact, a Convention imposing Upon one of the con- 
tracting parties obligations, while the other offers nothing in return, mi hit 
be interpreted as derogatory to the independence of the Sultan. But 
Russia does not require a bilateral Act. She will, on the contrary, be 
satistied with a note, and if the Porte reserves to itself the right to modify 
the Russian ultimatum, which it cannot sign under a threat without 
loss of dignity, its course is intelligible; but i, emboldened by foreign 
sympathy, it withdraws from that which it has already conceded by the 
note transmitted to Prince Menehikoff, and if it thinks that, notwith- 
standing the gravily of the circumstances, it can decline any description 
of diplomatic engagement, even such an one as should be confined to 
assurances given in a hote, it would, in the opinion of the Austrian 
Government, commit a grave error which might have the most disastrous 
consequences. wh iw | | 

Count Buol says he has expressed this opinion to the Porte, and hopes 
that similar instructions will be given to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe by 
Her Majesty’s Government. He will in_the meanwhile renew his most 
urgent demands against the occupation of the Prineipalities. 

He adds, that Count Giulay has received orders to omit no oppor- 
tunity of stating both to the Emperor and to his Cabinet that the military 
occupation of the Principalities must gratuitously aggravate the situation, 
and leave the Porte masters of the immense question of general peace, 
because from that moment the Sultan may when he pleases suspend the 
Treaty of 1841, and leave to fate and a unforescen accidents the peace of 
Murone and the mighty interests it involves. 
any Colloredo likewise read to me the despateh of Count Buol to

pation of the Principalities as a direct consequence of its * insufficient 
answer to the Russian Cabinet, and will have to beay all the responsibility 
of it; and Count Buol instruets Baron Bruck to urge the Turkish Govern- 
ment to take no precipitate step upon the occupation of the Principalities 
that would displease the Court of Russia, and render all future under- 
standing impossible. | ice 

1 expressed to Count Colloredo my regret that the Austrian Govern- 
ment, which professed to uphold the dignity of the Sultan, should blame
