The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 


(No. 199.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, July 11, 1853. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has this day communicated to me a despatch 
addressed by Count Buol on the 6th instant, to Baron Lebzeltern, stating 
that the Imperial manifesto, dated the 26th of June, had unfortunatel 
deprived the Austrian Government of the hope it had hitherto entertained, 
that the differences between Russia and the Porte might have been 
amicably settled without the occupation of the Principalities being 
considered necessary. 

Count Buol says that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh will have fore- 
seen, by his despatches of the 30th ultimo, the painful impression that the 
determination of the Emperor of Russia will have produced on the mind 
of the Emperor of Austria. By those despatches the Austrian Government 
had again implored (itérativement econjuré) the Imperial Cabinet well to 
weigh all the reasons of right and opportunity which were of a nature to 
make them desist from the occupation; and those representations having 
failed to modify the course that Russia had traced out for herself, it only 
remained for the Austrian Government to express its profound regret, 
which is all the more sincere as the difficulties: of the task which the 
confidence of Russia had assigned to them are increased. 

They will nevertheless, in the interest of peace, continue to use the 
conciliatory efforts at Constantinople, London, and Paris, which from the 
first they exerted in compliance with the desire of Russia; but their 
chances of success will be exceedingly weakened if Russia delays in 
supporting them efficaciously. 

The Austrian Government has neyer concealed from the Russian 
Cabinet the lamentable effect that the occupation of the Principalities 
must produce on public opinion in Europe; and interpreted, as such a 
measure is susceptible of being, as a first act of flagrant hostility, it would 
entail imminent danger of war; and even if the Sultan, yielding to the 
advice of the Powers, did not treat it as an act of war, it must aggravate 
all the difficulties of a pacile arrangement, 

The Austrian Government, however, renews its carnest entreaties to 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, that the occupation should at least be 
circumscribed within the narrowest possible limits; and that with respect 
to its object and duration, precise explanations should be given of a 
nature to calm the uneasiness to which this act must give rise—explana- 
tions which are all the more necessary because the Manifesto of June 26 
gives to the question proportions more vast than it hitherto possessed, 
and places iton a ground where it is impossible for Austria to identify 
herself with Russia, and which appears to the former infinitely to increase 
the difficulties as well as the dangers of the situation, because by appeal- 
ing to the relizious sentiments of the Russian people, the risk is incurred 
of arousing Mussulman fanaticism. | 

The question of the Holy Places having been settled to the satisfaction 
of Russia, the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh assured that of Vienna that it 
had nothing more to desire except a guarantee for the future, Sinve that 
time the Sultan, with the intention of complying with the demands of 
Russia, has solemnly confirmed the privileges of the Greek clergy in his 
empire; and has called all Europe to witness his immutable will to main- 
tain those privileges for ever; and he is prepared to reiterate the most 
positive assurances on the subject to the Emperor of Russia. How is it 

H 2 


=o. ot ea, 


o+ 


possible, then, adds Count Buol, to reconcile these facts with the passage 
of the manifesto, where it is said that the Ottoman Porte has attacked the 
rights of the Greek Church; that she has ended by threatening them with 
total destruction; and that every effort to bring the Ottoman Government 
fo better sentiments has been fruitless, But if the rights of the Greek 
Church had been thus threatened, how comes it that the Patriarch of 
Constantinople, far from raising any complaint, has solemnly and publicly 
thanked the Porte for the confirmation of the privileges and immunities of 
his Church. Lx 

Count Buol appeals to the wisdom and im artiality of the Russian 
Cabinet to say whether these contradictions will not explain the doubt 
and uneasiness that more than one Government interested in upholding 
the Ottoman Empire cannot fail to entertain; and he asks whether it 
would not serve the cause of peace, which all desire to preserve, if Russia 
would give assurances calculated to satisfy Europe upon her real 
intentions. . 

I requested Count Colloredo, and T also request your Lordship, to 
thank Count Buol for this communication, and to assure him that the 
frankness with which he has offered sound advice to the Russian Cabinet 
is most satisfactory to. Her Majesty’s Government, who hope that it may 
be productive of the desired resull, as the Kmperor of Russia cannot he 
altogether indifferent to the counsels of his Allies, nor set at defiance the 
public opinion of Europe; but should this unfortunately not be the case, 
and should the Emperor reject the proposals for arrangement that might 
be made to him, and persist in retaining forcible possession of territory 
belonging to ‘Turkey, Her Majesty's Government trusted that the 
Austrian Government would not remain neutral, but would come to the 
aid of the Sultan, who, having adopted the advice given to him by Austria 
as well as by England and France, has aright to expect that the Three 
Powers will cooperate together in his defence. 


I am, &e. |

My Lord, Berlin, July 7, 1852. 

1 SAW Baron Manteuffel this morning, when we had some conversa- 
tion on the aspect of affairs in the Kast. His Exeelleney said he had 
nothing of a satisfactory nature to communicate to me. He made some 
observations of a general nature on the Russian manifesto of June 26, 
which conveyed his marked disapprobation of this document, and then 
expressed his regret that the entrance of the troops into the Principalities 
should have followed so rapidly, He next informed me that Baron Bud- 
bere had communicated to him the proclamation which was to be issued 
by Prince Gortchakoff on crossing the Turkish frontier, pe 

This document, he said, was less objectionable than anything that 
had lately emanated from the Russian Government, and he observed that 
the terms of it appeared more reasonable; that an allusion which was 
made in it to the protectorate was fair enough; but he made some ironical 
remarks on the assurances given to the inhabitants of the Principalities, 
that they might continue their lawful occupations in full security, and that 
the laws aud general administration of those provinces would be respected. 
He said further, that the Russian Minister had read to him partof a letter 
from Count Nesselrode expressing his regret at the declaration of the 
neutral policy which Prussia intended to fo low, but that he hoped Mussia 
might nevertheless count on her impartiality, 

On my asking Baron Manteuflel whether he had learnt anything as 
to the future projects of the Russian Government, his Excellency said that 
Count Henckel was under the impression that the Emperor had no further

warlike intentions, and conceived that the moment was come when nepo- 
tiations would be practicable; arguing that it would be impossible for the 
Emperor after lis late declarations to recede from the measures which he 
had announced; that the refusal of the Porte to sign the projected note 
rendered the advance of the troops inevitable. 

I cannot say that Baron Manteuffel seems inclined to adopt this

No. 63. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received July 12.) 
(No. 341.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 3, 1853. 

IT is right that I should state to your Lordship, that as far as I am able to 
judge, the Russian Government are well satisfied with the prospect which they 
possess of being able to occupy the Principalities without having to encounter 
the immediate hostility of England and France, and will endeavour to pro- 
long both this occupation and the negotiation which will be required for 
bringing it to an end, | 

Various considerations suggest this policy: as, Ist. The expediency of 
giving time for popular feeling to subside in England. 2nd. The chances of 
circumstances arising which may tend to disturb the community of purpoee now 
existing between ourselves and the French, Ard. The advantage of keeping a 
large body of men at free quarters; and 4th. The value of a prolonged occupa- 
tion as having the etfect of aceustoming the Danubian Provinces to that state 
to which it is probably intended that they should ultimately be reduced, T say 
accustoming, and not reconciling, because, as far as 1 am able to form an 
opinion, nothing could be less welcome to the Wallachians or Moldavians than 
afresh visit from their Northern neighbours, unless, indeed, it were to have 
them as settlers and masters, 

As [learn from a person to whom these districts are familiarly known, 
they are hardly yet recovering from the effects of the last Russian irruption, It 
is believed here, that the troops must have crossed the Pruth on the Ist 
instant. 


The Manifesto which was inclosed in my despatch, No. 318, was read 
to-day in all the churches, 


| have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR, 


P.S.—The language of a person holding a situation about the Emperor's 
nevson, confirms the opinion which I had formed before conversing with him, 
is person conceives Russia to have a great advantage by having secured an 
entry into the Principalities, says, that in this position she can now well afford 
to wait, and is absolutely and sarcastically incredulous as to the charges of the 


occupation being borne by Russia. “ By the Sultan, he says, very possibly, by 
the Emperor certainly not,” 


No. 64. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,.—( Received July 12.) 


(No. 345. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 5, 1853. 

| HAD proposed to myself to offer your Lordship some refutation of the 
misrepresentations which are collected in the Russian circular, a copy of which 
was inclosed in my despatch No. 342, | have, however, given up that purpose, 
upon reflecting how useless it is to oppose separate contradictions to the various 
parts of a document, the whole of which is one laboured violation of truth, 

Your Lordship will have read with astonishment that the Governments of 
England and France have taken the initiative in the struggle which appears to 
have commenced, and that while the despatch of the Allied Fleets to the Darda- 


_hellea is spoken of as a mesure effective, all these menaces, and all that assem- 


blage of forces now poured into the Principalities, are described as measures 
purement eventuelles, 

Russia, then, as a preliminary step in a cause of outrage, is entitled to 
take possession of the Danubian Provinces whenever inclination or waywardness 
may suggest such movements, it being a the same time understood that the 


60 


fleets of England and France cannot be permitted to approach the coasts of the 
country where those acts of violence are to be perpetrated. 

At all events one portion of this paper, to which unhappily for his repu- 
tation Count Nesselrode has set his name, appears to me to possess considerable 
value. If any excuse were required for the Sultan's refusal to comply with 
the demands made upon him by Russia, it is handsomely provided by the 
Imperial circular. 

When the Russian Government can venture to declare seriously that the 
rights of which they now demand the simple confirmation, were assigned to 
them by the Treaty of Kainardji, no surprise is admissible at the Sultans 
repugnant to allow the signature of the bond which has lately been set before 
lim. 

If Russian interpretation can construe any provision of the Treaty of 1774 
into the grant of a Protectorate of the Greeks to the Emperor of Russia, then 
indeed, according to the same free reading, might the stipulations of Prince 
Menchikolf’s Treaty, Sened, or note, be understood as transferring St. Sophia 
to the use of the faithful of the Russian Greek Church. 

That, however, which is the most striking is the discordance between the 
confidential languace and the official acts of the Russian Government. There 
was scarcely less difference between the moderate pretensions announced by 
them during the first week of Prince Menchikoff’s residence at Constantinople, 
and the demands which led to his departure, than there has been between the 
conciliatory disposition professed since the event by Count Nesselrode, and the 
appeals and declarations which are made by the nee and the Circular. 

ave, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

M. DE BUOL has expressed himself to M. de Bourqueney in terms of 
great indignation at the occupation of the Principalities by Russia, and complains 
that the step should have been taken at a moment when Count Giulay was on 
his road to St. Petersburgh with an autograph letter from the Emperor Francis 
Joseph to the Emperor Nicholas, entreating him not to take this step. Count 
Buol is also annoyed that he should have received the intelligence of the 
accomplishment of this decisive movement in an indirect manner. 

Count Buol read to M. de Bourqueney the draft of an instruction to the 
Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh, insisting on the necessity of Russia 
limiting the number of troops by which the Principalities are to i occupied, 
and the time during which they were to remain.

My Lord, Berlin, July 12, 1853. 

M, DE LE COQ, upon whom I called to-day at the Foreign Department, 
read to me two despatches which have been addressed to the Representatives of 
Prussia at Constantinople and at St. Petersburgh, upon the Eastern question. 

‘The instruction to Baron Wildenbruch is an answer to a despatch which 
he had addressed to his Government, pressing for information to euide him in the 
dificult circumstances which were likely to arise; and he is directed to express 
to the Porte the good feeling entertained towards it by the Prussian Government, 
und their desire to assist in bringing about a pacific solution of the questions at 
issue between ‘Turkey and Russia. It suggests that the Porte should be induced 
to sign some document, consistent with her honour, that would be accepted at 
St. Petersburgh; in retarn for which it was hoped the Russian Government 
would not hesitate to give assurances declaring the absence of all intentions of 
interfering with the independence of ‘Turkey; these assurances to be drawn up 
ina formal manner, and to be previously concerted amongst the great Powers. 

_ Baron Wildenbruch is directed to communicate freely and to act tn concert 
with his colleagues, Tut to follow that line which will ensure to Prussia entire 
independence of action now and hereafter, 

A copy of this despatch has heen forwarded to Count Henckel at St. Peters- 
burgh, as in answer to one in which he had reported the favourable reception 
that the so-ealled Project of Baron Bourqueney had met with, and he is informed 
She it is intended for his guidance in any discussion that may arise on the 
subject, 

_ M, de le Coq mentioned that these two despatches would be sent to 
Chevalier Bunsen for communication to your Lordship, so that it is unnecessary’ 
for me to say more of their contents. He added, that he had read them to 
Baron Budberg, who appeared satisfied with them; and he said further, that 
that Minister's language has become much more conciliatory ; and that to judge 
from it, it would appear that the Russian Government were desirous that the 
question should be peaceably arranged, and would even be thankful to any 

avernment thal would assist in bringing about so desirable a result. 

Lasked hin) what Baron Budberg had said on the question of the Russian 
answer to the Porte being concerted with the Great Powers. He replied— 
requesting that I would consider what he said was-in the strictest confidence, — 
that the Russian Minister did not believe his Government would object to this. 

1 rejoined, that 1 was glad to hear this, for if Baron Budberg spoke the 
feelings of the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh, there was a satisactory opening for 
negotiations ; Lut that | was apprehensive he might not be well infurmed of their 
real impressions on this point, for M. de Kisselett had held totally different 
language to M. Drouyn de Lhuys in a late discussion of this question. 

M, de le Cog told me further, that he had seen a eopy of one of the last 
Austrian despatches to St, Petersburgh, and that it was drawn up in a less 
conciliatory and rather upheesding tone, and that he thought it not so well 
calculated to produce the esired effect as the Prussian instruction, which was 
more in the light of an appeal to the Emperor's generosity, |

No, 79. 


Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received July 15.) 
(No. 348.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 8, 1843. 

AS your Lordship will have learned from a preceding despatch of mine, 
No. 292, the publication of the diplomatic circulars in the “Saint Petersburgh 
Journal,” is attributed here by official persons to the necessity which existed for 
some reply being made to the attacks which during the latter weeks has been 
directed against the Russian Government by the public press of England and 
France. 

Whether this publication has benefited the cause of Russia, and has had 
the effecting of reconciling European feeling to the late course of diplomacy in 
Turkey, are questions to Pian; Limagyie only one answer can be returned. 

“As regards public feeling in this country, I have considerable hesitation in 
expressing an opinion, because a foreign resident in St. Petersburgh has in peint 
of fact but slight opportunities of estimating it correctly, 

As far, however, as the observation of those better acquainted than myself 
with the country is to be taken asa guide, I should say that the effect of the 
circulars, which have been read exclusively by the educated classes, has not 
been such as was expected, 

I hear of many Russians who have not scrupled to declare that these 
papers do not contain a straightforward exposition of views ; that if it is desir- 
able that Turkey should be invaded, it would be better that the attack should 
be made at once than that an unsatisfactory or unintelligible cause of quarrel 
should be assigned, 

With the uneducated classes the case is widely different; they have no 
means of forming an opinion for themselves, and when they are told, as they 
are in the manifesto, that the orthodox religion is in danger from the ruthless- 
ness of the Turks, there are rio suerifices which they would not be ready to 
make for its defence, 

How far it is allowable to appeal to religions feelings upon grounds which 
are not warranted by facts, is a point which appears not sufficiently to have 
occupied the attention of the Russian Government. There is a flagrant ana- 
cronism in imputing the wish of subverting the Greek religion to the most 
tolerant Caliph that ever oceupied the Ottoman throne, und that at the precise 
moment when his best efforts are empioyed for ameliorating the condition of his 
Christian subjects. 

l understand that, at the same time that the manifesta was read in the 
Russian churches, prayers were put to the Almighty for the success of the 
Imperial arms against the Turks. 

This step again involves one of those inconsistencies of which so many 
have been observable in the late foreign policy of Russia, At one moment we 
have been told that most unfortunately for Russia the authority of the Sultan is 
lost, and his empire upon the point of falling to pieces; while at another those 
precise measures are taken which are the best calculated to bring about results 
thus officially deplored, 

One day, it is stated, that the Power of Russia is such that a movement—a 
fillip given by the Imperial Government—is suflicient to overturn Turkey; on 
the next, prayers are put up in the churches for the support of Heaven in the 
attempt about to be mude against this almost Grontrate tte 

y degrees, however, the impartial observer of what is passing here almost 
leaves off attempting to reconcile inconsistencies and to explain obscure passages. 
So much of what has been of late to be witnessed is in contradiction as well 
with the repeated declarations, the Mabitue) policy, and best interests.of Russia, 

.2 


70 


that, like a person copying extracts from an unknown language, he confines 
himself to the endeavour of reporting faithfully that which he endeavours in vain 
to comprehend. : 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 8, 1853. 


1 HAVE acquainted Count Nesselrode with the contents of your Lordship’s 
despatch of the 28th ultimo, marked Secret, No. 12d. 

His Excellency expressed his warm satisfaction at hearing that a communi- 
cation made in fact to the Queen by the Emperor, was not to be brought to 
public knowledge. 

He commented further upon the difficulty of keeping up a system af 
confidential communication with a Government ready, upon oceasion, to make 
their communications generally known. 

1 begged to remind his Excellency that the wish, which lie had expressed, 
had been attended to; but that, as 1 had before stated to him, according to the 
practice of Constitutional Governments, foreizn eommunications can only reach 
the Sovereien through the responsible adviser of the Crown.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Eurl of Clarendon.—(Reerived July 15.) 
(No, 350.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 8, 1853. 

1 HAVE held this morning what appears to be a very important conver- 
sation with the Chancellor, 

it commenced by my saying that 1] had a serious question to put to his 
Excellency, IT would ask whether, after the publications which had heen lately 
made hy the Russian Government, I, in common with every one else who 
desired peace, was to continue my endeavours towards finding an amicable 
solution tor the difficulties which were thickening around us. | 

Cherchez toujours, Count Nesselrode answered ; and bear im mind, that the 
solution is now the easier in consequence of the oceupation of the Prineipalties 
having been effected. 

This might be so, L replied; but to my apprehension, what was difficult 
before ig rendered much more so by a iilitury movement and by. olficial 
publications. 

Count Nesselrode said, that he would repeat that the entry of the Prin- 
cipalities made it easier for the Emperor to make some abatement of his 
demands, but did not explain this opinion; with regard to the publication of the 
circulars and manifestos, he desired again to state that such an address to the 
wiblic was indispensable after the attacks made upon Rusgia by the press of 
éngland and France—attacks which Her Majesty's Government had never sought 
to mitigate by any observation as to the real views of the Russian Cabinet. 

Atter a pause Count Nesselrode made some observation as to the back- 
wardness of the friends of Russia in not proposing some scheme of arrangement 
faccommodement). 

L replied that it appeared to me, on the contrary, that the wish of finding 
some mitdie course was that uppermost in the minds of all ressonable men; and 
that I myself, unfitted as [was to advise or suggest, had submitted a plan to 
Her Majesty's Government; as Lthought the time was come when, if serious 
consequences were to be averted, great frankness ought to be employed on all 
sides, | would state to his Excellency what my plan was, only premising that 


71 


since it was made events had progressed, and that I could not take upon myself 
to state whether my suggestion would meet the approbation either of Her 
Majesty's Government or of the Cabinets of France and Austria. It was this:— 

). The publication of a hatti-sheriff confirming the privileges enjoyed by 
the Greeks, whether in virtue of prescription or of the stipulations of treaties, 
with special mention of the arrangements made by the two late firmans respect- 
ing the holy places. 

% The notification of this hatti-sheriff to Russia, either ina letter from 
the Sultan or from the Grand Vizier, to be brought here by a special aiplomatic 
agent from his Highness. 

3. ‘The official communciation by the Porte of copies of the hattt-sheritf 
to the Missions of the Great Powers at Constantinople. 

The Chancellor, although by degrees and cautiously, gave me to understand 
that the terms were such as would be aceepted by the Emperor; the only point 
to be kept in view was, he said, that if ohjections which he considered unreason- 
able were to be maintained against the signature of the note by the Porte, some 
equivalent security must be found against the violation of the terms of the 
Jerusalem firmans. 

How, Count Nesselrode then asked, did [ contemplate that this proposition 
should reach the Emperor ? 

[replied that I must again remark that L was speaking in my own name 
and riot in that of Her Majesty’s Government; but that knowing the conciliatory 
feelings of that Government I had suggested that the proposal should be made in 
what would probably be the manner the most acceptable to the Emperor, thats, 
throuch the Austrian Cabinet. 

The Chancellor remarked that it was of course out of lis power to return 
anything like a definitive opinion to the plan which I had mentioned, but that it 
appeared to him, prind fucie, that something of the nature of what he termed the 
syettine-Seymour might be found acceptable, and that at all event whatever 
reached the Emperor at the hands of Austria was weleome and worthy of full 
consideration. 

The conversation then took suddenly a more animated turn: again Count 
Nesselrode desired to maintain the reasonableness of the terms proposed by 
Prince Menchikoit. 

After some discussion I snid that I really thought further argument useless ; 
that in general | had the bizhest respect for his Excellency's judgment, but 
that, as I had told him before, upon this subject IT had much less, because he 
was un interested party (en jeu), and that I must therefore be allowed to adopt 
an opinion which was not that of Her Majesty's Government or ot Lord 
Stratford de Redcliffe exclusively, but was shared hy the Cabinets of France, 
Austria, and Prussia, and specially by their Representatives at Constantinople. 

An altereation, which the well-known urbanity and good temper of the 
Chancellor were after a time exercised to restrain within due bounds, was then 
provoked by Count Nesselrode remarking that he was fully aware of the 
endeavours made by the Foreign Missions at Pera to defeat and annmilitlate the 
influence of Russia; that, reduced to its most simple expression, this was neither 
more or less than an attempt constantly made by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to 
reign paramount at Constantinople ; and that in these views never would the 
Emperor be brought to acquiesce, and never would he advise His Majesty to 
show such complaisance. | 

To this | replied, and with a certain warmth, that England had never 
sought to dispute the influence to which Russia was entitled in Turkey, and 
which, as we had lately read in a State paper, she possessed ina paramount degree; 
but that unquestionably if it was sought to sanites thot influence exclusive and 
dangerous to ‘Turkish independence, the opposition of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment mizht very securely be counted upon. ; 

With regard to personal allusions | said ; 1 am not fond of resorting to them, 
but as your Excelleney mentions Lord Stratford de Redclifie’s name, let me pro- 
nounce that of Prince Menchikoff. 1 did not, when he was named, endeavour 
to prejudice Her Majesty's Government against hin; | even refrained: afterwards 
from expressing what | felt us to his conduct : but allow me to tell you that no 
diplomatist who acts a8 he did, who displays the want of sincerity which he 
showed, can fail in putting himself upon bad terms with his callengues. 
The Prince proceeds to Constantinople, he knows the friendly disposition 


Pai 


72 


with which he is regarded by Her Majesty’s servants, and his first business is to 
seek out the Turkish Ministers, to make overtures or demands of which England 
knows nothing, and which he insists shall be kept from her knowledge ; and 
when, in process of time, his objects become a matter of publicity, he turns 
round and abuses his brother Ambassador because he is found to disapprove, as 
every one clse did, of Ins proceedings. 

Count Nesselrode said that this was a mistake ; that Prince Menchikoff had 
shown the greatest openness towards Lord Stratford de Redeliffe; that he had 
at once and fully explained to his Lordship the nature of his views. 

M. le Comte, I said, we are at present at variance as to facts; itis sometimes 
easy to reconcile opinions, it is impossible to reconcile contradictory statements 
of facts. 

At least, said Count Nesselrode, you must admit that Prince Menchikoff 
hig at a very conciliatory spirit; this was shown by the successive abatements 
in his demands upon the Porte. 

1 am sorry to be unable to make any such admissions, I replied; Prince 
Menchikoff might have shown moderation in acting as he did, supposing his 
original demands to have heen reasonable; but, as had been seen, they had 
been held by all impartial persons to be of a very different character. 

The conversation then, in consequence of the self-possession and kind 
courtesy of the Chancellor, was softened down tu its ordinary tone, and | took 
leave of his Excellency telling him that I should acquaint your Lordship with the 
unauthorized plan of reconethation which [ had had the honour of detailing to 
him. 

I would only beg your Lordship to pardon me if I express the hope that 
the terms I have sketched out may not be granted to Russia should they not 
meet with the approbation of the French Cabinet.

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, July 8, 1859. 

IT is very far from my wish to throw doubts upon the intentions of the 
Austrian Cabinet ; nothing can be fairer than their professions, as reported in 
Lord Westmorland’s despatch No. 241. 

At the same time 1 would state to your Lordship that the language 
held here by the Austrian Mission appears to me hardly to tally with that 
employed by Count Buol in his conversations with Her Majesty's Minister. 

Ag far as 1 can make out, only two despatches have been received by Baron 
Lebzeltern respecting the aggressive policy of the Russians, and the latter and 
stronger of the two is Te resented to meas only expressing the hope either that 
the occupation of the Principalities would not tixe place, or, if definitively 
decided upon, that it would be of short duration, | Bi 

It is unfortunate that in consequence of the absence of her Minister, 
Austria should be feebly represented at this moment at St. Petersburgh; as I 
cannot but fear that expressions not very strong mm themselves, became still less 
energctic when employed by a temponiry Chargé d’Atluires accustomed to those 
forma of deferent regard which for a long time have been observed by the 
Austrian Chancellerie in their communications with that of Russia. 

Happily, however, natural policy, position, and interests are such, that 
until a partition of Turkey shall be actually agreed upon, it 18 hardly possible 
that any amount of friendly feeling on the part of the Austrian Government 
can he sufficient to permit their acquiescence in the extension of Russian 
supremacy at the expense of ‘Turkey. ee ' 

Austria can hardly admit of the mouths of the Danube being in the holding 
of Russia; and the Head of the House of Hapsburgh cannot be the willing 
champion of Greek privileges and pretensions at Jerusalem. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

IN writing my despatch No. 40, of yesterday's date, [ had not time to 
mention certain details of my conversation on that day with M. Qrouyn de

His Excellency observed upon the difficulty of replying adequately to the 
Jast Russian Circular on account of ils mendacity, since it was rather a delicate 
matter to convey to a foreign Government that it had not spoken the trath. 

He considered Count Nesselrode as acting under compulsion in putting his 
namie to so senseless, truthless, and affronting a document, which he charac- 
terized as authorising the employment against Russin, by Enelind and Vrance, 
of two or three fleets and as many armies, were they so disposed. 

His Exeelleney said, he proposed publishing the Russian Circular and his 
reply on different days, and he asked iny opinion. | replied, that 1 thought the 
bane and the autidote had better again go together, to whieh he agreed. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys dwelt upon a topic on which he has already mucde 
remarks to Lord Cowley, namely, the similarity between Russia’s attitude at 
present and when she was proceeding to the partition of Poland, adding, that 
on that occasion also England had tried to prevent the catastrophe by proposing 
au form of Convention. 

I remarked that the partition of Poland could not have taken place had 
Austria and Prussia not combined with Russia, and that such a combination was 
hardly to be expected against Turkey; that, moreover, Enghind and France 
were determined to defend ‘Turkey, whereas Poland had fallen undefended, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys may perhaps be said to suffer from what has been 
called Russophobia; and one of his observations was, that, were great care not 
taken, anda fearless and determined front opposed to Russia, the whole of 
Europe might sooner or later become © Parkified.” 

His Excellency insisted upon the necessity of bearing in mind that Russian 
civilization was not like English or French, and consequently that the confidence 
to be placed in Russian assurances was of a peculiar kind: 

From one of his Exeellency’s expressions | should gather that he would 
much like a Treaty between France and England guaranteeing Turkey,

BARON BRUNNOW has communicated to me the circular despatch, 
dated ‘°°, which Count Nesselrode has addressed to the Russian Missions. 

It is difficult. to express the astonishment and regret with which Her 
Majesty's Government have read in this despatch the declaration that the 
Principalilies lave been invaded and oecupied in consequence of England and 
France having disregarded the recommenrlations of the Russian Government,

The passages of the despatch which contain this extraordinary statement

“En posant cet ultimatum h la Porte, nous avions plus particuli¢rement

plus avant qu’ils ne I’étaient déja dans ta question Thonneur et la dignite de 
'Empereur.” 

“)‘autre part, les deux Puissanees maritimes n'ont pas ere devoir déférer 
aux considérations que nous avions recommandées i leur sérieuse attention. 
Prenant avant nous l'initiative, elles ont jugé indispensable de dévancer imme- 
diatement par un mesure effective, celles que nous ne leur avions annonces 
que comme purement éventuelles, puisque nous en subordonnions la mise 4 effet 
aux résalutions finales de la Porte; et qu'au moment méme ot j'écris, Fexécu-

dans les parages de Constantinople Elles occupent déja les eaux et ports de Ta 
domination Ottomane & portée des Dardanelles. Par cette attitude avancee les

toire, qui, comme nous le leur avions fait pressentir, devait ajouter 4 la crise de 
nouvelles complications, 

“Ey présence du refus de la Porte, appuyé par li manifestation de la France 
et de l'Angleterre, il nous devient plus que jamais impossible de modifier les 
résolutions qu'en avait fait dépendre Vimpereur. 

“Bn consequence, Sa Majesté Imperiale vient Wenvoyer au corps de nos 
troupes stationné en ce moment en Bessarabie Vordre de passer la fronti¢re 
pour occuper les Principautes.” 

With respect to the first passage, 1 have to observe that Count Nesselrode’s 
despateh of June 1, to Baron Brunnow was not communicated to Her Majesty's 
Government till June 8, and therefore the order sent a week before to Admiral 
Dundas, to proceed to the neighbourhood of the Dardanelles; was not issued in 
disregard, as Count Nesselrode’s circular alfirms, of considerations brought to 
the knowledge of the British Government. But even if the case had been 
otherwise, anil no orders had been issued, it was im yossible for Her Majesty's 
Government to suppose that the threat to aceupy the Principalities would be 
rendered null by the Porte aceupting the terms which a few days before it had 
unhesitalingly rejected; and on the Sth of June, therefore, Her Majesty's 
Government were compelled to consider the oceupation of the Prineipalities 
inevitable + and they conelude that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh is not now 
prepared to admit that the note of Count Nesselrade to Reshid Pusha contained 
an empty menace, the exeeution of which was never seriously contemplated, 
But, in fact, Count Nesselrode's note of May 81, communicating the hostile 
intentions of Russia, would of itself have been sutlicient to justify Her 
Majesty's Government in taking mensures for the protection of Turkey. 

i shall now proceed to place on record at what time, and for whint reasons, 
the British fleet was sent to the Turkish waters. 

Prince Menchikoff, acting, it must be assumed, on the orders of his 
Government, stated in his note of the 4th of May, of which a copy was 
received in London on the 18th of May, that any further delay in answeriyg 
his proposals respecting the Greek Church, could only be conniaeesd by him as

This succession of menaces, addressed to a Power whose independence 
Russia had declared her determination to uphold, and in support of claims so 
much at variance with the assurances given to Her Majesty’s Government, 
together with the vast military and naval armaments which for months had 
been preparing on the very contines of Turkey, left no doubt on the mind of

as Her Majesty's Government adhere now, as firmly as in 1841, to the princi- 
ples which that ‘Treaty records, and believe that the maintenance of European 
peace is involved in the maintenance of the Ottoman Empire, they felt that the 
time had arrived when, in the interests of peace, they must he prepared to 
protect the Sultan; and upon learning the abrupt departure of Prince Menchi-

ae Malta, slould be pliced at the disposal of Her Majesty's Ambassador at

On the 2nd of June L communicated to Baron Brunnow the measure taken

It is thus clearly established that the British fleet was not sent to the 
waters of Turkey in disregard of considerations submitted to Her Majesty's 
Government by the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and that on the day before the 
instructions to Viscount Stratford de Redeliffle left London, the decision to 
occupy the Principalities was taken by the Russian Government; and I suy 
that decision was taken, because the Russian Government could never for one 
moment seriously have expected the submission of the Porte to the terms, " sans 
variante,” that a regard for its own dignity ane security had n few days before 
compelled it to decline, Yet Count Nesselrode in his circular despatch of

waters and ports can only be balanced by a military position on the part of 
Russia. 

But Her Majesty's Government must in the strongest terms protest against 
this assertion; and they deny that any resemblance exists between the position 
of the combined fleets in Besica Bay, and tnat of the Russian armies in the 
Principalities. The fleets have the same right to anchor in Besica Bay as in 
any port of the Mediterranean. Their presence there violates no treaty and no 
territory ; it infringes no international law; it is no menace to Turkish inde- 
pendence, and it assuredly ought to be no cause of offence to Russia; 
whereas by occupying the Principalities, Russia does violate the territory of the 
Sultan and the special ‘Treaty which regards that portion of his dominions : 
it is an infraction of the Law of Nations, and an act of direct hostility against 
the Sultan which he would be justified in meeting by a declaration of war, 
and by a requisition to the allied squadrons to come up to Constantinople for 
his defence; and, lastly, it is an act so dangerous as a precedent, and so 
violent on the part of a powerful State towards one whose very weakness 
should be its protection, that throughout Europe it has created feelings of alarm 
and reprobation, ‘To admit that any similarity exists, or that any comparison 
ean with trath be established, between the position of the English and French 
fleets outside the Dardanelles, and that of the Russian armies within the Princi- 
palities, is manifestly impossible, 

It is with deep regret that Her Majesty's Government thus find them- 
selves compelled to record their opinions upon the recent invasion of the 
Turkish territory; but they consider that the withholding of those opinions 
would be an abandonment of duty on their part, and might render it difficult 
for them hereafter to interfere in defence Taggers of Treaties which con- 
stitute the International Law of Europe, and which are the only effectual 
guarantees of general peace and of the rights of nations. 

The sufferings which the occupation of the Principalities must entail upon 
the inhabitants, will doubtless be much alleviated by the Russian Government 
taking upon itself the entire charge of that occupation. 

As I have so often, and at such length, discussed the demands of Russia 
upon the Porte, it is hardly necessary forme to remark upon the other portions of 

ount Nesselrode’s circular despatch, which in fiet adduces no new fact or 
argument in support of those demands. 1 must, however, express the convic-

My Lord, Vienna, July 12, 1853. 

WITH reference to the statements contained in my despatch No. 265, as 
to the movement of a brigade of infantry which had been ordered to assemble on 
the frontier of Servia, I have now the honour of reporting that this brigade will 
consist of the three regiments of infiuntry, Nicholas, Haynau, and Constantine, 
and that they will be placed under the orders of General Coronim, who. is 
Governor of the Austrian province of Servia, 

These troops are destined for any service which may be required upon the 
frontier, where at present there is no other force assembled which might be 
available in ease of disturbances.

No. 99. 


Mr. Jerningham to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 19.) 
(No. 54. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, July 18, 1853. 

IN the course of conversation to-day, M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed the 
strongest regret that the two fleets had not passed the Dardanelles upon the 

Lussians passing the Pruth, and he entered upon a variety of reasons for his 
opinion, of which the following appeared to me the principal; that if Russia 
means peace she would not have made war because France and England had 
done only as much as herself, whilst, if she means war, peace will not be pre- 
served by our stopping at Besika Bay; that if, as he believed would be the case, 
we should have eventually to order the fleets to advance, Russia would be able 
to exclaim that we had ruined the negotiation; that as the position of Besika 
Bay was a weak one, and as that of the Sea of Marmora would have been a 
strong one, the latter would have allowed England and France to be more con- 
ceding to Russia than the former, and that to have at once passed the 
Dardanelles, immediately upon Russia's giving us the right to do so, could not 
have failed to produce a great moral effect in our favour throughout Europe, the 
opposite of which he regretted to perceive had arisen from our attitude at Besika 

ay; whilst that bold but rightful step would also have done as much as could be 
done to control Russia. 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys farther observed upon the impossibility of the fleets 
remaining where they are throughout the winter, supposing Russia to show a 
determination to spin out the occupation of the Principalities, 

His Excellency reverted strongly to his belief that the present crisis would 
have been prevented by the two fleets going to the Dardanelles when that of 
France went to Salamis. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys aggravated his gloomy view of the general state of 
things by expressing his conviction that we shoule soon hear of Greek insur- 
rections in Bulgaria and elsewhere, which he believed Russia to be doing her 
best to bring about. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) 3. H. JERNINGHAM.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 20.) 
(No. 527.) 


My Lord, Paris, July 19, 1853, 
THE messenger who ought to have left Constantinopte on the 5th instant 
not having yet arrived, although M. Drouyn de Lhuys received his despatches of 


the same date two days ago, I am apprehensive that something must have 
vecurred to delay him on his journey. 


86 


It does not appear, however, from the contents of M. de la Cour’s 
deapatches, that the missing messenper could have been the bearer of any 
intellizence of importance. M, de la Cour states, that no progress had been 
made by the Porte in the compilation of a note, as advised by the four Powers, 
to replace that insisted upon by Prince Menchikoff; but that steps were taking 
to urge the Ottoman Government to show a little more alacrity. | 

Another despatch alludes, with gloomy forebodings, to the insufficiency of 
the meens of the Porte to meet the pecuniary sacrifices which the present crisis 
in her affairs calls upon her to make ; and it mentions, on the other hand, that 
an excitement, which may end in an outbreak, is to be observed in more than 
one part of the ‘Turkish dominions among the Christian subjects of the Sultan, 
an excitement which ig not without its echo in the neighbouring kingdom of 
Greece. 

A third despatch recounts the late unfortunate event at Smyrna, and states 
that the French Consul, at the request of his colleagues of Austria and the 
United States, had taken the refugee Kosta under his protection until it was 
finally settled to which of them Kosta is to le given Up.

(Signed) COWLEY,

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Barl of Clarendon.—( Received July 20.) 
(No. 39d.) : 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, Judy 12, 1853, 


COUNT DUVAL DE BEAULIEU, Secretary of the Belgian Legation 
at Constantinople, has passed the last four years in Turkey, and has been 
eneaged during the greater part of that lime in visiting various parts of the 
country. 

He happens to be at this moment at St, Petersburgh, and, as the oppor- 
tunity was fivourable for haying an impartial opinion, L asked him what was to 
be thought of those accounts of persecutions of Christians by Turks, of which 
we have lately heard so much through the Servian press, 

Count Duval's reply to the inquiry was very explicit, 

His extensive journies had satistied him that no systematic persecution ol 
the Christian subjects of the Porte took place, and that individual eases of 
oppression and wrong were extremely uncommon ; the great majority of the 
colplaints upon this subject were absolutely unfounded. 

“Tis is not all; what had struck Count Duval de Beaulicu in the relations 
of Grecks towards Turks was the insolent bearing of the former, who are very 
generally disposed to treat the Mahomotans as an inferior and intruding race.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 20.) 


(No. 355.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 12, 1858. 

ON the night of the 10th instant, 1 called upon the Chancellor at his villa. 
His Excellency, who was in conversation with several persons, left his chair to 
say a few words privately to me; ‘ Votre proposition,” he said, ‘ ave vous 
envoyée en Angleterre? faites nous la parvenir, et le plus tot possible, le moment 
est favorable—fuites nous la parvenir par Vienne.” I replied, that I had already 
written to your Lordship upon the subject, and that with his sermission | would 
make an inquiry of his Excellency ;—Was it true, as it had been stated to me, 
that the Government had intimated to the Porte their willingness to receive & 
Turkish negotiator? 

Count Nesselrode replied that T must be aware that all diplomatic inter- 
course with Constantinople had ceased ; that any communication between the 
Government und the Porte was carried on through the medium (par Ventremise) 
of the Austrian Cabinet. ; 

This 1 consider to have been, if nota direct, at all events an affirmative 
reply to my inquiry, 

My French colleague acquaints me that he has been seeking a solution for 
the question which at present causes such general embarrassment, and that he 
may have found it ina note which he proposes to substitute for that: presented 
by Prince Menchikolf, 

This “projet de note’ he read to me; it is composed of passages liken 
from the notes of Prince Menchikoff and Reshid Pasha, and offers perhaps a 
better method of putting an end to an unfortunate complication than the plan 
which I took the liberty of submitting to your Lordship. 

1 will not conclude my despatch without remarking upon the singularity of 
the eagerness now shown by the Russian Cabinet to come to terms with ‘Turkey. 
or, in other words, to modify its original demands, inmediately alter the publica- 
tion of the cireular containing the words: “En presenee du refus de la Porte 
appuyé par la manifestation de la France et de la Grande Bretagne, il nous 
devient plus que jamais impossible de modifier les resolutions qu’en avait fait 
dépendre |"Empereur.”” 

As | before stuted, however, T find myself very constantly obliged to record 
apparent coutradictions, without haying the means of reconciling them,

Tneclosure in No. LOG, 


Amended Copy of Memorandum from the Four Representatives to the Porte. 


AYANT reeu de lu Porte communication officielle de la lettre adressée en 
dernier lieu par M. le Comte de Nesselrode & Reshid Pasha, et la réponse du 
Ministre Ottoman & son Excellence le Chancelier de Russie, et plus tard ayant 


occupation of the Principalities. 


In cither o: these two cases, it is no exaggeration to slate that the Bastern 
question would be virtually surrendered. 1 mean by the Bustern question, the 
maintenance of the Ottoman Empire in its present degree of independence and 
territorial integrity, attended with the effect of averting that violent disturbance 
of European interests which could hurdly fail to ensue on any signal infraction 
of the principle. But in thus putting forward the point of political counter.

progress of trade and the prospects of social improvement in this quarter, with 
all their respective bearings on our national industry and international sympa- 
thies, It rests with Her Mujesty’s Government, and not, of course, with me, 
to determine the value of these interests, compared with the risks and sacrifices 
at war. 

The chief advantage which Turkey may hope to derive from not pushing 
its right of hostilities to an extreme, in the event of a simple occupation, is, that 
time will thus be gained for attempting further negotiations, far effecting a more 
complete concert aniong the Powers agreeing in opinion with Turkey, and for 
completing the preparations of defence on this side of the Danube, But, 
although it is probable that the Turkish forees will make a steadier resistance

Henceforward that extensive Empire of which Constantinople is the

Inclosure 7 in No. 108. 
Uonsul Wood to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(Extract.) Damascus, June 7, 1653. 


THE unusual excitement which prevails in Damascus in consequence of the 
apprehensions entertained at the capital of a war with Russia, coupled. with the 
disaffection occasioned by the really deplorable laxity and corruption of the local 
authorities, has produced a state of things that has added much to the general 
insecurity. 

The most formidable Arab tribes have occupied the country from Merg, four 
leagues from Damascus, to Karieteyn, and are ready to avail themselves of any 
confusion that might occur to pillage and plunder. 

But the worst feature under present circumstances is the highly agitated 
state of the population of this city, All the classes of the Mahometans are most 
anxious to see the embarrassments of the Porte increase, and herself involved in 
a disastrous war. ‘They wish to see her humbled in the hope that her officers in 
Syria will cease to persevere in a system of administration prejudicial to the 
interests of the effendis and grandces, whose property has been sequestered under 
various pretexts, and has been so heavily taxed as to have reduced their incomes 
to one half, and to the artizuns and tradesmen who find themselves at the mercy 
of rapacious tribunals and polive officers. 3 ; 

To aggravate a state of things which is already unsatisfactory the locusts 
have partially destroyed the crops, while the disaffected districts have not been 
brought under cultivation.

Inclosure 8 in No. 108. 
Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(ixtract.} Erseroom, June 24, 185. 

| HAVE inquired of various persons coming from Georgia whether any 
military preparations were making there. Some have said that troops were 
being assembled at Ghumri; others, and those the most numerous, that every- 
thing was perfectly quiet, but that war was talked of as imminent. Our Pasha 
says that troops have certainly been collected at Ghumm, but in so quiet a way 
as scarcely to have attracted public observation. Tt appears to me that no 
important movement of troops can have been made; but it is not unlikely that 
the Russians may fear that, in case of war, a simultancous attack might be com- 
lined between the Daghestanlees: and the ‘lurks, anid in that idea the garrison 
of Ghumri may have been strengthened, 

| cannot see that Russia would derive any advantige from the present 
occupation of Erzeroom; to do that, and to mitintain a sutlicient foree to resist 
the attack of the Caucasian tribes, which would certainly be made were war 
commenced, would require a larger force than she could conveniently withdraw 
from those points where the principal struggle must take place; and were she 
victorious there, she could at any time occupy Erzeroom. | therefore conceive 
that the object of Russia is probably to maintain her positions in Georgia, 
without any addition to the forces she his there, which, though sufficient for 
defence, for offensive operations would searee suffice. In the last invasion at 
this part of Turkey, the number of Russian soldiers did not exceed 10,000, 
though they were aecompanied by a vast number of irregular native levies, but 
then ‘Turkey had no disciplined troops; now there will be here, perhaps, a force 
of 2),000 diseiplined troops, besides irregulars, so that it would be scarce sale 
for Itussia to venture on an invasion with an army of less strength; and I doubt 


95 


whether she could detach so large a force from Georgia without offering too 
ereat an advantage to the Caucasian tribes; so that I do not apprehend that we 
shall see a Russian army in Erzeroom for the present. 


Inclosure 9 in No. 108. 
Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract.) Erzeroom, June 25, 1856. 

IN every part of the country the Koords are actively engaged in robbing, 
both on the high roads and in the villages. . 

It is said that within a few days about seven battalions will have come in 
from Harpoot ; and some time since, seventy picces of artillery set out on the way 
hither by a circuitous route, as the direct one was not practicable for guns. The 
detachments in the various out-stations have been called in, but | trust some 
troops will be left there, as the country will be at the mercy of the Koords, and 
incalculable injury to the cultivators will ensue. 

The militia has been called out; and altogether the force to be collected 
here will, it is said, amount to about 40,000 disciplined troops. 1 hope that 
with such an imposing force the Porte and the General may not be tempted to 
make an attack upon Georgia, as, from the want of skill in the Turkish officers, 
there would not be much hope of success. But if Russia were to meet with 
reverses in Europe, so as to disable her from succouring Georgia, and if an 
European force were landed in that country to cooperate with the Turkish force, 
then indeed a forward movement, combined with an attack on the part of the 
Caucasian tribes, would not fail to drive the Russians out of Georgia, for they 
would find few friends among the natives, were they to experience a reverse. 


Inclosure 10 in No, 108. 
—— to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(fxtract.) Erzeroom, June 25, 1855. 

THERE is no communication whatever between Ghumri and Batoom, on 
account of the want of roads through the almost inaccessible country which 
separates the two places, Any news from the former town would naturally find 
its way through Kars to Erzeroom,; and I believe Mr. Brant is writing to your 
Excellency on this subject. 1 do not think it probable or possible for the 
Russians to march from Ghumri on Batoom. The port could be occupied at 
any time by Russian vessels of war, or by troops marched by the frontier along 
the sea-shore. The country around Batoom is untenable, on account of its 
mountainous and densely-weoded character, so that the port alone could be 
occupied, and could, I imagine, be easily retaken at any moment.

(Extracts.) Monastir, May 19, 1853. 

I HAVE the honour to transmit, herewith inclosed, a translation into 
Turkish from the Greek language, of an incendiary and anonymous address 
which was, during the last month or two, as [ am informed, cirenlated in the 
neighbouring provinces of Thessaly and Salonica, It seems to have failed 
exciting disturbance of any kind, however it may have contributed to the recent 
pretties, 


Monastir, June 10, 1853. 

Aoni Pasha is of opinion that it is exceedingly imprudent to leave the 
provinces of Thessaly and Thrace, the inhabitants of which are notoriously 
disaflected, and ready to join the Hellenes on the first opportunity, thus denuded 
of all regular detence, 

Only 6,500 Albanian irregulars, picked men, are to be levied for Shumla, 
Considering the numerical force of the bands whieh Albania can furnish, if 
necessary, this is a very inconsiderable body indeed; and, coupled with the fact 
already mentioned, that all the regular troops are to be withdrawn from Thessaly 
and Thraee, leads me to infer that, in the event of the rising of the Greeks in 
these provinces, it is intended to employ the Albanians against them. How far 
a plain of this kind would he consistent with good policy, to say nothing of 
humanity, Linust leave your Excellency to judge; believing, for my part, such u 
result (whether casual or contemplated) by no means improbable. 


Inclosure 13 in No. 108. 
Consul Longworth to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract, Monastir, June 23, 1853. 

AS | had the honour to state in my last despatch to your Excellency, some 
alarm and uneasiness have been experienced by the inhabitants of Monastir 
at the complete evacuation of the place by the Nizam or regular troops. The 
Austrian Viee-Consul, M. Westermager, having requested me to join him in 
representing to Aoni Pasha the danger of leaving the town in this defenceless 
state, | deemed it advisable (though by no means concurring with him as to the 
extent of that danger, or of the disorders which he believed had actuatly taken 
place), to recommend that a small number of regulars should be detained here, 
i they could be spared without causing inconvenienee and embarrassment with 
regard to the military combinations now in progress. Aoni Pasha as well as the 
civil authorities at once acquiesced in the propriety of the suggestion, but said 
they could not venture to infringe the orders of Omer Pasha, who had positively 
instructed them to send forward all the regular troops. 

The Austrian Vice-Consul, who appeared to labour under considerable 
excitement, then wished me to enter into a joint protest with him on the 
subject; but this | informed him Ef did not feel justified in doing. ‘The fuct is 
that although public security might be promoted by the detention ef a few 
companies of infantry at Monastir, there are in the precarious social condition 
of Ruropean Turkey many other places where a still more urgent necessity 
might be pleaded for their presence; and yet if all such claims were attended to, 
serious obstacles would be opposed to the concentration of the Turkish army at 
Shuma.

Inclosure 15 in No. L0G, 
Consul Saunders to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 


(Extracts, ) Prevesa, April 13, 1853. 

The greater part of the villages along the whole line of boundary in 
Thessaly and Epirus, as wellas the entire districts wherein these villages are 
situated, are almost exclusively tenanted by Christian subjects of the Porte in a 
state of extreme destitution, 


June 2, 180d, 

The frontier districts of Thessaly and Epirus appear likely to cause con- 
siderable embarrassment to the Government in the event of pending negotiations 
assuming a less pacilic character. 

The rural population, oppressed by fiscal exactions, and subjected to 
intolerable acts of violence and injustice, cannot be expected to entertain any 
but the most rancorous feelings towards their persecutors. ; 

The inhabitants of the greater part of these villages being moreover 
exclusively Christians, and seeing no other prospect of relief open to them, are 
continually thronging the foreign Consulates with the view of seeking some 
friendly intervention. 

After thus depicting to your Lordship the disastrous condition of these 
frontier districts from various causes, it may be readily conceived that for some 
time past the emigration of whole families to Greeee, which can only be accom- 
plished by stealth, has been practised to a considerable extent; and that parties 
so circumstanced, together with the whole body of Suliots, Chimariots, and 
other Epirotes domiciled in Greece will be eager to avail themselves of the first 
favourable occasion of promoting disturbances in this province.

(Extracts) Scutari, June 1, 1853. 

ALL that remains to protect these districts are three battalions of regular 
troops and 1200 irrepular Topehi, who are quartered on the borders. All the 
desperate characters have raised their heads again, and acts of rapine and 
robbery are agam very frequent at the expense of the Christians. . 

Osman Pasha, the Governor of this province, is & Mussulman, and sees with

vengeance of their enemies, live in a continual state of alarm. It must, however, 
he borne in mind that the Christian population of these districts is three times 
greater than the Turkish, and if they have been hitherto kept down it was 
merely by the hope of political improvement under the promising administration 
of Omer Pashia, 


Scutari, June 8, 1853. 

There now remain in these parts only three companies, incomplete, of 
regular troops, distributed among the various fortresses in this district.

reports from Scutari, Monastir, and Prevesa, annexed to this instruction. You

me by the late Grand Vizier, the appointment of a more trustworthy Pasha at

of could at length be effectively redressed. But it is with extreme disappoint- 
ment and pain that I observe the continuance of evils which affect so deeply the 
welfare of the empire, and which assume a deeper character of importance in the 


jresent critical state of the Porte’s relations with Russia. You will read this 
instruction to his Highness; you will communicate fully the contents of the

adopting adequate measures for the repression of crime and the protection of the 
Sultan's loyal and peaceable subjects without further delay. [ am aware that 
the Porte’s attention is principally directed at present to them defensive prepara- 
tions which cannot with safety be dispensed with; but it cannot be denied that 
the matters now brought into notice have an immediate bearing on the same 
wreat interest, and cannot be neglected with safety more than with justice

Inclosure 2 in No. 110. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to M. E. Pisani, 


Sir, Therapie, July 4, 1853, 

| HAVE frequently had occasion of late, and indeed for some years back, 
to bring to the knowledge of the Porte such atrocious instances of cruelty, 
raping, and murder, as 1 have found, with extreme concern, in the Consular 
reports, exhibiting generally the disturbed and misgoverned condition of many 
parts of Roumelia, and calling loudly for redress from the Imperial Government. 
The charneter of these disorderly and brutal outrages may be said with truth to 
be, in general, that of Mussulman fanaticism, excited by cupidity and hatred 
aeainst the Sultan's Christian subjects. 1 will not say that my friendly and 
virrnest representations have been entirely disregarded, On the contrary, 1 have 


106 


sometimes had the satisfaction of being instrumental towards the repression of 
erime, the alleviation of individual suffering, and the reeall of incapable magis- 
trates. But the evil, nevertheless, has not been permanently removed, and the 
effect of every partial check has been of short duration. 

It is evident. that the present political circumstances of the empire must 
tend directly to increase the temptations to crime, and to bring a much wider 
extent of country within the range of disorderly and outrageous passions. ‘The 
Mussulmans are excited by the prospect of war. The Rayahs, from their 
nuinbers, especially in the European provinces of Turkey, are objects of fear, no 
less than of hatred and cupidity. The movement of troops; the calling out the 
Rediff; the concentration af regulars on the frontier; the demand of supplies ; 
the scarcity of money; the pressure for payment of arrears; the anticipation of 
future taxes, concur to spread alarm among the peaceable, and to hold out a 
clearer prospect of impunity to the violent. The Pashas and subordinate 
Governors are perplexed ; individuals possessing local wealth acquire a licentious 
influence; and unless some powerful remedies be applied without further delay, 
it is to be feared that the authority of the Central Government will be com- 
pletely overpowered in some of the provinces, and that the people, despairing of 
protection, will augment the disorder by resorting to lawless means of self 
preservation, 

For the sake of the empire itself, no less than from motives of humanity, | 
am inexpressibly anxious to engage the Porte’s attention, ere it be too late, to 
this abundant source of evil and danger. | am well aware of the difficulties 
under which the Government labours, and that it is far more easy to desenbe 
any mischief and to trace it to its causes, than to find an efficient remedy, Yet 
such is the magnitude of the evil, and such the danger of its extension under 
present cireumstances, that the necessity of checking its progress, and restoring 
some degree of confidence among the tributary classes, Is scarcely subordinate 
to the duty of preparing the means of resistance against an invading foreign 
aiviny. 

“Tn addition to the numerous extracts of my Consular correspondence which 
I have furnished to the office of Foreign Affairs with reference to this subject, | 
now inclose, for special consideration, the intelligence which has reached me 
fram-an. official source in Bulgaria, Reshid Pasha will learn from its contents 
how erying is the evil—how urgent the peril, even in a province where a very 
considerable portion of the regular army is being at this moment collected, 

The more pressing and obvious wants are these; the correction, by means 
of explination and control, of that fanatical and licentious spirit which new 
inflames the Mussulman population; some special means for the protection of 
the loyal and peaceably disposed, whether Mussulinan or Raynh; an efficient 
responsibility on the part of the local governors and magistrates towards the 
Supreme Government; a more regular and judicious exercise of authority in the 
collection of supplies, and the direction of persons acting in concert with the 
army; relief for the labouring. and the rural classes, by means of extraordinary 
aids obtained by the Porte from other sourees, and applied to the payment of 
the forces, and other immediate wants of the State. 

| abstain from offering any suggestions of a more particular kind, in the 
belief that the Porte is the best judge of its own resources, and in the hope that 
it will adopt every remedial measure to be found within the range of those 
resourees, 

You will leave a copy of this instruction with Reshid Pasha, after reading 
and fully explaining its contents to his Highness; and you will request that it 
may be brought, without delay, before His Majesty the Sultan and the Council 
of State, to the end that it may be taken into serious consideration; and that 
the Porte’s decision may be communicated to me for the information of Her 
Majesty's Government, 

Yours, &e, |

WE have at length received official intelligence of the entrance of the 
Russian army in Bessarabia into the Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia, 
The crossing of the Pruth at Sculeni began at 8 o'clock in the forenoon of the 
ord instant. 

Inclosed herewith is a copy of Consul Gardner's despatch to me, trans-

document agree with the conditions on which I had recommended the Porte not 
to withdraw the Hospodars, I have every reason to believe that they will remain 
in their respective Governments for the present. 

There are two passages in the Proclamation to which I beg leave to draw 
your Lordship’s attention ; one is that describing the conditions on which the 
Emperor is stated to abstain from offensive hostilities against Turkey, and the 
other indicative of the manner in which the pledge of not charging the inha- 
bitants of the Principalities with the expenses of the occupation is to be 
redeemed. It cannot be necessary for me to trouble your Lordship with any 
comment upon the interpretation to which, in different ways, each of then is 
liable.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Recerved July 20.) 


(No. 144.) 
My Lard, Therapia, July 9, 1854. 

THE sudden dismissal of the two principal Ministers of State, the Grand 
Vizier and the Seeretary for Foreign Affairs, without a knowledge of any cir- 
cumetances calculated to satisfy the public curiosity, has thrown the whole 
capital into a state of astonishment and anxiety. As this important change 
took place at the very moment when intelligence was received of the occupation 
of Moldavia by a Russian army, it was natural to ascribe it 1o some intrigue 
connected with the feeling of the Government towards Russia. The leading 
members of the diplomatic body had every appearance of being taken by 
surprise, and the Sultan s Ministers, both these who were dismissed and those 
who were retained in office, disclaimed all knowledge of the Sultans motives in 
taking so questionable a step at the present juncture. ‘The prevailing impression 
was that the war party hid obtained the ascendant, and that measures, not 
unlikely to precipitate an appeal to force, were to be expected. 

For my own pe I determined to seck information at the fountain 
head, and 1 accordingly sought and obtained an audience of the Sultan this 
morning. 

His Majesty received me with his usual aflubility, and I had scarcely stated 
the object of my visit, when he assured me that the partial change of Miniateis 
which he had ordered, was exclusively attributable to personal causes. Without 
entering into particulars, he told me that some of his Ministers had occasioned 
so much vexation by their personal jealousies that in self-defence he had been 
obliged to. remove them. His idea, under this supposed necessity, was fo 
replace the late Grand Vizier, Mustapha Pasha, by the Commander of the 
guard, Mehemet Rushdi Pasha, and Reshid Pasha by the Tate Governor of 
Smyrna, Aali Pasha, 

L took the liberty of submitting to His Majesty whether the critical cir- 
eumatances in Which his Empire was now unfortunately placed, did not impose 
upon hin the duty of making all secondary considerations give way to the 
principal point; and whether the stability of his administration, and the conse- 
quent respect inspired by it, were not objects of greater consequence than 
obtaining relief from the annoyance of those personal differences which his 
Imperial authority was fully able, if properly exerted, to control, and perhaps 
even to remove altogether. 

These and other observations, pressed upon His Majesty's attention with 
becoming respect, failed not, 1 am happy to say, in producing the desired effect. 
The two Pashas, Mustapha and Reshid, are restored to their former posts; and 
the Sultan, by my advice, has urged upon them 80 strongly the paramount duty 
of devoting themselves exclusively to the public interests m this time of crisis 
that the causes of the late untoward changes are, T trust, not likely to be repeateil 
for the present, 

| was the more desirous of bringing the Sultan to this resolution because | 
found that he intended toname Aali Pasha to the direction of the Foreign Office, 
and 1 bad reason to know that the appointuient of that distinguished individual 
go soon after the late occurrences at Smyrna would give offence, most unseason- 
ably, to the Court of Austria. 

“T cannot conceal from myself that a certain degree of inconvenience Is 
attached to a reinstatement, following so immediately upon a dismissal, of such 
high funetionaries. Rut | am convinced that the balance of evil was on the side 
of perseverance in an untimely and injudicious change, and that the: sense of its 


Ll] 


being necessary to return 80 promptly to the preceding state of things is well 
calculated to discourage a repetition of such hazardous experiments. 

1am happy to add that, although the coincidence of these occurrences with 
the festival of Bairam has occasioned a delay in the transaction of public 
business, my audience afforded me an opportunity of urging the Sultan to 
persevere for the present in a course of moderate counsels, notwithstanding the 
aggressions of Russia, and of receiving the most satisfactory assurances in that 
respect from His Majesty's own lips. Since my return to Therapia I have 
learnt that orders have been given to submit the protest, which is already drawn 
up, to the deliberations of the Council, and to prepare a proclamation directed 
to the maintenance of public tranquillity, by explaining fully the existing 
differences between Turkey and Russia, as well as the friendly relations subsisting 
gencrally between the Porte and the leading Powers of Christendom. It may seem 
strange that the second part of this explanation should be necessary ; but it 
appears that the presence of the British and French squadrons in the Dardanelles 
‘s considered by some ignorant Turks as rather having reference to their own 
eventual interests than to the protection of Turkey in case of further aggression 
from Tussia. 

L have, &c. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Consul Longworth to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(Extract.) Monastir, June 23, 1853. 

FIVE months’ arrears of pay are owing to the whole army, officers and 
men, which creates much murmuring and discontent. The military chests are 
apparently empty; and Omer Pasha was compelled to have recourse to the 
inerchants of this place for so small a loan as 60,000 piastres. There was some 
talk of riising a million by anticipation, on the Temetuat or property tax in this 
and the adjoining districts; but no steps that Tam aware of, have yet been 
taken for that purpose. It is very questionable indeed if such a sum could be 
raised at present, as the resources of the people are said to be completely 
exhausted, and the jails overflow with insolvent tax-payers. 3,000 out of the 
7,000 irregulars that were to have been raised in Albania refuse to march unless 
they are paid three months’ hire in advance, and an allowance of 80 instead of 50 
piastres a month; among these are 1000 Miridit or Christian Albanians, though 
in consideration of their privileges and exemption from Haratsh they are bound 
lo serve gratuitously, 

Information has within the last few days been received from Osman Pasha 
of Seutari, that the Montenegrins have again begun to harass and plunder their 
neighbours, and seem to be preparing for an incursion on a formidable seale, into 
the Turkish territory ; he has necontingy sent large reinforcements of irregulars 


to Spuez. There is at this moment, I believe, a Russian Consular Agent 
reaident at Cettigne.

No. 116. 


Mr. Jerningham to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved July 21.) 


(No. 55. Confidential.) | | 
My Lord, Paris, July 18, 18030. 

SINCE the departure of the messenger, | find I have omitted to mention 
that M. Drouyn de iba s observed to me, that many months ago, In writing 
to Lord John Russell, he predicted the mischievous course pursued by the 
Emperor Nicholas, feeling confident that the armaments at Sevastopol und in 
Bessarabia could not but signify injurious designs. 


lt4 


| told his Excellency I must do him the justice to say, that when, in the 
carly part of the year 1 had occasion to observe to him that Her Majesty's 
Government placed reliance on the assurances of the Emperor of Russia, he 
showed a disinclination to concur. 

It may perhaps be said that the armaments in question were as much at 
variance with the language of peace, as was the Emperor's fixed idea of the 
impending fall of Turkey with his expressed wish for her perpetuity; that, 
though Russia talked as if she wished the Porte’s preservation, she acted as if 
she desired its downfall; and that the said fixed iden may have had some sort 
of connection both with the alleged Greek prophecy that the present year would 
see St, Sophia restored to Christianity, and with the fact that the Prince of 
Montencgr attacked the Turks immediately on his return from St. Peters- 
burgh. 

It may be as well to mention, that having expressed to M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys the opinion that a vital point at present was the adherence of Austria, 
his Excellency not only agreed with me, but seemed to trust in such support. 

When M. Drouyn de Lhuys maintained that the present crisis would not 
have arisen had England agreed at the outset to a bolder line of conduct, it was 
of course easy to retort, that neither the crisis nor the question would have 
arisen had not France made her untoward move about the holy places; but, as 
your Lordship is aware, no one condemns that step more than M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, and the subject therefore appeared to me as beside the matter under 
consideration, 

lis Execlleney’s reason for the above-mentioned opinion seemed to he, 
that the carly junction of the two fleets would have made it impossible for the 
Emperor Nicholas not to feel convinced from the first that England and France 
were determined to act in concert, and consequently that, unless bent on war at 
any price, His Majesty would not have gone as far as he has, 

The argument of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that the stronger position of the 
Soa of Marmora would have rendered it easier for England and France to make 
concessions to Russia than docs the weaker one of Besika Bay, may perhaps 
find its answer in the reflection that the Power most called on to concede is 
Russia, and that the stronger we leave her position for a time, the easier ts it for 
her to concede. 

Lhave, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. JERNINGHAM.
