Sir G, A. Seymour to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Received July 21 .) 


(No, 461.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 15, 1853. 


IF the late reckless policy of the Russian Cabinet has been of a nature to 
cause the apprehension of the whole of Europe, it has served not less effectually 
to cause a perturbation here which will probubly require a longer time to calm 
down. 

What the sums are which have been expended in naval and military pre- 
parations, and in those practices which on extraordinary occasions are so exten- 
sively employed by Russian agents, will probably never be known to the public, 
but their eflect is already shown by the state of the Russian Treasury. ‘Already 
before one of the ucts of hostility have taken place, of which so many would 
follow the completion of Prince Menchikoff's plans, the exigencies af the State 
have beeome such that there is serious question of having recourse to those

A CONVERSATION which I had this morning with the Chancellor was 
more satisfactory than any which I have held for some time with his Excellency. 

Count Nesselrode professed himself much gratified by the assurances which 
I gave him of the conciliatory disposition by which Her Majesty’s Government 
are still animated, in despite of all that has of late occurred, and expressed his 
confidence that under this state of things a disturbance of the European peace 
was not to be feared. 

His expression was that he now felt very sanguine as to the future, sinee, as 
Her Majesty's Government were intent upon finding some solution of the 
present difficulty which would be acceptable to the Emperor, he was convinced 
that these means of eseape from danger would be diseovered. 

His Excellency spoke of various plans which had been devised, and added 
(I thought incautiously) that of course Russia would select that which pleased 
her the best: he himself leaned to: the plan proposed by M. de Bourqueney ; 
this however was, | observed, little thought of at Paris. or in London, indeed, | 
added, it was now understood that the idea had originated not with M. de 
Bourqueney but with Baron Meyendortt. 

Count Nesselrode then reverted to my own suggestion, and again expressed 
the wish that this plan should reach St. Petersburgh as soon as possible through 
the Austrian Cabinet, 

{ will not conceal from your Lordship that this anxtety impresses me with 
the belief that the terms whieh | had devised are of a nature too favourable for 
Russia, though at the same time Ido not hesilate to express my conviction of 
its being for the general interests of Europe that the Emperor should be well 
satished with the arrangement which may be definitively decided upon.

afterwards dropped the idea. IT then observed that I trusted there would be 
found at St. Petersburgh a disposition to listen to reason, and that we might 
confidently look to a pacific solution of the question. He believed this would 
be the case; but he added, that he had received intelligence of consideralle 
reinforcements having marched into the Prineipalities; that the army of occu- 
pation already amounted to 50,000 men; and that he also heard of the advance 
of further Russian forees towards the Turkish frontier, 1 told his Excellency 
that all this proved more.and more the necessity of a close union amongst those 


Li? 


who were opposed to the encroaching policy of Russia, and that I hoped he 
would write to St. Petersburgh in a stronger sense than he had hitherto done ; 
that Austria had changed her language, and had done so from seeing the little 
attention that had been bestowed by the Emperor and his Cabinet to various 
suggestions that had been sent in what might be ealled a mild and supplicating 
tone; that it was now more essential than ever that we should unite, and bring 
our moral weight to bear together on the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh; that we 
were all agreed as to the injustice of the proceedings of Russia in this question ; 
and that it was only by showing her that there was no second opinion in the 
matter among the great Powers that we could insure success and a continuation 
of the blessings of peace. 

Baron Manteuffel assured me that it was his intention to write in this sense 
to St. Petersburgh; but I regret to say that the King has already left Berlin ; 
and his Excellency intends to return again to-day to the country, where he 
purposes remaining a week, so that it ts improbable any fresh instructions of 
importance on Eastern affairs will issue from the Prussian Foreign Office for 
some days to come. 

I availed myself of the opporlunity of this conversation to read to Baron 
Manteuffel some passages in your Lordship’s late despatches to Lord Westmor- 
land Nos, 189, 197, and 199, and drew his Excellency’s particular attention to 
the various observations which your Lordship had made to Count Colloredo on

Treaty of 1841; the good advice Her Majesty's Ambassador had given to the 
Porte not to declare war against Russia, in retaliation for her unjustifiable 
conduct in occupying the Principalities ; as well as the justice of your remarks 
us to the Emperor of Russia's apparent desire to give himself the benefit of a 
state of peace for preparing further armaments. 

T read to him the observations which your Lordship addressed to Count 
Colloredo, as reported in your No, 197, to the Earl of Westmorland, relating to 
the question of a simultaneous evacuation of the Principalities and departure of 
the combined fleets from Besika Bay. He appeared struck with the truth of

[ then drew Baron Manteuffel’s seta attention to the last part of your 
Lordship’s despatch to Lord Westmorland No. 199, where you express the

which had been made to him, and persisted in retaining forcible possession of 
territory belonging to Turkey, the Austrian Government ecula: not remain 
neutral, but come to the aid of ‘Turkey; and asked him what Prussia would do 
in sucha case ? His Excellency's reply was, that the occupation of the Princi- 
palities was not of that immediate importance to Prussia which it was to

confidentially that the Prussian Government was quietly preparing for eventu- 
ilities; but he would not say anything which approached to a belief that Prussia

policy which she had laid down for herself in the present erisis.

My Lord, Foreign Office, July 22, 1853. 

A FEW days ago Count Walewski informed me that his Government were 
desirous to concert with Her Majesty's Government as to the measures to be 
taken, and the instructions that should be sent to the French and English 
Ambassadors at Constantinople in the event-— 

1. Of Russia rejecting all measures of conciliation. 

2, Of the occupation of the Principalities being prolonged; and 

3. Of the presence of the combined fleets being necessary at Constantinople 
im consequence of serious events. | 

I told Count Walewski that I -could give him no decisive answer without 
consulting the Cabinet; but 1 begged to remark that the second contingency 
appeared to be unnecessary as being included in the first, for the Emperor of 
Russia, if he refused all offers of conciliation, would certainly continue ta occupy 
the Principulities, and, on the other hand, he must immediately evacuate them if 
his differences with Turkey were arranged, 

{ wed Count Walewski what were the “serious events” to which the third 
hypothesis alluded; and his Excellency said that the despatch of M. Drouyn de 


119 


Lhuys was not very clear on that point, but that he understood them to refer 
not to any attack on the part of Russia, but to internal commotions, 

T have since informed Count Walewski that in the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government it would be unjust towards the Representatives of England and 
France at Constantinople to throw upon them the responsibility of acting upon 
hypothetical instructions, and that as much would depend upon the nature of 
the terms proposed to Russia, and the reasons assigned by her for rejecting 
them, and that as authentic information upon the subject could only be received 
at London and Paris, while vague ramours would only reach the Ambassadors, 
it would be highly imprudent for the Governments of England and France not 
to keep entirely in their own hands the decision of a question upon which the 
peace of Europe might depend, particularly as the Ambassadors had ample 
power under their instructions to protect the Porte against any hostile attack 
that might be attempted by Russia in the fhilure to effect a peaceful arrangement 
by negotiation. 

In the meanwhile, however, I said that Her Majesty’s Government would 
take into their serious consideration, and would desire to concert with the French 
Government as to the measures which should be adopted if all the different 

rojects for settling the question should prove unsuccessful, but that at present 
it appeared to them unnecessary to contemplate the case of suspending the 
Treaty of 1841, in order that the naval forces of England and France might he 
employed in the internal affairs of “lurkey. 
Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Sir G. H. Seymour to ihe Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeeived July 25.) 


(No. 365, Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 16, 1853. 

A WANT of time prevented my offering you the Wetails of the communi- 
cation to which LE alluded in my despatch No. 357 of the 13th instant; and | 
the more regretted my inability to write to your Lordship at length, as these 
details possess considerable interest, 

I will only premise that they formed the substance of a conversation which 
had been held by one of the senior employes of the Foreign Office with a person 
in whom I have full confidence, who has had the kindness to bring this conver- 
sation to my knowledge, upon condition that his name shall not appear, 

“Our position,” said the Russian employé, “is one of extreme difficulty 
and embarrassment. We ure perfectly aware of it, and we are in a hurry to 
extricate ourselves, 80 that we can only do so in a creditable manner. 

“Tn general, every step taken in our foreign policy is taken advisedly and 
alter duc deliberation, On this occasion the Emperor has been betrayed—that 
is the word—by the rashness of the Sclavonian party, by Prince Menchikoff, and 
M. de Séniavine, who were powerfully supported by the Grand Duke Con- 
stantine. 

" These persons actuated, the two first by their fanatical Russian feelings, 
the latter still more even by his dislike to his eldest brother and the peaceable 
policy which he always advocates, circumvented the Emperor, and persuaded 
him that by good management and sudden movements an advantage could be 
derived for the Greek Church, which would produce a great effect in Russia, 
and which was attainable without visk or difliculty. 
 * The result has been what you see. The preparations for this undertak- 
ing have exhausted the Treasury. We have spent about thirty millions of 


* Tn copies sent abroad, the word “méme" is to be omitted, at Baron Bruniow's request, 


Ven 


silver roubles since the Ist of January upon our armaments, and we find that 
we have aroused the jealousy of the whole of Europe. This comes of neglect- 
ing the advice of the Chancellor, and of the Russian party getting a temporary 
ascendancy. 

“Se the affair now stands, If pressed, the Emperor will fight his way 
through his difficulties as he ean, for he will not bear disgrace; but you may be 
sure that if honourable means of retreat can be found, His Majesty will gladly 
avail himself of them.” 

The person in question proceeded to speak of Prince Menchikoff, and 
observed that it might be taken as certain that he went to Constantinople with 
the firm determination of what he termed “de brouiller les affaires.” 

“Did you hear,” he continued, “of a speech which the Prince made in the 
hearing of several persons, as he was upon the point of embarking at Odessa ?— 
‘J'ai bien Vintention,’ he said, speaking of the Turks, ‘de les mener rondement ; 
je les connaig ces gens la, et quand d leur miserable Sultan je me propose bien 
avant de le quitter de lui faire avaler du pore.” ; 

I request your Lordship’s attention to the picture thus offered of Russian 
manners in the middle of the nineteenth century, 

The policy of the Emperor's whole life is defeated, and the peace of Europe 
placed in danger, by the intrigues of a couple of fanatics, assisted by the wild 
ambition and perverse disposition of a youthful Prince; while one of these 
conspirators, at the very moment of undertaking the most important office with 
which the confidence of his master could invest him, cannot repress a ribald 
joke, which would have been unbecoming in his great grandfather, the fortunate 
pastrycook’s boy. . 

The picture would have been incomplete if this aged jester had not been the 
person who, immediately afterwards, came forward as the calumniator of one of 
the most eminent of European diplomatists, by whose firmness his acts had been 
foiled, and if, in process of time, his own vile intrigues had not been brought 
(though indirectly) to the knowledge of the English Mission by a confidential 
servant of the Imperial Foreign Office, in general so distinguished by its myste- 
rious discretion, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, Berlin, July 22, 1853. 

| CALLED this morning on M. de le Coq, in the absence of Baron 
Manteuffel, and he informed me that a further instruction had been addressed to 
the Prussian Minister at Constantinople. He read me this despatch, the main 
object of which is to recommend the adoption of the “ projet-Bourqueney,” and 
to urge Baron Wildenbruch to use all his influence with the Porte to accept any 
reasonable propositions that are made for the termination of the negotiations now 
pending in the Turkish eapital. 

When M. de le Coq had finished reading this paper, 1 observed that it con- 
tained nothing new, that it showed that no material change had perhaps come 
over the independent policy of the Prussian Government in this question ; but I 
eaid the tone of the instructions was designed to engage the Porte to sign a note 
which she had already refused to do, and to adopt an arrangement less calculated 
than others which had been brought forward to maintain the dignity and 
independence of Turkey. 

I then told M. de le Coq that a Project of Convention had been sent to 
St. Petersburgh by Her Majesty's Government for the settlement of the question, 
but that we did not yet know whether it had been favourably received or not, 
and 1 gave him this paper to read, After he had perused it, he observed that it 
appeared to him to contain everything that Russia could require, and that he 
should write to Count Henckel at St, Petersburgh by this evening's packet to 
support the project, and to add the weight of Prussia in recommending its 
adoption. 

1 told him he would do well to write in this sense, but that we were 
disappointed at the falling off that had occurred in the policy of Prussia, and had 
expected that she would have persevered in viewing the Eastern question in the 
manner she had done at the commencement, “To this M. de le Coq replied, that 
it was useless for the Prussian Government to press matters in a stronger tone 
at St, Petersburgh, that her remonstrances would not be listened to, and would 
not advance the objects we had in view; but that he could assure me that there 
was no change in her sentiments and desire to do everything in her power to 
uphold the dignity and integrity of the Tarkish Empire.

My Lord, Vienna, July 20, 1853. 

I READ to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No. 199; and he 
observed with much satisfaction your Lordship's approval of his conduct in the 
advice he had offered to the Russian Cabinet, and generally of his despatch to 
Baron Lebzeltern of the 6th instant, which had been communicated to you by 
Count Colloredo. 

Count Buol read to me the reports he had received from Count Colloredo 


of his interviews with your Lordship, which are in conformity with your 


despatches Nos, 197 and 198. 

I drew Count Buol’s especial attention to the last paragraph in the despatch 
No. 199, in which your Lordship expresses the hope that, in the unfortunate 
event of the Emperor of Russia’s rejecting the proposals for arrangement that 
might be made to him, the Austrian Government would not remain neutral, but 
would come to the aid of the Sultan in cooperation with England and France. 

Count Buol observed that he had not changed the opinions he had 
expressed to me, and which I fully reported to your Lordship in my despatches 
Nos. 241 and 251, and which met with your Lordship’s approbation, and that 
he still considered himself as entirely united with your policy with respect to the 
Turkish Empire. Ue would employ every means in his power to maintain its 
independence and integrity; he would take no engagement with Russia not to 
oppose her by arms; and he would take none for engaging in hostilities on 
either side; but if he should be called upon to carry out an armed intervention 
on the frontier, it would be in support of the authority and independence of the 
Sultan, 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

My Lord, Vienna, July 20, 1853. 

M. DE BOURQUENEY received last night despatches from the French 
Ambassador at Constantinople, duted the 10th instant, M. de la Cour gives an 
account of the Ministerial crisis which took place on the 7th instant, which was 
brought about by the efforts of Mchemet Ali, to induce the Sultan to adopt a 
more energetic policy towards Russia, and to resent the occupation of the 
Principalities. 

M. dela Cour represents the Sultan as having been greatly irritated by that 
measure, and consequently inclined to adopt the suggestions of a more warlike 
policy. The Sultan sent to the Grand Vizier and to Reshid Pasha, to announce 
to them that he was under the necessity of replacing them by Mehemet Ali and 
Ali Pasha, the late Governor of Smyrna. 

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, under these circumstances, waited upon the 
Sultan, and brought before him the extreme danger to which he would expose 
his empire, and succeeded in persuading him to reconsider his decisions. 

The two Ministers were reinstated, with some engagement that they should 
not again be exposed to similar treatment. M. de lu Cour highly praises the 
conduct of Lord Stratford; and Baron Bruck, in a letter ta Count fuol, does 
the same, 

M. de la Cour does not consider the position of affairs in Constantinople as 
satisfactory; he thinks the warlike feeling of the Turks has been roused, and 
may lead to excesses, ;

No, 141. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received July 29.) 


(No. 366.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 20, 1853. 

I HAVE been very desirous of representing to your Lordship what effect 
has been produced in Russia by the publication of that very inflammatory 
manifesto, from which it might have been inferred by the ignorant that the 
Greek religion was in danger in consequence of the violence and fanaticism or 
the Turkish Government; but | have found myself, as indeed [ still am, unable 
to speak very confidently upon the subject. 

Public opinion in ee has but a languid circulation, and its pulsations 
almost escape the observation of those strangers who, like myself, have no access 
to the classes of society in which it is probably most perceptible. 

If. however, Lam unable to state to your Lordship what is felt here, anc 
to what results warm religious feelings have led, lam able to oppose a contra- 
diction to many of the statements upon the subject which have been put forth 
by the public press, and even by a journal of such importance as the Times.” 
[t has not been my fortune to witness any indication of religious excitement, 
nor have 1 been able to hear of any, although I have been anxious to gain 
information upon the point, and have made extensive inquiries as to the indica- 
tions which may have been remarked by others, The one single instance at 
fanatic excitement of which I have heard, is that of a servant who quitted his 
master that he might enlist to fight against the infidels. 

As for those exhibitions of joy, those illuminations which are stated to have 
been witnessed at St. Petersburgh when the manifesto was published, nothing 
was known of them here till the accounts to which I allude were read in the 
English and French papers. 

As regards the upper classes, what may perhaps be made out is a dread of 
war without a reasonable motive, which will occasion fresh demands for men 
and equipments, while, by putting an end to commerce, it will deprive the landed 
proprietors of a large portion of their incomes. Whut may be discovered among 
the lower and middle classes, is an indifference which leads to the helief that 
they doubt the existence of any danger to their religion. 

Were that danger real and apparent, I have no doubt that religious zeal 
would be unequivocally manifested by the richer of the mercantile class in 
willingness to contribute to the exigencies of the State; among the poor, in an 
eagerness to offer thei personal services. 

As I have alluded to the public press, | may take this opportunity for 
remarking that the ignorance which it has betrayed upon Russian affairs hus 
been very remarkable of late. Even in an article of the “Times,” which is 
rupposed to have been received from a St. Petersburgh correspondent, and 
which professes to give a list of the present Cabinet, I read (independently of 


133 


other inaccuracies) the names of two men, Count Wronschenko and Prince 
Wolkonsky, whose public services terminated a twelvemonth since by their 
death. 

According to a letter from Moscow which has been placed in my hands, the 
only effect produced by the manifesto, although besompaned by a political 
sermon by the chief ecclesiastical authority of the town, has been an increased 
belief in the imminence of war, and a disposition on the part of persons in trade 
to contract their mercantile operations. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

(No, 372,) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 22, 1853. 

BY the arrival of the messenger Drury, I have been put in possession of 
your Lordship’s further despatches down to No, 133 inclusive, 

Although not directed to do so by your Lordship, I have not hesitated to 
read to Count Nesselrode your Lordship’s despatch No. 130 of the 9th instant. 

The grievous difficulties from which the whole of Europe ts at present 
suffering have proceeded mainly from concealment and underhand dealing, and, 
as certainly none of the views entertained upon the great question by Her 
Majesty's Government are such as any one can be ashamed to profess, | was 
desirous that the Chancellor should know from your Lordship’s own language 
what was the opinion entertained in England of the Russian manifesto. 

In the course of the conversation which ensued, Count Nesselrode again 
endeavoured to establish an analogy between the position occupied by Russia in 
the Principalities, and that taken up by France and England at Besiea Bay. | 
entreated him not to press a point which, if insisted upon, would lead to serious 
consequences, as 1 would not conceal from him that Her Majesty's Government 
would never lend themselves to recognize that any such rnatlarity existed, 
Among other arguments or clucidations which I employed, I made use 
of this, 

* Your position,” I said, “ M. le Comte, ts that of a person who has broken 
into the house of our friend; ours ig that of being found fault with for having 
taken up our station at the corner of the street in which that act of violence has 
been committed.” . 

This conversation, which took place on the 20th instant, ended in an 
amicable manner by Count Nesselrode observing in pleasing terms that he 
would not conceal from me that the idea of « misunderstanding so serious as to 
lead to war between Russia and England was one which his sense and feelings 
rejected ; that he had no doubt of the willingness of Her Majesty’s Government 
to withdraw their ships as soon as possible from the Dardanelles, and that 
nothing would be more agreeable to the Mmperor than to receive from the Porte 
such assurances as would enable His Imperial Majesty to recall his troops from 
the Principalities, 

| ought perhaps to have mentioned, that the Chancellor remarked upon 
the too great stress which was commonly laid upon the independence of Turkey, 
while but little attention was bestowed upon her actual existence. The aceounts 
from Turkey of the fanaticism of the Turks, and of the sufferings of the 
Christians, were, he said, dreadful, and might lead to serious consequences. 

[replied that it appeared to me a little extraordinary that Her Majesty's 
Government and that of Austria, both in general tolerably well informed, should 
have heard nothing of these persecutions, hut if in truth the fanaticism of the 
‘Turks had been awakened, it was hardly to be wondered at when they no 
doubt thought both their religion and their existence in danger; that the

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clirendon.—( Received July 29.) 


(No. 374, Secret and Confideatial.) 


My Lord, St. Peteraburgh, July 22, 1853. 

JUDGING from a conversation which I held on the 20th instant with the 
Chancellor, | am inclined to believe that the Russian Government are prepared 
to lend themselves to some arrangement with Turkey similar to that which was 
alluded to in my despatches No, 339 and No, 350, but which they would prefer 
being embodied in a Convention. ) 

In expressing this opinion, however, | am bound to reflect, that while 
professing a willingness to come to terms and even to hasten negotiations, 
the Russian Cabinet (if listening to sinister suggestions) may be desirous of 
gaining time under the appearances of being disposed to negotiate; nor must it 
be forgotten that late transactions have offered a fresh example of the Emperor's 
liability to be acted upon by domestic influences. 

As often as the influence of the Grand Duke Constantine is allowed to 
exert itself, so often, I apprehend, will the Emperor be liable to such aberrations 
from his hubitual policy as have been lately witnessed in the gratuitous quarrel 
sought by Russia of the Porte, 

As 1 once before stated, the Grand Duke Constantine is, probably from 
calculation, a bigot in religion, his prejudices and aspirations are those of his 
race, and his dislike to his elder brother would of itself render him little favour- 
able to the cause of peace and tranquillity.

No. 146. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon, — (Received July 30.) 


(No, 149.) 
My Lord, Therapica, July 16, 1853, 

SOON after the late readjustment of the Turkish Ministry 1 took oecasion 
to visit the principal members of the Cabinet with the view of impressing upon 
their minds the extreme importance of acting with unity and steadiness under 
the present critical circumstances of the Empire. 1 endeavoured to convince 
them of the danger which must necessarily accrue not only to the Empire but to 
themselves also, if they continued to be swayed by private interests and personal 
jealousies at a time when all their energies ought to be applied exclusively to the 
service of their Sovereign. I must do them the justice to say that they took my 
admonitions in good part, though each conceived them to be more applicable to 
his colleagues than to himself. I found at the same time that, with some 
trifling shades of difference, they all took the same view of the Russian demands, 
and, however anxious for the maintenance of peace, were unanimous in their 
resolution to oppose them to the last. I left them with the impression that 
there would soon be more to apprehend from their rashness thun from their 
timidity.

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 147. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 30.) 


(No, 150.) 
My Lord, Therapia, July 16, 1853, 

THE Porte had prepared its protest against the occupation of the Danubian 
Prineipalities before the official intelligence of that aggression had reached 
Constantinople. But the festival of Bairam, the momentary change of Ministers, 
and the unavoidable formalities of this Court, occasioned a delay of several 
days before it was communicated to the foreign Representatives. I have already 
sent a manuscript copy of it to your Lordship, and | have now the honour to 
inclose a printed one. It will be found to contain the principal ideas suggested 
in your Lordship’s instruction to me, No. 51 of this year. Reshid Pasha 
udmitted them with much readiness into his draft, to which an explanatory form 
was given, with the view of making the protest more palatable to Russia. His 
Highness, at my suggestion, accompanied it with a note to the four Kepresen- 
tatives. A copy of this document is inclosed herewith, and on its receipt T lost 
no time in proposing to my three colleagues a meeting, at which we might take 
both the note and the protest inte consideration. 

The proposed interview has since taken place at my house, and Tam happy 
to state that we found no difficulty in determining the course to be pursued by 
us under the circumstances, A memorandum of what passed at our meeting 16 
inclosed herewith. Your Lordship will observe that we concluded by agreem 
to apply for a conference with Reshid Pasha. His Highness has since appointec 
an early hour to-morrow for receiving us. 

In the course of our interview to-day, the Austrian Minister read the draft 
of a letter which he had prepared for Reshid Pasha to address to Count Nessel- 
rode, I submitted to my colleagues the propriety of leaving his Highness free 
to draw up his own letters, and my amendment prevailed, 

| take this opportunity to mention that the Austrian proposal of a “ fusion” 
of Prince Menchikoff’s parting note with that prepared by Reshid Pasha had 

reviously dropped, the Pasha having paused in his composition, apparently 
seenuse | declined having anything to do with it apart from the other Represen- 
tatives, and the Internuncio eee acquiesced in its relinquishment on account 
of the delay and consequent change of circumstances. 

For my own part, I am persuaded that our best chance of making an 
impression at St. Petersburgh lies in the plan traced out in your Lordship's 
instruction No. 81 of this year, though in following it out. in concert with the 
French Ambassador, 1 hope not to lose sight of what advantage may be derived 
from the concurrence of Austria and Prussia, by so far adapting their respective 
ideas to it as to promote our conciliatory views without compromising that 
principle on which the Porte has taken its stand, 

The other Representatives appear to entertain no doubt of a marked 
improvement in the disposition of the Russian Government. Though ! have no 
direct information on the subject myself, Tam unwilling to suppose that their 
impressions and those of their respective Courts are without any solid 
foundation. 

IT have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, Therapia, July 16, 1853. 

THE copy inclosed herewith of a report addressed to me yesterday by M. 
Pisani, may serve to give your Lordship some idea of the difficulties which beset 
my course of proceeding here. 

I particularly solicit your Lordship’s attention to the language held, as it 
would seem, by my French colleague to Reshid Pasha, ; 

I do not at all partake his opinion concerning the inexpediency of hasten. 
ing the publication of the protest, and as to what he says of a Convention 
proposed by Her Majesty's Government, | should have had no idea of his 
meaning were it not for a private letter which I received by the last opportunity 
from Lord Cowley. His Lordship has given me to understand that the objec- 
tions of the French Government applied to the form rather than to the sub- 
stance of a Convention as proposed by your Lordship, and that the idea would 
in all probability drop without further discussion. 

I have taken the hint suggested by this communication, and desisted from 
pressing the offer of an explanation of the Treaty of Kainardji as part of the 
propitiating experiment now in preparation for St. Petersburgh. It appears that 
the French objections ta any conventional form are extended by M. de la Cour 
to that point also. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, Therapia, July 15, 1853, 

HAVING last night waited on Reshid Pasha, he communicated to me very

confidential letter from the latter addressed to Reshid Pasha, 

In the course of the day M. de Wildenbruch called on his Highness, and in 
communicating to him orally the contents of the said despatch, observed that 
although its purport was at variance with his opinion and against his conscience, 
vet he hod a duty to fulfil, that of endeavouring to carry into execution the 
orders of his Government,

Porte could not accept any proposal until she is aware how the protest will 
operate upon the minds of the Four Powers, under whose consideration that 
paper has been respectively submitted.

that given to the Prussian Envoy. Moreover, he communicated to him the 
despatch of the Prince of Moldavia, as well as its inclosures, and made the 
romurk that, after all this, the Porte could not with propriety take upon itself

BEARING in mind your Lordship's instruction respecting the principles 
on which Omer Pasha may be directed to carry on his operations touching the 
Danube, | beg to submit to you the two memorandums inclosed herewith ; the 
one relating to defensive operations on this side of the river, the other indicating 
how far it may be desirable to leave unmolested such vessels of war as the 
Russians may employ on the river itself, above its junction with the Pruth. I 
am indebted for the former of these papers to Major-General Macintosh, who 
was lately here, and | have communicated it to Reshid Pasha, and through his 
Highness to the Council. ' 

With respect to what is recommended in the other memorandum, T learn 
from that Minister that the Council objected to its adoption, probably on some 
ground of form; but the same suggestions are about to be put into a different 
shape, with better prospects of being accepted. 

Your Lordship will learn from the letter inclosed herewith in copy, and 
addressed by Prince Gortchakoff to Reshid Pasha, who sent it to me, that the 
Russians profess the intention of acting with moderation similar to that which | 
have recommended to the Porte.

Inclosure | in No. 152. 


Memorandum relating to Defensive Operations south of the Danube. 


THE line of the Danube is so extended, and the nature of the country in 
its immediate vicinity so favourable for a large manoeuvring army, if opposed to 
to one in the state of training, beyond which the Turks have not advanced, that 
it seems almost hopeless that they should, unless powerfully aided, meet thelr 
opponents successfully in such a locality. It may, therefore, be submitted that 


144 


the best plan of procedure would be, only to garrison the fortresses on the 
Danube, and to strengthen duly the line of the Balkan at as early a period as 
possible, as the best situation im which an army could receive the assuilants. 
With this view, everything should be done to put Shumla and Varna in as com- 
plete a state of preparation to receive their garrisons as possible; and, moreover, 
the passes leading through the mountains in the rear should be artificially 
strengthened with field-works looking towards these fortresses. Heavy cannon, 
such as ship guns, might be placed in these works, which could not be easily 
used against the troops on this side in the event of any portion of the works 
falling into temporary possession of the enemy, 

It would be impossible to prepare such works at a period when active 
operations might be going on in the field; and the expense would be greatly 
diminished by employing the troops which are already in that neizhbourhood in 
their construction, before their dispersion renders this impossible, 

here is a range of low mountains, called the Lesser Balkan, behind the 
great range, and looking towards the sea, the pass through which, near Paki, 
should also be strengthened, with a view to its occupation. A force landing 
behind the pass through the Balkan, in rear of Varna, might otherwise turn the 
main position, and even penetrate from thenee into the country. 

Should the enemy sueceed as before in reaching Adrianople, it is believed 
that the capital might still be defended by occupying a position which extends 
from the erecks of Buyuk-Chekmejeh, and Koutchouk-Chekmejeh towards the 
Black Sea. This position, however, ought also to be artifically strengthened. 
The peninsula on the European side of the Dardanelles ought to be strengthened 
against a land attack by works across the narrowest part of the isthmus north- 
east of Gallipoli, as most of the batteries on that side of the strait could be 
easily carried from the heights behind them, if left as they now are. It would 
also be very desirable that the Gulf of Saros, behind that peninsula, should be 
accurately surveyed, and the soundings near the isthmus correctly laid down, a 
facility for doing which is, 1 presume, afforded by the present vicinity of the 
fleet. [say this in the belief that no such survey at present exists, as in the 
event of our ships having at any period to act there, and possibly to land troops 
it would be found of great utility. | 

Works are to a certain extent in progress in rear of the batteries on the 
Bosphorus, which was a precaution much called for. 

_ The other localities adverted to would require a careful examination of 
skilful officers of engineers, who would afterwards lay down the works and 
superintend their execution, and I fear that the Turkish military establishment 
does not afford a sufficient number for such on undertaking; and it is the impres- 
sion on my mind that the whole staff arrangements in this country are still very 
deficient, ; ‘ 

Therapa, July 6, 1853. 


Inclosure 2 in No, 152, 
Instructions to Omer Pasha. 


( Translation.) 


THE Russian forces having occupied Moldavia and Wallachia in a military 
manner, declaring at the same time that they do not thereby intend war against 
the Sublime Porte, and the Porte itself having taken the resolution of suspending 
its right of war under a reference to those Powers which signed the Treaty of 
1841, you are directed not to enforce the rights of treaty against Russian vessels 
of war which may go up the Danube beyond its confluence with the Pruth 
provided they do not touch at any point on the right bank of the Danube or 
tuke possession of any place there, or land troops on the same side of the river 
or push forward under the fortifications of Roustchouk, Silistria, or Wiadin i 
any of which cases a different view may be taken, unless there should be Pahidn 
to believe that the vessels In question had been forced by a strong wind or other 
incidental cause upon the Bulgarian coast,

Prince Gortchakoff to Reshid Pasha. 


M. le Ministre, Jassy, Phare: 1853. 

JE remplis Jes ordres de mon auguste Souverain en faisant parverur cette 
lettre & votre Excellence pour l’informer de l’entrée des corps darmée placé sous 
mon commandement dans les Principautés de Moldavie et Valachie. 

Mieux que personne votre Excellence connait les raisons qui ont nécessité 
cette mesure. Gouvernement Impérial n'y a recours qu'aprés avoir épnisé 
tous les moyens de persuasion, toutes les vols diplomatiques, toutes les démarehes 
de conciliation qui lui étaient dictées par son sincere désir de rester dans les 
meilleurs rapports d'amitié et de bon voisinage avec la Porte Ottomane. 

Aujourd’hui encore, en faisant entrer son armée dans ces provinces plactes 
en vertu des Traités sous la suzeraineté du Sultan et la protection de l'Empereur, 
Sa Majesté ne déclare pas la guerre i Ja Porte, Elle attendra que la Gouverne- 
ment de Sa Majesté le Sultan, mieux conseillé, mieux éclairé sur les intentions 
et les demandes légitimes de la Russie, y fasse droit sur la base des Traités 
existans. 

Il dépend uniquement du Gouvernement Ottoman d'aceélérer une entente 
sincére et reciproquement satisfaisante. Ce moment sera aussi celui ol les 
troupes que je commande rentreront dans ies limites qu’elles viennent de 
franchir. . 

Les orires que je remplis en occupant militairement les Principautes me 
prescrivent de m'abstenir de tout mouvement hostile et agressif contre les 
troupes et les garrisons Turques stationnées au-dela du Danube. 

C’est au Gouvernement de Sa Majesté le Sultan de juger s'il doit adresser a 
ses commandant militaires les memes ordres, afin d’éviter toute collision regrettable 
quiune démonstration offensive de leur part en deci du Danube amenerait 
nécessairement entre nos forces respectives. 

Je suis, &e.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Karl of Clarendon,—(Received July 30.) 


(No. 158.) 
My Lord, Therapia, July 18, 1853, 

RUMOURS, on which I place but little reliance, continue in some measure 
to prevail here of an intended massacre, in which the Turks would be the 
executioners und the Christians the principal victims. There is no doubt that 
considerable excitement exists among the Mussulman population, and it is more 
likely to increase than to diminish, But the Porte is deeply interested in pre- 
venting any kind of disorders here; and hitherto, with the exception of some 
trifling incidents, the public tranquillity has been admirably preserved. 

On the occasion of a visit which I made to the Captain Pasha a few days 
ago on board his magnificent flag-ship, a three-decker, [ passed close in front of 
the whole crew, amounting to 1100 men, and witnessed the exercise of the guns, 
without remarking a single glance or gesture of ill-will, and much gratified by 
the zeal, activity, and skill displayed throughout. 

I have nevertheless been careful to provide, as fur as | can, against the 
worst, by requesting Admiral Dundas to station a couple of large steam-vessels 
in these waters, and by prevailing on the Sultan to issue on explanatory pros 
clamation calculated to remoye erroneous impressions from the minds of the 
people. ‘The execution of this last measure has been delayed, but it is now on 
the point of being carried into effect, and | hope to good purpose. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLITFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Recetved July 30.) 
(Na. 161) 
My Lord, Therapia, July 19, 1858. 

I FORWARD herewith, for your Lordship’s information, a despatch which 
1 have uddressed to-day to Her Majesty’s Envoy at St. Petersburgh, and I 
request your Lordship’s carly attention to the delicate questions which form the 
subject matter of its contents. 

I have communicated with the French Ambassador, as well on the question 
of urging the evacuation of the Principalities, as on that of eventually with- 
drawing the two squadrons to some distance from Besika Bay. He appears to 
hold the same opinion as myself on both subjects, and will, no doubt, take the 
commands of his Government thereon.

Constantinople, July 19, 1853, 
IN the identical letter addressed by M. de la Cour and myself to you and 
General Castelbajac, mention is made of the very natural expectation entertained 
here that the evacuation of the Principalities by Russia will accompany the 
nomination of a Turkish Ambassador to St. Petersburgh, supposing the prelimi- 
nity agreement respecting religious privileges may be satisfactorily settled. 1 aim 
U

148 


prepared to learn that the Porte makes a formal condition of that measure. 
Indeed it is not easy to conceive how an independent Government, not yet 
reduced to despair by the necessities of war or the hazards of insulation, could 
make up its mind to send out an Embassy to Russia while two of its provinces 
are forcibly occupied by that Power. . 

It is principally owing to my sense of the difficulty arising from this cause, 
that I have concerted to throw out the prospect of a retirement of the squadrons 
from the immediate neighbourhood of the Dardanelles as a facility for the 
evacuation of the Principalities. 

I send a copy of this despatch to Her Majesty’s Government, with a request 
that their view of the matter may be transmitted to you with the least avoidable 
tlelay.

THE proposed conference of the four Representatives with his Highness 
the Ottoman Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs took place on the 17th 
‘nstant, The memorandum, inclosed herewith, which, though unsigned, has 
received, like the preceding one, inclosed with another despateh, the sanction of 
Reshid Pasha and my three colleagues, will inform your Lordship, without going 
into details, of what passed between us on the occasion, We have since 
employed our best exertions in preparing to carry into effect the conciliatory 
proceeding which we then agreed to adopt. 

| have now the honour of forwarding liérewith to your Lordship the 
several despatches which, in addition to the two memorandums, | have drawn 
ip, subject to the assent of my colleages, or upon a general understanding with 
them. Their contents will serve, | trust, to explain whatever is necessary to 
enable Her Majesty's Government to form 4 correct judgment of the course 
which we have agreed to pursue in the hepe of confirming the improved 
dispositions supposed to exist at St. Petersburgh, and of securing them in favour 
of a peaceful arrangement on sate and honourable terms, 

In common with the French Ambassador [ have found it necessary to make 
some concessions in point of form and expression to the delicate position of our 
German colleagues, to whose goodwill, within the limits prescribed by that 
position, | am bound, nevertheless, in justice to beur witness. 1 trust at the 
same time that while endeavouring to remove such obstacles as unnecessarily 
encumber the avenues to peace, we have not neglected to guard the rights of the 
Sultan and the interests of his Empire. 

I feel confident that your Lordship's indulgence will not be wanting 
wherever L have incurred responsibility for the sake of improving a favourable 
opportunity, or preventing an increase of the impending evils. 

| shall naturally be anxious to learn your Lordships opinion without loss 
of time, and I take the liberty of submitting, if the course now taken be 
acceptable to Her Majesty’s Government, that their approval may he conveyed. 
by telegraph to Vienna for further transmission by express to St. Petersburgh.

had come to the determination, with the sanction of His Imperial Majesty the 
Emperor, of calling upon M. de Bourqueney, Baron Canitz, and myself, to 
consult together, with the view of arriving at the adoption of some proposal 
which could be submitted to the Porte with the sanction of all our Govern- 
ments. . 

Count Buol explained that his object in making this proposal was, that if 
the note we might approve of was adopted by the Porte, it should be transmitted 
to St. Petershurzh with the same recommendation as to its acceptance as had 
been addressed to ‘Turkey. 

The other Ministers, as well as myself, having agreed to this proposal, as 
one which we would submit to our respective Governments, Count Buol stated 
that the note whieh had been proposed by M. Drouyu de Lhuys appeared to him 
to be the best foundation upon which we could proceed in the formation of the

approved by your Lordship, it was considered by the other Ministers as nore 
likely to be accepted by the Government of the Sultan, by whom auch strong 
objections had already been stated to any transaction in the form of a 
Convention. | 

The general opinion having, therefore, been pronounced in favour of the 
projected form of a note, I agreed to submit the proposal to your Lordship, and, 
as there would be no means of communicating with Constantinople until Friday 
next, by which time a courier from St. Petersburgh was expected, it was agreed 
that Count Buol should draw up the note and submit it for our consideration, 
by which time it was expected that the answers from our respective Governments 
would be arrived. 

The answer from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, agreeing to this proposal, has 
already been received from M, de Bourqueney, with the injunction only that the 
alterations in the original note, before they are adopted, are to be reported for 
the sanction of the French Government, and Count Buol has consequently pro- 
ceeded in drawing up the note, 

His Imperial Majesty the Emperor spoke to me of the anxiety he felt that 
the project proposed by Count Buol should be adopted ; and he expressed his 
regret that Baron Meyendorft, who had been invited to attend the contercnee, 
had net considered himself authorized to do so, His Majesty stated that he 
felt great anxiety for the settlement of these lamentable complications, and that 
he had used every exertion to prevent them, and would, now that they had 
arisen, continue these exertions to put an end to them,

HER Majesty's Government approve of your proceedings as reported in 
your despatches Nos, 286 and 202. 

Shortly after the rupture between Russia and the Porte, the Austrian 
Government were made aware by my communications to Count Colloredo and to 
your Lordship, that a conference was desired by Her Majesty's Government us 
the fittest mode of bringing the. designs of Russia upon ‘Turkey under the 
deliberation and control of the Great Powers of Europe, and Mer Majesty's 
Government therefore learned with much satisfaction that your Lordship, 
together with your French and Prussian colleagues, hud been invited by Count 
Buol to concert with him upon a plan of settlement that should be acceptable 
ulike to the Emperor of Russia and to the Sultan. 

As the mediation of Austria lag been accepted by Russia, Her Majesty's 
Government regret that the Russian Minister should not have considered 
himself authorized to attend the conference, to which he seems to have also 
heen invited by Count Buol; but Mer Majesty's Government hope that this toes 
not indicate a disinelination on the part of Tussta to accept the reasonable terms 
that will be submitted to her, and with respect to which it is natural to 
Ree that Count Buol has been in communication with the Cabinet. of 
St. Petersburgh. 

Upon this point, however, Her Majesty's Government are desirous: to 
receive precise information, as itis of the utmost importance that all unneces- 
sary delay should be avoided, both with reference to the increasing excitement 
which prevails in Turkey, and to the advanced state of the season, which will not 
permit of the combined fleets remaining much longer in the open Bay of Besika ; 
and T need hardly add that they will not move further from Constantinople so 
long as the Principalities are occupied by Russian troops.

differences between Russia and the Porte, to which reference was first made in 
my despatches Nos, 480 and 484, had been approved by Her Majesty's 
Government, : 
As there is some slight discrepancy between M. Drouyn de Lhuys' state- 
mont and the words which I have used in your Lordship’s name when speaking 
of this project, it may be as well to state that he never heard from me that your 
Lordship approved the note. 1 told him that you admired the cleverness with which 
it was drawn up, but that you were convinced, since Russia had declared that 
she would accept of no other note but that contained in Prince Menchikoff’s 
ultimatum, that the French project would not satisfy the Emperor. 
have. however, on more than one occasion assured the French Minister 
for Foreign Affairs that the project of Convention put forward by Her Majesty's 
Government was not conceived in any spirit of rivalry towards the French’or 
any other project of arrangement, and that if the French project was preferred 
Her oh Government would be quite ready to adopt it. 
_ Your Lordship is already aware that when the French project. was put 
forward, M, Drouyn de Lhuys had no expectation that it would succeed. Tp 
fact he only sent it to St. Petersburgh with the laudable design of proving that 
the French Government, to which such warlike propensities were attributed, had 
seriously occupied themselves in endeavouring to find a solution of the Eastern 
differences,

My Lord, Foreign Office, August 2, 1853, 

ON the 30th ultimo Count Walewski informed me that he had received 
instructions to propose to Her Majesty's Goyerument that in the event of Russia 
not accepting within a very short time, or not showing herself well disposed to 
accept, the measures of conciliation submitted to her, the fleets of France and 
England should without delay receive orders to enter the Dardanelles upon the 
first demand of the Porte. 


;

162 


I told Count Walewski that | adhered to the opinion I had several times 
expressed to him upon this subject, and that I could see no advantage in hypo- 
thetical agreements which would never supersede subsequent discussion and 
deliberation between our respective Governments, nor materially influence their 
decision upon events as they arose. 

Count Walewski assured me that he was far from wishing for any formal 
Cngagement or even understanding, but simply for an exchanee of “opinion 
between the two Governments as to the course that in certain eventualities it 
might he desirable to pursue. 

[ then said that T would read to his Excellency the concluding faragraph of 
a despateh I had written to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, and which had received 
the approval of more than one of my colleagues. ‘The paragraph is as follows: 

“In the event of any further act of aggression by ltussia, or of undue delay 
on her part in accepting the terms for an amicable arrangement that may he 
proposed to her, Her Majesty's Government, in conjunction with that of France, 
will be prepared to take more active measures for the protection of Turkey aainst 
it Power of whose hostile designs there will then exist no reasonable doubt.” 

Count Walewski expressed his satisfaction, and I requested his Excellency 
eluirly to understand that the term of delay to be granted to Russia and the 
Hiture mode of operation were still left quite free and open fir diseussion between 
the French and Mnglish Governments, To this Count Walewski entirely 
assented. :

No, 170. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 2.) 


(No. 385. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, July 26, 1853, 


THE Chancellor spoke to me yesterday, of his own accord, of the Projet 
de Convention between Russia and Turkey, proposed by the English and Irench 
Crovernments. 

He did not conceal from me that the objections which he entertained to 
the plan were slight; but observed, that he could give no positive answer until 
he had received some despatches, which in the course of a day or two must 
reach him from Vienna, 

The objections, such as they were, to be made to the Projet de Convention, 
were three: that the preamble, he thought, might be abridged; that special 
mention inight be made of the late firmans, relating to the holy places; and 
that some phrase might be employed which could connect (rattacher) the 
Sultan's engagements to the Treaty of Kainardji, and to the promises lately 
made by His Highness to the Greek Church. 

I replied, that, without having authority to speak in your Lordship’s name, 
I was convinced that your Lordship looked to the essence of the proposed Con- 
vention, and not to particular phrases; that all that was desired was that the 
affair should be terminated in a manner suited to the interests and consistent 
with the dignity both of the Emperor and the Sultan. 

The conversation proceeded for some time in an amicable strain, and con- 
cluded by Count Nesselrode observing, that I might be convinced that the 
Kussian Government was as desirous as that of Her Majesty could be that a 
peaceable and satisfactory solution of the difficulties should be arrived at. 

It was agreed between Count Nesselrode and myself that I should call 
upon him again on the 29th instant, by which time he considers it certain that 
he shall be in possession of the despatches expected from Baron Meyendortf. 

I hear from several quarters that the language of the Court at Peterhoff is, 
that all danger of a war is past, and that a settlement of the Oriental question is 
close at hand. 

This and other indications induce me to believe that some arrangement 
more acceptable to the Russian Government than that devised at London and 
Paris must have been brought forward, with a certain prospect of success, by 
the Austrian Mission at Constantinople. 

M. Balabine, who was the last of the Russian Mission to quit Pera, has 
returned to St, Petersburgh. 

The language of this gentleman is less conciliatory than that of his superiors 
—1t circumstance to be accounted for, probably, by his having been for a certain 
time under the orders of Prince Menchikoff. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

despatches addressed by you and by M. de la Cour to Sir Hamilton Seymour

Inclosure in No, 182. 
Proclamation. 


(Translation. ) Constantinople, July 13, 1853. 

I'T has been already stated in the Turkish official “ Gazette” that Russia. 
having broken off official relations with the Sublime Porte on certain matters on 
which they could not come to an understanding, withdrew her mission from 
Constantinople ; and that, in consequence of the extensive preparations made by 
that Power by sea and by land, the Sublime Porte had made some military 
urangements and defensive preparations, wholly for precaution and her own 
protection. 

The real cause of the existing dispute with Russia is the desire of that 
Power to obtain a binding and exclusive engagement from the Porte concerning 
the religious privileges of the Greek churches and priesthood, which the Porte 
cannot in justice be expected to give. 

Now these religious privileges, granted in the reign of his deceased Majesty 
Mehemed Khan, of glorious memory, and confirmed during the reigns of his 
illustrious successors, have been maintained ever since. In imitation of this 
noble example of his Royal predecessors, His present Majesty has likewise 
ratified and corroborated them. It never even entered into the imagination of 
any one to violate the ancient privileges granted a proprio motu by the Imperial 
Throne, . 

It hos been repeatedly declared, in a friendly and sincere manner, that the 
Porte did not refuse to give assurances sufficient to remove the doubts on which 
the Russian Government establishes. this dispute, in the same manner as the 
Porte can give assurances to the whole world in a matter so firmly settled; and 
that whereas, if one Government should enter into an engagement, having the 
colour or force of Treaty, with another, concerning the religious privileges of a 
nition consisting of so many millions of its subjects, the independence and 
sovereign rights of the Power thus bound would be impaired, such on engagement 
could not be consented to. 

_ _While no necessity existed for persisting to such an extent in this matter, 
the Government of Russia would not desist from its pretensions, and, indeed, the 
passage of the Russian troops across the Pruth to take temporary possession of 
and hold the Provinces of Wallachia and Moldavia, has been a subject of painful 
surprise to ihe Sublime Porte. ‘This violation of the frontier is an infraction of 
existing Treaties, and has been immediately protested against, according to 
International law, that is, the Sublime Porte has officially and publicly notified 
ta the Great Powers that she cannot accept such a wolation of Treaty. 

Since divers States, connected by the ‘I'reaties which they have contracted, 
constitute the links of mutual security with respect to territorial possessions and 
sovercign independence; since agreement and cooperation are the means now 
generally employed when serious disputes like the present arise; since, more- 
over, Russia has proclaimed that her real object was not to make war upon the 
Porte, but to hold possession of Wallachia and Moldavia as a guarantee until 

Zz 


V2 


such times as her claims are satisfied: and since all the Great Powers, without 
exception, have displayed sentiments more or less favourable towards Turkey, 
while two of them, England and Franee, being Powers on which, from their 
quality of maritime States, the Porte relies with special confidence, have 
given a practical manifestation of their friendship and goodwill, the Porte is 
engaged in communicating according to custom with the above States ; and 
meanwhile, as she cannot possibly accept a proposition so detrimental to her 
independence and sovereign rights, she has adopted the unanimous resolution of 
assuming in her own defence an armed attitude, as well upon the Danube as 
upon her Asiastic frontier. 

~ Such, then, is the real cause of the dispute with Russia, and the present 
aspect of the question. The Sublime Porte has at the same time been duly 
careful to adopt all necessary measures, and to make for her defence every 
requisite disposition of troops and ammunition. 

The duty, therefore, of all the Porte’s subjects, according to their several 
conditions, will be to continue in the tranquil prosecution of their respective 
concerns, agriculture, and commerce, and to hold themselves ready to execute 
any orders which may be issued to them by the Imperial Government. 

As it has been clearly established in previous statements that, however the 
pretensions. of Russia may relate to the religious privileges of the Greeks, 
neither the Greek people nor their Chiefs have any knowledge or participation 
therein: and the Sublime Porte is convinced that they are in every respect 
satisfied and grateful towards their Sovereign, and that they are concerned more 
than any other at such pretensions being put forward, itis on these accounts 
by no means fitting that any resentment should be felt towards them in this 
respect: and as the Greeks are equally faithful subjects of our gracious Master 
with the Armenians, the Catholics, the Protestants, and the Jews, it behoves all 
the Sultan's subjects, without exception, to be on good terms with cach other, 
not acting hostilely, nor using abusive language, nor committing any action 
contrary to the Supreme will, but attending to their own concerns. 

‘The above dispositions and decision, as well as the admonitions as above stated, 
are the result of the deliberation of a general Council, comprising the Sheikh-cl- 
Islam, the learned Chiefs of the law, the Seraskier, and all those in military 
office, and the other Ministers and public servants, and held in the presence of 
the Grand Vizier; and an Imperial firman having also been issued on this subject, 
any one disapproving of this decision, and acting in contravention to these 
decisive admonitions, will be held a disobedient subject, and severely punished. 


: _ 


No. 183. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendan.—(Received August 3.) 


(No. 167.) 
My Lord, Therapie, July 23, 1853. 

AT the last meeting of the Four Representatives, held at my house on the 
40th instant, | submitted for consideration a draft of a note, or part of a note, 
which might, if accepted by the Porte, be proposed to the Russian Cabinet as 
the final arrangement of the question of religious privileges, which a ‘Turkish 
Extraordinary Ambassador would, if received at ot. Petersburgh, be authorized 
to conclude. 

This suggestion was favourably received hy my colleagues, and, when sub- 
sequently communicated to Reshid Pasha, by his Highness also, wlio tnitl it 
before the Council and submitted it to the Sultan. Approved by both, after 
some alteration of no real importance, | bave now the honour to bring it 
officially under your Lordship’s notice. It is inclosed herewith in its amended 
shape; and [hope to obtain the consent of the other Representatives, as well 
as of the Turkish Minister, for sending it jointly to Vienna and St Petersburgh 
by way of supplement to the identic despatch ulivady forwarded, in copy, with 
my previous correspondence to your Lordship, and as offering to Russia, in 4 
full thougl simple forin, the utmost amount of satisfaction which the Porte can 
with safety give on the main point of difference, 

The importanee of not losing time will, I trust, excuse me for transmitting 


173 


it at once to Her Majesty’s Ministers at Vienna and Petersburgh, with an urgent 
recommendation to-use it without delay in carrying out the concerted plan of 
reconciliation now on its way to those capitals. If it be true, as confidentially 
stated in some official correspondence, that the Emperor of Russia is ready to 
declare his respect for the sovereign rights of the Sultan in return for a declara- 
tion securing the privileges of his Church in Turkey, he can hardly object to a 
mode of arrangement wich meets his demand without requiring any counter- 
declaration on his part; especially when it is considered that the offer will, in all 
likelihood, be brought before His Imperial Majesty with the concurrence and 
support of his allies in the Treaty of 1841, and that the Porte consents to make 
it while two of her provinees are oceupied by Russian troops, and to confirm tt 
by means of a special embassy to Petersburgh, notwithstanding the rupture by 
Russia of her diplomatic relations with that Bowen 

A process, so humiliating to any independent empire, may be supported for 
the sake of peace and in consideration of past errors; but it is evidently most 
desirable to shorten it by all available means, and to make it, in case of 2 sture, 
the passage to a more determined and progressive state of things. 1 submit that 
a powerful Government, insulated by the opinion of Europe, cannot be allowed 
to triumph in its wrong, without inflicting a heavy blow on that international 
morality which best controls the spirit of aggression, and insures the continuance 
of peace. The worst form of triumph, I conceive, would in the present instance 
be that whieh, by prolonging indefinitely a state of harassing encroachment on 
the one side, of exhausting efforts on the other, of disturbance and excitement 
on both, would finally leave to the weaker and injured party no resource but 
that of ruinous conflict or degrading submission, With no pretensions to fore- 
sicht, I cannot conceal my apprehension that if the last reasonable prospect of 
bringing Russia to terms by negotiation were allowed to close in despair, the 
responsibility would rest with those who are deterred from the performance of 
duty by the sacrifices it necessarily involves, 

have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE, 


Inclosure in No. 183. 
Project of Note. 


AWARE of the deep interest taken by His Majesty the Emperor of Russia 
and by the vast majority of his people in all that concerns the religion which 
they profess, and fully appreciating the motives of that interest, I had much 
pleasure in making known to your Excellency the firmans which the Sultan, my 
racious Sovereign, promulgated at the end of Shaban in this year; and for the 
removal of all doubts, | now assure you on behalf of the Sublime Porte that it is 
the sincere intention of His Imperial Majesty, reserving the sacred rights. of 
sovereignty towards his own subjects, to secure to the Greek, or Orthodox Church, 
by means of those firmans duly enforced, the enjoyment of the privileges thereby 
confirmed, and also of such other privileges and immunities as may hereafter be 
ranted by His Majesty to any other sect whatever of his Christian subjects. 

The Sublime Porte entertains no doubt that the assurance grounded on the 
above-mentioned firmans, which have inspired confidence everywhere, will give 
satisfaction to Russia also.

The French translation which neem panied the Turkish original is inclosed here- 
with. Your Lordship may observe that it differs slightly in two or three expres- 
sions from the English version which | forwarded with a preceding despatch, and 
which would not be unlikely to prove the more acceptable of the two to Count 
Nesselrode. If the difference were deemed to be of any importance at St. Peters-

expressions when the note should be finally prepared for transmission to the 
Russian Government. ne 

Reshid Pasha then proceeded to make us a formal declaration in the name 
of his Government, and the terms of the declaration having been consigned to 
paper in his presence, | beg to refer your kre for their exact ela to the 
memorandum inclosed herewith. It is certain that the Sultan and his Council 
have taken their line definitively, that they now consider themselves as making 
the last permissible effort for peace, and that their minds are made up for the 
consequences of a failure. Your Lordship will not fail to notice the last pari- 
graph of the Porte’s declaration. It stands in marked contrast with the tneite- 
ment to a religious war paraded in the Emperor of Russia's manifesto. 

The whole declaration was received by my colleagues without the slightest 
show of objection. ‘The decision and firmness which it exhibits, accompanied 
as they are with fresh materials und renewed endeavours for an accommodation, 
appear to me, if | may hazard an opinion, both well-timed and creditable to the 
Porte, I hope they will be so viewed by Her Majesty’s Government. _

apologise for writing to the former in French, I found it convenient for com-

our despatches on this occasion to St. Petersburgh. : 

I repeat my former request, that your Lordship will be kindly pleased to

of Her Majesty’s Government with regore ¥ the proposed course of proceeding.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—({Received August 3.) 


(No, 294.) 
My Lord, Vienna, July 29, 1853. 

_ COUNT BUOL called a conference this day of the French and Prussian 
Ministers and myself, and brought under our consideration the communications 
he had received from Baron Bruck, and those also that the Turkish Ambassador 
had been instructed to make to him, and which had been transmitted from Con- 
stantinople on the 20th instant. Count Buol stated that, having taken the 
Emperor's orders upon these various communications, he could not agree to the 
proposals made to him, He must decline to transmit the note of Reshid Pasha 
to Count Nesselrode to St, Petersburgh, or to recommend it, or the documents 
with which it was accompanied ; nor could he advise the Ambassador to forward 
it, or to prepare to forward it, in the manner which had been recommended by 
the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople. He felt that these 
communications were not of a nature to encourage any hope that they would be 
well received by the Russian Cabinet, and therefore he entirely objected to them. 
He then stated that the Emperor had determined to adhere to the recommenda- 
tion to the Porte of the project of note which Count Buol had drawn up, and 
which had been assented to by the Three Powers, and which he would transmit 
by special Envoy, who would probably be the bearer of an autograph letter from 
himself to the Sultan, calling upon him to adopt it as the only means he thought 
likely of coming to a satisfactory arrangement. ; 

Count Buol suid that if the Porte agreed to this recommendation, the 
Emperor would make every exertion to obtain the consent of the Emperor of 
nets to receive the note, which should be transmitted by an Ambassador from 

1¢ Porte. 

Count Buol did not contemplate sending this communication till the day 
after to-morrow, so that the members of the Conference would have time to 
receive the decision of their Governments with regard to his present proposal ; 
and he strongly recommended that we should lose no time in applying for their 
directions, and for the orders which they would desire to have transmitted to 
their respective Ministers at Constantinople. 

This declaration on the part of Count Buol rendered any discussion of the 
arrangement proposed by the Porte und by the Representatives at Constantinople 
impossible; each of us, however, communicated the objects proposed by our 
respective Ministers, and I particularly brought before the Conference the 
assurance I had received in a private letter from Lord Stratford that a further 
eoncilintory proposal to be inserted in the note to be presented by the Ambas- 
sador, upon his arrival at St, Petersburgh, was likely to be adapted by the Porte, 
and would be transmitted in two days from the date of the last despatches. 

Count Buol declared that, after having received the Emperor's orders, he 
could not alter the measure which he had been ordered to carry out; he did not 
conceive that uny addition made to the mode of addressing the Emperor, by 
sending a protest against his proceedings, could render the communication more 
likely to be accepted by him; he also conceived that this proposal, which was at 

resent only to inquire whether an Ambassador would be received at St. Peters- 
Murgh to enter into negotiation as to an arrangement, was of a nuture to occasion 
so much delay at a moment when an early settlement was of the greatest conse- 
quence, that, upon that ground alone, he could be no party to it. He believed 
also that the proposal of the eventual retirement of the fects from the neighbour. 


hood of the Dardanelles, in return for the immediate evacuation of the Princi- 
pulities, was not likely (in face of the declarations lately made) to be accepted by

probable that his (the messenger’s) services might be required for the purpose of 
cornmunteation with Constantinople, 

Upon leaving Count Nesselrode 1 drove to the French mission, and related 
the whole of what had passed between the Chancellor and myself to General 
Castelbajac. 

As usual, this proof of confidence was warmly responded to by my French 
colleague, who immediately said that in the event of a reference to Constan- 
tinople becoming necessary, he should be prepared to write to M. de la Cour 
requesting him to give his best support to the overtures which would be made 
by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Porte. 

The French Minister went further, and stated that in the event of this 
reference becoming necessary through the failure of Baron Bruck’s plan, he 
should be quite ready to join me in the responsibility of adopting the alterations 
in the Projet de Convention alladed to by Count Nesselrode, so as to avoid the 
loss of time which would be incurred by a reference ta London and Paris. 

Like myself, General Castelbajac however doubts whether, when the 
moment shall arrive, the Russian Cabinet will agree positively to accepting the 
Projet de Convention, without consulting the Austrian Ministry. 

IT have to reproach myself with having through forgetfulness omitted to 
question the Chancellor as to the correctness of the report, according to which 
the payment of the tribute owing by the Hospodars of the Principalities las 
heen prevented by the military authorities of Rasta. I am, however, assured 
positively that such is the fact, and that the justification of an act which appears 
to be in contradiction with promises, is attempted on the part of those in 
authority by the excuse that it would be childish to place in the Sultan’s hands 
the means of carrying on war with Russia. 

I beg to conclude my despatch with two observations relating to persons, 

It is highly agreeable to mete perceive that the conduct of Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople is becoming so well known and so much appre- 
elated by all unprejudiced persons, as to offer the best refutation of the calumnies 
with which he had been so improperly assailed, and 1 find constant satisfaction 
in the relations which exist between my French colleague and myself. 

Itis highly desirable, at a crisis like the present, that the greatest confidence 
should prevail between the French and English Missions: in Russia, and unques- 
tionably General Castelbajac does all in his power to promote this common 
object. 

Ihave, &e.
