The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 5.) 
My Lord, 


Vienna, July 31, 1853. 
SINCE 1 had the honour of addressing to your Lordship my despatch 
No, 204 of the 27th instant, I received, on Friday the 20th, your Lordship’ 
telegraphic message of Thursday, stating “that you agreed to the modifications 
proposed, and that 1 was to announce to Lord Stratford de Redelitle that Mer 
Majesty's Government desires that the project should be adopted by the Porte 
unless some other arrangement had already been made.” And on this day | 
have received your Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of yesterday's date, which 
Instructs me to suspend * the transmission of the despatches from Constantinople 


addressed to St. Petersburgh, until further orders ;"’ and adds, “In the moditi- 


184 


cations of the French note suggested by Count Buol, we propose, after the word 
‘Sultan,’ to add, ‘restera fiddle, &c. ;" and after * culte Chrétien,’ to add, ‘et que 
Sa Majesté regarde, Xe.’ ‘These changes are desirable for the purpose of 
ensuring the acceptation by the Porte; nevertheless we do not mmitke of it an 
absolute ‘sine gud non,’ Inform Count Buol and your colleagues. 

I transmitted both these telegraphic messages to Count Buol, and this 
morning he called a conference, at which he explained his great satisfaction at 
the approbation your Lordship had given ta the modifications proposed by him 
in the French note, and at the decision you had come to, to suspend the trans- 
mission to St. Petersburgh of the propositions which had come from Constan- 
tinople. Count Buol then stated that he at. once adopted the changes your 
Lordship proposed in the note he had drawn up, and this was approved by the 
ather members of the Conference, 

Count Buol then adverted to the despatches he had received from Constan- 
tinople, of the 23rd instant, and stated that the Turkish Ambassador had 
communicated to him those which he had received, and which, he supposed, were 
of the same purport as those transmitted to Faron Bourqueney, M. de Canitz, 
and myself, ‘This having been found to be the case, Count Buol stated that he 
considered these communications as in no way altering the character of the 
proposals from Constantinople which had been discussed at the last conference ; 
there was no change in them, with the exception of the official form given to the 
note hereafter to be presented to the Russian Government by an Ambassador from 
the Porte if his mission was accepted, and which had already been Neate made 
known and considered at that conference; and with respect to the declaration 
made by Reshid Pasha to the Representatives aul Constantinople, he did not 
consider it as applicable to his own proposals, which protected the honour und 
the best interests of the Porte as effectually as the measure Reshid Pasha had 
adopted. Count Buol therefore looked upon the propositions as unaltered, and 
he adhered to the deciéion he had taken with regard to them. 

He then read to us the modifieations which had been made in the draft of 
his note, aud consented to by the three Governments to which they had been 
submitted; and also the despatch by which he instructs Baron Bruck to bring 
that note before the ‘Turkish Government as the one proposed to be addressed 
to Count Nesselrode and signed by Reshid Pasha. He submitted this despatch 
for the approval of the members of the Conference, which we all unanimously 
eave. Qount Buol then stated that these documents would be forwarded to 
Constantinople to-morrow evening by a Colonel, who would also be the bearer 
of an autograph letter to the Sultan from the Emperor, im which His Majesty 
would, in the strongest manner, recommend to the Sultan the adoption of the 
proposals now submitted to him, as bemg the best calculated to terminate the 
differences unhappily existing between his Government and that of Russia, with 
the maintenance of his honour, his dignity, and independence. Count Buol 
called upon cach of the members of the Conference to engage our respective 
colleagues in Constantinople, in conformity with the instrtictions we had received 
from our Governments, to give their support to his proposition, assuring us that 
to their powerlul influence and exertions he looked with the firm expectation 
that they would sueceed in convincing the Turkish Government that it was. 
made in the most friendly spirit, and with the conviction that it offered the best 
—perhups the only—chanee of terminating with honour, and with the least delay, 
the unfortunate complications Which menaced the prosperity of their own Empire 
and the peace of Europe. 

L have, &e. 


(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

No. 194. 


Lord Bloonifield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved August 5.) 


(No. 307. Confidential.) | 

My Lord, Rerlin, August 3, 1854, 
ALI EFFENDI, the Turkish Chargé d'Affaires, called on me this tnorning 

and communicated to me the copy of a memorandum signed by Reshid Pasha 

dated Balta Liman, the 23rd ultimo, which had been delivered by His Highness 


185 


to the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople, together with the 
draft of a note which the Turkish Government propose to address to the 
Russian Government asa means of settling the differences between them. 

In reply to Ali Effendi’s inquiries as to. my opinion of these documents, 
and also of the note which Reshid Pasha had addressed to Count Nesselrode on 
the 20th ultimo, when transmitting to the Russian Chancellor a copy of the 
Porte's protest against the occupation of the Danubian Principalities; I said 
that they appeared to be drawn up in moderate language, but that I could say 
nothing as to the prospect of the note being accepted ut St, Petersburgh, and 
that as Twas uninformed of the opinions of my Government respecting this 
project, my private opinions could he of no value. 

Ali Efendi then spoke of the cruel position in which Turkey was placed, 
saying, that England and France had approved of her resistance to the demands 
of Russia, and that now when Russia had taken possession of portions of her 
territory, they had prevented her from adopting active measures against her. 
I replied that whilst the object of England and France had been to support 
Turkey, these Powers had also deeply at heart the prevention of open hostilities, 
which explained the position of our fleets at Besikn Bay, ready to sail ata 
moment's netice, but that we still hoped the differences woulil be settled by 
negotiation, 

Ali Effendi became then « good deal animated, and threw out hints that if 
the British and French Governments had not appeared in earnest at the com- 
mencement of the erisis, the Porte would not have offered such determined 
resistance to the demands of Russia, und that now in the moment of danger, 
when they had made every reasonable concession short of sacrificing their 
independence, England and France were hanging back, . 

T endeavoured to demonstrate that this was not the case; that it was not 
only our duty as friends, but our interest as allies, to support Turkey, and that 
she might count on us, and on our desire to assist in the maintenance of her 
independence, 

The conversation dropped at this paint for a few moments, and Ali Effendi 
resumed it, saying, “ If you do not give us some other support than that which 
we have received froin you up to this time, and see us sate through our present 
difficulties, you will lose your intluence at the Porte; for it is clear that we 
must henceforth submit to everything Russia chooses to dictate: Russian 
influence will predominate, and we shall find it better to rest on her friendship, 
hollow as it may be, than to rely on that of two distant Powers who showed a 
willingness to come forward in our support, but who, after encouraging us to 
resist, retreated before the complications which a war with Russia might pro- 
duce, Such," said Ali Effendi, “is the present feeling at Constantinople, and | 
conjure you to let it be known to your Government betorett is too late.” 

[ replied that his alarms were exaggerated ; that they were no doubt dictated 
by the dangers which threatened his country, but that he would always find 
England to be the true friend of Turkey. 

Having addressed a few questions to him as to whether he had seen much 
of the Logothete Aristarchi who is now here, and whom he had brought to m 
house some days ago, he replied that he had held several conversations with 
him. Well, then, [snid, this explains mach of your present impressions, The 
Logothiete has, no doubt, been poisoning your mind with all sorts of histories, 
which he has been told by Baron Budberg, the Russian Minister; and [ strongly 
recommend you to be on your guard as to every word which the Logothete 
utters: that his reputation at Constantinople, I believed, was not of the best, 
and that, though he had come here ostensibly for the purpose of placing his 
sons at some establishment of education, he was perpetually at the Russian 
Legation, and had algo been much, us 1 understand, with Baron Meyendorft 
during the fortnight he passed at Vienna, and that he was, most probably, 
geeupied at the present moment in intriguing in favour of Russia, 

Ali Effendi replied, that the Logothete hud certainly told him that Baron 
Budberg had shown him some dooumerits, the tendency of which was to raise 
the character of Russia in this question, to prove her power, and the inutility of 
the Porte's counting upon any material assistance from the Western Powers. 
He appears to have attempted to show that we were deterred from more active 
Interierence than anchoring our tleets at Bosika Bay by the hostile attitude of 
Russia, and to have endeavoured to prove that all resistunce was useless, und 


186 
could only hasten the downfall of Turkey ; and that if she wished to exist, she 
niust look to Russia as her best friend. , 

[ repeated to Ali Effendi, before he left me, that he must be on his guard 
as to the Logothete Aristarchi, and not place too much reliance on anything he 
told him, for it was evident that he was acting in opposition to the interests of 
Turkey. ; 

I think it right to make this report of my interview with the Turkish 
Chargé d’ Affaires, as a proof of the ability with which the agents of Russia turn 
to aceount every opportunity of advancing their interests, and the facility with 


which they find ready engines for their work. 
I have, &e. 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lord, Vienna, August 3, 1853, 

1 HAVE the honour of forwarding, together with their inclosures, two 
despatches, from Mr. Consul-General Fonblanque, Nos. 35 and 3%, addressed to 
your Lordship, and transmitted under flying seal to me. 

I brought the subject of these despatches under the consideration of Count 
Buol, who expressed his extreme surprise that the circumstances which had 
taken place at Belgrade, and the communications which had been directed to be 
made to the Prince of Servia and to the Pasha of Belgrade, should have been so 
misunderstood, and that the Prince should have partaken of this error to such 
an extent, as to have protested against 4 supposed violation of his rights. 

Count Buol repeated to me the order which had been transmitted to the 
Austrian Consul-General, which was to explain to the Prince and to the Pasha, 
that the Emperor had determined upon sending a brigade of infantry to the 
neighbourhood of Peterwardein and towards the frontier of Servia, in ne con- 
nexion whatever with the movement of Russian troops in the Principalities, but 
for the sole purpose of giving security to that part of his empire, which might 
in ease of war, if it should unfortunately take place, be menaced by any outbreak 
or disturbances; and he was also to stale that, ifin the provinces under their 
authority any insurrection should take place, they might count upon the assist- 
ance of this force to aid in its suppression. 

Count Buol stated that in the first instance the Prince returned his thanks 
for this communication, but that afterwards he was induced to take exception to 
it, and he had protested in the manner described by Mr, Fonblanque. 

Count Buol said that he had now replied to that document, complaining of 
the spirit of distrust in which it had been drawn Ups and explaining the motives 
in which the original communication had been mace.

separate proposition for the settlement of the matters in dispute between Russia 
and the Porte had been submitted to the Turkish Government by the Prussian 
Minister at Constantinople; without any previous communication of this intention 
being made either to Her Majesty's Government or Her Majesty's Ambassador 
at Constantinople ; and for his Excellency’s more complete information, I read to 
hin your Lordship’s despatch No. 173 of the 2nd imstanb. 
Baron Manteuffel replied that he had already received a despatch on this 


deseribed : and on my telling him that it appeared to me Baron Wildenbruch’s, 
conduct should be censured, he said that he could not say more until he received 
his own report of his communication with Reshid Pasha, and that he would then 
speak to me further. 
I rejoined that the facts must be as your Lordship had stated them, because 
they rested on written documents which had been dellverey is the Porte.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl af Clarendon. —( Received August 8.) 


(No. 311, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, August 5, 1853. 


HAVING received a private letter some days ago from Her Majesty's 
Minister at Dresden, informing me that Baron de Beust had stated to him that 
the Prussian Government had given assurances at St. Petersburgh that, in the 
event of a Turkish war, they would side with Russia, | deemed it right to 
mention the circumstance to Baron Manteutiel, who expressed the greatest 
astonishment at such false intelligence being promulgated by the Saxon Minister 
for Foreign Affairs. I then observed to his Excellency, that as it was probable 
that Baron de Beust had used the like language to other members of the Diplo- 
matic Body at Dresden, it would be well if he were to direct the Prussian 
Representative’s attention to the subject ; and | have the honour to inform your 
Lordship that his Excellency has adopted my suggestion, and instructed Baron 
Lehndorff to inquire of Baron de Beust the source of the false intelligence which 
he had received, and to give it the most unqualified contradiction. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 9.) 


(No. 579.) 
My Lord, Paris, August 8, 1853. 

THE Constantinople post of the asth ultimo has reached Paris this 
morning, but Lord Stratford's messenger isnot yet arrived. M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
‘forms me that he has received three despatches from M. de la Cour, one 
relating to the position of the Turkish army in the Balkan, which in the opinion 
of the French officers in the Turkish service is too extended ; the second stating 
that, although the decision had been taken by the Sultan to recall the Huospodars 
from the Principalities, the order was not gone to them, but that instructions 
had been sent to fire on any Russian vessels which might aseend the Danube 
higher than its confluence with the Pruth; and the third giving some details of 
the position of affairs at Constantinople. In this fast despatch M. de la Cour 
reasserts the great difficulty which the Representatives of the Four Powers had 
experienced in inducing the Porte to nceept the note to Count Nesselrode, which 
was eventually stopped at Vienna, and he says that the war party is in the 
ascendant, and that the language of Reshid Pasha himself is less pacific, 

That Minister does not hesitate to declare that it is preferable for the Turks 
to perish in the struggle than to endure the uncertainty and expenses of their 
present position. 

M. de la Cour appears to apprehend that Reshid Pasha may not be able to 
retain his place.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receited August 9.) 


(No. 581.) 
My Lord, Paris, August 8, 1853: 

M. DE BOURQUENEY mentions in a despatch to M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
dated the 3rd instant, that he had informed Count Buol that the French Consuls 
at Jassy and Bucharest were furnished with instructions to strike their tings 
should the Government of the Hospodars be suspended, and he inquired what 
line it was intended to pursue in regard to the Austrian Consuls. | 

Count Buol replied that the position of the Austrian Consuls in the 
Principalities was essentially different from that of the English and French 
Consuls, the latter having 4 diplomatic character which the former had not. 
The Austrian Consuls had only to superintend the commercial affairs of 
Austrian subjects, and their presence m the Principalities was a necessity. 

Count Buol added that he did not believe that the Hospodars would obey 
the orders of the Porte to quit their seat of Government; but he did not the less 
blame the proceedings of Russia in regard to them and their relations with the 
Sultan, which he characterised as being at variance with the promises made by 
Russia on entering the Principalities.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 9.) 


(No. 171.) 
My Lord, Therapia, July 25, 1853. 

A GENERAL Council was held yesterday at the Porte, including, together 
with the Ministers and members of the ordinary Council, aay distinguished 
and experienced persons no longer in office, ‘The course adopted by the Porte, 
as already communicated to your Lordship in my despatches of the 20th and 
a%rd instant, and the Sultan’s proclamation, of which a draft has already been 
forwarded to England with my previous correspondence, were unanimously 
approved. Tt was decided at the same time that the proclamation should receive 
an amendment suggested by me, to the effect that the Mussulman subjects of 
the Porte should be distinetly enjoined ‘1 common with the rest to live in 
harmony with their countrymen of other ereeds, 

The ‘Turkish Ministers propose to enter seriously to-morrow on the con- 
sideration of such measures as may be advisable for them to adopt in order to 
maintain good order and to afford effectual protection to the Ravahs during the 
unavoidable withdrawal of the regular troops. 

{ have submitted to Reshid Pasha a few suggestions, which may possibly 
assist in giving a ens result to their deliberations. I was glad to find that 
his Highness, of his own accord, had directed my previous communications on 
this important subject to be collected, with a view to bringing them more 
pointedly under the notice of his colleagues. It is, no doubt, to be regretted 
that they have remained so long without more than a partial attempt at redress, 
but the pressure of still more urgent business and the uncertainty of the Porte's 
position might fairly excuse even a more protracted delay. I trust that the nest 
suceceding step will be towards the introduction of those improvements in justice 
and administration which | have so often recommended to the Sultan and his 
Ministers, and which are daily becoming more essential to the safety and future 
welfare of this Empire. 

1 have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

No, 216. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Receiwed August 11.) 


(No, 401.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, Angust 4, 1853. 


A CONVERSATION which I have held with a person who is well 
acquainted with the proceedings of the Prussian Mission tends completely to 
confirm Lord Bloomfield's opinions, both as to the object of the Prussian Cabinet 
being to preserve its independence of action in the Turkish Question, and as to 
the desire felt at present at Berlin to prevent the return of General Rochow 
until he ean do so without incurring that risk of Russian disapprobation which 
would attend any attempt on his part to throw blame upon the conduct of this 
Government. 

I would suggest that another feeling may possibly exist on the part of His 
Prussian Majesty's advisers, and that they may not be sorry to recommend 
themselves to the Russian Court, at the expense of their rivals, by the contrast 
which their inactivity in a good cause presents to the zeal which has been shown 
lately by the Austrian Cabinet. 

"Wien the Prussian Government alleges that their favourable representations 
at St. Petersburgh would be more likely to produce evil than good consequences, 
they assert that which cannot be admitted. : 

‘The late policy of Russia has been of a nature to displease the whole of 
Europe, and the best chance of procuring its amendment would have been that 
it should have been met by a general ery of disapprobation. 

Those, however, who are in the wrong require but little encouragement to 
persevere in error, and a backwardness on the part of any of the Great Powers 
to withhold their expression of regret and blame for what has passed would, | 
am convinced, be considered as indicating their approbation. 

1 have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No,:217. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received August 11.) 


(No. 403. Confidential.) 
My Lard, St. Petersburgh, Auguat 5, 1853. 

VARIOUS indications are observable here, which if properly considered 
might suggest to the Government that the course upon which they have lately 
entered is attended with danger, against which their million of bayonets would 
not protect them. 

When the Emperor visited Cronstadt a month ago, he was painfully struck 
by the absence of foreign shipping; the same observation 1s to be made now, 
and the consequence is that freights have advanced in a remarkable manner— 
coals, for instance, which are usually brought from England at a charge of Os. 
ner ton, are now imported at a cost of 11. 2e., the result’ being that very serious 
inconvenience is felt by the manufacturers, and that some of these, if the evil is 
to continue, will be obliged to suspend operations. 

If such be the effects of a panic, which has never assumed very serious 

roportions, it may not be difficult to caleulate what would be the consequences, 
Tio not say of an attack, bat of a simple blockade of the Gulf, Commerce 
would be annihilated, credit destroyed. and the Government cut off from its 
principal resource; even now L apprehend that the want of funds is severely 
felt, for at Cronstadt there appears to be an inability to go on with the works 
which had been commenced for widening the docks, urgent as was the necessity 
for these works, and earnest as is the attention now bestowed upon naval affairs. 

Among the consequences of a war, there is one which should seem to have 
escaped the notice of the Government; they have a number of steamers, and-as 
long as peace is preserved with England and France they possess the ineans of 
sending them to sea, The facility, however, ends with peace, for besides that 


197 


these vessels would be captured if they ventured out, their means of navigation 
are entirely dependent upon foreign supply. 

These are among the considerations which lead me to imagine that Russia 
has yet to learn to what she might expose herself by a collision with Western 
Europe, and which induce me to believe that, long-and heavy as may be her 
sword, her cuirass. would upon trial be found defective. ; 

At the same time, that the growth of Russia in power of all sorts has been 
unparalleled by any country unless it be by the United States cannot he 
questioned; und that, unless checked, it will at no distant period weigh most 
onerously upon the whole of urope, appears to me no less certain. 

We have had hitherto the security of a Sovereign whose respect for Treaties 
antl whose moderation prevented the misuse of vast resources and unlimited 
authority: recent events, however, show that the security has fallen in value, 
and that Western Europe must henceforward rely more upon the power of 
resisting Northern encroachment than upon the disposition of the North to 
refrain from encroaching. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 218. 
Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receiwed August 11.) 
(No, 404.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 5, 1853. 


IT is my agreeable duty to acquaint your Lordship, that upon waiting upon 
the Chancellor this morning he stated that he had the satisfaction of informing 
me, that the Emperor had signified his acceptance (acceptation pure et simple) 
of the Projet de Note which had been received from Visa and a copy of 
which was dispatched on the 24th ultimo from Vienna to Constantinople. 

The satisfaction at this result, at this probable termination of an arduous 
affair, which the Chancellor expressed, was very visible in his countenance. 

Intelligence of the Emperor's decision will be sent off to-morrow to Baron 
Bronnow, and has been already conveyed by telegraph to Vienna, 

Count Nesselrode said a few words regarding the fresh proof offered by the 
Emperor of his love of peace; and for himself would only observe, thut it must 
be in my recollection that he had taken a more cheerful view of affairs from the 
time that intelligence had been received of the occupation of the Principalities, 

On my side | was cager not to establish the claim of having taken a right 
view of the ‘Turkish question by recalling past transactions, and [ refrained 
accordingly from reminding his Excellency that the form of declaration now 
ussented to by the Emperor was very much what I had suggested to His 
Imperial Majesty in a conversation which immediately followed the news. of 
Prince Menchikoll’s being withdrawn from Constantinople, 

Before leaving the Chancellor, being desirous of acting upon the orders 
conveyed in your Lovdship's despatch No. 149, I remarked that I must beg to 
call his attention once more to the occupation of the Principalities, and: to 
express on behalf of Her Majesty’s Government the hope that the occupation 
would cease us soon as the note should be signed. . 

Count Nesselrode thought it would be premature to give a direct answer to 
my question; and would inquire if it were suspected that the Russian army 
intended to remain in the Principalities permanently ? 

My question, I replied, did not imply that suspicion; but 1 felt obliged to 
make an inquiry which was justified by intelligence which had reached Her 
Majesty's Government, of roads and bridges which were in a course of con. 
struction, and of contracts for several montha which had been made. 

The Chancellor rejoined that he evidently could not speak positively until 
he should know whether the Turkish Government were prepared to sign the 
note which had been sent them; thatin the meantime he could only state, that 
the Emperor was desirous that the occupation of the Principalities should not be 
prolonged by one day beyond the term which was absolutely necessary. 

I had been anxious that my. French colleague, who called upon the 


a 


198 


Chancellor a little before me, should have made inquiries of the same nature ; but 
this he declined doing, and he was indeed r that I should forego my avowed 
intention. General Castelbajac was disposed to consider the immediate evacua- 
tion of the Principalities after the signature of the, note as a matter of course, 
and thought that to raise any doubt upon the point, besides being unnecessary, 
might be considered to imply a distrust in the good faith of the Russian 
Government, | 
[ have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clorendon.—(Recetved August 12.) 


(No. 587. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paria, August 11, 1853. 


DURING an interview which I had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys this after. 
noon, his Excellency expressed an intention of writing to-morrow to M, Castel- 
bajac, stating the satisfaction of the French Government on learning the 
conciliatory disposition manifested by the Emperor of Russia in regard to Turkey, 
and declaring that the French Government, relying on the Emperor's good 
faith, regarded the differences which existed between Russia and Turkey as 


settled. But inasmuch as the French Government trusted to the Emperor of 


Russia's pal to order the immediate evacuation of the Principalities, so His 
Imperial Majesty should trust to the loyalty of France for the departure of the 
French fleet from Besika Bay. 


19%) 


I observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys that I considered the latter part of the 
despatch to be imprudent, and that I thought it would be better to omit it. 
After some discussion, in which the French Minister stated that he had only 
intended the phrase to which I objected as a guidance for General Castelbajac in 
case the departure of the fleets was urged upon him, he said that he would alter 
the last paragraph thus: that the General was to ask no question respecting the 
evacuation of the Principalities, but that the French Government, being desirous 
of obliterating the last traces of these unfortunate differences, would be glad to 
hear without loss of time whenever orders were sent for that evacuation. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys added that he should send this despatch by post, and 
that the Russian Government might draw its own conclusions from the desire 
which would thus be expressed in in it. 

. I have, &c. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

No. 224. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetwed August 15.) 


(No. 406.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 9, 1853. 

SOME of my diplomatic colleagues have observed, as 1 have done, that: the 
language of official persons in speaking of Eastern affairs is constantly that too 
little attention has been bestowed upon the Russian mission at Constantinople ; 
that Russian influence had been allowed to fall off, and that it had become 
therefore necessary that this influence should be revived by some extraordinary 
exertion. 

Of all the excuses which can be offered for the late transactions of the 
Russian Cabinet in Turkish affairs, this appears to be the most illogical, as it is 
in other words a declaration of the Sultan being called upon to pay the price of 
a fault which is not bis,and is the fault of the party by whom reparation is 
sought, 

L should probably not have noticed this attempt at excusing a mischievous 
licy by an unreasonable argument, but for the circumstances of iny having 
veard it insisted upon by a person whom | do not feel at liberty to name, but 
who is likely to hold no other language than that which is in use at court. 


202 


| observe among my colleagues and other persons the best qualified to 
form 4” correct opinion, a mistrust as to the immediate termination of the late 
quarrel in consequence of the Emperor’s acceptance of the Projet de Note 
drawn up at Vienna, 

Some of these persons imagine that the Sultan’s accession to the proposed 
ternis may be difficult to obtain. Others anticipate revolutionary movements, 
caused either by the turbulence of the Christian population or the fanaticism of 
the Turks; while the Minister of Greece, whose opinion (when not prejudiced) 
is one of the most valuable, is possessed with the apprehension of the Sultan's 
throne, and even life, being in danger from the machinations of his brother. 

M. Zographo likewise speaks of the disorderly proceedings which invariably 
and unavoidably attend both the gathering and the disbanding of Turkish 
armaments, and apprehends that from one or other of these causes disturbances 
may result, the extent of which it is difficult to calculate. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR. 


No. 225. 
Sir G. A. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 15.) 


(No. 408.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 9, 18535. 

THE French Minister who attended the exercises at the Camp of Krasno- 
Selée on the 6th instant, was very graciously received by the Emperor, who 
spoke to him of the satisfaction which he felt at having been able te. promote the 
cause of peace by giving his consent to the plan of arrangement which had been 
proposed at Vienna. 

His Majesty, however, added, that although he had consented to the plan, 
he felt by no means certain that the same course would be taken by the 
Porte, 

According to the account which General Castelbajac gave me, His Imperial 
Majesty appears to be possessed with the idea of the Sultan's authority being 
greatly shaken, of Turkish affairs being in a state of great disorder, and of some 
crisis being at hand by which the Ottoman Empire may be placed in the greatest 
danger. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

déclaration, pensait conserver votre Altesse et son Altesse le Prince de Valachie 
dans vos postes respectils, . 

Cependant, nous apprenons par la lettre qui vient d’arriver de la part de 
votre Altesse que la Cour de Russie a ordonné que vous, ainsi que le Prince de 
Valachie, eussiez A rompre vos relations avee Constantinople, et  suspendre le 
tribut établi, qui doit étre payé & la Sublime Porte ; ce qui lui a causé heaucoup 
de surprise. 

Comme la Cour de Russie a entamé le systéme de ces provinces par 
l'endroit qui regarde immédiatement la puissance proprictaire, c'est-i-dire, par 
ses bases fondamentales, la Sublime Porte voit clarement que dans cet état de 
choses l'exercice de 'autorité légitime dans les Principautés de Walachic et de

Par conséquence, la Sublime Porte, ainsi que ses droits sacrés et incon-

été aussi communiquée officiellement aux Grandes Puissances. 

IL faut done que vous, conformement aux ordres émancés du Tréne Impérial 
4 cet égard, yous quittiez de suite la province, et s‘il arrive que vous agissiez

Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to the Hospodar of Wallachia. You will

racket to him with your own hands, requesting that he will appoint an early 
aie for your return in order to know whether he has any communication to 
make to you. ; , 

If he should invite you to stay, you will of course do so; but neither in 
the one case nor in the other are you at liberty to declare your knowledge of the 
contents of the packet, until he opens himself to you, or by his continued silence 
obliges you to inquire what course he means to take. a | 

One of two things will happen. Prince Stirbey will either obey the orders 
of the Porte, or he will remain at Bucharest contumuciously. 

In either of the two cases you will suspend your Consular functions, and 
cease hoisting your flag. 

You will be careful to inform the Chief-Acting Wallachian authority that

No, 225. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received August 15.) 


(No, 319. Confidential.) 


My Lori, Berlin, August 12, 1853, 

GENERAL ROCHOW, the Russian Envoy at St. Petersburgh, who has 
been on leave of absence for several months past on account of his health, 
returns to his post to-morrow. 

In reply to an inquiry which | have just made of Baron Manteuffel as to 
whether General Rochow was charged with any special instructions respecting 
the Eastern Question, his Excellency said that in order that that Minister should 
be completely informed on the subject, he has been occupied reading the 
correspondence connected with it, which was to serve as lis guide in communi- 
eating with the Russian Government; that he had no new directions to give him, 
hut that he was not to conceal that a disapprobation of the late measures of the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh continued to be felt by the Prussian Government, 
though they now hoped the difficulties would be speedily brought to an end, 

I inquired further whether General Rochow would urge the evacuation of 
the Principalities, and was given to understand that the desire of the Prussian 
Government was that this should take place as early us possible, and that 
General Rochow would do his best to advance this object, but that he (the 
General) apprehended that it would be wiser to leave the question. to the 
Emperors decision rather than to urge it, for that he firmly believed that His 
Imperial Majesty had no intention of his troops remaining there unnecessarily, 
but that he would not give way to pressure. 

Baron Manteutfel seemed to agree as to the prudence of following this 
course, Lut was by no means inclined toadmit the justice of the principles which 
it involved, and said something of the personal confidence with which the 
Emperor of Russia had inspired General Rochow, hinting that this might perhaps 
be carried too far, but that still the General was avery useful servant of the 
Crown, and that he was put to a good deal of embarrassment by the desire 
which he had frequently expressed of retiring from his present diplomatic post, 
and which he had again urged on his consideration. 

It may be right that I should add to this despatch, that in consequence of 
the Emperor of Russia having expressed disappointment at not seeing any Prussian 
officers of rank at the review this summer, Ne King ordered General Lindheim, 
who commands at Breslau, and who is already personally known to His Imperial 
Majesty, to-proceed to St. Petersburgh, and the General has already left Berlin 
for this purpose, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No, 238. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received August 16,) 
(No. 599.) 


My Lord, Parts, August 15, 1853, 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has received some interesting details respecting 
the Russian army from Bucarest, dated the 4th instant. M. Ponjade, the 
French Consul, states that after an appearance of uncertainty as to their move- 
ments, the Russian troops have moved close up to the Danube, upon which, as 
high as Galatz and Ibraila, they have gun-boats, He states the number of 
Russian troops between Ismail and Gemnitza to be 115,938, the details of which 
he gives; besides, reinforeements are said to be advancing in all directions. 
Everything indicated the certainty on the part of the Russians of a campaign, 
and the prevalent idea in the Principalities is that the Russians are only endca- 
vouring to gain time, and will eventually march further. M. Ponjade adds that 
those who remember the last Russian occupation say that the present troops are 
in a far better state, both of discipline and equipment. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

My Lord, St, Petershurgh, August 11, 1853. 

IT appears that General Castelbajac, upon his visit to the camp last week, 
was received with even more favour and distinction than | had been aware af, 
and that the Emperor conversed more with him than with any of his military 
guests, not excepting General Giulay, 

In talking over with me again lis conversation with the Emperor, the 
Marquis Castelbajac remarked that he had at first intended to have withheld 
from mea part of His Imperial Majesty’s observations, but that he felt bound 
upon reflection to dismiss this reserve, and to acquaint me that His Majesty, 
ater speaking of the distracted state of Turkey and the total loss of all authority 
by the Sultan, had concluded by stating that it was clear that the Western 
Powers were not aware of the danger which constantly threatened; but that for 
his part he regarded it to be so imminent that, as soon us the present difficulties 
were surmounted, he should consider it of great importance that the Allied 
Powers should occupy themselves with an eventuality (eventualité) which must 
be near at hand, 

It is very apparent to me that General Castelbajac did not reply to the 
Eimperor’s observation (or it may be overture) as an English diplomatist would 
have done, and that, instead of insisting upon the expediency of propping up i 
sinking empire he dwelt rather upon the expediency of no fresh arrangement 
with regard to Turkey being made till the Allied Powers should be consulted. 

[ need hardly state to your Lordship, that General Castelbajac's communi- 
cation was made to me in the strictest confidence. 

[ will not conclude my despatch without reporting to your Lordship that 
in speaking of the prospect of an arrangement with Turkey, the Emperor added ; 
“Ainsi, done, General, je ne doute aucunement que nous nurrivions & une 
bonne entente pourvu que les autres soiont d’aussi bonne fot que nous!” 

As in this country there prevails. the habit of giving a mol dordre, which, 
once employed by the Mmperor or his Ministers, is repeated by the persons 
belonging to the Court; this same phrase has been made use of to me two or 
three times by my Russian acquaintances,

(No, 420. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 11, 1853. 
I WOULD take the liberty of offering the following short observations, 


which are suggested by the perusal of your Lordship's despatch to Viscount 
Stratford de Redclitle marked No, 136. 

It is certain that the Russians believe in the power which they possess of 
overrunning Turkey and putting an end to the Sultan’s role in Europe when 
they think fit; and as regards myself | do not hesitute to express my conviction 
that their confidence is well founded. Whether England and France would not 


210 


he able to compel Russia to drop her prey, and whether she would not have to 
pay dearly for her flagitions attack, that is another question, and one which 
might probably be answered affirmatively. 

Icanwhile, however, there can, I think, be no doubt that any remains of 
authority which the Sultan may possess over his European provinees would be 
destroyed, and that the Ottoman Empire would remain a ruin which all the 
power of the most powerful States would be incapable of reconstructing. 

The conduct of the Russian Government in the late transactions has been 
such that it is impossible the most confiding should place any reliance in their 
professions and promises: putting these, however, aside as valueless, | would 
venture to observe to your Lordship that I have no doubt of Russia being sutti- 
ciently sensible of her own weak points to be very much disinclined to engage 
in war against England and I’rance, united as they are at present. 

For that reason I believe that the Emperor has no actual intention of 
extending his encroachments upon Turkey; and, beyond that, I believe that he 
will be induced to withdraw his troops from the Principalities, 

His Majesty may not have obtained all that he had in view, but according 
to his views he has carried out the great objects, of obliterating the eficet of 
Freneh and Austrian interference in Turkish affairs, of reigning paramount in the 
apprehensions of his southern neighbours, and of having givena fresh and perhaps 
a fatal shock to the independence of that country whose existence, according to 
the set phrase of Russian diplomacy, is of greater value to Russia than to any of 
the other States of Europe, 

At a time when the inhabitants of Constantinople may be supposed to be 
under great apprehensions from the anticipation of a Russian invasion, it has 
been, | must confess, with no slight satisfaction that | hive ascertamed that the 
inhabitants of St. Petersburgh were not unmoved at the contingency of the 
combined flects of England aud France making their appearance before the walls 
of Cronstadt. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 12, 1853. 

IN reply to your Lordship’s despatch of the Ord instant, No. 165, it is 
only necessary that I should state that your inquiry with regard to the Emperor's 
acceplance of the Projet de Note prepared at Vienna, was answered by antici- 
vation by the despatch No. 404, which Thad the honour of addressing to your 
Eandelin on the Sth instant. 

With respeet to your Lordship’s despatch No. 157 of the 2nd instant, [ beg 
to state that I waited yesterday upon Count Nesselrade, to whom | reported the 
substance of your observations upon the conduct of the Russian authorities in 
mreventing the payment of the tribute due by the Hospodars of Moldavia and 
Vallachia to the Porte. 

No act, L remarked, of the Russian Government had given so much offence 
in ‘Turkey as well as in England and France, the sensation produced having been 
all the stronger from the allies of Russia being at the time occupied in bringing 
wbout an amicable arrangement of difficulties which might be scceptable to the 
Mmperor. | 

‘The Chancellor observed that he was nware that my visit announced clouds, 
but that he was willing to believe that these clouds were upon the point of being 
dispersed, 

“You reproach us,” he said, “with our conduct in the Principalities, and 
you suspect that our object is to gain tine and so prolong our occupation of 
them. Upon the first point I will observe that nothing can be mote circumspect 
thin our conduct has been; we hive made no changes in the administration of 
the country, we pay for everything, and shall leave the Prinetpalities in o 


211 


better state than that in which we found them. As for the tribute money, 
we could not allow it to be handed over to the Sultan—you would not have 
done so yourselves; it is inconsistent with the very character of a military 
occupation that the occupying Power should allow supplies of money to be sent 
to the enemy.” 

I here interrupted the Chancellor to observe that the Sultan was not the 
enemy of Russia, that the two countries were not at war: his Excellency 
admitted the correction, and substituted the word “adversary” for * enemy.” 

I begged to inquire whether it was at least understood that the tribute- 
money was reserved for the later use of the Sultan? ‘To this question the 
Chancellor could return no definitive answer; the Emperor's pleasure not having 
been signified, no determination had taken place. 

Then, | said, for God's sake, decide the question at once, and decide it 
according to what is on all sides expected of you. 

The Chancellor resumed: “ Now,” he said, “about the delays which we 
are supposed to be desirous of interposing. The note which is intended to 
setile affuirs reaches us ona Tuesday; on the following day our acceptance of 
it, without the slightest alteration, is sent off by telegraph as far as Warsaw, and 
from thence by a feld-jiger to Vienna, where it arrives on Saturday; we sub- 
scribe, without hesitation, to the slight changes made in the note at London and 
Paris, antl the acknowledgment of our acquiescence reaches us again on the fol- 
lowing ‘Thesday—a rapidity of communication of which there has been hitherto 
noexample. “This does not look like a desire to protract affairs. Now,’ Count 
Nesselrode said, “ let me proceed further: you wish to see us out of the Princi- 
palities; I beg of you not to speak to us upon that subject; we are persuaded 
that you are anxious to beable to withdraw your ships from Besika, | entreat 
af you to believe that on our side we are just as desirous of leaving the Princi- 
palities ; these things are better not spoken of—they will come naturally and of 
themselves.” 

I again took an opportunity of expressing the sincere hope that the non- 
conclusion of affairs would not place the fleets under the necessity of entering 
the Dardanelles before the approach of autumnal weather. 

Count Nesselrode expressed his conviction that long before that time the 
decision of the Porte (respecting which, however, lhe would remark that he felt 
considerable misgivings) must be Known; that the Emperor proposed setting off 
for Warsaw in the firet days of September; and that before His Majesty's 
departure all doubts, he was satisfied, must be removed, 

Reverting to the subject of the evacuation of the Principalities, | observed 
that it was highly important that the Emperor's intention of withdrawing his 
troops should be made known to the Turks, os a means of obtaining their 
wihesion to the proposed arrangement, 

Count Nessclrode replied, that no such declaration was necessary—that the 
thing spoke for itself; indeed, that the Emperor’s intentions upon this point 
had been made known in his manifesto. 

I feel called upon to admit that some considerable time has elapsed since 
any conversation in which I have been engaged with the Chancellor has lelt so 
favourable an impression upon my mind as that of which I have thus submitted 
the principal details to your Lordship,

‘THE extract, which I inclose herewith, of M. Pisani’s daily report to me, 
has interest enough to induce me to call your Lordship's attention to its cou- 
tents. The langunge held by Reshid Pasha to M. Pisani is the more remark. 
able, as it did not originate in any message or inquiry for me,

It has come to my knowledge in a confidential manner, that the day before 
yesterday M. de la Cour, while paying a visit to the late Seraskier, now Com- 
mander of the Guards, Mehemet Rushdi Pasha, said, in reply to a question from 
the latter, that France was quite ready to send troops in aid of the Porte, but 
that it would be difficult to disembark them from the Black Sea, and impossible 
to march them through Germany. It appears, moreover, that the French 
Ambassador subsequently sent word to Reshid Pasha that he bad written to his 
Government on that subject. ; ; 

Other ideas, grounded on the eventuality of war, are also entertained by 
M. dela Cour. Amongst them are the military occupation of the Dardanelles 
jointly by England and Franee, and the independence of the Danubian Prinet- 
palities. Whether they proceed from himself or from his Government, I cannot 
presume to say. It would seem, however, pretty clear that schemes of so much 
importance ought not, under present circumstances, to be lightly or prematurely 
thrown out, If the motives for entertaining them are sufficient, it is but 
reasonable to expect that they should not be broached here, except upon an 
understanding with Her Majesty's Government. ' . 

The Turkish Ministers are evidently gaining confidence in thetr means of 
resisting Russia. It has been reported to me, as the opmion of a Prussian officer 
lately returned from Bulgaria overland, that the passes of the Balkan are now so 
well fortified as to defy the attack of any invading army.

Inclosure in No. 240. 
Proclamation, 


(Translation.) Constantinople, July 15, 1853. 

IT hasbeen alreadystated in the Turkish official “Gazette,” that Russia, having 
broken off official relations with the Sublime Porte on certain matters on which 
they could not come an understanding, withdrew her mission from Constanti- 
nople; and that, in consequence of the extensive preparations made by that 
Power by sea and by land, the Sublime Porte had made some iilitary arrange- 
ments and defensive preparations, wholly for precaution and her own protection, 

The real cause of the existing dispute with Russia, is the desire of that 
Power to obtain a binding and exclusive engagement from the Porte concerning 
the religious privileges of the Greck churches and priesthood, which the Porte 
cannot in justice be expected to give. 

Now these religious privileges, granted in the reign of His deceased Majesty 
Mehemed Khan, of glorious memory, and confirmed during the reigns of his 
illustrious successors, have been maintained ever since. In imitation of this 
noble example of his Royal predecessors, His present Majesty has likewise 
ratified and corroborated them. It never entered even into the imagination of 
any one to violate the ancient privileges granted @ proprio motu by the Imperial 
Throne. 

It has been repeatedly declared, ina friendly and sineere manner, that the 
Porte did not refuse to give assurances sulficient to remove the doubts on which 
the Russian Government establishes this dispute, in the same manner as the 
Porte can give assurances to the whole world in a matter so firmly settled; and 
that whereas, if one Government should enter into an engagement having the 
colour or foree of Treaty with another concerning the religious privileges of a 
nation consisting of so many millions of its Bubieoe the independence and 
sovereign rights of the Power thus bound would be impaired, such an engage- 
ment could not be consented to, 

While no necessity existed for persisting to such an extent in this matter, 
the Government of Russia would not desist from its pretensions ; and indeed the 
passage of the Russian troops across the Pruth, to take temporary possession of 
und hold the provinces of Wallachia and Moldavia, has been a subject of painful 
surprise to the Sublime Porte. ‘This violation of the frontier is an infraction of 
existing Treaties, and has been immediately protested against, according to 
international law ;—that is, the Sublime Porte has officially and publicly notified 
to the great Powers that she cannot accept such a violation of Treaty. 

Since divers States, connected by the Treaties which they have contracted, 
constitute the links of mutual security with respect to territorial possessions and 
aovercizn independence; since agreement and cooperation are the means now 

snerally employed when serious disputes like the present arise; since, moreover, 
Rossii has proclaimed that her real object was not to make war on the Porte, 
but to held possession of Moldavia and Wallachia as a guarantee until such time 
as her claims are satisfied; and since all the great Powers, without exception, 
have displayed sentiments more or less favourable towards Turkey, while two of 
them—England and France—being Powers on which, from their quality of 
maritime States, the Porte relies with special confidence, have given a practical 
manifestation of their friendship and goodwill, the Porte is engaged in com- 
municating, according to custom, with the above States; and meanwhile, as she 
cannot possibly accept a proposition so detrimental to her independence and 
sovereign rights, she has adopted the unanimous resolution of assuming, in her 
own defence, an armed attitude, as well upon the Danube as upon her Asiatic 
frontier, 

Such, then, is the real cause of the dispute with Russia, and the present 
aspect of the question, The Sublime Porte has at the same time been duly 
careful to adapt all necessary measures, und to make for her defence every 
requisite disposition of troops and ammunition of war, ‘The duty, therefore, of 
all the Porte's subjects, according to their several conditions, will be to continue 
in the tranquil prosecution of their respective concerns, agriculture, and com- 
merce, and to hold themselves ready to execute any orders which may be issued 
to them by the Imperial Government. 

a 7 


214 


‘As it has been clearly established in previous statements that, however the 
pretensions of Russia may relate to the religious privileges of the Greeks, neither 
the Greek people nor their Chiefs have any knowledge or participation therein ; 
and the Sublime Porte is convinced that they are in every respect satisfied and 
grateful towards their Sovereign; and that they are concerned more than any 
other at such pretensions being put forward; it is, on these accounts, by no 
means fitting that any resentment should be felt towards them in this respect ; 
and as the Greeks are equally faithful subjects of our Gracious Master with the 
Armenians. the Catholics, the Protestants, and the Jews, it behoves all the 
Sultan’s subjects, without exception, to be on good terms with one another, not 
acting hostilely nor using abusive language; in short, the Mussulmans, as well 
ns the other subjects of the Porte, shall live on good terms with each other, none 
among them whatsoever committing any action contrary to the supreme will, but 
attending to their own concerns. 

The above dispositions and decision, as well as the admonitions as above 
stated, are the result of the deliberation of a General Council, comprising the 
Sheik ul Islam, the learned chiefs of the law, the Seraskier, and all those 1 
military office, and the other Ministers and public servants, and held in the 
presence of the Grand Vizier; and an Imperial firman having also been issued on 
this subject, any one disapproving of this decision, and acting in contravention 
to these decisive admonitions, will be held a disobedient subject, and severely 
punished.

Supposing the latter to be as stated, I fear we must conclude that, if

No. 243. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received August 18.) 


(No. 188.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 4, 1893. 

THE affairs of Servia have suddenly assumed a character of unusual 
interest. It was to be expected that Austria would observe the population of 
that country with a watehful and jealous eye; nor have indications of something 
more than vigilance been wanting, if the accounts of her military movements 
along the frontier, and the suspicions attached to Meyenhoffer’s mission and 
Milosch’s letter he not altogether misplaced. 

| merely allude to these circumstances in the persuasion that Mr, Fons 
blanque has given to your Lordship the same information respecting them which 
he has addressed to me, ‘The increase as well as the movement of Austrian 
troops on portions of the whole frontier line from the Adriatic to the Carpathian 
Mountains had drawn the attention of others also, and naturally of the Porte 
itself. No one, however, appears to have been quite prepared for the intelli- 
gence which arrived by express from Belgrade on the evening of the 30th 
ultimo, purporting that the Austrian Consul there had announced the intention 
of his Government to occupy Servia by a military force whenever any appear- 
ance of disorder in that provinee should require the execution of such a 
Measure, 

Mr. Fonblanque’s statement was fully confirmed by letters which arrived 
here at the same time from the Pasha of Belgrade, the Servian authorities, and 
the French Consul. Extracts from Mr. Fonblanque’s reports to me are inclosed 
herewith, not so much for your Lordship’s information, os he has, no doubt, 
written direetly to London on the subject, but as the ground on which my reply 
to the Porte’s communication was to be founded, 

The salient points of the case, beside the threat af occupation, were the 
absence of any disorders in Servia, and the protest, or remonstrance, of the 
Servian authorities. 

These circumstances had determined Reshid Pasha to support the Servians 
in their resistance to a forced occupation, even before he sent his first message 
to me announeing the facts, [tis almost unnecessary to inform your Lordship 
that I approved of his decision, ‘The principle, of itself, is highly objectionable, 
and could not he applied without prejudice to the Porte's a alates There 
would also be danger of its: causing much bloodshed, as the Servians, however 
rashly, would in all likelihood resist the invasion, which could hardly occur 
without giving Russia, the protecting Power, a right to interfere too, 

On the other hand, it was obviously desirable that the Porte in opposing a 
dangerous pretension should act with prudence ; taking care to give no unneces- 
vary smbrage to Austria, and to seeure the attachment of the Servinns, without 
putting too much power into their hands, 

Under these impressions | waited on Reshid Pasha, who had requested to 
see me, and the result of our conversation was, thet the Porte should lose no 
time in seeking an explanation with the Austriqn Cabinet, not only by means 
of the Internuncio, but also through the channel of its own Aimbassador at 
Vienna; and that contidence should be expressed in the intentions of Austria, 
the inconvenience and hazard of accepting the proposed occupation pointed 
out, and the present tranquillity of Servia appealed to in proof that the measure 
would be wholly superfluous. It ware further agreed that the Porte should, 

oP 2 


216 


nevertheless, declare its readiness to meet the views of Austria by taking pre- 
cautions against any eventual disturbance ; that orders should therefore be issued 
for collecting a Turkish army near the frontier of Servia, and increasing the 
small military foree, together with the native police, in Prince Alexander 
service ; and that the Sultan should appoint a Commissioner of rank with power 
to regulate these several operations and provide for such contingencies as might 
be expected to arise. 

It was subsequently suggested by the Council, that a reinforcement should 
also be sent to the garrison of Belgrade. 

This course of proceeding was communicated to Baron de Bruck the day 
before yesterday, at a conference which took place between his Excellency and 
Reshid Pasha at the house of the latter, and on his Highness" invitation. 

It appears from what Reshid Pasha stated to M. Pisani that the Internuncio 
was satisfied with it, and that being requested to explain the communication 
made at Belgrade by the Austrian Consul-General, he aid that it was incumbent 
on his Government to prepare for every emergency, and that in offering to 
contribute to the repression of any disturbances which might break out in Servia, 
it contemplated the extent to which disorder might be carried if not immediately 
quelled. 

L have thought it best not to seek any direct intercourse with Baron de 
Bruck on this delicate subject. In concert with the French Ambassador T had 
faken occasion, before the arrival of the last intelligence from Belgrade, to 
afford him an opportunity of explaining the military movements ordered by his 
Government along the frontier, and his answer was not. sa explicit us to 
encourage any further attempts without the advantage of aright to push the 
inquiry home. I have preferred writing to Lord Westinorland; and a copy of 
my letter to him is inclosed herewith for your Lordship's more complete 
‘aformation. ‘The original is forwarded to Vienna by the post of to-day. 

T cannot conclude without an appeal to your indulgence, my Lord, when 
the course of proceeding which L have recommended comes under the considera- 
tion of Her Majesty’s Government. Several objects, not ensy to be reconciled 
with each other, were to be simultaneously provided for, and it is rare bub some 
hazard must be incurred, when that is the case. Under present circumstances 
every occurrence 15 complicated by the position in which Russia has placed 
herself towards this. empire, The Servians are not without longings for inde- 
vendence, and the chance of a war must naturally tend to excite their hopes. 
Fnvaded. ‘auch were the case, by Austria, and ill-supported by Turkey, they 
might turn once more towards the protecting Power and make a very serious adidi- 
tion to the dangers which already menace the very existence of this empire. 

In my occasional interviews with the Servian Agent I have always advised 
him to lean upon the Porte, as holding outa better hope for the future prospects 
of Servia than any to be derived from a closer connexion with Austria or with 
Russia. Such counsels can, nevertheless, avail but little if the Porte, as time 
advances and the motives of independence inerease, coutinties to maintain 
without relaxation thut system of jealousy and mistrust which appears more or 
less in all her dealings with the Christians. The Sultan stands im need. of 
assistance from every side, and ‘n order to obtain it he must ineur those risks 
which are inseparable from weakness. If Servia is to resist an Austrian occu~- 
pation, it must be entrusted with the means of resistance, and the best security 
against an abuse of those means is surely to be found in the contidence with 
which they are granted, The approach of a Turkish army, however explained, 
would otherwise he a souree of apprehension and a motive with the Servians for 
hastening to sever the tie which still connects them with Turkey,

( Extract.) Belgrade, July 24, 1853. 

IN my No. 38 to the Secretary of State I mentioned that, on the 22nd 
instant, the Austrian Consul-General formally, though verbally, notified to 
Bessim Pasha that if disorders should oceur in Servia, two Austrian brigades 
would be ready to enter the Principality on an application to him, either from 
the reigning Prince, or from the Turkish Governor of Belgrade. 

This morning M. Simitch, the Servian Minister for Foreign Affairs, called 
on the Pasha to state his subsequently acquired and quite certain information, 
that the Austrians would occupy the country when they saw fit, without waiting 
for any application from hence, I doubt whether they will allow time for an 
answer to be received from Constantinople on Bessim Pasha’s reference. 

The Imperial forees assembled close by are quite strong enough for the 
comtemplated invasion of Servia, but I should mention that their greatest con- 
centrations are in the directions north of Orsova, whence, L suppose, they will 
second, over the lower districts of Servia, some Russian movement to take the 
‘Turkish army in flank and in the rear, 

[venture to think your Lordship will agtee that the purpose now indicated 
by Austria with regard to Gervia is even a less excusable aggression than the 
Russian one in Moldavia and Wallachia. 

Under an aspect of aflairs so threatening, and surrounded by circumstances 
justifying suspicion of disloyalty, I rejoice to acquaint your Excellency that the 
Servian Government has prepared a protest against any violation of the soil by 
Austrian troops. It will be sent to Colonel von Radisavlievitch to-morrow 
morning, and, at the same time, a Tatar will be dispatched to Constantinople. 

It seems quite evident that Prince Michael's letter was a device for exciting 
the troubles of which Austria intended to profit in go insidious & manner.

Consul-General Fonblanque to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(Extract.) Belyrade, July 26, 1853, 

1 AM now enabled to inclose the Servian Minister's letter to the Austrian 
Consul-General. It does not bear out the description, originally given, of a pro- 
test, but the latter part contains a sufficiently firm remonstrance against Austrian 
occupation without a request from the Prince. Still it is as muchas the strained 
influence of M, de Ségur and myself could evoke. 

The recapitulated Austrian’ plea of “ traces of the Hungarian emigration 
still existing in Servia,” is either fanciful or fictive. No vestige of the kind 
remains ; but, on the contrary, the most dangerous feeling of the Servian masses is 
that rancorous one against the Turks, who evinced such sympathy with the Magyars 
as to be identified in opinion with the political refugees of three years since, — 

A strong popular feeling is evinced in Belgrade against the Austrians, and 
there are accounts of rather large bodies of peasants having assembled near 
Negotin to oppose the expected ruling at Milanovatz, Such bands will never 


a 


stand against regular troops ; a single discharge of grape-shot would disperse two 
thousand of them. . 

‘The Servian Government will at once send the treasure and special archives 
to Kragujevatz.

INCLOSED herewith is the copy of a letter sent from the Porte to Omer 
Pasha, with instructions to his Excellency to transmit it under his signature to 
Prince Gortchakoff, 

Your Lordship will observe that the Porte is determined not to submit 
quietly to any attempt on the part of the Russians to increase their armed force 
on the waters of the Danube above the confluence of the Prath with that river. 

I dissuaded the Council from announcing, ly means of the same letter, its 
intention to occupy and fortify a small island on the Wallachian side of the 
river and opposite to the fortress of Widdin, to the defence of which, in case of 
war, it is thought that the possession of that island by the Turks would be 
essential. ‘This intention is not abandoned altogether, but only suspended until 
more certain information can be obtained. Tam not without apprehension that 
an attempt to carry it into effect might cause a premature collision between the 
forces of the respective Governments.

Inclosure in No. 245, 
Omer Pasha to Prince Gortchakoff. 


AS your Excellency is already aware from the answer addressed to you by 
the Porte, the passage of Russian ships of war up the Danube beyond the 
confluence of the Pruth with that river, is forbidden by Treaty; and I have 
therefore received instructions to prevent any vessels passing that point. In the 
event of any Russian vessels of war wishing, henceforward, to pass the point in 
question, they will be reminded, in the first place, in a friendly manner, of the 

‘reaty restriction, and, should they not comply, your Excellency will understand 
how impossible it is for me to permit such a thing. 

Previously to the receipt of these instructions, ships of war and pontoons 
(or gun-boats) had passed the point in question and gone to the neighbourhood 
of Galatz. It is to be hoped from your Excellency’s sound sense and judgment, 
that however this may be, the vessels and pontoons which have passed that point 
will go back, ‘They shall be permitted to do so unmolested; but if they should 
attempt to go upwards beyond Galatz, I shall be under the necessity of pre- 
venting them also, 

In conformity with the pacific feelings which continue to animate the Porte, 
and of her special consideration towards the Government of Russia, | have 
considered it my duty to make this communication to you beforehand, and I 
avail myself, &e,

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon, —( Received August 18.) 
(No. 195.) 


My Lord, Therapia, August 4, 1553. 
THE satisfaction which you have done me the honour to express in your 
instruction No. 116 of this year, at the course taken by the Porte with respect 
to Russia's occupation of the Principalities, will naturally increase in proportion 
as your Lordship finds reason to believe that the objects for which that course 
was advised are Hkely to be attained. I presume, under correction, that the 
objects in question were to postpone hostilities, to open unothur chance for 


220 


negotiation, to give time for defensive preparations here, and for public opinion 
to mature elsewhere: Appearances warrant 1 belief that in none of these 
respects were our anticipations ‘n error, It would seem, moreover, that forbear. 
ance on this side has had some effect in softening irritation on the other, while 
‘t ig certain that the Porte has been thereby spared the mortification of a defeat, 
without suffering the annoyance of any udministrative derangement, 

Your Lordship has probably been for some days in possession of the con- 
ciliatory, though final, proposals founded on the Porte’s explanatory protest, 
and forwarded from here on the 20th and 24rd ultime to London, Paris, and 

fienna. OF other experiments originating in an earnest desire to avoid the 
calamities of war, some, a8 your Lordship knows, have proved abortive, and 
come remain for consideration without the advantage of being accepted in the 
outset by either of the contending parties, Foremost among the latter 18 your 
Lordship’s draft of a Convention, which reached me, with its covering despatch, 
on the 31st ultimo. 

Under other circumstances, without reference to my own impressions, I 
should have lost no time in laying it betore the Sultan’s Government, and even 
as it was, 1 might have sheltered my responsibilty by doing 50; but strict 
obedience to the letter of my instructions would have furnished a poor com- 
pensation for the usclessness, aud perhaps the harm, eventually resulting from 
the step. 

Your Lordship had forwarded the Convention to me in ignorance of the 
plan of arrangement adopted here by the Four Representatives accepted defint- 
tively by the Porte, and transmitted to Vienna, for conveyance to Count 
Nesselrode in the manner most likely to prove agreeable to the Court of 
Russia. I could not take upon myself, nor would it have been reasonalle for 
me, as 1 conceive, to propose the Convention as a substitute for that plan, 
which was in fact beyond our reach, especially after 1 had ascertained, by 
affording Reshid Pasha an opportunity of reading the Convention, that he was 
decidedly averse to it himself, and anticipated a similar degree of objection 
on the part of his colleagues. The form of a Treaty, founded expressly on that 
of Kainardji, involving an engagement in terms to Russia, and liable to be 
understood by that Power as extending over the Sultan's firman, could hardly 
fail of seeming dangerous in his sight. 

Aware that your Lordship has no predilection for one kind of arrangement 
more than for nother, movies the parties be satisfied on just and honourable 
grounds, L have not hesitated to act according to what appeared to me the true 
situation and requirements of the case, Should the plan adopted here, and long 
ere this received in London and Vienna, be found incapable of execution, the 
Convention may be subsequently brought forward with less disadvantage, if such 
be the course resolved upon, than if ++ were now officially presented to the 
Porte, and officially declined, as I have every reason to believe it would be. 

With respeet to the Conventional form as preferable, in the actual cir- 
cumstances of Russia, to that of a note, | would venture to remind your 
Lordship that the Russian Cabinet showed no disinclination to accept the note 
submitted to it, asa projet, by General Castelbajac, though the terms of that 
note must have been thought sufficiently sale to ruurd the Sultan's rights from 
any eneroachment or dangerous innovation, 

I cannot bring this despatch to a conelusion without recording a cireum- 
stance reported to me two days ago by M. Pisani. His words are these: ‘In 
talking on the Russian question, Reshid Pasha declared to Baron de Bruck 
officially that the Porte is decided neither to accept any new proposal, nor to 
add a single word to the lust Projet de Note. We are ready to dic,” said he, 
“rather than sacrifice our independence and sovereign rights to Russia.” 

I have, &e, 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 247, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed August 18.) 


(No. 196.) 


My Lord, : Therapia, August 6, 1853. 

__ THE Servian Agent at the Porte having called here yesterday, I learnt from 
his conversation that he viewed with some feelings of mistrust the measures 
about to be taken by the Porte with respect to his country. His apprehensions 
appeared to be chietly directed to the effects of a supposed concert between the 

urkish and Austrian Governments to the disadvantage of Servia, declaring his 
conviction that, if such apprehensions were realized, an insurrection of the 
Servian peasantry might take place, and afford the Austrians an opportunity of 
accomplishing their worst purposes, 

Though 1 suceceded in calming his excitement to a certain degree, by 
explaining to him the real position of affairs, and impressing upon him the 
advantage as well as duty of inducing his Government to hold firm to the Porte 
in loyalty and reasonable confidence, I felt the necessity of putting Reshid Pasha 
upon his guard, and advising him to carry into effect the proposed measures 
with a due regard to the character of the Servians and the state of parties in 
their omy 

Nith this view I sent Mr. Alison to his Highness a few hours ago, and 
the points which I desired him to press upon the Pasha, were the following’ 
first, to enter into no concerted agreement with Austria, but simply to remon- 
strate against an unsolicited occupation of Servia, and announce the precautionary 
measures intended by the Porte; secondly, to address a letter of approval and 
encouragement to the Prince of Servia, enabling him at the same time to explain 
to his Government and to the public the views of the Porte and its confidence 
in their loyalty; thirdly, to post the army of observation at a certain distance 
from the frontier of Servia, and not to divide it into more than two separate 
brigades at most ; fourthly, to select a Commissioner already known to the 
Servians, and not to increase the garrison of Belgrade beyond an additional 
battalion. 

To all these propositions Reshid Pasha most readily assented. 


I have since received visits from the Internuncio, and also from the Servian 


The former, being the first to enter upon the subject, assured me that the 
sole aim of his Government was to let any parties in Servia who might be 
disposed to cherish revolutionary projects, know that the Austrian forces were at 
their post. He added, in reply to an inquiry from me, that he was satisfied with 
the Porte. 

The latter told me that he hud seen Reshil Pasha subsequently to 
Mr. Alison’s visit, and that his conversation with his Highness had revived his 
confidence in the intentions of the Porte towards Servia, He, nevertheless 
retained some portion of his previous anxiety, and endeavoured to persuade me 
that the tranquillity of Servia would be best maintained in the present state of 
parties there by a postponement of the intention to send an additional battalion 
and a Commissioner to Belgrade, until he could learn from his Government in 
what manner those measures would probably be construed on the spot. 

2 On the whole, I trust that the necessary measures will be carried inte 
a feat re proper degree of prudence, and consequently without danger of 

At the same time, I do not quite understand why the Austrian Goy 
should be so eager to adopt precautions with a view to the chance of ate han 
it speaks with so much confidence of the peaceable disposition of Russta. . 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

of his Government towards Servia. 

M, Nicolayevitch, the Servian agent, assures me that there is no truth in 
the suspicion expressed therein, and that the views of the Servians do not 
extend beyond certain improvements in their present political or rather admunis- 
trative position, expressed in a paper which he placed confidentially in my hands 
not long ago, and a copy of which I have new the honour to submit herewith to 
your Lordship. ; : 

With respect to the French Consul at Belgrade, I can easily conceive that 
he lays himself open to suspicion by an excess of zeal and activity; but it does 
not appear from the language of M, Nicolayevitch that he is much in the conti- 
dence or favour of Prince Alexander’s Government.

My Lord, Foreign Office, August 18, 1853. 

1 HAVE to acquaint your Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government 
ipprove the course pursued by you in regard to the draft of Convention inclosed 
1 my despatch No. 116 of the 9th of July, under the circumstances stated in 
yur despatch No. 195 of the 4th of this month, that draft having been sent to 
Cnstantinople without knowledge on the part of Her Majesty's Government of 
th proposals forwarded from Constantinople to Vienna. 

Her Majesty's Government have no predilection for one form of arrange-
