My Lord, Paris, August 18, 1853. 

M. DE HUBNER has made a communication to M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
respecting the attitude taken by the Austrian Government in regard to Servia. 
Count Buol mentions M. Fonton’s mission to Belgrade on the part of Russia, 
and says that the Austrian Consul-General will have directions to support that 
gentleman in his endeavours to improve the administration in Servia under the 
present Prince, and to free that country from the revolutionary element which 
pervades it; and Count Buol hopes for the assistance of France for the same 
purpose. He declared at the same time that there wus no truth in the imputa- 
tions made against Austria of protecting the Obrénowitch family, and of 
wishing Lo disturb the present reigning Prince; and that if Austrian troops enter 
Servia, it will be to defend and protect the Porte against internal outbreak. 

M. Drouyn de Liuys replied to M. Hiibner that his general views agreed 
with those of Count Buol, that it was right to support the present reigning Prince; 
that if reforms in the administration of government were necessary, they should he 
counselled; and that France was equally with Austria opposed to revolution: 
bul, when the assistance of France was asked, he niust inquire what Count Buol 
meant by revolution, Men and acts must be named belore he could give an 
answer: for, in fact, what Austria called revolution others might think improve- 
ment, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys availed himself again of this opportunity to declare 
that there could not be a greater mistake than to suppose that the French 
Government was an enemy to liberal institutions. 


241 


Tn the conversation to which I have referred above, M. de Hiibner informed 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys that the Austrian Government, although admitting the 
right of the Porte to recall the Hospodars, regretted nevertheless that that step 
had been taken. I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My dear Lord, Therapia, August 4, 1853. 


YOU have probably learnt from Me. Fonblanque that the Austrian Consul- 
General at Belgrade has offered military assistance to the Servian Government, 
with a view to the suppression of any disorders which may arise under present 
cireumstances in Servia, accompanied with an intimation that the proposed 
auxiliary foree might eventually enter the Principality, whether the oceupation 
was or was not agreeable to the naunl auclenns 

2H 2 


| « 


202 


I take it for granted that Mr. Fonblanque has also informed your 
Lordship of the respectful remonstrances addressed by M. Simitch to Baron 
Radislavievitch, in reply to his rather startling communication. 

I have now to pul you in possession of the manner in which the intelligence 
has been received by the Turkish Ministers, and of the measures which it would 
geem that they are inclined to adett in consequence. 

The impression made upon them was to all appearance a painful one, in 
which the feelings of surprise and mistrust predominated. 

L have endeavoured to soften their apprehensions in 80 far as the idea of an 
understanding between Austria and Russia is concerned; but I could not, on any 
sound principle, blame the immediate resolution which they adopted to support 
the Servian authorities in their resistance to an unsolicited occupation. 

The course which they have in mind to, pursue is, at the same time, well 
qualified to meet any legitimate expectations of the Court of Vienna, It is, in 
substance, as 1 understand, to form an army of their own on the frontier of 
Servia, to allow the Prince of Servia to increase his own small military force and 
police, to augment the garrison of Belgrade, and to appoint u high commissioner, 
empowered by the Sultan, to communicate with the local authorities, and to 
watch over contingencies as they arise. 

I know not whether these intentions are conveyed to Vienna by the post of 
to-day, or, indeed, whether they are yet definitely settled. But 1 presume that 
no time will be lost in apprising the Austrian Cabinet of the view taken by the 
Porte of its late communication with the Servian Government, and lam certain 
that Baron de Bruck is already in possession of its sentiments in that respect. 

I have done what depends upon me to encourage the Porte in giving the 
most considerate and amicable form to its declaration, which I venture to hope 
will be received with satisfaction at Vienna, 

Your Lordship will bear in mind that there are no disorders at present in 
Servia, and that the Austrian troops may be better employed in muintaining 
order within their own frontier than in carrying alarm into a country unwilling 
to receive them. 

| have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

THE following passage occurs in Count Nesselrode's circular despatch of 
the %=: “Sciemment et volontairement nous ne chercherons a exciter aucun 
soulévement parmi les populations Chrétiennes de la Turquie.” 

With reference to that assurance, I transcribe a pussage in the despatch 
from Her Majesty’s Consul in Bulgaria, of which I inclose a copy : 

“The agents of Russia. have been most active in widely spreading the 
cireulars and manifestoes which have issued of late from St, Petersburgh. 
Within the last few days, the circular of the Russian Government, which 
represents the causes of the impending hostilities to be of a religious character,

Sir G. H. Seymour to Count Nesselrade. 


(Confidential. ) 
Dear Count Nesselrode, St, Petersburgh, Auguet 14, 1854, 

IT js often in the close neighbourhood of port that the chances of shipwreck 
become the greatest; this must be my excuse if my anxiety respecting the 
success of an arrangement calculated Lo insure peace increases as the conclusion 
ef our negotiation draws near. 

If | have carried away a correct impression of our last conversation, you 
are not free from anxiety, from the notion of the Turkish Government being 
little disposed to accede to the measures now pressed upon them on the part of 
the allies. 

It is indeed but too obvious that late transactions, diplomatic aud militiury, 
miust have had the tendency of awaking to a degree that spirit of fanaticism 
which had previously slept, and that it will require all the fnendly exertions of 
the foreign Representatives at Constantinople to calm down feelings which have 
been worked upon by apprehensions, religious and political, by which the 
Turks are at last possessed. 

Again, then, I would venture to remark to your Exeellency, that nothing 
will so much conduce to the success of the pacific attempts of your allies— 
nothing will so much tend to dissipating the unfounded but very considerable 


235 


apprehensions of the Turks—as any act on your part which will prove that the 
overtures which the Sultan is recommended to make, will be met in a friendly 
spirit by the Emperor, | 

It is certain that it must be under a sense of pain that the Porte are 
prepared to send an Ambassador to St. Petersburgh at a time when a portion of 
the Turkish empire is occupied by a Russian army, as certainly it could 
misbecome neither the magnanimity nor the power of the Emperor to determine 
that the withdrawal of the Imperial forces should at all events commence as 
soon as the Turkish negotiator arrives on Russian ground. | 

‘The point is one to which my Government attach very great importance, 
and attention to it would not only be very acceptable to your allies, but would 
be very reassuring to that Government whose weakness you have been among 
the first to deplore. 

The immense importance of the questions at issue will, Lam sure, excuse 
me for addressing you this fresh representation. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR. 


No. 260. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received August 24.) 


(No, 427. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 16, 1853. 

ACCORDING to an opinion very commonly received, the most skilful and 
successful diplomacy of Europe is that of Russia. 

Were the fact so, it would not be surprising, the Imperial Government. pos- 
sessing in the funds at its command, in the unity of its action, in the passive 
obedience of its agents and subjects, facilities which exist in Russia alone; but 
beyond this I venture to regard the opinion as an erroneous one. 

If it had been the Emperor's purpose (which even now Ido not believe) to 
have taken forcible possession of the Principalities, the great point should have 
been to have brought about a state of things which would have given a colour to 
if it had not justified this act of violence. 

No stich intelligible ground of quarrel was established ; no such show of 
reagon was made, and if may be almost enid that the motives assigned on the 
Emperor's behalf have been so futile that it is doubtful whether in his interests 
an unexplained breach of national rights would not have been preferable to one 
for whieh such miserable pretexts have been offered. 

Again, a diplomacy conducted with even ordinary skill would not, in pursuit 
of an object, have lost sight of others to which an almost equal importance is 
attached whenever the neglect has been most apparent throughout the course 
of the present transactions with ‘Turkey. 

It was the policy of the Russian Cabinet to cause the Emperor of the 
French to be looked upon as the intended violator of Treaties, and to exclude 
him from the Council of Sovereigns; the effect of Russian diplomacy has been 
to enable him to dispel the suspicion, and to assign him a place, and a very pro- 
minent one, in that Council. 

It was their policy to prevent any close alliance between the Governments 
or the people of England and France, and themselves have brought about that 
intimacy, 

It was their policy to maintain Austria in « state of submissive tutelage, and 
they offered her the most eligible occasion for emancipating herself, and for 
manifesting what is here termed “ her ingratitude.” 

Tt was their policy to preserve their hold wpon the rest of Germany, anil 
the rest of Germany witnesses with indignation an enterprise which has all the 
appearance of an act of hostility against the commerce af every State of the 
Confederation. = 

Above all it was, or it ought to have been, their policy that the Head of the 
State should retain that proud position which his supposed disinterestedness and 
respect, for ‘Treaties had obtained for him, and which is now lost beyond the 
power of recovery, 


236 


If in all this any great skilfulness has been displayed, then must those who 
hitherto have been esteemed the most successful masters of diplomacy have been 
undeserving of their reputation. 

But it may be said, that Russia having had a bad cause to defend, has at 
least shown great Ingenuity in the defence which her diplomatists have set up 
for her, 

Really, my Lord, those who make this assertion can hardly have read the 
State Papers which the Imperial Chancellerie have put forth; for assuredly tt 
would have been better that the Blondoffs and Labenskis should have kept 
silence than that, by rushing into print, they should have exposed themselves to 
the refutation of every tolerably conducted newspaper. The Foreign Depart- 
ment of St. Petersburgh has been seen to be unequally matched against the 
Paris “ Charivari.” 

It has indeed been remarked, that the great difficulty of late in arguing 
with a Russian agent, was not that of putting Russia in the wrong, but of not 
putting her to such a degree in the wrong as would render a return to more 
correct ways difficult, from the excess of her departure from a straight course. 

As regards the Russians, | must allow that those with whom my habits 
and duties bring me into intercourse approve of all that the Emperor has done, 
and approve, | may add, in the same official phrases, 

With respect to the strangers whom I see, and | refer more especially to 
the Members of the Diplomatic Body, having been one and all of them upon 
my arrival here loud in their admiration of the Emperor, who was then spoken 
of as the Protector of European society, they are now (with a solitary excep- 
tion) unanimous in disapproving his conduct, and in considering it as subversive 
of those principles by which society is held together. 

One of my colleagues has not hesitated to state to me, that having been 
long resident here, it had furmerly been his pride to be placed at the Russian 
Court, while now all that he desired was to withdraw himself from a post 
for which he felt unfitted—no longer comprehending what is going on around 
him, or the motives which have led to these strange movements, 

I venture, then, to assert, that if Russian diplomacy is to be judged of by 
the doings, sayings, and writings, which have lately occupied my attention, no 
opinion can be more erroneous than that which would assign to it the character 
of pre-eminent dexterity, 

Some little talent was shown in the assurances with which a settled purpose 
was denied at the commencement of Prince Menchikoffs mission, but there 
began and there ended the only skilful exertion of Russian diplomacy as exerted 
in ain European field, which has come under my observation, 

In candour it must, however, be admitted, that there is no sound diplomacy 
where there is no knowledge of facts, that is, where truth is not allowed to 
prevail; whereas a Russian funetionary only writes or says that which it is 
acceptable to his master to learn, 

Much of the mischief which has lately occurred has been occasioned, first, 
by the remarkably incorrect estimate taken ly the Emperor of the rights secured 
to him by Treaty ; and in the second place, by that want of courage which 
prevented his servants from venturing to point out the errer. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H, SEYMOUR,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No. 33d.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, August 26, 1863. 

ON the 20th instant Count Walewski informed me that he had been 
instructed Phe Government to propose that orders should be dispatched forth- 
with to the British and French Ambassadors, to send for the fleets to Constanti- 
nople on October the Ist, if the Principalities were not evacuated before that 
ime. 

I told his Excellency that 1 did not understand what advantage was 
expected from sending such orders so long before the time they could be acted 
upon; and that, as the chief difficulties with Russia appeared then to be over- 
come, it would be desirable to wait for the answer that might daily be expected 
from Constantinople. If the Porte aceepted the note, and Russia still refused 
to evacuate the Principalities, it might be necessary for the fleets to enter the 
Dardanelles long before the Ist of October; but if, on the other hand, the note 
was rejected by the Turkish Government, a different course of action might be 
thought expedient by the Governments of France and England. Count 
Walewski appeared to admit that his proposal was open to these objections, and 
did not press the subject further. |

(Signed) CLARENDON.

Nessclrode, and he regretted to say that the tone of them was not satisfactory. 
That the Emperor had reproached Genera] Rechow with ‘the conduct of the 
Prussian Government, stating that if their language to the Maritime Powers 
had been different, the resistance of England and France to his just claims on 
Turkey would have been less decided, and the difficulties with which the 
qperiion was now surrounded would have been greatly diminished ; but His 
imperial Majesty said that, notwithstanding ull that had taken place, he had 
no intention of retaining possession of the Principalities, and that if the Turks 
ugreed to the Vienna arrangement, his troops would leave them in five days,

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 19, 1853. 

A PERSON in whom I can place entire reliance acquaints me that Count 
Orloff, in conversing the other day with one of his familiar friends, by whom the 
statement was made to my informant, expressed plainly his opinion as to the 
likelihood of a speedy arrangement of difficulties, and of the arrangement being 
short-lived. : ; , 

“We shall probably,” said Count Orloff, “ settle this business very shortly ; 
but you may rely upon it, before six months are passed we shall be at war with 
the Turks.” ne 

I beg of your Lordship to call to mind how much this opinion agrees with 
those which T have heard expressed in other quarters, and with the apprehen- 
sions by which I myself have long been possessed. ih A 

Just at present public opinion runs strongly against Russia; France and 
England are Abe united against her pretensions ; and Austria (as far as we 
are aware) has not begun to entertain those visions of extended Empire which 
will hardly be long resisted, if once it be proved to her satisfaction that the 
downfall of the Ottoman Empire is certain and imminent. ee 

The very position too in which Russia would find herself after a reconcilia- 
tion with Turkey upon the basis of the arrangement lately made at Vienna, 
would afford grounds for mistrusting her intentions, since every one must feel 
that the object attained was far from being commensurate with the immense 
sacrifices made for its acquirement, ; 

The Emperor, in fact, would have subscribed to terms which he himself 
told me on the 30th of May he was determined not to listen to, y 

| have taken care to inform my French colleagues of Count Orloff opinion, 
as reported at the beginning of my despatch.

assurances are expected as to the Emperor's intention of ordering the evacuation 
of the Enlai as soon as the Vienna note shall have been delivered or even 
signed; on the other, not only (as my correspondence will have shown) is the 


Imperial Government disinclined to Ee this distinct engagement, but my 
92 


240 


colleagues of France, Austria, and Prussia, have shown themselves to be very 
little dis sed to press for it. 

If T had no other object in view than to guard against personal responsibility, 
it might be easily obtained by calling upon the Government in season and out of 
season for that which the Emperor should in fairness concede, and which Her 
Majesty's Government have a perfect right to expect; I have been, however, 
unwilling to take this course, partly because ] am desirous of not allowing any 
marked difference to be observable between the conduct of the French Envoy 
and mine, and partly because in the event of a failure of the negotiation, now 
considerably advanced, the blame would probably be thrown by the other parties 
upon the injudicious pertinacity of the English Mission in asking for pledges in a 
manner which implied suspicion in the Imperial intentions. 

These considerations will, however, no longer restrain me, 80 s00n @S I shall

(No. 437.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 19, 1853. 


LOOKING to the contingency of a removal of the fleets from Besika Bay 
to Constantinople, I thought it advisable to state to Count Nesselrode (whom | 
saw this evening), that the anchorage of the former place was becoming danger- 
ous, and that a letter from Mr. Consul Yeames acquainted me that several 
English and French vessels had gone ashore there in a late gale. 

Count Nesselrode remarked that it was only surprising to him that the two 
fleets had not repaired to Mitylene, where he understood there was excellent 
anchorage, and which was not further than the Russian harbour of Sevastopol 
from Constantinople. 

His Excellency again expressed his ap rehensions that the proposed note 
would be rejected by the Sultan. He was desirous of knowing what, in that 
contingency, would be the line taken by Her Majesty's Government. 

Not being able to supply the desired information, I replied that I did not 
share his fears; and that i believed the contingency to be one which had not 
been contemplated. 

In a guarded manner | glanced at the consideration which, for the present, 
deterred me from saying more upon a subject respecting which Her Majesty's 
Government felt go much anxiety, as that of the withdrawal of the Russian forces 
from the Principalities. 

Count Nesselrode begged me to believe that importunity upon this point 
would be caleulated to defeat the propos object; the Emperor's word had 
been, his Excellency observed, pledged by an open declaration: to doubt that word 
would of course be very displeasing to His Imperial Majesty. 

In the absence of any renewed and more distinct engagement, even this, 
acknowledged by the Minister, of a self-imposed engagement by which the 
Sovereign 18 bound, appeared to me to be of value. 

I have, &c.

My Lord, Vienna, August 23, 1853. 

COUNT BUOL read to me the report he had received from the Austrian 
Consul-General at Belgrade, detailing the result of the explanations he had 
given to the Prince of Servia, with reference to the protest His Highness lately 
addressed to the Austrian Government against their supposed intention of 
carrying out a military occupation of his country without his consent. 

‘The Consul having assured the Prince that he had never intended or been 
authorized to convey any such impression, but that the sole intention of his 
Government was to assure His Highness and the Sultan that if their rights 
were attacked by insurrectionary movements, oF menaced in any other manner, 
they might rely upon the assistance of the military force of Austria to support 
them; he received from the Prince the declaration that he was atheetly 
satisfied with these explanations, and he acknowledged that he had been preci- 
pitate in making his protest against the supposed intentions of the Austrian 
Government. His Highness also stated that he should desist from carrying 
out the armament of the Servian provinces which had been commenced, and 
that he believed the Government of the Sultan would no longer think it 
necessary to place a corps d'armée on his frontiers. 

The Austrian Consul-General reports the arrival of M. de Fonton (the 
Russian Chancellor of Legation in ienna) at Belgrade, and expresses his 
belief that the opinions given by that gentleman as to the good feelings and 
good intentions of his Government towards the established order of things in 
Servia, and the maintenance of the ‘T’reaties with reference to that country, will 
have the best effeet in securing its tranquillity and peace,

My Lord, Vienna, August 25, 1853. 

| HAVE this day transmitted to your Lordship two telegraphic despatches, 
both from Baron Bruck to Count Buol, the one of the 18th an the second of 
the 19th. I am happy to say this last despatch gives & more favourable expla- 
nation of what has taken place at Constantinople, as to the Vienna project of 
note, than the former one, os it states the acceptance of that note with modifi- 
cations by the Sultan. 

‘These modifications have been viewed by Count Buol with great regret, 
because they do not appear to have been sufliciently necessary to have imposed 
upon the Turkish Government the abligation of insisting upon them, in oppo- 
eition to the advice of the Governments its allies, with the certainty of ocea- 
sioning delay in the arrangement of the questions at issue, and the risk of 
reopening a discussion which, by the aceeptation of the note by the Emperor of 
Russia, might have been considered as nearly cloged. 

Count Buol hopes, however, that this most regrettable delay may be the 
only check which may arise to the Dron settlement of these affairs, as the 
modifications in the note are generally rather verbal than affecting any material 
interests; and Baron Meyendorff has expressed his expectation and belief, that 
they will not prevent the accept ‘on of the note as it will now be forwarded to 
St. Petersburgh. 

The only alteration which appears to be of any particular importance is the 
one in the third paragraph, which inserts the words “ par la Sublime Porte” after 
the words ‘Ja protection.”

Lord Cowley to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received Auguat 30.) 


(No. 640. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, August 29, 1853. 

M. DE LHUYS, who has been absent for a few days from Paris, was 
expected to return here to-day, but is not-arrived; it is supposed that he has 
been summoned by the Emperor to Dieppe. 

M. de Thouvenel, whom I saw this afternoon, was good enough to 
communicate to me (in confidence, as he had no authority to do so) the 
substance of the despatches of the 15th instant, received yesterday by the 
regular packet from onstantinople. M. de la Cour at that date foresaw the 
result which has since been communicated by telea eet of the negotiations 
between the Representatives of the Four Powers and the Porte to induce the 
atter to accept the text of the Vienna note. 

He gives, | am sorry to say, a very unsatisfactory account of the state of 
the negotiations, and of matters in general at Constantinople. The Turkish 
Ministers were unanimous in their opinion not to accept the Vienna note 
without modifications and without guarantee that in its modified form it should 
not become in the hands of Russia an instrament for future attack. If this 
could not be obtained, it was better in their judgment to continue the struggle 
at once, and persist in defence of their honour and independence. Reshid Pasha 
was looked upon with suspicion, as the representative of a pacific policy, and 
every effort made, even by his colleagues, to ensure his downfall; and he himself, 
in order to secure his place, had become as warlike in language and as 
untractable in negotiations as the most violent of the anti-Russian party. The 
very acceptance of the Vienna note by Russia, instead of proving an assistance 
to the Four Powers, was a fresh embarrassment, “ Russia,” say the Turks, 
‘would not have accepted what it would be fit for the Porte to agree to.” It 
waa considered an insult to ask the Sultan to accept the note without the 
power of altering a single word. 

M. de la Cour adds that he cannot conceal from himself that the behaviour 
and language of the Divan is in painful unison with the public feelings. 

On the other hand, a correspondence which had taken Bec between 
Omer Pasha and Prince Gortchakoff, made a collision on the Danube if not 
probable at least very possible. Omer Pasha had, as your Lordship knows he 
was instructed to do, theeatened to fire on Russian boats ascending the Danube 
above a certain height. The Prince had replied that the fire would be returned, 

Thave, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


No. 271. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No. 337.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, August 30, 1853. 

HER Majesty’s Government learn with sincere satisfaction from your 
Excellency's despatch No. 633, the views entertained by M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
in regard to Turkey and tothe proceedings of Russia in reference to that Empire ; 
and this satisfaction arises not alone on account of the sound and disinterested 
policy which those views indicate, but because they cannot fail more closely to 
cement the alliance and friendly feelings which now bind the two countries 
together. 

The communications that have passed during the last six months between 
them can leave no doubt as to the sincere desire of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment to maintain the integrity of the Turkish Empire, or consequently of their 
readiness to cooperate with France in any measure for preventing its dismem- 
berment. 


245 


Her Majesty's Government have reason to believe that similar views are 
entertained by Austria and Prussia, and they agree with M. Drouyn de Lhuys as 
to the importance of ascertaining the opinions of the Emperor of Russia upon the 
subject, although they doubt whether the present moment would be favourable for 
the purpose. ‘The settlement of pending differences between Russia and Turkey 
would appear to be the fitting opportunity for guarding against the recurrence 
of events such as those which have lately caused so much alarm and ineon- 
venience ; but should the Emperor of Russia refuse to associate himsell in the 
proposed course of policy, Her Majesty's Government consider that his determi- 
nation, however much to be lamented, should not deter the Four Powers from 
actine in concert with respect to Turkey, and agreeing as to the measures best 
caleulated to ensure the maintenance of peace and the existing balance of power 
in Europe. 

Her Majesty's Government do full justice to the disinterested policy of France 
upon this subject, as developed to you by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, but they claim 
equal credit for that of Great Britain; and they desire it to be distinctly under- 
stood that territorial aggrandisement is neither sought for nor desired by the 
people of England. 

As very erroneous ideas have at times existed with respect to our views 
upon Egypt, Her Majesty's Government wish also that it should be distinctly 
understood that we have no other object than to preserve a free communication 
through that country with our Indian possessions, and that no arrangement 
eould answer our purpose better than that which now exists. 


Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord, Therapia, August 11, 1853. 

AT alate hour of the evening, the day before yesterday, | received from 
Lord Westmorland a despatch, transmitting to me in copy his reports to your 
Lordship of the 29th and 31st ultimo, by way of reply to the proposition which, 
founded on your Lordship’s instructions to me, and adopted by the Porte, I had 
forwarded to Vienna on the 10th and 23rd of the same month, in concert with 
the Representatives of Austria, France, and Prussia, with the view of its being 
subsequently conveyed to St. Petersburgh and laid before the Russian Cabinet. 

he information thus transmitted to me shows that the Austrian Govern- 
ment has stopped, or rather, in so far us they are concerned, set aside, the letter 
addressed to Count Nesselrode by Reshid Pasha, together with the Porte’s 
ultimatum and declaration, superseding them by a projet de note to which the 
French and British Governments had given their assent, before they knew 
anything of the plan of arrangement adopted here. 

The Internuncio’s language, as addressed repeatedly to me, and, as | 
understand, to M. de la Cour also, had not prepared us for this. Baron Bruck 
had every appearance of entertaining a strong persuasion that: the proporals 
forwarded from Constantinople would be favourably received at St, Petersburgh, 
and that the Porte’s explanatory act of protestation alone contained enough to 
satisfy the Russian Government, 508 

Be that og it may, there was no room to doubt that our communications 
had been suspended ut Vienna, and that the Internuncio would eall upon the 
Porte to give up its ultimatum in favour of the Austrian note. : ; 

It was, moreover, evident that Her Majesty’s Representative at Vienna, in 


252 


transmitting to me the three telegraphic despatches inclosed with his despatch 


to me of the Ist instant, expected that I should feel bound to support the 
Internuncio’s demand. | 

Tt remained for me to consider, what course it behoved me to take in 
expectation of direct instructions from Her Majesty's Government. 

Looking to the telegraphic despatches I o served, that although your 
Lordship had directed the transmission of our communications to Petersburgh 
to be suspended, and had accepted, in concert with France, Count Buol’s note 
amended in London, desiring me to be informed that Her Majesty's Government 
wished it to be adopted by the Porte, there was no evidence that your Lordship 
had received my despatches of July 20, anda moral certainty that you had not 
received those of the 23rd, when the last of the telegraphic notices was 
sent from England. lie 

On the other hand, it was to be presumed that your Lordship would lose 
no time in sending back the ‘‘ Caradoc” from Marseilles with instructions to 
me, after receiving my despatches of the 23rd; and it was reasonable to expect, 
on a calculation of dates and distances, that any instructions forwarded by that 
fast steamer would reach me in three or four days, 

Such being the state of the case, and considering that as the Austrian note 
had been already transmitted from Vienna to Petersburgh, the delay of a few 
days here was of little importance, I determined not to forego unnecessarily 
the prospect of acting with the advantage of your Lordship’s deliberate 
instructions. S' 

When, therefore, the French Ambassador, wishing to compare notes with 
me, called here on Tuesday night, and the Internuncio on the following 
morning, I declined taking any official step or expressing any official opinion 
until | had allowed a fair time for the arrival of the expected despatches from 
England, they both did me the honour to acquiesce courteously in the intinia- 
tion; and the Internuncio informed me, that he had communicated the 
substance of his instructions on the preceding night to Reshid Pasha, but had 
not received from His Highness any reply committing him to an opinion, 

When, at an early hour next day, fsaw the Ottoman Minister, he contirnied 
Baron Bruck's statement, and on my part I was careful not to express any 
opinion respecting the merits of the Austrian note. I left him with an under- 
standing that the new proposal would not be submitted to the Council before 
the 14th instant, unless my instructions arrived in time to admit of an earlier 
meeting, Not having found the Prussian Envoy at home when I called upon 
him, | am unable to say how he is circumstance on this occasion; but it ts 
natural to suppose that if he had received fresh instructions from his Court on 
the question of common interest, he would not have left me in ignorance of their 
tenor. : 

It is proper for me to state in conclusion, that T have not yet received, 
though | have seen, the Projet de Note transmitted from Vienna.

The Porte to the Bey of Servia. 


(‘Translation.) August 8, 1853. 

THE reply given by your Highness to the communication of the Austrian 
Consul at Belgrade relative to the introduction, on certain grounds, of troops 
into Servia, was such as might be expected from your sound judgment, and has 
met with His Imperial Majesty's approval. 

The Porte cannot consent to admit the troops of any Government whatso- 
ever into Servia, one of her provinecs; and as the Sublime Porte attaches much 
importance to the preservation of the actual state of things in Servia under your 
Highness’ rule and administration, his Excellency Chekib Effendi has been 
specially appointed by His Majesty to advise with your Highness on all necessary 
matters. 

Of the troops under arms in different quarters owing to the dispute which 
has arisen between Russia and the Porte, those which are in the neighbourhood 
of Servia will afford every necessary support to your administration. 

His Majesty the Sultan is animated with the best dispositions towards

Inclosure 2 in No. 275. 
The Porte to the Ottoman Embassy al Vienna. 


(Translation ) August 8, 1$43 

EXPLANATIONS having been demanded of the Austrian Legation here 
on certain communications made by the Austrian Consul at Belgrade to the 
Pasha in command and to the Prince, concerning the entrance of Austrian troops 
in Servia, grounded on certain doubts with reference to a change in the present 
tranquil position of that province, it was stated in reply that the Austrian 
Legation here had no information on the subject, but that the military prepara. 
tions made in the neighbourhood of Servia were only of a precautionary nature 
intended to intimidate the Servians; that some parties in Servia wanted to avail 
themselves of the present difficulties, with the idea of creating troubles: in 
the province; that this would neither suit the Sublime Porte nor Austria, who 
had so many Servian subjects; and considering that the Servian Administration 
would not be strong enough to meet such a contingency, Austria intended, in 
order that things should not come to that pass, to stifle and put down any such 
movements whether they manifested themselves or not. i 

It is inferred from this statement that it is the intention of Austria to move 
troops into Servia; but on the other hand, it was stated at length to the Inter- 
nuncio that His Imperial Majesty the Sultan is, praise be to God, strong enough 
to put down any seditious movements which might take place in Servia and one 
of his provinces, and that the necessary measures will be looked toy that the 
Prince will be py on his guard, and that a funectionary of distinction may be 
sent to Belgrade on a special mission, to act as circumstances may require, 80 
that there would be no necessity whatever for Austria to move troops into 
Serviay that the Sublime Porte could never consent to such a thing, and that 
Austria ought ta beware herself of such bad examples, | 

His Excellency the Internuncio admitted that there would be no occasion 
for Austrian troops, if such prompt and effective measures were tuken by the 
Porte. 

Your Excellency will observe from these details that the Porte, in the fulfil- 
ment of its administrative duties, is engaged in taking every measure for securing 
the tranquillity of Servia, A special letter has been also sent to the Prince to 
ps him on the alert; and your Excellency is now instructed by order of His 
Majesty the Sultan to make known officially, and once for all, to his Execllency 
the Austrian Minister for Foreign Affuirs, Count Buol, that the Porte cannot 


255 


consent to the introduction of troops by Austria into Servia, and that, in short, 
she cannot admit such a thing on whatever ground or pretext 1t may he sought 
to found it. 

Your Excellency will therefore make this communication duly te Count 
Buol, and communicate his answer to me without delay.

No. 276. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 31.) 


(No. 214.) 
My Lord, Theramia, August 13, 1853, 


YESTERDAY evening, between 5 and 6 o'clock, Her Majesty's steam- 
vessel “Caradoc” arrived here, with your Lordship’s despatches of the 2nd 
and 3rd instant, At an early hour this morning I waited on Reshid Pasha, and 
communicated to him the substance of your Lordship's instructions relative to 
the projet de note already received from Vienna. 1 called his attention to the strong 
and earnest manner in whieh that paper was recommended to the acceptance of 
the Porte, not only by Her Majesty’s Government, but also by the Cabinets of 
Austria, France, and Prussia, I reminded him of the intelligence which had 
arrived from St. Petersburgh the day before by telegraph, purporting that the 
Emperor of Russia had signified his readiness to aceept the same note. I urged, 
moreover, the importance of his engaging the Porte to come to a decision with 
the least possible delay, and I put him at the same time in full possession of 
the motives by which your Lordship had been actuated in approving the 
detention at Vienna of His Highness’s letter to Count Nesselrode, and the 
transmission to St. Petersburgh and Constantinople of the above-mentioned 
projet de note, which had already received the eanction of the Four Powers, 
when the Porte’s ultimatum reached Vienna. I added that the two Projects, 
besides being identic in form, would be found on exammation to be essentially 
similar in their general tenor, not only with each other, but even, it might 
almost be suid, with the note originally prepared by himself for communication 
to Prince Menchikoff. 

The Pasha listened with a very good grace to all 1 said, and acquiesced 
silently in the change of plan which I had explained to him, and of which he 
had been previously apprised. He gave me, however, to understand that there 
were parts of the note whieh were not satisfactory to him, and to which he 
anticipated objections on the part of his Government. 

Of the passages thus pointed out as exceptionable, two only appear to 
involve considerations of any weight, presenting, in the one case, a question of 
fact, in the other a question of unsafe interference on the part of Russia, 

In the beginning of the second paragraph the Emperors of Russia are 
represented, hypothetically, as having at all times displayed an active solicitude 
for the privileges and immunities of the Greek Church, ‘The fact, however, 
according to Reshid Pasha, is that the Sovereigns of Russia never displayed their 
veal on behalf of those privileges before the negotiation of the Treaty at Kainardji, 
Ile therefore proposes to draw a distinction between the general freedom of worship, 
at all times an object of interest to Russia, with respect to the Greek Church, 
and the privileges granted to its clergy especially maintained by the Ottoman 
Sultans, marking that difference by the use of corresponding terms in the note. 

Again, ut the end of the third paragraph, a form of expression is used, 
which, in the Pasha’s opinion, if not amended would have the effect of extending 
Russian patronage over all those subjects of the Porte who belong to the Greek 
Church and its establishments, A consequence of this description ts appre- 
hended, from the terms of the Note, because they would entitle Russia to 
jarticipate in the concessions made to Austria by the Treaties of Carlowitz, 
Belgrade and Sistova, which include all persons of the Roman Catholic persuasion 
in Turkey, without any reservation as to the Sultan's subjects. This danger 
was carefully avoided in the projet de note drawn up here. 

For your Lordship’s more complete information, I have the honour to 
inclose herewith the Articles of the Austrian Treaties which bear upon this 
question, and ulso a paper exhibiting all He passages in Count Buol’s projet de note

My Lord, Theramia, August 14, 1853, 

THE projet de note transmitted from Vienna was laid before the Council 
to-day by Reshid Pasha. All the Ministers were present to the number ot 
seventeen, including the Sheik ul Islam, A stormy debate ensued, and the 
majority of the Council declared it to be their firm intention to reject the new 
proposal, even if amendments were introduced. ‘They founded this determina- 
tion on the preference they gave to that draft of a note which the Porte had 
decided on forwarding to St. Petersburgh through the Austrian Cabinet, and on 
the declaration which had been formally made by Reshid Pasha when he con- 
signed it on the 28rd ultimo to the Four Representatives, purporting that 
nothing beyond the terms of that raft would be aceepted by the Ottoman 
Government, [t was their opinion that no necessity obliged the Porte to. recede 
from its former resolution in order to yield to a proposal which was not in 
accordance with their views. 

The Minister for Foreign Affairs having submitted that the new projet de 
note was founded in some measure on the draft which he had himself prepared 
for Prince Menchikoff, the Council decided that time should be allowed for its 
incmbers:ta compare the two papers at their leisure. 

The adjournment which followed is not to extend beyond to-day or 
to-morrow. 

Inclosed herewith is the list of the members who were present, The 
statement which precedes is the substance of M. Pisani's report to me on the 
authority of Reshid Pasha,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(LReceived August 31.) 


(No, 219.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 14, 1853, 

1 HAVE to offer my acknowledgments for the endeavours made under your 
Lordship's instructions to do justice to my diplomatic character and conduct 
during the late negotiations here, I have observed in the various corre- 
spondence transmitted for my information Sir H. Seymour’s recital of what 
passed between him and Count Nesselrode when he communicated to his Excel- 
lency your Lordship’s instructions respecting me. I have been too long 
aceastomed to indications of prejudice and unexplained ill-will from that quarter 
not to be prepared for more, and | feel obliged to Sir Hamilton for having done 
whatever depended upon him to set my conduct in a proper light. The 


259 


Emperor of Russia has done me more honour than he intended, more indeed 
than I can presume to deserve, in attaching so much importance to my personal 
influence. What little eredit I may be supposed to enjoy, beyond what is 
naturally due to me as the Queen's Representative, has arisen In & great 
degree out of my resistance to proceedings sanctioned by His Imperial Majesty, 
which have had the effect of identifying the performance of my duty with the 
natural feelings and vital interests of this Government and its subjects of all 
classes. 

But while I am more or less indifferent to attacks originating in causes 
which have obtained for me your Lordship's confidence and the approval of Her 
Majesty’s Government, | observe with far other sentiments the beginnings of a 
jealous and insidious course of action brought to bear upon my position here by 
those who profess to have views in common with Her Majesty's Embassy, and 
whose instructions I have been led to suppose are essentially similar to mine as 
to the great object of our present solicitude. 

It appears that Baron de Bruck has been actively employed during the last 
two or three days in visiting the Turkish Ministers and other members of the 
Council with the view of recommending Count Buol’s note to their acceptance. 
| am far from meaning to criticise so laudable a display of zeal, but looking to 
what passed in the Ottoman Council to-day, I may be allowed to question the 
success of his exertions, and to express my surprise that some of the Ministers 
who voted for rejection, sans phrase, were exactly those whom he had visited, 1 
revret, moreover, to learn that the language employed by his Excellency in 
pleading the cause of peace was understood to imply both jealousy of my 
influence and mistrust of Reshid Pasha, who is not of course pleased with the 
kind of appeal which he has made at the present critical juncture from the 
Minister for Foreign Affairs to that Minister's colleagues in the Council. I have 
reason to believe that Baron de Bruck used so little disguise as to tell Reshid 
Pasha himself that while he pretended to uphold the independence of his country 
against Russia, he did not hesitate to place it in a state of dependence on me. 

What does this mean? Is there anything in my correspondence, anything 
in my conduct,to warrant a suspicion that I counteract the Internuncio when his 
objects are legitimate, and above all similar to those of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment? I appeal to your Lordship’s knowledge of my proceedings, and T would 
also appeal to the Internuneio’s immediate predecessor, the late Chargé dAffatres. 
Or is the spirit of Austrian policy, as applied permanently to this country, at 
varianee with the salutary advice which, under the instructions or with the 
approbation of your Lordship, 1 tender from time to time to the Sultan and his 
Ministers? If so, L can understand, however little | may admire, the foresight 
which has led Baron de Bruck, even while we are acting in concert, to lay a 
foundation for the overthrow of British influence in my person at this Court, 

The French Ambassador has rivalled the Internuneio in locomotive activity 
during the last few days. His principal object has, no doubt, been the acceptance 
of Count Buol’s note. He has also applied for an audience of the Sultan, as like- 
wise has Baron de Bruck, the latter having to present an autograph letter from 
the Emperor of Austria, and M. de la Cour wishing, as he says, to address the 
Sultan on the present state of affairs. 

When Reshid Pasha informed me that M.de la Cour had applied for an 
audience, he added that the French interpreter had inquired whether he meant to 
attend, and on his expressing a wish to know my opinion, 1 advised him by no 
means to volunteer a retirement. ‘Lhe Pasha appears to have acted in con- 
sequenee with becoming spirit, as your Lordship will perceive on reading the 
extract, inclosed herewith, of M. Pisani’s report. 

If M. de la Cour, like M. de Bruck, was minded to disparage Reshid Pashe, 
and also by a side wind to impair my influence with the Sultan, I trust that his 
‘ntention is foiled for this time: But it is not the less my duty to apprise your 
Lordship of some passages in the conduct of that Ambassador, which seem, in 
my humble judgment, to be rather inconsistent with an earnest anxiety to 
hasten the acceptance of Count Buol’s note, 7 would not dwell upon his having 
assisted Reshid Pasha in preparing amendments to that note, as he might have 
been actuated by mere good nature, though it is evident that such assistance 
given out at such a moment could hardly fail to diminish the chances of a com- 
plete acceptance, But I learn that he has informed the Ottoman Minister of 
Count Walewski’s proposals to your Lordship, and led him to believe that the 


260 


two Governments of France and England are already prepared to take ulterior 
and active measures in support of this Empire. He had before made some 
inquiries of the Pasha with reference to the disembarkation of troops on the 
Turkish coasts, and he now inquired whether the Porte was disposed to consider 
the Dardanelles as already open to the passage of the squadrons. On receiving 
a Beenie answer, his Excellency said that he should speak with me upon the 
subject. 

When M. de la Cour ealled shortly afterwards to execute this intention, | 
avowed my knowledge of what had passed on the question of ulterior measures 
between your Lordship and Count Walewski, but added my conviction, that 
Her Majesty's Government, though by no means blind to the eventual exigencies 
of the future, had not contemplated the adoption of any such measures in the 
present state of the negotiations. 

Lam the more particular in mentioning these circumstances, because | think 
it unlikely that M. de la Cour should take any step or employ any language not 
fully authorized by his Government. aie ;

M. E, Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(Private and most Confidential.) 
(Extract.) August 13, 1853. 

M. DE LA COUR told this morning Reshid Pasha that he thought of 
having his audience quite in a private manner, and consequently he would save 
him the trouble to assist, 

His Highness replied that he might have a private interview with the 
Sultan if he liked, but could not have it without his being present ; and that the 
intention he expressed denoted a want of confidence on his part. 

“It is true’ added the Pasha, “that the British Ambassador had a private 
interview with the Sultan, accompanied only by his first interpreter; but it must 
he borne in mind that there was no Minister for Foreign Affairs at that time. 
During the Ramazan Lord Stratford had a private audience of the Sultan, but | 
was present. Should you insist upon avoiding my being present, I shall consider 
it as un offence, and shall tender my resignation.” 

Upon this M. de la Cour answered that he never intended to offend his 
Highness, but only wished not to intrude upon his valuable time, in a moment 
when he was overwhelmed with business.

Inclosure in No. 279. 
M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Therapia, August 14, 1859. 

RESHID PASHA informs me that Baron de Bruck called on him to-day 
at the Porte to urge the necessity of accepting, without further delay, the draft 
of the note approved by the Emperor of Raley 

His Highness replied that the draft in question might perhaps be adopted, 
but with amendments; but as it now stands it was utterly impossible. © You 
saw,” said the Pasha to the Internuncio, “ all my colleagues, and | suppose you 
are in possession of their opinion on the subject.” He answered in the athrma- 
tive; and added, that some appeared rather well disposed, and others very 
adverse, ‘“ As to making alterations,” continued he, “1 think it very difficult 
and almost impossible, the note being already accepted by the Emperor.” 

Upon this Reshid Pasha observed, that the Emperor, who was to receive 
the note, ought not to be so particular about the wording ; whereas the Porte, 
who was to give it, ought of course to be careful and weigh every word. I 
really cannot conceive, said the Pasha to Baron Bruck, how the Cabinets could, 
previously to consulting the Porte, which is so deeply concerned in the matter, 
submit the proposal to St. Petersburgh. More than once, said he, the Porte 
was told by the Four Representatives, both verbally and in writing, that she was 
the best judge in the pending question, and now, in contradiction to all this, the 
Cabinets take upon themselves to draw up u note without the knowledge or 
concurrence of the party more immediately interested, and have it also accepted 
by the Emperor,

No, 280. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 31.) 


(No, 221. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therupia, August 16, 1853. 


| HAD a long and interesting conversation last night with Reshid Pasha, 
whom I met at the French Ambassador's, where an entertainment was given in 
honour of the Emperor Louis Napoleon's name or birthday. 

His Highness told me he had attended in the morning at three audiences, 
the concurrence of which had obliged the Council to postpone its udjourned 
meeting till to-day. It appears that M. de la Cour and Baron Bruck had, each 
in his turn, advised the Sultan with earnestness to accept the Austrian note, and 
that the Sultan had replied to both in gracious but general terms, committing 
himself to no opinion, and without any difference but that which was caused by 
the presentation of a letter from the Emperor of Austria. 

The third audience had been given to General Prim, and Commander 
Reares, who, as your Lordship knows, is on his way to the Turkish camp, and 
who may be supposed to awaken the sympathies of ‘Turkey at a moment when 
the Spanish and Ottoman Courts are both excluded from diplomatic relations 
with Hussia. 

The Pasha then confirmed what M. Pisani had previously reported to me 
respecting the state of opinions in the Council, and assured me that there was 
no chance of obtaining a majority in favour of neoe RHE Count Buol’s note. 
The only way to avoid a complete retusal was, he said, to propose the note with 


certain modifications. He could not, himself, sign the note us it was then 
worded. He gave credit to Her Majesty’s Government for the most. friendly 
intentions, and lamented on that account the more deeply that the dangerous 
extent, as he conceived, to which concession had been carried at Vienna should 
have been overlooked in London, He could not, he said, conceal from me 
that a persistence in the same course would alienate the sympathies of this 
country from England, and place our influence here on a footing quite different 
2M 


262 


from that on which it now stood, It was unnecessary for him to tell me how 
much he should personally regret so unfortunate a change, but it would not be 
in his power to prevent it. 

I endeavoured to counteract these impressions to little purpose. He saw 
the objections to our proposal in strong colours, insisted upon the fatal con- 
sequences of accepting it in its present shape, and intimated that it would have 
been better for the Porte to yield in the first instance, than to have been so 
strenuously encouraged and then, as he thought, so unreasonably abandoned. 

All that [ could obtain from him was an assurance that he would endeavour 


to een his amendments in the most conciliatory terms, and preyail, if 


possible, upon his colleagues to allow a sufficient interval between the decision 
of the Ministerial Council, and the meeting of the General Council, which would 
ensue, for communication with the Four Representatives. 

It was evident, on the whole, that Reshid Pasha’s disapproval of Count 
Buol’s note had been strengthened by the opposition declared to it in Council, 
and that he could not hope to carry his plan of amendments unless he took 
eolour in some measure from the hostile party. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 31.) 


(No, 222.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 18, 1853. 

AS soon as 1 saw reason to believe that the Turkish Ministers were 
resolved not to accept Count Buol’s note without amendment, not being 
authorized to use intimidating language, | felt myself free, and indecd compelled 
hy a sense of duty, to suggest some form of decision which might present the 
character of an acceptance, and yet leave room for such an adjustment of terms 
as would completely secure the Porte. My conversation with Reshid Pasha at 
the French Ambassador's, following on what I had learned from ML. Pisani of 
the opinions entertained by a majority of the Council, gave certainty to my 
convictions onthat score. | nevertheless abstained, though not without difficulty, 
from making any admissions calculated to encourage the Porte in its resistance. 

The Ministerial Council was to meet again on the following day, and would 
probably take its decision on the pending question. I employed the interval in 
trying to discover some adequate expedient, and finally settled upon the only 
one which seemed to offer a chance of suecess. It was simply that the Porte 
should signify its acceptance of the note under its own construction of the 
objectionable passages, and, for securities, rely on the assent dnd sanetion of the 
Four Powers, A proposition to this effect, accompanied with the necessary 
explanations, was conveyed to Reshid Pasha by my direction, while the Council 
wis sitting. Mr. Alison, who had charge of the message, was instructed to 
wilthold it from the Ottoman Minister until he had ascertained, which it was 
not diffienlt for him to do, that the turn of the deliberations evieed a manifest 
intention to throw out the note in its present form. Tt was under these cirenm- 
stances that the Pasha received my suggestion from Mr Alison, and, on fis 
return to the council-roomt, submitted it, as such, to his colleagues before the 
clove of the debate. This, my Lord, is what he has since told me, adding that 
the proposal did not meet with favour from the assembly. 

On calling yesterday, to learn from his own lips the exact state of the ease, 
I found that Reshid Pasha had drawn upa note or memorandum, exphinatory 
of ibe Porte's abjections, and expressive of a grateful deference to the Four 
Powers, but declining the object of their friendly recommendations, unless it 

mply amended in his sense, He translated the whole paper verbally for 
ormation. [could only return his confidence by urging once more the 

sooimtment which the Porte’s refusal would occasion to the Powers most 
ted in its welfare, and reminding him of the consequences which were but 
coo bieely to ensue from such ao decision, ‘The tone and language of his 
oou)position appeared to be unexceptionable, and T confess that in substance it 


263 


struck me as justifying, more than I felt myself at liberty to admit, or had even 
in some respects anticipated, the course which his Government was prepared to 
adopt. 

Perceiving my reserve, the Pasha was deeply affected; his eyes overflowed 
with tears; forgetful for a moment of his rank, he kissed my hand, and in the 
most moving terms implored me not to forsake his country in the midst of 
distresses and dangers which it could not avoid without an unworthy sacrifice. 
The scene was to me a most painful one, and not the less so from ta ing place 
in the presence of a Greek, whose age, ex] erience, and British sympathies 
entitle him to my respect, and whose religion did not prevent him from taking, 
to all appearance, a cordial share m the Vasha’s sentiments, 

Returning home with very uneasy reflections, I determined to make one 
more effort. before the meeting of the Great Council, in order if possible to 
imvest the Porte’s decision with that character of constructive acceptance which 
might enable your Lordship to exert a powerful influence, and, in concert with 
France and the other Powers, realize the proposed arrangement im terms 
satisfactory to the Ottoman Government, and on that account more likely to 
earry with it the general approval of Europe, My notion was, that the note or 
memorandum proposed by Reshid Pasha should contain by way of resumé, a 
passace identical with the draft inclosed, and that I should propose at a mecting 
of the Four Representatives a form of reply more or less sinnlar to the words 
inclosed herewith under letter (3).

nothing better under circumstances fraught with danger to this Empire, and with 
serious disturbance to the most important interests of society. 

Such as it is, | have directed M. Pisani to propose it confidentially to 
Reshid Pasha, as coming personally from me, and I have reason to think that 
his Highness will adopt the suggestion, if he can suceced in obtaining the 
Council's assent.

WE still give a decided preference to the last note prepared at Constanti- 
nople; but-acknowledging the friendly intentions of the Four Powers, and out 
of deference to their earnest recommendations, relying at the same time on their 
continued sympathy and support, we are willing to accept, and do in fact adopt, 
the note arranged by them, similar as it is in form and intent to our own, 
provided that the passages already pointed out as being of a doubtful and 
dangerous signification, should be understood in the sense explained by us and 
modified accordingly in the terms of expression, with the assent of the Powers, 
and the security resulting therefrom.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receired August 31.) 
(No. 223.) 


My Lord, | Therama, August 19, 1853. 

_ 1AM fully aware of the honour conferred upon me by the serious attention 
which, as your Lordship has been kind enough to inform me, Her Majesty's 
Government have paid to the subject matter of my report No. 132 of this year. 
Encouraged by so flattering a mark of consideration, I venture to submit a few 
remarks suggested to me by passages of your Lordship’s despatch No. 136, in 
reply to mine. 

___ In advising the Sultan to meet the occupation of the Principalities by a 
simple protest and appeal, 1 had a two-fold object in view : first, to afford time 
for endeavouring to settle the pending difference by a well-concerted and defi- 
nitive negotiation ; and secondly, to prepare for the effectual employment of 
other means in case negotiation should fail. I was deeply impressed with) a 
foresight of the evils attending hesitation and uncertainty, when Russia had 
taken so aggressive a position, when public feeling was so completely roused 
and when such vast interests were at stake, not only here, but in Europe also. 
Tt was not then in weakness, or with a view to any sacrifice of principle, but in 
the strength of a good cause, and in order to obtain a successful issue—in peace 
if possible, but at all events to obtain it—that L tendered the advice which Her 
Majesty's Government have honoured with their approval. 

I have felt from the first that a question of so much moment as that whieh 
has been brought into play by Russia, could not, if once it passed the bounds of 
diplomatic discussion, be brought to the desirable solution by any partial or 
limited application of foree. At the same time it was evident that the principle 
for which the Porte was contending could not be surrendered without a virtual 
abandonment of what is called the Eastern question; nor could it be visconti 
or doubtfully vindicated with any degree of satisfuction to public opinion, or Any 
fair prospect of durable tranquillity. — . Tee 

_ Under these impressions, on the departure of Prince Menchikolf, I sub- 
mitted to your Lordship whatever occurred to me at that time as to the dangers 
which threatened Turkey, and the momentous interests to which she could 
tay nel in soliciting the continued good offices and active support of Great 
ritain. 

_ When at a later period the Russian troops were about to enter the Princi- 
pee | implored your Lordship with increased earnestness to contemplate the 
astern question in all its magnitude, and to purse a course of policy which 
would successively enlist every kind of exertion in favour of a triumphant 
Issue, 

In proportion as | urged the claims of Turkey to a degree of support 
from England, which might eventually invelve us in war, | felt: more stronel 
the duty of not concealing the weak points of this Empire, but, on the contrar : 
of giving them a distinctive place in any calculation to be made of its internal 
resources, and of the means which might be required from without for its 
defence. 

My starting points in argument were, the vastness of the interests at stake 
the urgeney of making timely provision for their security, and the heavy demands 
ubich might be thereby entailed on British generosity, good fnith, and rese- 
ution. ) 

: It was no more an object of mine to gloss over the oppressions of Turkish 
administration than to conceal the vulnerable points of the Turkish Empire 
Of course I did my best to obtain the correction of those evils which are always 
rife in declining or misgoverned countries ; but L did not understand that the 
merits of the Eastern question were of a strictly administrative nature. I 


265 


thought that the Porte’s dependence and the balance of power in Europe were 
considerations of primary importance, and that the exigencies of the crisis were 
rather to be used for pleading the cause of improvement than the want of 
sufficient progress in that respect was to be viewed as a motive for leaving the 
crisis to take care of itself, 

Great, no doubt, is the peril to which Turkey would be exposed in a single- 
handed contest with Russia, and it is probable that without succours from 
abroad the Sultan's Government would be compelled ultimately to submit, But 
there is also much danger in a continuance of the present state of expensive 
and irritating preparation ; and the Porte, unassisted, may find a fatal result in 
the one case as in the other, There arc, no doubt, reasons for exhausting all 
the means of negotiation to avert a disaster ; but there are also reasons for 
pushing negotiation with vigour to a definite end, and still more for preparing 
and combining other and stronger ways of rescue in ease of diplomatic failure. 

| learn from the close of your Lordship’s despatch, that Her Majesty's 
Government, though determined to leave no honourable expedient untried for 
the preservation of peace, are equally determined to maintain that principle 
which is now the main object of contention, and to take in due season, should 
it he necessary, more active measures for the protection of Turkey. 

With such prospective intentions, Her Majesty’s Government will learn 
with pleasure that the apprehensions of disturbance and massacre in the Turkish 
Provinces, and of fanatical exasperation against. the Christians here, have been 
nowhere realized. Ihave reason to believe that much exaggeration has pre- 
vailed on those subjects, Greatly asa thorough redress of grievances, accom- 
panied with administrative reform, is needed in Turkey, the present state of 
alarm and excitement among the Turkish population has not, with a few local 
and transient exceptions, had the effect of increasing the evils which existed 
before. Even among the Greeks and in Bulgaria the expectations of Russian 
partizans have not been fulfilled. 

The Turkish authorities on their side have been so careful to repress any 
tendencies to disorder among the Mussulmans, that the painful cireumstanices to 
which I drew attention some time ago have not been followed hy the conse- 
quences then apprehended. 

Lam able, on the contrary, to state, without fear of contradiction, that in 
all which concerns the political proceedings and military operations directed by 
the Government and its principal functionaries, a most creditable display of 
firmness, cnerzy, and prudence has been maintained. ‘The capital and its neigh- 
bourhood have enjoyed unbroken tranquillity, notwithstanding apprehensions 
which at first seemed to warrant the adoption of precautionary measures, The 
country las been traversed in various directions by bodies of armed men—regu- 
lars, irregulars, militia, and policemen—without oceasioning any complaint of a 
<erious nuture not immediately attended to. ‘The defences of the Bosphorus, of 
the Balkan, and of the Danube, have been brought, in the opinion of competent 
judges, to a state of comparative efliciency, with admirable speed. ‘The army 
and navy are both described, by officers who have reported them, a8 most respect- 
able in numbers, discipline, and exercise. Even money and provisions are in 
some way or other procured in sufficient quantities to supply the wants of the 
moment, and no serious anxiety appears to be entertained by the Government 
in these respects. 

The success which has hitherto attended the progress of these operations 1s, 
no doubt, a source of confidence at the Porte; and a portion of the spirit of late 
exhibited there is traceable to that cause, as well us to the fear of emburrassment 
likely to result from dispersing the army and dismantling the squadron, without 
a satisfactory arrangement, obtained, if not by military, at least by diplomatic 
exertions. ) 

T need not repeat that such exertions are at the same time caleulated to 
undermine the strength of the Empire. But surely they also give the Porte an 
additional claim to European sympathy, and to Europe an additional motive for 
rescuing the object of its solicitude from peril and ruin. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

I have already prepared your Lordship for the Porte’s decision, which 
however it may fall short of the hopes entertained in London, 1 beg to recom- 
mend to the serious and candid appreciation of Her Majesty’s Government. It 
‘s the result of much earnest deliberation. It unites the opinions of all parties. 
It was voted unanimously by a Council of sixty members, comprising the most 
distinguished statesmen of the capital, whether in or out of office. If it does 
not completely represent the public feeling of this country, it only fails in being 
framed with too much forbearance and moderation. j ; 

Your Lordship will observe that the Porte rather accepts than refuses the 
jlan of arrangement recommended to it by the Four Powers, and that the 
interpretations which qualify its acceptance are accompanied with arguments 
and explanations worthy of deliberate attention. ‘ 

I have no hesitation in stating it as my firm conviction, that if the Porte 
be not secured from her present apprehensions of Russian interference, she will 
incur the hazards of war in preference to a tame acquiescence in terms of 
accommodation which she can never be persuaded to reconcile with her safety 
her honour, or her repose. I may add, in conclusion, that the Sultan and his 
Ministers, though much disappointed of late, continue still to reckon upon the 
sympathy and support of the British Government, and [am persuaded that the 
accomplishment of their hopes would be accepted with more pratification from 
that quarter than from any other. |

The sovereign rights and independence of a nation are sacred and inesti-

of the note in question, all Governments have mature experience and local 
knowledge concerning their own affairs, and the conclusions therefore come to 
upon those matters which are submitted to their judgment are not without real

The refusal to assent to the arrangement now put forward, after the

My Lord, Therapia, August 20, 1853, 

AGREEABLY to the instruction contained in your Lordship's despatch 
No. 135 of this year, | have made inquiries as to the causes which delayed the 
completion of that letter, which, under the name of “ fusion,” was to have been 
composed by Reshid Pasha. 

Having addressed my inquiry to the Pasha himself, his Highness informed 
me that sundry incidents had retarded the composition; that while it was 
among the papers submitted to the Sultan, the invasion of the Principalities 
became known, and called away his attention to the Protest, 

On looking back to the dates of that period, I perceive that M. Bruck’s 
suggestion was made about the 22nd of June, and submitted to the Sultan on 
the following day. 

How long it remained with the Sultan T cannot say, for papers sometimes 
remain in the Seraglio u considerable time. But it appears that Reshid was 
occupied with his “fusion” on the 20th, and that next day Baron de Bruck 
proposed clandestinely a separate and wholly inadmissible version, copy of which 
was forwarded at the same time to your Lordship. The suggestion having been 
approved by the Council, was before the Sultan on the 4th of July, and the 
festival of Bayram, which occupies three or four days, followed on the 6th, a day 
before the intelligence arrived of the Russians having erossed the Prath and 
entered the province of Moldavia. On the same day Reshid Pasha, was 
dismissed, a a ministerial crisis, which occupied three days, succeeded, 

On the whole, my Lord, it may be stated with some degree of confidence, 
that the delay and final relinquishment of the “ fusion,” however! the 
‘‘ suzestion” may have been approved by the Sultan, are traceable more or 


271 


less to all the successive causes just mentioned. It may be added, that Reshid 
Pasha had no confidence in the success of the proposed notion, and the cireum- 
stances, joined to the natural effects of the Ramazan and Bayram, which are as 
much “thieves of time” as procrastination itself, might account for a much 
longer delay, The “fusion” was finally dropped in consequence of the act of 
protestation naturally taking its place, at a moment when the Pasha found 
that I could not assume the responsibility of giving an opinion on the paper he 
had imperfectly prepared, until it was officially communicated tu the Four 
Representatives.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received August 31.) 
(No. 229°) 


My Lord, Therapia, August 20, 1853. 

THOUGH | scrupulously abstained from expressing any private opinion on 
the merits of Count Buol’s note while it was under consideration at the Porte, 
| think it incumbent on me to state frankly to your Lordship that the decision 
of the Couneil has in no degree surprised me In making this avowal I have 
exclusively in view those passages of the note to which the Porte objects. It 
really appears to me, with all deference to your Lordship’s superior judgment, 
that the first two of the objectionable passages could hardly stand as they are 
without exposing the Porte to inferences not borne out by facts, and eventually 
to pretensions that it would be equally inconvement, if not dangerous, to admit 
or to resist. 

With respect to the third amendment, its adoption would seem indis- 
pensable, unless it be intended to give Russia the full enjoyment of that right 
of interference which is secured to Austria by her Treaties with the Porte, and 
in particular by that of Sistova. Such a convession when practically claimed 
by Russia, would leave her nothing to desire as to the means of exercising & 
powerful influence on all the concerns of the Greek clergy, and interfering even 
on behalf of the Greek laity subjects of the Porte, 1 have the honour to inclose 
herewith, in copy, the Article of the above-mentioned Treaty to which | 
particularly refer. Confined to Austria, the privilege in question may be 
exercised with little inconvenience to the Porte; but in the hands of Russia, 
applicable to twelve millions of the Sultan's tributary subjects, the same right 
becomes a natural object of suspicion and well-founded apprehension. 

It cannot be necessary for me to trouble your Lordship further on this 
subject, important and delicate ag itis. 1am convinced that Her Majesty's 
Government will give it their fullest consideration, in a spirit of perfect fairness 
to all parties; and I venture to hope thut the result of a further investigation of 
its merits will be favourable to the just interests and expectations of the Porte. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.
