Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received August 31.) 


(No. 641. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, August 29, 1853. 


HAVING profited by the absence of M. Drouyn de Lhuys from Pans, to 
pass a few days at Dieppe, I had the advantage of being able to communicate 
directly with the Emperor on the receipt of the telegraphic intelligence from 
Constantinople that the Ottoman Government had refused to accept without 
modification, the propositions made by the Conference of Vienna for the settle- 
ment of the Eastern question, His Majesty received me with his usual affability, 
and entered at once upon the subject on which 1 had desired to see him, He 
did not conceal his disappointment ab what had occurred, nor bis displeasure at 
the little deference shown by the Porte to the counsels of the Four Powers. He 
said that England and France were placed, by this conduct of the ‘Turkish 
Government, in a position of extreme embarrassment ; and that, for his part, he 
knew not what to advise. He thought, however, that more stringent instructions 
should be sent to the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople, 
with a view of yet obtaining the compliance of the Porte with the propositions 
made from Vienna, and already aceepted by the Emperor of Russia. 

I remarked that, unfortunately, this was not all that was required, since 
M. de la Cour had by telegraph given the French Government to understand 
that the signature by the Porte of the note, even if the modifications were agreed 
to by Russia, depended on the previous evacuation of the Principalities, and on 
certain guarantees—not very clearly explained—against attacks of a like nature 
for the future. Now, it was not likely that the Russian Government would 
accept the latter conditions, even if they admitted the modifications. What, 
then, was to become of the fleets, if both parties heltl out? To remain at Besika 
during the winter months, was all but impossible. ‘Lo retire, W tile the Russians 
remained in the Principalities, was not to be expected ; and yet, to advance 
within the Dardanelles at the moment when Russia had shown herself more 
voneiliatory, and the Porte had pefused to act upon our advice, would haye the 
appearance of a measure of hostility towards the former, and of approbation of 
the conduct of the latter, 

The Emperor said, that as long as the Russians were in the Principalities, 
the fleets could not, in his opinion, retire» but were there no other sate anchor- 
uges to which they might resort, without going to Constantinople? My know- 
ledge of the localities enabled me to tell him that there was an anchorage at 


274 


Gallipoli, towards the other end of the Dardanelles, at the entrance of the Sea 
of Marmora; and I believed also, at this end of the Dardanelles, between the 
first and second castles. There was also the well-known Bay of Vourla, in the 
Gulf of Smyrna. Going to Vourla, however, would have somewhat the appear- 
ance of a retreat. 

After some reflection, the Emperor said that, upon the whole, he was 
inclined to advise the passage of the Dardanelles whenever the fleets could no 
longer remain at Besika, He should wish them to anchor as near as possible to 
the mouth of the Dardanelles, in order that the change of position might not be 
considered a demonstration against Russia: aud he thought that England and 
France might now, or later, when the change of station took place, address an 
amicable explanation to Russia, stating that the move had been rendered neces- 
sary for the safety of the fleets at the advanced season of the year; and adding. 
that the fleets would leave the Dardanelles whenever the Russian troops quitted 
the Principalities, Perhaps the equivalent thus offered to Russia might enable 
her, with less sacrifice of dignity, to recross the Pruth. His Majesty said that 
he should write immediately in this sense to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, and I said 
that I should inform your Lordship. : “a 
___M. Drouyn de Lhuys returned to Paris this evening; and I having arrived 
in the interim from Dieppe he sent immediately to desire to see me, I found 
him in possession of the Emperor's letter, and much disturbed at the news 
which had accumulated in his absence, from Constantinople. He asked ue 
directly whether I had communicated the Emperor's view to your Lordship ; 
and, on my replying in the affirmative, whether you had expressed any opinion 
upon them, | replied, that there had not been time to receive your answer, but 
that I conceived it unlikely that your Lordship, or Her Majesty’s Government 
would form any decided opinion until you were in receipt of the despatches 
brought to Marseilles by the “Triton.” M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared to have 
pal te the Kmperor’s conclusions as to the best course the two Governments 
cou d now take. He saw but one difficulty to entering the Dardanelles, that 
being the possibility of a refusal on the part of the Porte to give the necessary 
firmans. 

1 observed, that if the Porte was so blind to her own interests as to refuse 
the firmans, the flects might proceed to Vourla; and that if such «a movement 
under such circumstances, was looked upon in the light of a retreat, it would he 
a retreat undertaken to show the respect of the two Powers for the very Treat 
which they had invoked against the encroachments of Hussia. Nor should it be 
forgotten that we had always declared that the fleets would remain at Besika as 
long as it suited us, and no longer ; that in returning to Vourla we were consult- 
ing our own interests, not submitting to any condition; and that it was not 
impossible that a spontaneous move of the kind on our part might induce the 
Russians to a correspondent spontaneous movement on the Pruth. 

Your Lordship will be kind enough to bear in mind that these were not 
arguments used to counsel the retreat of the fleets to Vourla, but suggestions of 
what might be said were such a retreat deemed advisable, I was particularly 
careful throughout this conversation to give it a confidential character as 
between two persons reviewing what was possible and practicable under various 
circumstances, 

'T thought it, however, expedient on account of certain expressions which 
bud escaped the Emperor in the conversation alluded to in the beginning of this 
despatch, as well as from the tenour of some of M. de Lhuvs' observations Lo 
caution the latter against too great blame of the Turks in any despatches he 
might address to General Castelbajac. However much he might regret and 
eensure the conduct of the Porte in refusing our advice, regret alone should be 
expressed at St, Petersburgh, censure should be kept for Constantinople. Nor 
considering the opinions we had expressed to the Russian Government both in 
regard to the armed occupation of the Principalities, and to the conduct of the 
Russian authorities since that occupation, would it be consistent with our honour 
or our dignity to upbraid the Turkish Ministers, beeause they refused to send a 
friendly cane to a Sovereign so long as that Sovereign held forcible posses- 
sion of a part of the Sultan’s dominions. [ reminded M. Drouyn de Lhuys that 
in expressing regret that the point had not been more clearly defined by the 
Vienna Conference, I had foretold that it would be the stumbling block at the 
last moment, and | said that although diplomacy might yet find means to remove 


275 


it, the opprobrium of creating it ought to rest with the Russians. Nor would it 
be fair to diminish the responsibility which belonged to them by expressing 
disapprobation at the Porte’s still insisting on the vindication ofits sovereign 
rights. In fact, by any other language we should be turning the tables and 
putting Russia in the ritht and the Porte in the wrong. 

I should add that M. de Lhuys’ apprehensions that the Porte may refuse the 
firman to enable the fleet to pass the Dardanelles are founded on the fact that 
M. de la Cour asked some time back for provisional firmans for the passage of 
the fleet, in case its presence at Constantinople should become necessary, and 
that Reshid Pasha declined complying with the request. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


No, 290. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received August 31.) 


(No. 645,) 
My Lerd, Paris, August 30, 185d. 

M. DE LHUYS received this morning the despatches from M. de la Cour, 
brought to Marseilles by the “ Triton.” | have scen nothing of Lord Stratford’s 
messenger, and presume that he is gone straight to London. | 

M. de la Cour’s latest despatch is dated the 20th instant. That, and 
others of a previous date, detail the efforts made by himself and his colleagues 
to induce the Porte to accept the Vienna note without modifications. M, de la 
Cour had even had an audience of the Sultan ; but all, as your Lordship knows, 
ta no purpose. Copies of the note, as definitively modified by the Porte, and of 
the official note addressed by Reshid Pasha to the Representatives of the four 
Powers, accompany M. de la Cour's despatches. 

The Ambassador enters again at some length into the aspect of affairs at 
the Porte, He evidently considers the situation to be one of considerable 
danger. He imagines the feeling of Reshid Pasha to be a desire for war, 
founded on the conviction that France and England must still perforce side with 
Turkey, and that the war will therefore be a successful one for the Sultan, and 
obtain for him guarantees for the future which will materially strengthen his 
tottering power; and M. de la Cour does not doubt that, if the Ottoman 
Government is deceived in this hope, the Sultan will change his Ministers and 
endeavour to make terms with Russia directly, But he is also of opinion, that 
such a change of policy may cost the Sultan his throne and his life. 

The perusal of these despatches and their inclesures had, upon the whole, 
put M. de Lhuys im better spirits as to the final result. He regrets, of course, 
the introduction of any modifications into the Vienna note ; but he certainly 
considers them to be alterations for the better, and hopes that the Russian 
Government will subseribe to them, He thinks the tone of the note addressed 
to the Representatives of the Four Powers moderate ; and as the promise of the 
evaeuation of the Principalities, and not the immediate reality, appears to be 
asked for, and as the Four Powers, and not Russia, are applied to for guarantees 
for the future, he is inclined to think that these points may be arran ed satis- 
factorily if Russia does not demur to the proposed modifications of the note. 
Before | left him, M. de Lhuys again reverted to the question of the future 
movements of the fleets. He said, that the more he considered the matter the 
more he felt convinced that the Porte wonld make great difficulties to granting 
the necessary firmans to pass the Dardanelles, particularly if there was any 
latent idea in the Sultan’s mind of treating directly with Russia. But a refusal 
would be very humiliating to the two Powers, and he should almost prefer that 
the fleets should weigh anchor, and go and sal about within reach of the 
Dardanelles and watching the course of events. 

| remarked, that if the fleets were to act as he proposed, nothing would be 
more likely to precipitate an understanding between the Porte and Russia. 
then suggested that the Porte might herself be made the arbiter of their future 
movements. Let the Ottoman Government be informed that the fleets could 
not remain during the winter where they now were, and let them be asked 


276 


whether they preferred that the fleets should pass the Dardanelles or seek 
a secure anchorage elsewhere. If she preferred the latter, the necessity of 
consulting the Porte’s wishes would be an answer to all cavillers against what 
would appear to be a retreat; if the former, we should pass the Dardanelles at 
the Porte’s desire; and if the Porte wished to save appearances with Russia, she 
might fix the limits within which the permission to anchor would be aecorded ; 
for instance, she might say that, without firmans, the fleets should not pass the 
second castles. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he wished to see the Emperor on the whole 
question; and that he should go to Dieppe for that purpose. I propose accom- 
panying him, and shall have the honour of writing to your Lordship from 
thence, M. de Lhuys promises me, in this critical position of the question, to 
send no instructions referring to it which shall not have been previously 
submitted for your Lordship's corsideration. 

I venture to hope that your Lordship will take the same course, 

M. de Lhuys is of opinion that it is desirable, if possible, to charge the 
Conference of Vienna with the care of drawing up an answer to the note 
addressed by the Porte to the Four Powers, in order to keep in action the union 
which has been established. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Vienna, August 28, 1853. 

T HAVE the honour of forwarding the despatches* which I have received, 
under flying-seal, from Lord Stratford, with the request that they should be 
transmitted to your Lordship with the utmost practicable expedition, 

These despatches are confirmatory of the telegraphic despatches which | 
forwarded on the 25th and 26th instant. T waited upon Count Buol to inquire 
the impression made upon him by these communications, and the measures he 
‘ntended to take upon them. Count Buol stated that he should write by 
messenger this day to St, Petersburgh, charging Baron Lebzeltern to state to 
Count Nesselrode that he greatly lamented the modifications which the Porte 
had thought it right to introduce in the Vienna note, as it had originally been 
forwarded to Constantinople with the approval of the Four Governments ; 
but that he strongly recommended their adoption as a means, without any 
loss of dignity to His Majesty the Emperor of Russia, of bringing these 
unfortunate differences to a close. Count Buol would also remark, that the 
Porte having required an assurance as to the evacuation of the Principalities, he 
would leave it to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to state what answer he was to 
return ; that, knowing that it was the intention of the Emperor that these Prin- 
cipalities should be evacuated, he could only express his anxious desire that the 
earliest period for its commencement should be named, 80 that he might make 
that communication both to the Porte and to the other allied Governments, with 
the view of preparing the execution of this most desirable object. 

Count Buol stated, with respect to the declaration in the note of Reshil 
Pasha: “ Que la Sublime Porte attend encore une garantie de la part des Hautes 
Puissances contre toute ingérence de,” ke.; that as this did not refer to the 
Russian Government, but to the allies in general, he should not bring it forward 
officially at St. Petersburgh; that it was a question rather to be treated after 
the pressing difficulties of the present moment should be arranged ; and as it 
was not made by the Porte a condition of that settlement, he should abstain 
from making aby further comments with regard to it.

No: 292, 
The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G. H. Seymour. 


(No. 203.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, September 1, 1853. 

HER Majesty’s Government earnestly hope that the modifications proposed 
by the Porte of the note sent from Vienna may receive the assent of the Emperor 
of Russia. 

His Imperial Majesty accepted the note upon condition that no change in 
‘¢ should be made at Constantinople, and he is, therefore, perfectly free to reject 
the modifications. But Her Majesty’s Government are confident that the 
Emperor, animated bya spirit of justice, will admit that the Turkish Government 
have aright to express their opinion upon the note they are required to sign, and 
their scrupulous attention to forms is no small proof that they recognize the 
binding character of the engagement they are about to contract, while there can 
he no doubt that the note as amended will effectually secure the maintenance of 
existing Treaties and of the status quo in religious matters which Russia has 
throughout declared to be the objects she had in view. 

I am, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON, 


P.S.—In the event of the modifications not Leing accepted, you will 
endeavour clearly to ascertain from Count Nesselrode the reasons of their 
rejection.

My Lord, Foreign Office, September 2, 1853. 

COUNT WALEWSKI called upon me yesterday and held precisely the 
same language upon the Eastern question as that of the Emperor and M. de 
Lhuys to your Excellency. 

Count Walewski lamented that the Turkish Government had declined to 
uecept the note, and said that their decision caused great difficulty as to the 
disposal of the fleets, which could not remain much longer in the Bay of Besika; 
but if they were sent to a more distant anchorage, it would appear as if France 
and England were retreating ; and that the preferable course would perhaps be 
for them to enter the Dardanelles without proceeding to Constantinople or 
beyond the castles, an explanation being at the same time given to the Emperor 
of Russia that this change of position had been rendered necessary by the 
advanced state of the season, and that the fleets should withdraw altogether if 
the Principalities were evacuated. | 

I suid that without consulting my colleagues, ull of whom, with the exception 
of Lord Aberdeen, were out of town, | could give no definitive answer upon a 
question so important as that of settling where, under existing circumstances, 
should be the winter quarters of the fleets, and, according to this suggestion, 
involving the violation of a Treaty: but it HP Bee to me that the longer they 
could remain at their present anchorage the better; and I understood that 
during the month of September there would be no danger in their so doing, but 
that no decision could be taken until we know whether the Emperor of Itussia 
would accept the modification proposed by the Porte. If he did, minor 
difficulties might easily be overcome ; but if he rejected them, he must give his 
reasons, and we should then, more clearly than at present, be uble to judge what 
course it would be fitting for England and France to adopt.

(Signed) CLARENDON,

No. 294. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeeived September 2.) 


(No. 442, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 23, 1853, 

GENERAL DE ROCHOW returned to St. Petersburgh on the 20th 
instant, from his visit to Robscha, where he had held a very long conversation 
with the Emperor, who, as he stated, had recapitulated to him with remarkable 
clearness and talent the various events connected with the Turkish question 
which have occurred during the last five or six months, making it of course 
appear throughout his narration that his conduct could not have been other than 
what it has been. 

Before leaving me General de Rochow said, ‘The sum is this. All now 
depends upon the Sultan's acceptance of the note: in that case the affair is 
finished, 1 do not venture to give you any advice, but I will express an opinion 
and a wish; 1 will say that I desire eagerly that you may refrain from pressing 
upon the Government the evacuation of the Principalities, because 1 am con- 
vinced that such representations will do harm, 1 can, 1 think, give you my 
word of honour, yes, | can almost give my word of honour, that the orders for 
the retreat of the troops will be issued as soon as the Turkish Minister arrives 
here; and I will add that according to my belief the Emperor is eager that the 
order should be given as soon as possible.” 

Upon my inquiring of General de Rochow upon what evidence he formed 
his opinion as to the Emperor's eagerness to fall back from 4 position 
which had been taken up with considerable forwardness (empressement), ite 
replied that he had ascertained that although up to the present time the reports 
of the sanitary condition of the Russian troops was satisfactory, considerable 
anxiety was felt as to the maladies to which they would be exposed if not 
very speedily withdrawn from their present quarters. 

The Prussian Envoy desired to feria me of the former understanding 
which existed between us. He should be always glad to give me any information 
which he had the power to offer, but would beg of me to consider these com- 
munications as made in strict confidence. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

IT has been my duty, in compliance with the instruction given to me in 
your Lordship's despatch No. 181, to read to the Chancellor Mr, Colquhoun's 
despatch of the 29th ultimo, marked No. 22. 

His Excelleney observed that no reliance was to be placed in the supposi- 
tions or statements of Mr. Colquhoun with regard to the Russians, his strong 
fvelings against Ruasia being a matter of notoriety. 

With respect to the “mass of 40,000 or 50,000 men who could be brought 
to bear on any one given point,” this, Count Nesselrode said, was about the 
amount of the Russian forces in the two provinces; while Mr. Colquhoun 
himself states in another despatch, that from 40,000 to 50,000 men were to be 
quartered within a rayon of 15 miles round the capital, 

‘That with regard to the ‘settled unshaken determination to cross the 
Danube,’ all that need be said is that the Government have a settled determina- 
tion of not allowing them to pass, unless it should unhappily prove that the 
Sultan should decline eigning the note; in that case he said he could take no 
engagement—‘' ce sera alors comme alors.” 

The truth is, Count Nesselrode observed in conclusion, that Mr. Colquhoun, 
perceiving that a great deal of irritation prevails, has been doing his best to 
increase it; instead of water, he secks to throw oil on the fire.

supplies; and equally to be rejected are all suppositions founded upon any 
enmity entertained towards a connection of Prince Ghika, that Prince being

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewwed September 2.) 


(No. 452.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 26, 1853. 

| HAD the mortification of learning to-day from the Chancellor that the 
news of the Sultan’s acceptance of the note which had been communicated to 
me on the 24th instant is incorrect, the Government having received intelligence 
from Constantinople of a later date by three days than that of the day on which 
the Sultan's consent had been supposed to be given, and this intelligence stating 
that no decision had been taken by the Porte. 

The Chancellor alluded to the orders sent by the Sultan to the Hospodars 
to withdraw from the Principalities, and stated that news had been received of 
their having declined to obey the summons. I replied that in that case 1 took 
for granted that they would be recalled by the Porte. 

Count Nesselrode observed that this could hardly be, inasmuch as, without 
the consent of Russia, the removal of the Hospodars would not be legal. 

I begged to remark in return that a very anormal state of things had been 
ereated in the Principalities, and that if the removal of the Hospodars by ‘Turkey 
constituted an illegality, that an illegality at least as striking was involved in 
their oceupation by a Russian army. 

The Chancellor could not admit that the Russian Government had acted 
illegally or wrongfully, and would repeat that the removal of the Hospodars 
could not be valid without the Emperor's consent, which certainly would not be 
given ; at the same time he did not apprehend that in the event of the note being 
signed by the Porte this incident would give rise to any serious complication.

My Lord, Paris, September 2, 1853. 

| HAD some conversation yesterday with Vely Pasha, who, evidently 
alarmed at the false position in which the Porte has placed herself, and at the 
displeasure evinced by the French Government, came ostensibly to inquire 
whether I could suggest any means by which the Ottoman Government could 
extricate themselves, but in reality to find out whether the opinion of [Her 
Majesty's Government agreed with those of the F rench, and whether the lite 
eonduct of the Porte had altered the friendly feelings of [ler Mujesty’s advisers 
towards ‘Turkey. In doing this he endeavoured to explain the necessity for 
his Government to act as they had done, his arguments being identical with 
those addressed by Reshid Pasha to the Representatives of the Four Powers at 
Constantinople, 

I said that no doubt Her Majesty's Government were much disappointed 
at the turn which the Eastern question lad taken, in consequence of the 
refusals of the Porte to accept the solution proposed by the Four Powers, and 
that they could not but feel that their position towards Russia, who had 
accepted that solution, became necessarily modified, Further than this I could 
not say, us When I last heard from your Lordship you were not in possession of 
Lord Stratford's despatches explanatory of the conduct of the Porte, Speaking 
unofficially, | thong it greatly to be regretted that if the Porte considered 
the Sultan’s honour and independence were not sufficiently assured on certain 
points by the proposed note, the Turkish Goverament did not adopt thie sugees- 
tion of ler a bait Ambassador at Constantinople, and, while signifying their 
acceptance of t 


he note as being offered by the Four Powers, place on record in 
a separate paper their interpretation of the objectionable passages contained 1 
it. This or some other mode might casily have been found to guarantee the 
Porté against undue admissions; whereas the Porte having now declared the 
note to be unacceptable, except with certain modifications, rendered the offer of 
any advice very difficult. Perhaps Russia would admit the modifications, ut 
if she did not I thought the Porte would do wisely to reconsider its decision, 
and, trusting to the good intentions of the Four Powers, sign the Vienna note, 
With regard to the question of the evacuation of the Principalities, and to 
cuarantee against ull similar attacks for the future, | remarked that no condition 
of the kind had accompanied the note which Reshid Pasha had declared himselt 
to be willing to sign. He had then evidently intended to trust to the honour of 
Russia for the one, and to the continued friendship of the Four Powers for the 
other. It was difficult indeed to see in what way guarantees could be given, and 


284 


Turkey ought to take the present attitude of Europe, united in remonstrating 
against the unjust and aggressive acts of Russia, as the surest guarantee which 
could be offered. If, therefore, any opening was given from Vienna or elsewhere, 
af which the Porte could avail herself, to reconsider her late determination, | 
was sure she would do well to profit by it. 

In the course of this conversation Vely Pasha said that he was instructed

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
éNo, 283.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 7, 1853. 

I'T appears from a despatch from Count Nesselrode to the Russian Minister 
ut Vienna, dated the 22nd August, which has been shown to me by Count 
Colloredo, that subsequently to the acceptance by Russia of the Vienna note, 
Baron Lebzeltern was instructed to inquire of Count Nesselrode what steps 
would be taken for the evacuation of the Principalities in the event of the 
Porte's agreeing to the note without alteration, 

The reply of the Russian Government seems to have been a reference to 
the terms of the Circular of 7322, and more particularly to those of the Mani- 
festo, 25 establishing clearly the temporary character of the occupation, and the 
intention to bring it to a close as soon as the Porte signed the note which Russia 
had stated she looked upon as a sufficient satisfaction; and as soon as that note 
should be delivered at St. Petersburgh by a Turkish Ambassador, orders would 
be immediately issued for the return of the Russian troops within their own 
frontier. 

This being the case the Emperor was somewhat surprised and grieved at 
the question which had been put to him; but he was led to suppose that 
Austria shared the doubts which had been stated in the British Parliament, 
that independently of the satisfaction required of the Porte, Russia required, as 
the condition of the eyacuation of the Principalities, the previous withdrawal of 
the English and French squadrons. 

Russia disclaimed any such interpretation of the cireular. She never 
required that the squadrons should quit their position before the Russian troaps 
quitted theirs; what she meant was, that, in the existing circumstances, the 
presence of the two squadrons had the appearance of menace and pressure 
directed towards Russia, and so long as that menace and pressure lasted, Russia 
could not abandon her military position. But now that the Maritime Powers, 
instead of employing their squadrons to encourage the resistance of the Porte, 
were engaged in advocating at Constantinople the plan of arrangement proposed 
ut Vienna, and thereby obtaining the satisfaetion due to Hussia, the cuse is 
different; und if, at the same time, the required satisfaction is offered by the 
Porte, Russia would no longer have any reason for muintaining the position 
which she had taken up, and she conceived that the Powers would, on their 

2 


ae ct, 


Shy _l os 


286 


side, no longer find it necessary to maintain theirs, after the reasons which had 
induced them to take it up had ceased to exist. And if the Powers, like Russia, 
have no intention of gratuitously prolonging the existing crisis, there was 
nothing to prevent the simultaneous withdrawal of their squadrons and of the 
Russian troops being the natural result of the settlement of the questions 
between Russia and the Porte, and being coincident in point of time without any 
sacrifice of honour on either side. 

If such is the solution desired by Austria, Russia will give her an assurance 
to that effect, which she may make use of towards the Maritime Powers ; and 
Russia repeats that she has no intention to raise, with reference to the with- 
drawal of the squadrons, any discussion of principle; and that, us far as she is 
concerned, if the note as drawn up at Vienna is delivered without alteration at 
St. Petersburgh by a special ambassador, the immediate evacuation of the 
Prineipalities will be decided. 

Count Colloredo having asked me what answer I wished him to give to this 
despatch, 1 said that the renewed pledge to evacuate the Principalities, given by 
Russia, was satisfactory, and in the name of Her Majesty’s Government I 
begged to thank Count Buol for having obtained it; but I must then, as on 
previous occasions, decline entering into. any discussion respecting the with- 
drawal of the fleets. The Austrian Government, however, could hardly doubt 
that they would not remain at Besika Bay a moment longer than was necessary.

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me a despatch from Count 
Buol, dated August 31, stating that on the 28th of that month he had sent to 
Baron Lebzeltern the modifications which the Porte desired to have made in the 
note which it was proposed from Vienna that the Porte should address to Russia, 
with instructions to express the hope that they would be considered by the 
Emperor of Russia as not of sufficient importance to induce him to change lis 
pacific intentions. Count Buol remarked to Count Colloredo upon the absence 
in the note returned from Constantinople of the concluding passage of the 
Vicuna note; and inferring from thence that those passages are not objected to, 
he has inserted them in the amended copy which he has sent to St. Petersburgh. 

Baron Lebzeltern, it appears, is further instructed to request the Russian 
Government to enable the Cabinet of Vienna to give assurances to the Porte in 
regard to the evacuation of the Principalities. 

Count Buol then goes on to observe, with reference to the expectation of 
the Porte to receive from the Powers 4 guarantee against any future interference 
on the part of Russia in its affairs. and against the eventual occupation of the 
Principalities, that the Internuncio had been instructed to declare to the Porte 
that Austria did not look upon the expression of this expectation as a condition 
on the realization of which the settlement of the existing differences with 
Russia was to depend; and that, for her part, Austria could not enter into any 
engagement such as the Porte seemed to contemplate, Austria considered that 
the Porte would find its best security against such contingencies in maintaining 
relations of friendship and confidence with all the Powers of Europe, and in the 
wisdom and eficaciousness of the measures which it might adopt for the improve: 
ment of its internal adiministration, and for the amelioration of the condition of 
its Christian subjects; and that Austria was of opinion that such a guarantee 
from the Powers as the Porte seemed to require would amount to 4 humihating 
avowal of weakness, and a virtual sacrifice of its independence, 

At all events. Count Buol observes, the question thus raised by the Porte 
ought not to be mixed up with that now pending; but appertanning, as it does, 
to the future, it should be entertained as one bearing on the general interests of 
Europe, and not exclusively and singly on those of the Ottoman Empire. 

Tam, &c.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received September 8.) 


(No. 456. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 29, 1853. 


IN one of the despatches which reached the French Mission by their last 
courier, M. Drouvn de Lhuys observes “that he has frequently asked himself 
whether the Emperor's ready acceptance of the Vienna note may not have been 
occasioned by His Majesty's belief that the note was likely to be rejected by the 
Porte.” 

It is certain that the same suspicion has frequently presented itself to 
my mind; and in proof of its having done so, T need only remind your Lordship 
that when Count Nesselrode spoke to me of that fanaticism which was likely to 
impel the Turks to refuse the proposal made to them by their allies, 1 took care 
to establish to what circumstances that fanaticism (supposing it to exist) was to 
be attributed. 

But L would venture to remark to your Lordship that, under all cireum- 
stances, it can hardly be otherwise but that the Emperor must be desirous of 
altering the situation in which he finds himself placed, which, notwithstanding 
the supposed excellency of Russian diplomacy, is a very disadvantageous one. 

Even in the supposition of His Imperial Majesty entertaining these umbi- 
tious views, which by some are attributed to him, and of his being determined 
upon carrying them into execution upon the first favourable opportunity, he 
niust sce that the occasion does not offer itself at present, when England ancl 
France are standing shoulder to shoulder, and when the utmost that Austria 
has been disposed to do in favour of their Imperial allies and benelactors was to 
lend her aid in extricating them from the false position in whieh they had 
placed themselves. 

Under such circumstances, even without reference to the line which might 
be taken by the Porte, it would be, I think, the obvious policy of Russia to 
adhere to the proposat of her allies, and to wait for hetter times. 

It is ign not considered in the nature of things that the harmony 


which has of late prevailed between the English and French Governments should 
be of eternal duration; and the Emperor, at the meeting which he proposes 
having with his Imperial friend at Olmutz, hopes probably to be able to show 
reason why that alliance, which recent events have a little shaken, should be 
made as intimate as heretofore. 


289 


I will conclude my despatch by repeating to your Lordship an observation 
of General Castelbajac, which appears to me to be very judicious. 

General Castelbajac, I should remark, has been very desirous of ascertaining 
the amount of the Russian forces in the Principalities, and, after having made 
the most diligent inquiries, has perfectly satisfied himself that they cannot 
execed 50,000 men, although, by having been a good deal moved about, their 
numbers have been made to appear much more considerable. 

In making this statement to me, General Castelbajac said, ‘‘ Il est elair pour 
moi que la Russie qui s’est fourvoyée dans cette affuire, qui a fait faute sur faute, 
avait cherché A rassurer l'Europe, et A intimider la Turquie. Malhenreusement 
pour elle c'est le contraire qui est arrivé. Les Tures n’ont pas eu peur, eb c'est 
UEurope qui s’alarme.”

No. 313. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 8.) 


(No. 457. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, August 29, 1656. 

ATTENTION appears to have been turned in Austria to the proceedings 
of the Russian Secretary of Legation, M. Fonton, who was known to have 
left Vienna for the purpose of visiting Servia. 

I am informed that M. Fonton had been instructed to report upon the state 
of that province; and that, in the despatches which he has written, he speaks of 
the tranquillity and order which he observed there. 

This circumstance gives me an opportunity of remarking upon the hollow- 
ness of Russian diplomacy, and the facility which it exhibits in dealing in a 
summary way with facts, 

Some three months since, as your Lordship will recollect, the “ Chan- 
cellerie” spoke in moving terms of the condition of Servia, of the uncertainty of 
property and life there, and the eruel treatment to whieh Christians were 
subjected, &c. 

It is probable at that period, either that the Russian Cabinet had not 
determined what should be the extent of their invasion into the Sultan’s 
dominions, or that they were anxious to prepare the public for an explosion for 
which some preparation had been made. 

Suddenly the Austrian Government takes alarm, or resorts to precautions 
whieh leads to the gathering of a force on the Servian border, a proceeding which 
Russia (no longer quite confident in the support of her Austrian ally) views with 
certain misgivings. ‘The necessities of the moment accordingly become different; 
it is important to prove to Austria that her military precautions are unnecessary, 
and with that view M. Fonton is dispatched to Servia, no doubt with instructions 
to find the country in a very satisfactory condition. 

It has been with some pleasure that I have reflected upon the entire 
incredulity which I had opposed at the time to Count. Nesselrode’s alarming 
Servian intelligence, and he, no doubt, recollecting the language he had held, 
has refrained from observing to me, as he has done to some other persons of the 
diplomatic corps, upon the tranquillity which prevails in Servia, 

At the risk of “throwing oil upon fire,” to use an expression which | 
borrow of the Chancellor, | have pointed out to the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires 
the contradiction in the language of the Russian “Chancellerie,” and have 
offered him what I believe to be the true explanation. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 318. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 9.) 
(No. 238. Secret.) 


My Lord, Therapia, August 24, 1853. 

‘THE French Ambassador, acting apparently under recent instructions, 
continues in some degree to take a line not quite consistent with the position 
in which we hai previously stood towards each other. The day before yesterday 
he sent to Reshid Pasha, repeating his proposal that the military commander of 
the Dardanelles should be instructed to Het the French squadron pass up to 
Constantinople, on the application of Admiral Hamelin, 

When Resid requested to know the meaning of this haste, he was told 
that the Emperor of Russia might take some precipitate resolution on learning 
the fate of Count Buol's note, and that if such a result were to oceur, the news 
of it would be likely to reach Paris much sooner than Constantinople, and that, 
consequently, as orders would probably then be given for the advance of the 
squadron, it was desirable that no obstruction should be encountered at the 
Dardanelles. 

When the French interpreter was further requested to state whether the 
English squadron was included in M. de la Cour’s application, he replied that 
he was not aware of it. I know from undoubted authority that on the same 
night Reshid Pasha received a visit from the French Ambassador, who 
communicated to him in strict confidence, that his Government intended to 

ropose a new Convention to supersede the Treaty of 1841, and in concert with 
tngland, Austria, and Prussia, to establish the Porte’s independence, together 
with the integrity of its empire, on more distinct and solid foundations. 

Reshid Pasha appears to be much pleased with this overture. He inquired 
whether M, de la Cour had said anything to me upon the subject, and received 
for answer that he was instructed to confine his communications to his Highness 
alone. The Pasha is of opinion that an arrangement in the sense proposed 
would be very advantageous to the Porte, but that Constantinople is the place 
at which it ought to be concluded, 

I culled upon M, de la Cour to-night, in ignorance of his secret proposal, 
and put him upon the subject of the squadrons. He kept strict silence upon the 
former question, but, touching the latter, told me that his communication to 
Reshid Pasha originated in what hod passed between our respective Govern- 
ments on the muppesiston of further concerted measures being rendered necessary 
by the refusal of Russia to accept any reasonable terms of arrangement. 1 
observed, in reply, that although your Lordship had agreed with Count Walewski 
in principle, you had differed in some degree as to the time of application, and 
that T was ignorant of any sufficient reason for bringing up the squadrons to 
Constantinople, while I felt strongly the inconvenience of exhibiting any 
difference in the proceedings of the two Governments on the pending question, 
The discussion proceeded no further, and I hope to find a sufficient remedy at 
the Porte, unless any occurrence altering my present impression should 
Intervene, 

Meanwhile, I solicit your Lordship’s timely attention to the disadvantage 
under which I shall have to labour, if the course thus taken by France on the 
one side, and by Austria on the other, be allowed to proceed without some 
counterpoise in fuyour of British influence, whose ascendency for the best 
purposes it has been my constant effort to uphold and improve. ; 

Whether the present negotiations terminate in peace or in war, it will 
doubtless be most desirable that some kind of barrier should be raised anningt 
the recurrence of any such attempts at encroachment as those which we are 
now resisting. But it is equally des 


a that the improvement of Turkish 
yt 


2o4 


administration and the relief of the Sultan’s Christian subjects from much unjust 
and oppressive legislation, should be simultaneously secured, not as the means 
of increased influence to any particular Power, but as an object of common 
golicitude, scarcely less useful to Europe at large than to Turkey itself. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 319. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received September 9.) 
(No. 239.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 25, 1850. 


IN writing to you on the 20th instant, | was so much hurried by my 
anxiety to send off the Porte’s note and the correspondence relating to it with 
the least possible delay, that I fear I must have expressed myself even more 
imperfectly than usual. 1 entertain this apprehension particularly with respect 
to those weak points of the Empire, or the causes of danger, to which in the 
conscientious performance of an important duty I had drawn your Lordship's 
attention in my despatch No. 132 of the current year. I have it now at heart 
to observe, that in exposing those vulnerable parts my purpose was hot to brand 
the Turkish Empire with a character of helplessness an incurability, but to 
prepare Her Majesty’s Government in time for the direction which an active 
and calculating enemy in the unfortunate eventuality of war would probably 
give to its offensive operations against this country. 1 was under an impression 
that it might seem presumptuous for me to suggest any means of counteraction, 
when those who wielded the power of Great Britain commanded so large a 
portion of the knowledge on which that power depends, 

Experience has since shown that in some respects the danger was expanded 
into undue proportions, and that insufficient credit was given to the Mussulman 
population of Turkey and its Government for those qualities and resources 
which are the best supports of an independent State. On this score I have 
already endeavoured to do justice to both; and the favourable accounts which 
had previously reached me from the army are amply confirmed by information 
conveyed to me this morning by General Sir Charles O'Donnell, who returned 
only yesterday from the scene of defensive operations in Bulgaria, after visiting 
the principal military stations, inspecting the Turkish camp under the auspices 
of its commander, and witnessing the field exercises of the troops. A corre- 
sponding spectacle is at this moment before me. I have only to raise my eyes 
from the paper in order to see two squadrons and a camp, comprising alto- 
gether between soldiers and sailors a population of nearly 30,000 men, The 
discipline and perfect quietness which reign among them would do honour to 
the most civilized nation; and though the surrounding villages are principally 
inhabited by Christians, not an instance of personal aggression, and scarcely 
two or three of accidental insult, have come to my knowledge. 

The extraordinary expenses incurred by the Government are no doubt 
heavy, but the Minister of Finance appears to have little anxiety for the future ; 
the advances required from capitalists are comparativel small ; individuals of 
substance are prepared to make voluntary sacrifices in aid of the State; and the 
founders of the Bank have made up their minds, as 1 am assured by one of 
them, to open their institution in October, with the assent of those parties in 
England who ure to supply @ large portion of their capital. It may be added, 
that notwithstanding the concentration of nearly 100,000 men in Bulgaria, a 
considerable urmy is collected on the frontier of Georgia; and no hesitation 
has been shown in proceeding to form a separate, though smaller, army on the 
frontier of Servia. 

What | remarked before as to the exhausting consequences of so much 
exertion still holds good; but the exertion itself, and its accompaniments, are 
not only creditable to the Porte and to the nation, but indicative to a signal 
degree of what they are still equal to when duly supported and prudently 
directed ; though it must be allowed that actual war would test their means of 
resistance far more severely than its probability or its approach. 


* 295 


_ To judge from present appearances no spirit of discontent and insubordi- 
nation is sufficiently matured to threaten an immediate outbreak in Bulgaria 
Servia, 0 r Albania. The Consular reports from nearly all the principal places of 
the Empire in Europe and Asia have greatly softened their original tone of 
alarm, and T am inclined to think, that notwithstanding the absence of the 
Sultan's regular forces, there is less disturbance and perhaps even less oppression 
than usual. 1 learn from your Lordship’s own correspondence that the appre- 
hension of fresh incursions from Montenegro is far from being well founded. 
The fanatical exeesses which were so. naturally dreaded and predicted after 
Prince Menchikoff's departure have hitherto been no more realized than the 
rumours of intended massacre when he was here at Easter. 

_ Looking to dangers from without, to the ambition of Greece and the 
animosity of Persia, | cannot affirm that the grounds of mistrust are removed ; 
but the Porte must be friendless indeed if means be not found, in the event of 
war, to impress on these countries the duty and interest of respecting a 
neighbour's rights unjustly assailed from other quarters. 

Not to weary your Lordship with superfluous or unreasonable remarks, I 
conclude under a strong impression, that if Turkey be pushed against her will 
to extremities, she will fight even single-handed with partial success, and if sus- 
tained by her maritime allies alone with corresponding determination, that she 
will have a hopeful prospect of getting through her present difficulties, and in 
some measure relieving Europe from a constant source of political anxiety and 
commercial embarrassment. 

Though it cannot be denied that the vices of Turkish Administration, and 
the future relations subsisting befween the Mussulman and Rayah classes of the 
Empire, have improved but little in proportion to the need and promise of 
improvement, prejudices are daily softening down, and sounder principles are 
gradually gaining ground. The nearer contact of ‘Turkey with Europe, its 
greater dependence on some of the Christian Powers, and a progressive acquaint- 
ance with their manners, which passing events occasion, can hardly fail to 
advance the work of civilization; and the Turks would not be men if gratitude 
for benefits received did not induce them to respect the superiority of their 
benefactors, and to rely with some de of confidence in their counsels. 

I have &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Sir, Therapio, August 22, 1853, 
THOUGH 1 received on the 14th instant your answer to my despatch of 
the 4th, 1 delayed the repetition of my instructions, partly in the hope of 
learning from your next communication that on further reflection you had acted 
in obedience to their contents, Being now in possession of your despatch

No. 15 of the 11th instant, which shows that you still remained in error, while 
your colleague, the French Consul, acting under instructions from M. Boujade 

at Bucharest as well as from his Ambassador, had hauled down his Consular flag, 

as M. de la Cour informs me, I have to repeat my instruction that you cease to 

hoist yours from the receipt of this despatch, and, in concert with M, Testa, 

exeoute in all respects the instructions which I addressed to Mr. Colquhoun on 

the th, and sent to you in copy that you might act in the same manner. 

The Hospodar’s excuses are not accepted at the Porte, and the orders 
reviously sent to him are to be repeated. There is no question of intrigue as 
is Highness appears to have supposed. The Porte in ordering his retirement 

for the reasons known to you, acted on political and not on administrative’ 
grounds. It was his obvious duty to obey the Sovereign's command. 

T abstain from any remarks upon your despatch of the . The 
correspondence must necessarily go to-Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of 
State for Foreign Affairs. 

I expect to hear from you in reply to this instruction without any unneces- 
gary delay.

Inclosure in No. 325, 
Consul-General Yeames to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract. ) Odessa, August 22, 1853. 

THE whole of the 4th Corps d'Armée is now between the Proth and the 
Danube, excepting its reserves, which are still kept far in the rear. The three 
divisions of infantry comprise twelve regiments or forty-eight battalions, and one 
battalion of riflemen and one of sappers are attached to it. There is further a 
brigade or eight battalions belonging to one of the divisions of the Sth Corps 
quartered in and about Jassy, thus making fifty-cight battalions; and if the 
present strength of the battalion be estimated at 700 men under arms, | believe 
this appreciation will exceed rather than be below the truth. At most, there- 
fore, the infantry may amount to 40,000 men. Of regular cavalry there are the 
4th and Sth Divisions, comprising together eight regiments of lancers and 
hussars, and, lam told, four or five regiments of Cossacks. It is with reserve 
that I should state the actual foree of horsemen to be 10,000 to 12,000. Of 
artillery, twelve batteries or ninety-six guns are attached to the three divisions 
of infantry, and two batteries or sixteen guns to the cavalry. 

On this side of the Pruth, four battalions of the 15th Division of Infantry, 
belonging to the Sth Corps d’Armée, are at Leova and Riekness, and tour 
battalions at Ismail, where they had been sent by forced marches early in July, 


in consequence of a report, now considered absurd, of some hostile plan of 


attack on the part of the Nekoasopti, a fugitive remnant of the old Tapoooques, 
settled about Puleha and Isakeba, ‘The |4th Division of Infantry is now quar- 
tered between the Dniester and Odessa; and the remaining division of the 5th 
Corps (the 18th) is stationary at Sevastopol, he reserves are arrested on the 
left side of the Dnieper. 

The 3rd Corps d’Armeée ts still moving to take up the former position of the 
4th Corps, facing the Polish frontier of Austria. 

The flotilla in the Danube consisted in January last of about thirty gun- 
boats stationed at Ismail, and a few more may have come from Nicolayeff. Of 
this force a statement was lately made in the House of Lords monstrously 
exaggerated. 

A partof the fleet has been throughout the season at sea for evolutions, 
at no distance from Sevastopol, and the troops there have been practised in 
embarkation and landing. 

The intelligence lately received here has raised the hope ofa speedy cessa- 
tion of all warlike measures, and that peace will secure the prosperity of these 
ports, which otherwise would be annihilated.

No. 324. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 9.) 


(No. 666. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, September 8, 1853. 


M. DE HUBNER made yesterday a communication to M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, which the latter repeated confidentially to me. 

Count Buol informs the Freneh Government that the Emperor of Russia 
has addressed a despatch to the Austrian Cabinet, announcing his intentions in 
regard to the Principalities, His Imperial Majesty does not mean to make the 
evacuation of them depend on the departure of the English and French fleets 
from the neighbourhood of the Dardanelles ; but he will not order the Russian 
troops to recross the Pruth until a Turkish Ambassador shall have reached 
St. Petersburgh and placed in his hands, without any alteration, the note drawn 
up at Vienna, of which His Majesty has signified his acceptance. 

As a similar communication will no doubt have been made te your Lord- 
by Count Colloredo I do not enter into the minutiw of the Russian despatch, — 

M. de Hiibner added, that Count Buol considered this decision of the 
Emperor of Russia to be quite satisfactory, and trusted that it would meet with 
the approbation of the French Government. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that, with regard to the fleets, he could only 
repeat what M. de Hiibner knew, that France would not permit any condition 
respecting their movements to be made, With regard to the Emperor of 
Russia's intentions relative to the Prineipalities, he could say nothing officially 
without taking the orders of the Emperor; but he had no objection to state, as 
his personal opinion, that the Emperor of Russia’s conduct appeared harsh in 
the extreme. There were different stages at which His Majesty might have 
announced his intention to onder the evacuation of the Principalittes—upon the 
acceptation of the note by the Porte; or upon the nomination of an Ambassador 
to proceed with it to Russia; or upon the departure of that Ambassador from 
Constantinople; or upon his arrival at Vienna; or again, upon his reaching 
St. Petersburgh ; or lastly, upon the actual receipt of the note from the hands 
ai that Ambassador. The Emperor had chosen the last, and consequently the 
most humiliating to the Porte, Now Turkey, and with her France and England, 
had also different stages at which they might consider this matter as settled. 
Upon the acceptance of the above-mentioned note by the Emperor of Russia, or 
upon lis promise to evacuate the Principalities, or upon orders being sent for 
that pupae or upon the commencement or during the progress of the evacua- 
tion, or lastly when the last Russian soldiers should have crossed the Pruth, 

After giving me these details of his conversation with M. de Hiibner, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he wished I would inquire of your Pea at 
which of these stages Her Majesty’s Government would consider that the Porte 
might direct her Ambassador to leave Constantinople. 

l said that 1 would not fail to convey his inquiry to your Lordship; but 
that T thought that it should be addressed rather to the Porte, who must be the 
supreme judge as to the moment when it would be compatible with her honour 
to direct a special embassy to proceed to Russia. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

IN reply to the inquiry which, at the request of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, your 
Excellency hus addressed to me in your despatch No. 666, marked confidential, 
| have to state that Her Majesty’s Government entirely agree with M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys thet the course which the Mmperor of Russia proposes to pursue. is

the most illiberal and humiliating towards Turkey that he could adopt; but in 
answering a categorical question of the Austrian Cabinet which threw some 
doubt upon the Emperor's previous assurances regarding the evacuation of the 
Principalities, it was, perhaps, not to be expected that he should lower his 
demands with respect to receiving the note before the orders for withdrawing the 
Russian troops were given, in ignorance, as he then was, whether the note would 
be accepted by the Porte; but whenever a note is agreed to, it is to be hoped 
that the remonstrances which should then be addressed to His Majesty by the 
Four Powers, will induce him to act in a manner consistent with the dignity of 
the Sultan, 

It should be remembered that the offer to send an Ambassador to St. 
Petersburgh first emanated from the Porte; before the evacuation of the Princi- 
palities, itis true; but the offer was subsequently repeated, without relerence to 
their evacuation, in the note sent by Reshid Pasha to Vienna, and it was, for the 
first time, made an absolute condition in the note addressed by Reshid Pasha to 
the Four Representatives at Constantinople. 

It seems then to Her Majesty's Government that in the event of the 
Turkish modifications being accepted by the Emperor of Russia, or of any form 
of note being agreed upon between the two Governments, the Turkish Ambas- 
sador at Vienna might be charged to be the bearer of it to St. Petersburgh, but 
that he should not take his departure until he had reecived such assurances 
respecting the evacuation of the Principalities as the dignity of the Sultan would 
demand. 

The Emperor could hardly refuse to give the necessary orders for with- 
drawing his forces when he knew that the note he was prepared to accept had 
actually arrived at Vienna; while, on the other hand, the Turkish Ambassador 
would not set foot on the Russian territory until the honour of the Sultan was 
siutistiead,

My Lord, Foreign Office, September 10, 1853. 

| HAVE to acquaint your Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government 
approve the language which you held to M. de la Cour, as reported in your 
secret despatch No. 238 of August 24, with reference to a proposal which he 
had made to Reshid Pasha, that conditional orders should be sent to the Pasha 
of the Dardanelles, for permitting the French squadron to pass through the 
Strait on the application of the French Admiral. 

Her Majesty’s Government regret that this demand should have been made 
by M. de la Cour, without communication to your Excellency, and also without 
any communication to Her Majesty’s Government by that of France that such 
a demand would be made; and a representation will be addressed to M. de Lhuys 
in order to prevent the recurrence of acts which might lead the Porte into the 
error of supposing that there was any difference in the policy of the two Govern- 
ments. Your Excellency will of course understand that the instructions which 
you have already received with regard to the disposal of the British fleet remain 
in full force. 

It is the wish of both the English and French Governments—and that wish 
there is reason to believe is shared in by Austria and Prussina—to come to an 
arreement for better securing the future independence and integrity of the Otto- 
man Empire; and your Exeellency will find a distinct proposition to that effeet 
in Lord Cowley’s despatch No. 633 of August 24, of which ao copy was 
transmitted to you in my despatch No. 179 of the 8th instant. 

In my answer to Lord Cowley, No. 337 of August 30, of which a copy 
was transmitted to you at the same time, you will see that Mer Majesty's 
Government, while concurring in the views of the French Government, think 
the proper time for giving effect to them would be when the question now 
pending between Russia and the Porte is settled. In the meanwhile Her 
Majesty's Government observe with satisfaction that the opinions of the Austrian 
Government, of which you will find an account in my despatch to the Earl of 
Westmorland No, 284 of the 7th instant (also sent to you in copy on the 6th), 
respecting the future policy of the Porte and the administration of the internal 
affairs of Turkey, are in harmony with those of Her Majesty's Government,
