No, 328, 
The Earl of Clurendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(No, 184) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 10, 1853, 

HER Majesty's Government have had under their serious consideration the 
note addressed by Reshid Pasha to the Representatives of the Four Powers at 
Constantinople.on the [9th of August, axplining the modifications proposed by 
the Porte to the project of note seat from Vienna, 

Reshid Pasha appears to complain that the Porte was not consulted; und 1 
have to observe that the course peso pursued by the Porte, when a pra- 
posal for settlement was submitted to it, appeared to render subsequent consulta. 
tion inexpedient, as leading only to further loss of time. For it must be borne 
in mind, that on the 22nd of June the Internuncio, in pursuance of instructions 
given to him by Count Buol in anticipation of the possible refusal of the Porte 
to comply with the requisition contained in Count Nesselrodo’s letter to Reshid 
Pasha of the Slst of May, suggested to the Porte aguin to examine Prince 
Menchikoil’s proposed note, and to compare it with that which Reshid Pasha 
was himself prepared to address to the Prinee previously to his departure from 
Constantinople; and if the Porte was inclined to propose any alteration in the 


306 


Russian draft which it could accept itself, and which was likely to be accepted 
by Russia, the Internuncio offered to convey to his Government the proposals 
of the Porte as the basis of its further mediation, and with a view to preparing 
a favourable reception for the Ambassador whom the Porte intended to send to 
St. Petersburgh. | : 

Upon this suggestion being made known to your Excellency, and to your 
colleagues of France and Prussia, by Reshid Pasha and also by the Internuncio, 
you assembled the Representatives of the Four Powers at your house, and they 
concurred in agreeing to suggest to the Turkish Minister for Foreign Affairs to 
frame a draft of note which should combine Prince Menchikoff’s draft and that 
of Reshid Pasha, in the hope that a note might be drawn up which should be at 
once acceptable to Russia, and should at the same time not trench upon the 
principle which the Porte considered essential for the maintenance of its sovereign 
rights. ; x 

This suggestion was laid before the Sultan, and, as stated in your Excellency s 
despatch No. 145 of the 9th of July, after an unexplained delay of several days, 
returned to Reshid Pasha with His Majesty's sanction; but no subsequent 
communication was made either to your Excellency, or, as far as you knew, to 
your colleagues, on the subject, . 

Her Majesty’s Government thought it most unfortunate, as well as ungra- 
cious towards the Austrian Government, that this opportunity for effecting an 
arrangement should thus, and without even a reason for it being assigned, have 
been neglected; but it was not unnatural for the Austrian Government to 
suppose that a repetition of the request would be useless ; and considering that 
the oceupution of the. Principalities. was fraught with danger, nat to Turkey 
alone, but to the peace of Europe, Count Buol thought it advisable to call 
together the Representatives of England, France, and Prussia, and with their 
concurrenee to prepare a note that might prove acceptable both to Russia and 
to the Porte. | 

With this object they took the note which had been drawn up by the 
French Government, and which having been at one time communicated by the 
Freneli Minister at St. Petersburgh to Count Nesselrode, liad been favourably 
received; and Her Majesty's Government and the French Government were 
consulted as to udopting this note with certain modifications that it seemed to 
require; and both Governments replied that, without seeing the modilications, 
they could give no assent; bot upon their being transmitted and carefully consi- 
dered, they appeared to be unobjectionable, and were approved, although after- 
wards an alteration was made by Her Majesty's Government more effectually to 
guard the interests of Turkey. And it is hardly necessary to add, that if the 
English und French Governments had not concurred in thinking that those 
interests were protected, and that the principle for which we had all along been 
contending was maintained, neither Government would have assented to the 
note, 

When things had thus far advanced the Turkish project arrived at Vienna, 
lt consisted of the protest against the occupation of the Principalities, inclosed 
in a note from Reshid Pasha to Count Nesselrode, and to be followed by another 
note less definite in its meaning than that which he had been ready to address 
to Prince Menchikoff. Such a proposal could not have led to the renewal of 
diplomatic relations between the two countries—it was sure to be declined by 
Russia; the forwarding it to St. Petersburgh could only have been productive 
of further loss of time—a consideration of the utmost importance; and a prefer- 
ence wus therefore unanimously given to the note which in substance had been 
well recetved at St. Petersburgh, and which there was every reason to expect 
would meet the views of the Turkish Government. This project was received 
at Constantinople on the 9th ultimo; but it was not until the 19th that the 
note was accepted with modifications. | ae 

Hor Majesty's Government are far from denying that these modifications 
are in themselves unobjectionable; but they da not consider them of that vital 
importance, nor that they offer such additional security to Purkey, as to counters 
balance the risks to which the Ottomun Empire is exposed by further postponing 
the settlement ofthis unfortunate question. | 

Tho first objection taken by the Porte is to the following paragraph: “Si A 
toute Gpoque les Empereurs de Russie ont témoignsé leur active sollicitude pour le 
maintica dea immunités et priviléges de I'Eglise Greeque Orthodoxe dans 


SOT 


"Empire Ottoman, les Sultans ne se sont jamais refus¢s a les consacrer de 
nouveau par des Actes solennels.”' - 

Now it appears to be natural that the Emperors of Russia should exhibit 
solicitude for those who profess their religion, and are living under Mahomedan 
rile; but Her Majesty’s Government cannot consider that by the paragraph in 
question this solicitude shown in times past can be taken to have imposed any 
obligation, or to imply that the acts of the Sultans in favour of the Greek 
Chureh were not voluntary and spontaneous; and upon no construction of this 
passage could Russia found any future claim to require of the Sultan to 
perform such acts. The passage is simply historical, and may be true or false ; 
but Russia establishes no right, and Turkey takes no engagement by the recital. 
The Great Powers of Europe have at different times manifested their active 
solicitude for the Christian subjects of the Porte; none more frequently and 
energetically than England. They have done so in behalf of suffering humanity 
and outraged religion; and their just remonstrances have met with more or less 
suceess. But the power of the Sultan not to listen to them hag never been 
questioned ; and the mght of Christian Powers thus to interfere may again and 
again be exercised without prejudice to his independence. Can there be any 
doubt that the firmans which the Sultan of his own free will lately issued, were 
in consequence of the anxiety for his Christian subjects felt by his Christian 
allies; or that those Christian subjects will not obtain some alleviation of the 
suifvrings and injustice to which they are exposed, by the powerful protests 
whieh your Excellency a short time ago felt yourself compelled to address to 
the Porte? In listetting to such remonstrances and in acting upon them, the 
Porte acquires respect and esteem, but it parts with no right and contracts no 
engarement, 

Reshid Pasha says, with reference to the paragraph, that no one would 
consent to draw down upon himsel! the reproaches and the blame of his cotem- 
poraries, as well as posterity, by admitting the establishment of a state of things 
as injurious for the present as the future; or to put in writing words that could 
detract from the glory of institutions. that the Ottoman Emperors have founded 
by a spontaneous movement of their personal generosity and innate clemency, 
But the paragraph neither warrants any such interpretation, nor calls for any 
such censure; and if it did, it would be as applicable to Great Britain, to 
France, and to Austria, as to Russia. 

In considering the original draft of the note, the special attention of Her 
Majesty’s Government was directed to the Treaty of Kainardji, for the purpose 
of securing that the Porte should be called upon to do no more with respect to 
religious privileges than that to which Reshid Pasha says it is ready to consent, 
namely, to express ‘des assurances propres d faire disparaitre les doutes mis 
en avant par le Gouvernement de. Russie, et qui ont formé le sujet des dis- 
cussions.” 

But the paragraph states “que le Gouvernenient de Sa Majesté le Sultan 
restera fidéle & Ia lettre et 4 Pesprit des stipulations des Traites de Kainardji 
et d'Andrinople relatives 4 la protection du culte Chrétien.” 

To this there can be no objection, because Reshid Pasha says, ‘‘ Comme 
personne ne saurait nier que ce Traité existe, et qu'il est confirme par celui 
d'Andrinople, il est de toute evidence que les dispositions précises en seront 
fidélement observées,” 

The second part of the paragraph, however, is in no way dependent on the 
first, but on the contrary is disconnected from it. It does not say that as a 
consequence of the Treaty, the Sultan “ will regard,” &e., but the word ‘and’ is 
expressly introduced to cuard against such a consequence being assumed, The 
true reading, therefore, is, “the Sultan will remain faithful to the Treaties." His 
Majesty also “regarde comme ¢tant de som honneur de faire observer i tout 
jamais et de préserver de toute attcinte, soit présentement, soit dans Vavenir, la 
jouissance des priviléges spirituels qui ont lé accordés par les augustes aicux 
de Sa Majesté a l'Eglise Orthodoxe de l'Orient, et sont maintenus et confirmés 
par elle.” | 

Now if any part of this paragraph can justify the fears entertained hy 
Reshid Pasha of giving “au Gouvernement de Russie des motils de prétendre a 
exercer un droit de surveillance et d'immiscion dans de pareilles matidres,”” it 
assuredly is not the first passage nor its supposed connexion with the second ; 
but it is the second itself, by which the Sultan makes no ordinary cngngement, 


308 


but pledges his honour to maintain for ever inviolate all the privileges enjoyed 
by the Greek Church ; and this second passage is taken verbatim from the note 
which Reshid Pasha was prepared to address to Prinee Menchikoff, 

With respect to the third paragraph objected to by the Porte, the view of 
Her Majesty’s Government was precisely that which is taken in the note of 
Reshid Pasha, namely, “On ne saurait douter que le Gouvernement Impérial 
Whesitera pas 4 faire participer le rit Gree non seulement nux avantages qu'il a 
de sa propre volonté accordés aux autres communions de la religion Chretienne 
professées par les communautés ses sujettes, mais ausst & ceux qu'il pourrait 
leur octroyer 4 Vavenir.” 

The passage which follows the words “en outre” was meant to have a 
prospective sense, and the words “ mts Chrétiens’ were understood to apply to 
subjects of the Porte, 

It would be simply absurd to suppose that the idea ever could have been 
contemplated of extending to several millions of the subjects af the Porte reli- 
gious privileges granted at different times to the subjects of other Powers 
residing within the Ottoman territory. Her Majesty’s Government had not, 
nor have they now upon reconsideration, any fear that this passage could be 
interpreted in the sense attributed to it by Reshid Pasha; nor do they conceive 
that there is really any substantial difference between the passage in the Vienna 
note and the modification proposed by the Porte, which could leave room for 
misunderstanding hereatter. 

Such being the opinions of Her Majesty's Government, they cannot but 
regret the course that has been pursued at Constantinople. They do not question 
the right, or the propriety, on the purt of the Turkish Government, to examine 
closely the note that was proposed for their adoption; but if it had been signed 
subject to any reservations that the Porte thought necessary, or if the judicious 
proposal of your Excellency, as reported in your despatch No. 222 of the 18th 
of August, had been acted upon, great delay would have been avoided, and 
some important advantages might have been gained. 

Such a mode of proceeding would at once have removed the doubts which 
now generally prevail respecting the desire or intention of the Porte to effect a 
peaceful settlement ; and as the modifications proposed by the Turkish Govern- 
ment merely interpret the note in the sense intended by the Four Powers, they 
could not have hesitated to accept them, and thus give the Sultan a security for 
the future. In fact, they would have constituted themselves referees as to the 
true interpretation of the note, in the event of any difference arising hereafter 
upon it between the Porte and Russia, Not only were these modifications 
considered unimportant and as not altering the sense of the note by the 
Austrian Government, but by the Russian Minister at Vienna; and it might 
reasonably therefore have been expected, that if the note had been signed 
Russia would have joined the Four Powers inagreeing to its right interpretation, 

Your Excellency will understand that the modifications, although in the 
opinion of Her Majesty’s Government unnecessary, are not objected to as 
unreasonable, but that the mode of proposing them is likely to be productive of 
embarrassment, and to retard the solution of a question which Turkey is so 
deeply interested in settling; and they do not disguise from themselves that the 
Emperor of Russia, with reference to the condition upon which he reluctantly 
adhered to the note, may now decline to agree to the changes, notwithstanding 
that they have been strongly recommended by the Tour Powers to his 
meceptanee, 

Reshid Pasha in his note says, that in the event of the modifications being 
adopted the Porte will immediately send an Ambassador Extraordinary, upon 
condition of the evacuation of the Principalities; and he adds, that a solid 
guarantee will be expected from the Powers ‘contre toute ingérence 4 l'avenir 
et toute occupation de tems en tems des Principautés de Moldavie et de 
Valachic.”’ 

With respect to the first, it has always been considered, not only by Her 
Majesty's Government, but by the four Powers, that the evacuation of the 
Principalitics was the sine yud non of any arrangement being concluded on the 
part of the Porte; and they have no reason to doubt, but on the contrary they 
have cause to believe, that if the note had been accepted by the Porte the orders 
for the withdrawal of the Russian troops would long before this time have been 
given, 


S09 


As regards the solid guarantee expected by the Porte, Reshid Pasha must 
well know that it is utterly impossible for the Four Powers to enter into any such 
engagement. The term ‘ ingérence”’ by itself is most vague, and might be held 
to apply to the legitimate reclamations and remonstrances that, according to 
international law and usage, every Government is entitled to address to another ; 
nor could the Four Powers make such a proposal to Russia, and still less give 
any guarantee upon the subject, without reciprocally Imposing upon themselves 
similar conditions, and thus leaving the Turkish Government at perfect liberty to 
deal as it pleased with the religious, the social, and the commercial interests of 
their respective subjects throughout the Ottoman Bret In short, it would 
be as impossible to promise that for the future there shall be no “ ingérence” 
on the part of Russia, as it would be to undertake that towards that Power there 
shall never be a just cause of complaint given by Turkey; and if any such 
engagement were entered into by the Pour Powers, it might be justly considered 
by Turkey as an insult to, her honour, and a disregard for her independence 
which she would not endure. 

Equally difficult would it be to give a solid guarantee against any future 
occupation of the Principalities with reference to the peculiar Treaty which exists 
between the Two Powers respecting those provinces, and which under certain cir- 
cumstances (of which the Powers could not always constitute themselves judges) 
gives to Russia as well as to ‘Turkey the right of sending troops there. That 
Treaty, it is true, has now been grossly violuted ; but it is to be hoped that 
there will be no renewal of an act against which the opinion of Europe has been 
unequivocally pronounced, 

The Porte, however, may be well assured that its own interest can hardly 
exceed that of its allies in enileavouring by every means in their power to 
prevent the recurrence of events such as those which for some months past have 
endangered the peace of the world, | 

In conclusion, | have to observe that these last conditions were vot made in 
the note sent to Vienna, and which, without therm, the Porte was prepared to sign 
as i final settlement of the question, “There is consequently some reason to 
apprehend that they have since been brought forward, under the conviction that 
they could not be complied with; and should this unfortunately be the case it 
will verify the prediction of your Excellency made as long ago as the 16th of 
July, that there would soon be more to apprehend from the rashness than from 
the timidity of the ‘Turkish Ministers; and it will confirm the opinion lately 
communicated to Her Majesty’s Government, and which they gather also from 
the tone of your Excellency’s despatches, namely, “that the feeling of the 
‘Turkish Government is a desire for war, founded on the conviction that France 
and England must still perforce side with Turkey, and that the war will, there- 
fore, be a successful one for the Sultan, and obtain for him guarantees for the 
future which will materially strengthen his tottering power.” 

England and France will shrink from no obligation that their honour and 
their duty clearly prescribe, let the sacrifice be what i may of fulfilling that 
obligation. Although bound by no Treaty stipulations, they look upon the 
maintenanee of the Ottoman Empire as a great feature of European policy, and 
they desire to uphold the dignity and independence of the Sultan, But other 
interests besides those of Turkey ure committed to their charge, and belore they 
expose these to the dangers and the injury that war would inevitably entail, they are 
bound to take care that.no effort for the preservation of peace has been omitted; 
and it is, therefore, in the most friendly spirit, and with a sincere regard for the 
best interests of Turkey, that Her Majesty's Government advise the Porte not 
to be dazzled by the military preparations which with laudable zeal for their own 
defence they have lately made, not to yield to the religious fanaticism for which 
such just provocation has been eiven, nor to think that war under the present 
circumstances of the Ottoman Empire ean fail to be attended with consequences 
most disustrous: but, on the contrary, that they should exhibit a cordial 
readiness to adopt, and not a desire to evade, such an adjustment of their 
present unfortunate differences with Russia os they may think safe and 
honourable,

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, September 2, 1853. 

THE Russian Government are still without any details as to the objections 
entertained by the Sultan as to the projed de note in its present form, which 
was sent from Vienna. 

Their Vienna intelligence comes down only to the 25th ultimo, and 
acquaints them simply that the Sultan's acceptance of the note is subjected to 
its receiving several modifications, the nature and extent of which are not 
indicated, 

When I saw the Chancellor yesterday, he spoke to me with some animation, 
I should perhaps say asperity, of the conduct of the Turks. If they had, he said, 
the fhintest perception of their own interests, they ought to have given their 
adhesion to the projet de note with alacrity (des deux mains). That which the 
Emperor had received without change or hesitation in the course of twenty-four 
hours, should unquestionably have been received by the Turks with the same 
expedition ; their hesitation or their refusal was most deplorable, and it led to 
the suspicion of the Turkish Government not having been made sufficiently 
sensible of the dangers to which they were exposing themselves. 

L replied, that I regretted as much as Count Nesselrode could do that the 
note had not been accepted as it stood; but that when he blamed the Turks, I 
must only remind him that every allowance was to made for a people who were 
trembling not only for their religion, but for their very existence, ‘That it must 
not be forgotten that the late conduct of Russian agents in Bulgaria, who had 
been disseminating translations of the Imperial Circular and Manifesto, was 
caleulated to arouse the religious and political feelings of a sensitive people, and 
that it appeared to have that effect to such a degree, that the suspicions of the 
Turks were directed not only against their avowed enemies, but aguinst their 
Christian friends and allies. 

____Vhis I said T should remark, not so much asa reproach as in the way of 
history, and as explaining a resistance which Count Nesselrode had considered 
incomprehensible. 

The Chancellor retorted with considerable animation, that the conduct 
ascribed to Russian agency would have no influence upon the Turks, or upon 
their interests; that what must infallibly affect them would be the persccutions 
which the Christians were enduring in Bosnia, 

Of them, as I stated, I had no knowledge, and | thought that any facts 
bearing upon these accusations required close examination. 

The Chancellor proceeded to remark, that being unacquainted with the 
details of the alterations required by the Porte, and not having scen the 
Emperor since the arrival of the Vienna intelligence on the 80th ultimo, he 
really was unable to speak with certainty of the Emperor's intentions. He 
could only say, that after all the concessions which had been made by the 
Emperor, it might be conjectured that concession had reached its term: this, 
indeed, had been plainly stated in the despatch to Baron Meyendorff, signilying 
His Majesty’s acceptance [sane variente) of the Vienna projet de note. 

This despatch, dated the 26th July, was, Count Nesselrode said, known to 
your Lordship, and a eopy of it, which he took from his portfolio, he begged 
me to rend. 7 

In conclusion, the Chancellor expressed his apprehensions that no further 
Constantinople intelligence was to be expected before Tuesday next, the 6th 
instant, 

[may state to your Lordship that the language of military men lire is, 
that the evacuation of the Principalities must take place very speedily, if it is to 
take place at all this year, as the roads become so ie ) in the provinces and in 
Bessarabia after the autumnal rains as to be impassable for artillery, nnd very 
trying to troops of all descriptions, 

It appears to me that the Sultan's conduct at this crisis of affairs is deeply 
to be regretted. At this moment every day lost or saved is a matter of erent 
importance ; and whether the Emperor rejects the maditications desired at Con- 
stantinople, or whether he admits them, the loss will be on the Turkish side. 


dll 


In the by far less probable hypothesis, a dangerous question, after being 
made more serious, 18 left open as before. In the other, the unwillingness of 
the Sultan to bend to the suggestions of his alles would offer an unfavourable 
contrast to the readiness with which they were acceded to by the Emperor.

M, DROUYN DE LHUYS informed me this morning that he had

forbode the rejection by the Emperor of ussia of the modifications proposed hy 
the Porte to the project of note which His Majesty had aceepted, His Excel- 
leney seemed, however, to cling to the hope that some means would be found 
at Olmutz of bringing about an arrangement upon the Eastern question. The 
Emperor Nicholas was to leave St. Petersburgh the 13th, to reach Warsaw the 
19th, and to arrive at Olmutz on the 23rd. His Majesty had abandoned for the 
present the journey to Kiefl, Odessa, and Sevastopol, which he had previously 
“nnonneed his intention to undertake. M. Drouyn de Lhuys, after giving me 
this information, said that in the present state of the question four hypotheses 
were possible, two fayourable and two unfavourable : 

The Emperor might accept the note with its modifications, in which case 
his Excellency thought that the question of the evacuation of the Principalities 
ought to find an easy solution. A Turkish Ambassador might be sent to 
Vienna, on his way to St. Petersburgh, with the note signed, and await there the 
jasuing of the orders for the retirement of the Russian troops, setting out 
further on his journey on assurances being given by the Austrian Government 
that those orders were issued. ‘Che Emperor of Russia could hardly refuse his 
participation in an arrangement of the kind. Or, as your Lordship proposed, 
the note signed might be sent to Vienna, and orders given to the Ottoman 
Envoy at Vienna to proceed with it to Russia on ithe conditions stated above. 

Again, the Emperor might refuse the modifications. What was to be done 
‘ny that case? In his opinion the Porte should be invited to reconsider her 


ap 


decision, and, in order to induce her te do 50, the Four Powers might assure her 
that their understanding of the note did not differ from hers. Or, the Porte 
might sign the note and adopt Lord Stratford’s suggestion of making a separate 
communication to the Four Powers, stating the interpretation which she gave to 
the objectionable passages. 

These are the favourable hypotheses. The unfavourable were : 

The Emperor, in refusing the modifications, might say that the Porte, in 
not adhering to the note, had absolved him from all engagements, Or, His 
Majesty might refuse the modifications, putting forward as his reasons for so 
doing claims as objectionable as those urged by Prince Menchikoff. 

But in mentioning these last hypotheses, M. Drouyn de Lhuys added that 
he could not bring himself to believe that the Emperor would take a line which

and England could not hold a different language now from that which they had 
held in the beginning of this affair, and he could hardly hope that Austria and 
Prussia would go as far in their condemnation of Russia. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appears to think that some days will elapse before 
the Emperor of Russia's decision is known, and, indeed, that His Majesty may 
not declare himself before his arrival at Olmutz, Under these circumstances,

1 HELD yesterday a short but important conversation with the Chancellor. 

The subject of the late decision of the Porte having been broached, Count 
Nesselrode said that he could only confirm the decision for which his previous 
remarks must have prepared me. ! 

It would, he suid, be impossible for the Emperor, after the concessions 
whieh he had already made, to abate any further his demands upon the Porte, 
and to admit any alterations in a document which he had accepted with the 
ulterations in it made by the English and French Governments, and that within 
twenty-four hours, 

I begged to remind Count Nesselrode that | had upon more than one 
oecasion forewarned him as to the possibility of a Government acted upon by so 
many ¢ireumstances calculated to arouse religious and national feeling, bemg 
betrayed into imprudent resolutions ; and that now, as before, 1 would express 
the hope that general interests would not be placed in danger by too close an 
attention to resolutions adopted under the influence of such natural excitement, 

To this Count Nesselrode replied, that if 1 would only remember from whit 
point we had started, and to what the satisfuction which it was proposed to 
afford to Russia now amounted, it would be seen what the course must he which 
asense Of her dignity imposed upon Russia. 

© The note,” he suid, “ was not ours; we had no hand in drawing it up, nor 
indeed did it suit us; but we accepted it in the state in which it was received 
ftelle quelle) out of deference to the wishes of our allies; and beyond this point 
we have not, you will allow, been encouraged to proceed. You have seen by 
the newspapers of England, France, and Germany, that in acting as we have 
done, our motives have been misconstrued, and that we have been represented 
as having been compelled by the allied Powers to abate our pretensions, and 
to aceept a compromise which is unacceptable to us.” | 

In reply to further observations of mine, which went to show that the 
resolutions of the Sultan had been taken not so much from anti-Russian feclings 
as fram considerntions of his own security, and those which he was obliged to 
keep in view in fice of a party bent upon pushing matters to extremity, Count 
Nesselrode remarked, that he would repeat what he had long ago said to me, 
shat the Turkish Govermment had not been addressed ina proper tone; that 


Sig 


instead of being consulted, they should have been told that such and such terms 
were considered advisable, and must be subscribed to by them; that nothing 
was to be obtained from the Turks by persuasion, while every point is to be 
carried by decision and menace. Do not deceive yourself, Count Nesselrode 
continued to say; were it even possible for us to give way, nothing, you may be 
sure, would be gained by the concession; the triumph of the Turks would be 
cori and their ingolence would become such that war within six months 
would become inevitable, 

This same expression, as it will be in your Lordship’s recollection, was 
employed by Count Nesselrode upon a former occasion. 

As I was rising to take my leave, the Chancellor stated his intention of 
addressing to Baron Brunnow, by a messenger who would be sent off to London 
on the 10th instant, a despatch, in which the Emperor's final resolution and the 
grounds on which it is taken would be made known to him, for communication 
to Her Majesty's Government. ‘This despatch his Excellency promised to read 
to me if I would call upon him on the day previous to the messenger’s 
departure, 

1 should be wanting in duty if I failed to remark to your Lordship, that the 
unfortunate decision taken at Constantinople appears to have had the untoward 
effect of completely inverting the positions of the Emperor and the Sultan in 
the estimation of my diplomatic colleagues. Hitherto there has been on their 
part an all but unanimous readiness to blame the conduct of Russia towards the 

Yorte; there is now the same unanimity in blaming a resolution which, if acted 

upon, would be fatal to Turkey, and which is calculated to involve in serious 
difficulties those of her allies who were the most intent upon preserving her 
independent existence. 

I will only add, that a person very high in the Emperor's confidence 
observed to me yesterday, that he could affirm positively, and as a matter within 
his personal knowledge, that had the Sultan signified his unconditional aceept- 
anee of the Vienna note, the Imperial forces in the Principalities would be

No, 339. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G. H. Seymour. 


(No. 209.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, September 16, 1853. 

BARON BRUNNOW called upon me yesterday, and in the course of 
conversation inquired if I should object to inform him of the views and_inten- 
tions of Her Majesty’s Government now that the modifications of the Vienna 
note proposed by the Porte had not been adopted by the Emperor of Russia. 

replied that as the fact of their rejection alone was known by the telegraph, 
and that we were as yet ignorant in what manner or upon what grounds they 
had been rejected, I could not say what course it might be the duty of Her 
Majesty’s Government to pursue, but that I should have no difficulty in stating 
to him the views of Her Majesty's Government cting the modifications 
themselves; they were thought unnecessary, as affording no additional security 
or guarantee to the Porte, and because the note was originally framed, and of 
course was now interpreted by the Four Powers in the sense of the modifications ; 
and it. was therefore a matter of regret that they should have been proposed 
and insisted upon by the Turkish Government. The Four Powers, Rowever 
had not hesitated in recommending them to the acceptance of the Emperor, for 
they were not looked upon as altering the character of the note; and as the true 
meaning and intention of that note was not to confer any new power or right 
whatever upon Russia in Turkey, the Four Powers expected that the amend- 
ments would not have been disapproved by His Imperial Majesty, who on 
various occasions had declared that he looked for no new right nor increased 
power in Turkey, but desired simply the maintenance of existing Treaties, and 
the strict stafus quo in religious matters. 

The Emperor had, reluctantly as I was aware, accepted the note upon a 
condition (which might be binding upon himself, but could not be so either on 
the Conference at Vienna or on the Porte), that no change was made in it at 
Constantinople; but it must be borne in mind that it was on the part of the 
Sultan, and not of the Emperor, that the note was to be signed, and that the 
Turkish Government had therefore a right narrowly to examine the terms in 
which it was framed, and to propose any amendments they might think 
indispensable for the future safety and independence of the Ottoman Empire. 

The amendments were not viewed in that light by the Four Powers, and 
the course pursued by the Porte was the more to be regretted, as it delayed the 
evacuation of the Principalities, which they did not permit themselves to doubt 
would at once have taken place on the acceptance of the note by the Turkish 
Government. Nevertheless the modifications could not be disregarded, because 
they were thought to be of importance at Constantinople, and because they 
were not at variance with the intentions of the Conference at Vienna. 

But, | added, if the Emperor adheres to his intention of seeking no increase 
of power in Turkey, if he retains his opinion that the maintenance of the 
Ottoman Empire is a great principle of European policy, and that its dissolution 
would be a great European catastrophe, it was difficult to understand why he 
should object to these amendments of the note, or to believe that he would 
expose Europe to the dangers of war, and hasten the event he deprecates, rather 
than adopt certain modifications, unimportant as they were assumed to be, 
simply because they were proposed by the Porte. 

Baron Brunnow said that as he had not then received the despatches he 
was expecting from St. Petersburgh, he could give me no information as to the 
grounds upon which the Emperor had rejected the modifications, but he asked 
me if it was still the intention of Her Majesty's Government to cooperate with 
Austria towards bringing about a peaceful solution of the question; and I 
answered that such was their intention, as we had every reason to believe that 
no difference of opinion existed between the twa RUS is

My Lord, Vienna, September 14, 1853. 

| HAVE already reported to your Lordship by telegraph this day, that 
the despatches from Count Nesselrode announcing the decision of the Emperor 
Nicholas not to accept the modifications of the Vienna note which had been pro- 
posed by the Porte, had been received by Baron Meyendorfl. These despatches 
were communicated by the Russian Minister to Count Buol, who immediately 
requested the members of the Conference, Count Arnim, Baron Bourqueney, 
and myself, to meet him at his residence. : 

Count Buol placed in our hands the despatch of Count Nesselrode 
announcing the receipt of the Vienna note, amended according to the proposals 
of the Turkish Government; and after entering into various details as to the 
manner in which the original note had been submitted to the Emperor and had 
been accepted by him, Count Nesselrode announces that His Imperial Majesty, 
while adhering to his acceptation of the note as it had been originally presented 
to him by the Austrian Government, with the sanction of the Governments of 
England, France, and Prussia, declined to agree to any modification of it. 

Count Buol informed the members present that the despatch of Count 
Nesselrode had been communicated by the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to our 
respective Governments; and as it will consequently be in your Lordship’s 
possession before this despatch can reach you, I need not enter into any further 
deseription of its contents. anny 

‘ount Buol then stated that he admitted the perfect right of the Emperor 
of Russia (after having aceepted a proposal which had been submitted to him by 
the Four Powers) to refuse to adopt any alterations in the character of that note 
which the Governments in alliance with Turkey had not considered necessary 
for the maintenance of her dignity and independence; and although he had 
recommended to the Cabinet of His Imperial Majesty the adoption of the 
modifications, yet, as that advice had not been accepted, he felt that he hatl now 
no other course to pursue than to report this failure to the Government of the 
Sultan, and to reiterate to them in the strongest manner the advice he had 
originally given them to accept the note such as the Four Powers had proposed 
it. Count Buol remarked upon the importance of the Emperor of Russta’s 
declaration that in adhering to his acceptation of the original note, he was still 
in the intention (as'soon as it should be presented to him by an Ambassador) to 
order the evacuation of the Principalities, and from that moment to consider the 
relations between Russia and the Porte as reestablished. 

Count Buol stated that Baron Meyendorff had received a second despatch 
trom Count Nesselrode, expressing the great disappointment felt by the Emperor 
of Russia at the modification of the original note by the Porte, and his regret at 
the consequent delay in the execution of the order which had already been 
prepared for commencing the evacuation of the Principalities, and which would 
have tuken place immediately upon the Emperor's receiving the assurance that 
that note had been adopted by the Porte, and would be presented to him. 
Count Nesselrode declares in this despatch that this measure will still be carried 
out, if the Emperor should receive a satisfactory assurance from the Sultan in 
time for the evacuation to take place during the month of October ; later in the 
year it would not be possible to move the troops. Res ' 
‘Under these circumstances, Count Buol expressed his hope and his belief 
that the other Governments who had hitherto acted in concert with Austria in 
endeavourine to arrive uta peaceable solution of this question, would agree to 
the decision which, under the orders of his Sovereign the Emperor, he had now 
announced; and he requested each of the members of the Conference to call 
for the eurliest decision of their Governments upon this subject, and to recom- 
mend to them, in case they adhered to the course he had adopted, to lose no 
time in sending instructions to their Representatives at Constantinople. 

Count Arnim stated that, without waiting for more particular instructions, 
he adopted, on the part of the Prussian Government, the recommendation of 


425 


Count Buol., Baron Bourqueney and myself assented to the request of Count 
Buol, and with that view I addressed to your Lordship the telegraphic despatch 
of this day, to which T have already alluded. 

Count Buol read to the Conference the despatch he had addressed to the 
[nternuncio at Constantinople, directing him to use every means to induce the 
Turkish Government to adhere to the original note which had been submitted to 
them, and to represent to them that the Austrian Government adopted that

communicated to the Turkish Ambassador here, who has written to his Govern-

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Barl of Clarendon.—(Received September 19.) 


(No. 249, Secret.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 29, 1853. 

THE secret overtures urged upon the Turkish Ministers by M, de la Cour 
within the last few days, do not appear to have been attended with much 
suceess, The notion of a conventional agreement among the four, if not the 
five principal Powers of Europe, guaranteeing the independence and integrity of 
the Turkish Empire, offers naturally to the Porte an agreeable, though distant 
and uncertain, prospect. It required no advice from me, though I gave 1 when 
asked, to induce the Porte to make its acknowledgments for the idea, and to 
express the satisfaction with which it looked forward even to the voseibility of 
realizing such a plan, But the accompanying advice to accede to Count Buol's 
note, without the proposed modifications, experienced a different reception. 

Reshid Pasha has informed the French Ambassador, that neither he nor his 
colleagues are prepared to entertain any suggestion of that kind. It appears 
that the Sheikh-ul-Islam declared in Council, the day before yesterday, that he 
would rather break his seal than put it to a note like that which had been 
transmitted from Vienna. | aeuee 

If Lam rightly informed, as | believe myself to be, the French Ambassador 
called upon several of the Turkish Ministers separately, and held the same 
language to all that he held to Reskid Pasha, requesting each to guard a strict 
silence as to the nature of his communication. ‘This came out when they met 
together, and was the occasion of some merriment, The Ambassador fancied 
that he had made a favourable impression on Mehemet Ali, the Seraskier, but it 
wroved a mistake, He has shown a more particular anxiety that [ should be 

ept in ignorance of his proceedings. He sounded me yesterday respecting the 

Convention and the guaranty, but limited his confidence to the idea as proceed- 
ing from his Government, and as having been a subject of deliberation between 
your Lordship and Count Walewski, I told him that I was aware of something 
having naaaed between the two Governments, but that [ had no instructions 
thereon, and that in London the question was possibly considered a little 
premature, he ee A 

The Porte, meanwhile, persists in completing quietly and vigorously its 
defensive preparations. New levies, as 1 mentioned before, have been ordered, 
to the amount of 40,000 or 50,000 men. In some parts of the country the 
remaining portion of the redil, or militia, is called out, and from every quarter 
we hear that small detachments, of 400 or 500 men each, ure constantly 
embarking for Bulgaria, or marching towards one of the military stations, ‘The 
Porte has declined, for the present, sending orders to the Dardanelles for the 
eventual admittance of the French squadron.

Inclosure | in No. 347. 
M. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, Therapia, August 27, 1853. 

T HAVE the honour to report that M. de la Cour called to-day on Reshid 
Pasha at the Porte, and told him that the Convention he spoke of two days ago 
would not be entered into by the Four Powers unless the Porte accepted the 
note drawn up at Vienna as it stands; that the Porte would derive a great 
advantage by that Convention, if agreed upon; and that the acceptance of the 
note as approved by the Four Powers, without further delay, will have the best 
effect in urope, and will produce an important change in the public opinion in 
favour of Turkey. 

Reshid Pasha replied, that when the Cabinets and the public will be made 
acquainted with the well-grounded motives which induced the Porte not to 
adopt the note without the modifications proposed, he is pretty certain that the 
Four Powers, and especially England and France, will duly appreciate the Porte's 
objections, if indeed they wish to safeguard and maintain its independence and 
sovereign rights; but if, on the contrary, they are seeking for an opportunity to 
disengage themselves from their repeated promise to support the Sultan's rights, 
the Porte cannot force them to afford either moral or material assistance. but 
she will then be called upon to submit the whole question to the consideration 
of public opinion, and leave it to pronounce its judgment, which will be 
impartial and favourable to the Porte, 

All T can tell you, proceeded Reshid Pasha, is, that I will hy no means put 
my seal to a paper which, to my appreciation and that of my colleagues, is detri- 
mental to the honour, the dignity, and independence of my Sovereign and his 
Government, And, besides, how can we go back without dian raring ourselves 
in the eyes of our own people, towards whom we are engaged thus far? He 
moreover stated that so long as he (Reshid Pasha) remains in office, he will 
never give his assent to the acceptance of the note in question; and should the 
Porte he forced to show compliance, both he and his colleagues will instantly 
tender their resignation. If you think, he continued, that those who come after- 
wards will act otherwise, it is a great mistake. We are all unanimously deter- 
mined to adhere to our former decision. My sole regret is that the line pursued 
just now by the Western Powers will have for final effect to compel the Porte 
to throw itself into the arms of Russia, and come to some settlement which 
would probably change the policy of Europe, 

You mean, said the French Amb or, that the Porte would enter into a 
Treaty of offensive and defensive alliance with Russia: Europe will never allow 
the Porte to he preyed upon by Russia. In that case, observed his Highness, 
you must adopt a different view of the pending question, and not endeavour to 
humiliate the Porte by compelling it to act against its dignity and independence. 

M. de la Cour said that the Seraskicr Pasha, to whom he had paid a visit 
in the morning, seemed rather to like his proposal; and added, that he was alsa 
going to wait on the Grand Vizier to speak to him on the same subject. 

Reshid Pasha could not help observing to M. de la Cour that, if he recol- 
lected right, he thought that mm the despatch he communicated to him two days 
ago, there was only question of the Convention, and not a single word about 
the acceptance or rejection of the note, I suppose, said he, you will talk the 
matter over with the British Ambassador. M. de la Cour replied in the 
negative, and again recommended his Highness not to make any allusion 
whatever to your Lordship. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) E. PISANI,

Inclosure 4 in No. 348. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Consul Colquhoun, 


Sir, Therapia, August 29, 1853. 

I AM happy to assure you that your proceedings in execution of my 
instructions respecting the Hospodar, and the suspension of your Consular 
functions in consequence of the course pursued by his Highness, have met with 
my entire approbation ; and I shall have much satisfaction in learning that they 
have equally obtained the more important approval of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment. 

I avail myself of the same opportunity to acknowledge the zealous attention 
with which you have kept me informed of such occurrences in the Principality 
as necessarily carry with them a more than usual degree of interest under present 
circumstances. 

T have noted with particular satisfaction the general understanding and

My Lord, Therapia, September 1, 1853. 

| RECEIVED last night from your Lordship's office a printed copy of the 
speech delivered on the 20th ultimo to both Houses of Parliament by the Lords 
Commissioners, in Her Majesty's name. Anticipating the interest with which 
those paragraphs of it that allude to the Eastern question would be read by the 
‘Turkish Ministers, I sent it down at an early hour this morning to Reshid 
Pasha. M. Stephen Pisani being confined to his bed by indisposition, 1 directed 
Vir. Alison to take charge of it. Though Reshid Pasha was already informed of 
its contents, he received my communication with every appearance of interest, 
in the conversation which ensued, his language, as reported to me by 
Me. Alison, was that of a man who, in concert with his colleagues, had made up 
iis mind to hold firm to the decision taken, as your Lordship knows, by the 
Sultan and his Council. It appeared distinctly that the present Ministers are 
prepared to go to war rather than give way, and, if restrained by the Sultan, to 
resign; leaving to His Majesty the difficulty, perhaps the impossibility, of 


replacing them by a more pacific Administration. It may be conjectured that 


ac | 


they speculate on the war spirit roused in their nation and army, and the danger 
of disappointing it, for motives wherewith to counteract the fears, were such to 
predominate in the Sultan’s mind, of a contest singlehanded with Russia. The 
national will would thus, ay in former times. be brought to bear in a flood tide 
on the hesitations of the Palace, and prejudices which have hitherto obstructed 
the introduction of useful measures, particularly in respect of foreign capital and 
industry, would, they imagine, yield to the pressure of war and its accompanying 
necessities. 

An anonymous Turkish placard, which appeared two or three days ago on 
the gate of a mosque at Constantinople, may be taken as a shadow of the 
coming event, Its style is that of an educated person; and it was thought of 
importance enough to be conyeyed to the Sultan, who read it, however, without 
any apparent emotion. A translation of the writing in question is inclosed 
herewith. 

The Sultan reviewed the Egyptian army the day before yesterday. He was 
received with great demonstrations of loyalty by the squadrons as well as by the 
troops. His Majesty was in a single boat unattended; the appearance of the 
ships and the precision of the salutes were remarkable. |

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received September 19.) 
(No. 259.) 


My Lord, Therapia, September 5, 1853. 
I LEARN from undoubted authority that M. Argyropulo, the Russian 
interpreter, has lately visited two or three, if not. more, of the Turkish Ministers, 
under circumstances which have attracted attention. Yesterday he called upon 
Reshid Pasha, and leaving in doubt whether his visit was authorized or other- 
wise, talked over the Porte’s amendments to Count Buol’s note, His remarks, 
as repeated to me, may be summed up thus. He thought that Russia might 
accept the first amendment, but that the second and third would meet with 
determined resistance. In corroboration of this opinion he added, that the 
Court of St. Petersburgh would insist in having a full participation in all the 
religious privileges accorded by Treaty in past times to France and to Austria, 
He went a step further, and seemed to anticipate a perfect agreement between 
his Court and those of the other four Powers concerning the Austrian note. He 
apprehended that the Porte would find herself in the same insulated position 
from which the acceptance of that note had rescued his Government. 

It does not appear that Reshid Pasha relaxed, in consequence of M. 
Argyropulo’s remarks, from the determination which he had previously taken, 
in common with the whole Ministry and Council; but curiosity, and possibly 
some degree of uneasiness, has been excited in his mind by learning that 
Mehemet Rushdi, the late Seraskivr, a person of considerable influence, had 
been closeted with M. Argyropulo for more than an hour, and that the Pasha 
had made no mention of the circumstance cither to him or to any one of their 
mutual colleagues. 

I am informed, moreover, that the French Ambassador, though he told me 
that he had received nothing new from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, has twice resumed 
his solicitations to Reshid Pasha, either in person or by message, since the 
arrival of the last steam-packet on the Ist instant. In conversing with me, 
though he said nothing of his overtures to Reshid Pasha, he inquired whether | 
did not think that some opening towards further concession might be made at 
the Porte by means of Mehemed Rushdi Pasha, and the present Seraskier, 
Mehemet Ali, I replied that | had no instructions on which to act under the 
present circumstances; that whatever was to happen I conceived that, in 
common self-respect, the Porte must wait quietly for a reply to its demand 
of amendments, and that I should have thought that the leaders of the war party 
would be the last persons from whom spontaneous, not to say premature 
concession, was to be expected, 

If any change has really taken place in the counsels of any, or of all the 
Sultan's Ministers, I am ignorant of it; and the departure now preparing of the 
Egyptian contingent for Varna, seems to bear me out in continuing to believe 
the contrary. 

It cannot, at the same time, be doubted, that as danger approaches and 
difficulties thicken, the sense of responsibility and the apprehension of disastrous 
eventualities, weigh more heavily on the firmest minds ; and still less can it be 
denied that Turkey, encouraged by the approval of all Europe, animated by the 
appearance of the British and French squadrons at Besika Bay, and justly fearful 
of further invasion from Russia, has advanced into a position from which, if it be 
not providentially rescued or seasonably succoured, it can only escape by a 
sacrilice which it deems no less perilous than humiliating, or by a conflict but 

too likely to end in defeat or exhaustion. 

Hitherto the prognostications of massacre and insurrection have si 
failed. I have already paid a j

These alarms may be mere inventions, or at least exaggerations, but they 
carry enough of probability to make it imprudent to neglect them; and I have 
no doubt that they operate more or less on the minds of those who have attached 
their fortunes to the fate of the Government. 

The consequences to be apprehended from even a partial accomplishment of 
such contingencies need not be pointed out to your Lordship’s sagacity. The 
most immediate and inevitable would be one which, by placing the reins of 
government in the hands of an ignorant and high-spirited young man, under 
circumstances of unequalled dith aul; would increase immeasurably the hazards 
of the crisis, and stave off an impending catastrophe one to replace it by another 
less imminent, but, perhaps, in the issue, more fatal still.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 308.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 20, 1853. 

| INCLOSE copies of despatches* which I have addressed to Her Majesty's 
Ambassador at Constantinople, and to Sir G, H, Seymour, respecting the 
modifications of the note sent from Vienna that have been proposed by the 
Porte. 

[t is important that your Lordship should be in possession of the views of 
Her Majesty's Government upon this subject, as you are going to Olmutz, and 
may possibly have an opportunity of communicating with the Emperor of 
Russia, or with Count Nesselrode, who it is understood will accompany His 
Imperial Majesty. 

Your Lordship will perceive that Her Majesty’s Government considered the 
modifications to be unimportant, and regretted that they had been pro vosed, 
Her Majesty’s Government were accordingly prepared still to seamed that 
the note should be accepted by the Porte upon their interpretation of it, which 
was that of the Conference at Vienna ; for the Four Powers, who have anxiously 
laboured to effect a peaceful and honourable solution of the question, thought 
they did justice and gave ample security to the Porte by acting upon the decla- 
ration so repeatedly made by the Emperor, that he sought for no new right and 
no increase of power in ‘Turkey, but desired only the maintenance of existing 
Treaties, and the status quo in religious matters. Upon this principle, and with 
no other intention, the note was framed, and Her Majesty’s Government consl- 
dered that no other meaning could be attached to it; but the reasons given by 
Count Nessclrode in his despatch to Baron Meyendorff for objecting to the 
modifications induce Her Majesty’s Government to think that the apprehensions 
entertained by the Porte, so far from being groundless, are to a great extent 
justified by the construction put upon the original note by Count Nesselrode. 

I do not propose to enter into a discussion upon the objections raised by 
Count Nesselrode. It is sufficient to say, that they are at variance with the 
intentions of the Four Powers; and Her Majesty's Government feel that it would 
not be just or honourable, either towards the Emperor or the Sultan, to press 
the acceptance of the note upon the Porte so long #8 any misunderstanding 
existed upon its true meaning; and they feel, moreover, that the reestablishment 
of real and permanent friendly relations between Kussia and ‘Turkey, the object 
which the Four Powers have sincerely at heart, would be defeated if the note 
which they looked upon us the basis of reconciliation were hereafter to be made 
an cause of irritating discussion with respect to claims which it might be held to 
justify, and the resistance to them which, on the other side, would appear 


® See Now, $25 ond 329. 


335 


equally warrantable. The importance of avoiding all misunderstanding upon 
the question itself, and at the critical period at which it has arrived, cannot be 
exaggerated; and Her Majesty’s Government, therefore, in the interest of peace, 
and possibly as the last hope of perserving Europe from the danger which now 
appears imminent, are anxious to learn whether the Emperor is still determined 
to seek no new right and no further extension of power in Turkey; and as they 
feel convinced that His Imperial Majesty will not hesitate to renew his former 
declarations to that effect, they cannot either believe that he will object to such 
alterations of the Vienna note as would have the effect of quieting the alarm of 
the Porte, and that he will not, upon a misunderstanding that it is in his power 
to rectify, permit the recent negotiations to prove fruitless and thus expose 
Europe to the risks of war, which would entail the dissolution of the Ottoman 
Empire—an event which the Emperor, in common with all his allies, has never 
ceased to deprecate as a calamity of the greatest magnitude. 

Inthe event of your Lordship being honoured by an interview with the 
Emperor at Olmutz, you will govern yourself by the language of this despatch 
and its inclosures, and you will make the views of Her Majesty's Government 
known to Count Nesselrode, who, with reference to the importance and pressing 
nature of the subject, will doubtless overlook the irregularity of the communi- 
cation being made through your Lordship, who has no official relations with the 
Court of Russia. 

I am, &c. 


(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 312.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 21, 1853. 


COUNT COLLOREDO communicated to me confidentially, yesterday, 
two despatches, dated the 13th instant, which had been addressed by Count Buol 
to Baron Bruck, on the receipt of the intelligence of the refusal of the Emperor 
of Russia to acquiesce in the modifications which the Porte desired to introduce 
into the Vienna note. 

The first of these despatches purports to give the substance of the answer 
from St. Petersburgh; that the Emperor of Russia's consent to accept the 
Vienna note was contingent on ils acceptance, unaltered, by the Porte; that 
having renounced for himself the pretension to change the terms of the note, the 
Emperor could not admit that the Porte was entitled to make any alteration, and 
by so doing place Russia in a position of inferiority towards Turkey: that the 
Emperor had done all that could be required of him in accepting, without 
hesitation, a nute which, in various respects, could not but be distasteful to him; 
and that though entitled to make alterations if Turkey might doso, His Imperial 
Majesty had considered that the Porte would, like himself, look upon the note 
as not open to alteration, and on this understanding His Imperial Majesty had 
accepted it. That the Emperor, therefore, insisted upon the acceptance of the 
note by the Porte; and although released from his engagements by the refusal 
of the Porte, he was nevertheless still ready, on the arrival at St. Petersburgh of 
« Turkish Ambassador with the note unaltered, and without any conditions 
being attached to it, to withdraw his troops from the Turkish territory, 

Such being the tenor of the accounts from St. Petersburgh, Count Buol 
goes on to say, that nothing remained but to exhort the Porte duly to weigh the 
serious consequences of rejecting the only remaining chance of an amicable 
arrangement. Austria, undeterred by any feeling of pique at the rejection of the 
note which she had proposed, had urged Russia to accept the moditea ioe of 
which Austria herself did not approve, Whatever shades of difference might 
exist in the language and views of their Representatives at Constantinople, the 
Four Powers were unanimously of opinion that the note was worthy of accept- 
ance by the Porte, and was not calculated to prej udice either the interests or the 
dignity of the Sultan. With no less unanimity did they regret the hesitation 
shown by the Porte to listen to their advice; and the Austrian Government felt 
sure that they would now all agree ior NB the Porte no longer to refuse 
2A @ 


336 


accepting the note as it stood. At all events, if her counsels were again dis- 
regarded, Austria, while deploring the fatal consequences which must ensue from 
a fresh refusal on the part of the Porte to defer to the wishes of the Powers, 
could only consider her efforts to effect a reconciliation as at an end, 

In the second despatch Baron Bruck is directed to urge, not only the 
influential members of the Ottoman Ministry, but even the Sultan in person, no 
longer to defer adopting the only course which the state of affairs required; to 
press for the immediate dispatch of the note in its original shape by a special 
ambassador to Vienna, or that the Turkish Ambassador at Vienna should be 
authorized to seek an opportunity to place it before the Emperor Nicholas: and 
the Austrian Government would, in that case, endeavour to obtain an audience 
for the Ambassador before the Emperor of Russia set out from Warsaw on his 
return to St. Petersburgh, as the only means of effecting the evacuation of the 
Principalities before the winter. 

Count Buol goes on to say, that it might be suggested to the Sultan to 
accompany the note with an autograph letter to the Emperor Nicholas, in which 
His Highness might express the doubts which had occasioned the hesitation of 
the Divan, and so afford the Emperor an opportunity of tranquillizing the alarm 
which had been excited. Austria would, in that case, exert herself, and she had 
reason to suppose not without effect, to obtain still greater concessions for 
Turkey; for Austria could not doubt that the views of the Emperor were 
pacific, and his desire sincere to effect a reconciliation with the Porte; no better 
proof of which could be adduced than the fact that the Russian Army had 
already been ordered to prepare for the evacuation of the Ottoman. territory, in 
ease the Vienna note had been accepted by the Porte. In fact, Austria knew 
that the arrival of the Turkish Ambassador at St. Petersburgh would not have 
been waited for as a preliminary to the commencement of the withdrawal of the 
Russian forces. 

When Count Colloredo had finished reading these despatches he gaid, it 
was of the utmost importance that Her Majesty’s Ambassador at Constantinople 
should receive instructions similar to those which had been transmitted to the 
Internuncio, again to press the Vienna note on the acceptance of the Porte, 

In reply, I expressed my regret that such instructions could not be sent, as 
I had that morning received despatches from Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, stating 
that it was utterly impossible for the Turkish Government to agree to the note 
without modifications; but that the chief reason which must influence Her 
Majesty's Government no longer to urge the Porte on this subject, was the 
despatch of Count Nesselrode to Baron Meyendorff, explaining the grounds 
upon which the Russian Government objected to the moditications; and I could 
not help expressing my surprise, that no allusion should have been made to that 
document in the despatches which Count Colloredo had just read, for it was 
now clear that the Russian Government endeavoured to give to the note a 
construction not intended by the Four Powers who framed it. 

Count Colloredo said, that if instructions in the sense that Count Buol 
requested were not sent to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, there would be an end 
to the Conference at Vienna, I answered that that would be a matter of 
sincere regret. to Her Majesty's Government, who had considered that united 
opinion and action of the Four Powers upon not anly the present, but future 
questions, between Russia and the Porte, would tend to preserve peace and to 
uphold the Ottoman Empire; but that no advantage could be worth purchasing 
by dishonesty ; and Her Majest Ys Government would consider it nothing short 
of dishonesty to persuade the Turkish Government to sien the note, now that 
they were made aware that their interpretation of it was not that of the Emperor 
of Russia. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 21.)

My Lord, Paris, September 19, 1853. 


I HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
returned to Paris last nicht, I.received a note from him this morning, inviting 
me to call upon him. Upon proceeding to his residence I found that he had 
gone to the eae at St. Cloud, and it was not until a late hour this evening 
that 1 sueceeded in having an interview with him. 

He adverted immediately to the proceedings of the Conference of Vienna, 
since the refusal of the Emperor of Russia to accept the Vienna note, as modified 
by the Porte, was known in that capital. 

He read me two telegraphic despatches reecived from M. de Bourqueney, 
the one dated yesterday, informing M. Drouyn de Lhuys that the Representa- 
tives of the Four Powers had signed a Protocol for communication to the Porte, 
declaring that there was nothing in the note emanating from the Vienna Con- 
ference subversive of the sovereign rights of the Sultan; the other, dated 
9 o'clock this morning, showing that this declaration had not been obtained 
without considerable resistance on the part of Austria and Prussia, who had 
refused to subscribe to the more extended form proposed by Lord Westmorland 
in your Lordship’s name. 

Still M. de Bourqueney considers that a great point has been gained in 
obtaining any collective declaration whatever from the Representatives of the 
Four Powers, and he argues that there is nothing to prevent England and 
France from adding on their parts such further assurances os the nature of the 
ease may require. M. Drouyn de Lhuys hus adopted this view, and he pro- 
posed this morning to the Emperor that the French Government should adhere 
to the Protocol signed yesterday at Vienna, and that M. de la Cour should be 
further instructed to state to the Turkish Ministers that France would be ready 
to give this interpretation to the Vienna note whenever circumstances required 
her to doso. Under such assurances the Porte ought to be pressed to sign 
the original Vienna note. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys hoped that your Lordship would adopt the same 
course. He would have preferred that your Lordship’s projet of declaration 
communicated to him by Count Walewski, and strenuously supported by M, de 
Bourqueney, should have found favour at Vienna: but this not being the case, 
the next best thing in his opinion was to earry the Cabinets of Vienna and 
Berlin, as far as practicable, with those of London and Paris. Nothing need 
then prevent the two latter from giving for themselves such further explanations 
or assurances as they might think proper. ‘The Protocol of Conference, if it did 
nothing else, recognized the existence of Turkey, and asserted a principle in 
regard to her. He thought this preferable to no declaration at all. 

The Emperor agreed in this opinion, and it had been telegraphed to London 
for communication to your Lordship. No answer would be sent to Vienna 
respecting it until your Lordship's reply should be received. When I lett 
M, Drouyn de Lhuys at 6 o'clock, he was anxiously expecting it. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Paris, September 19, 1853. 
M. DE BOURQUENEY, in his telegraphic despatch dated this morring, 
of which mention is made in my preceding despatch, informs M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys that M. de Hiibner is desired to inquire what further steps the French 
Government will be ready to take should the Porte persist in her resolution 


ast 
ts 


oad 


to refuse the Vienna note without modifications. Count Buol is desirous that 
the Cabinets should not be taken by surprise (au dépourvu) as they were by the 
late refusal of Russia, but that some plan of action should have been agreed 
upon. He wishes that all the efforts of France at Constantinople should then 
be directed to prevent the Porte from commencing hostilities, Austria under- 
taking a similar task towards the Emperor of Russia. M. de Bourqueney adds, 
that he should not be surprised if a desire was expressed that the English and 
French fleets should come up to Constantinople to impose by their arrival 
upon the Porte, and that their presence in the Bosphorus should be turned to 
account to make Russia believe that they were acting es a pressure on the 
Porte, M. de Bourqueney appears to doubt the policy of such a proceeding. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys inquired of me what I thought of it. Ireplied that it 
seemed to me impossible to admit the parity which Count Buol seemed disposed 
to establish between the relative positions of Turkey and Russia. In fact, 
Count Buol’s proposition went to state that if Russia was allowed to remain 
quietly in the Principalities, she would give an equivalent by promising not to 
advance across the Danube, whereas the real state of the case was that Russia 
had no business in the Principalities, and that she would put herself still more 
in the wrong if she advanced further; while the Porte in abstaining from any 
attempt to drive the Russians back, was foregoing a right whieh, although it 
might be prudent not to exercise, was nevertheless a right that no one could 
contest. ‘The two Cabinets of England and France had, in the interests of 
general peace, counselled this moderate conduct to the Porte, and they might 
continue to counsel it abstractedly ; but it seemed to me next to impossible that 
they should admit it to be implied that Russia was making a concession in 
abstaining from further aggression. With regard to the appearance of the fleets 
at Constantinople, I said that I felt convinced that. Her NV ajesty's Government 
would never allow Her Majesty’s flect to be considered by Russia as intended 
to coerce the Porte into the acceptance of a note which she had a perfect right 
to modify or reject, however much it might be regretted that that right had 
been exercised, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared to coincide in this opinion, but he reserved 
to himself to reconsider it before he pronounced any deci ed judgment upon it.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 21.) 


(No. 695. Confidential.) 
My Lord, . Paris, Seplember 19, 1853, 

M. DE KISSELEFF communicated this afternoon to M. Drouya de Lhuys 
two documents, of which | have no doubt your Lordship has knowledge through 
M. de Brunnow; the one being a despatch stating why the Emperor of Russia 
has determined on rejecting the Vienna note as modified by the Porte; the 
other being a memorandum examining the modifications themselves, and show- 
ing the points on which the Russian Government differed from the interpretation 
sought to be put upon them by the Porte. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys described the first of these papers as being most ably 
drawn up; the second he thinks bad in argument and worse in principle. He 
eaid that a certain interference in the welfare of the Christian subjects of the Porte 
ig unmistakeably claimed in it as a deduction from the ‘Treaty of Kainardji. He 
told M. de Kisseleff that he regretted that he had read the second paper to him, 
as it opened afresh the whole discussion, and almost placed matters where they 
were at the beginning of this regrettable affair. 

M. de Kisseleff inquired what the French Government proposed doing. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that they were still anxious that the Porte should 
sign the Vienna note; that they still advised her to do so; but that Russia also 
should lend her aid, M. de Kisseleff rejoined, that that could not be, and that 
‘t rested with the Representatives who had proposed the note to insist on its 
acceptance. ‘ And indeed," he asked, " how could we assist you?” M, Drouya 


339 


de Lhuys answered that Russia might show a more conciliatory disposition 
towards Turkey ; that the Emperor had given, since the commencement of this 
affair, many satisfactory assurances as to his objects and intentions. Let His 
Majesty collect these together, and repeat them at Vienna. Such a proceeding 
would strengthen the hands of the Conference. M. de Kisseleff asserted that 
this was the business of the Conference, and not of the Emperor. “Am I to 
understand thereby,” exclaimed M. Drouyn de Lhuys, “that the Emperor of 
Russia declines to take his part with the other Great Powers in promoting the 
continuance of peace? Does he abjure the noble part he has layed until now 
‘n the Councils of Europe? What has induced France to interfere in this 
quarrel? A wish to prevent the dissolution of the Turkish Empire, because 
such a catastrophe would probably lead to an European war. But the Emperor 
of Russia has besides the duties of a neighbour to perform; and he claims to 
watch over the interests of cleven millions of the Porte’s subjects. Is he not 
then doubly bound to aid in the preservation of peace! and why should he try 
and devolve this duty on others? If such is his policy, let him state it openly. 
The Emperor of the French will not then shrink from the additional burthen 
sought to be laid upon his shoulders.” 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


P.S. September 20.—M. Drouyn de Lhoys, in referring again to this 
conversation, added, that M. de Kisseleff, seeing the bad impression made by his 
communication of the memorandum, said that it was not to be considered as an 
official ote nor too much importance given to its contents. M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys replied, that before he could consider it in any other light than an official 
communication, he must have an official declaration from M. de Kisseleff that it 
had no real value.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 21.) 
(No. 701.) 
My Lord, Paris, September 20, 1853. 


| HAVE just seen M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who read to me'a despatch which 
he had received this morning from Count Walewski giving an account of a 
conversation which that Ambassador had held with your Lordship yesterday in 
the presence of the Earl of Aberdeen. Count Walewski stated that your 
Lordship had read to him the copy of a communivation made to you b M. de 
Brunnow, giving the reasons why Russia refused to adhere to the modifications 
demanded by the Porte before the latter could accept the Vienna note; that 
these reasons showed that Rugsia put a very different interpretation upon the 
sense of the Vienna note from that intended by the Conference; that it 
appeared consequently to Lord Aberdeen and to yourself that any further 
proceedings at Vienna would be useless, for that it would not be fair to urge 
the Porte to sign a document which would give Russia such advantages as it 
was now clear the Russian Government expected from it, Count Walewski 
however continuing to press your Lordship to send instructions to Lord West- 
morland in the sense indicated in my despatch No. 692 af yesterday's date, you 
promised to give him a more positive answer to-day, 

Count Walewski states further that he insisted upon the necessity of the 
two Governments taking some decided resalution as to their fnture action, the 
ised crisis rendering any further hesitation extremely dangerous. Such, in a 
‘ow words, is the substance of a long despatch from the French Ambassador in 
London. 

After reading it to me, M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed himself as. still 
desirous that the declaration emanating from the Vieuna Conference should be 
sent to Constantinople, accompanied by such further assurances as the French 
and English Governments might think it expedient to give. 

He told me further that ufter his conversation with M. de Kisseleff yester-

day, to which reference is made in my despatch No. 695, he had sent a tele- 
graphic despatch to M. de Hourqueney desiring him to demand categorically of 
M. de Buol whether the Austrian Cabinet adhered to the Russian interpretation 
‘ven to the Vienna note or not. He appears to hope that this summary 
mand will foree an explanation unfavourable to Russia from Courit Buol, who 
will be placed in the dilemma of baving expressed an opinion in the first instance 
that the Turkish modifications were of no importance, and of expressing a

I observed that whatever might be the result of the step which he had

which may yet avert the storm ready to burst in the East, 
He will see the Emperor in Council to-morrow, and I am to have an
