The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received September 23.) 


(No. 350.) 
My Lord, Vienna, September 17, 18043, 
UPON the receipt yesterday of your Lordship’s despatch dated the 1th 
instant, | wrote to Count Buol stating that | should wish to communicate it to 
him, and that I thought it would be advisable to assemble the Conference. 
Count Buol appointed 3 o'clock, when I was met by my other colleagues. I 
read to them your Lordship’s despatch, and M. de Bourqueney also read the 
despatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys of the 12th, which he had received, and 
which contained the draft of « note to be addressed to Reshid Pasha, which is 
alluded to in your Lordship’s despatch, Count Buol stated what I have 
reported in my telegraphic message of yesterday’s date, that having already 
written to the Internuncio the despateh which he had read to us on a former 
day, directing him in the most anxious terms to press upon the Porte the 
importance of accepting the original note as it had been proposed by the Four 
Powers, he felt that it would be impossible he could now associate himself to any 
communication which appeared to hint less caleulated to obtain the object which 
all the Powers were anxious for; and he particularly remarked upon the absence 
in the note proposed by the French Government, of any mention of the recom- 
mendation to adopt the Vienna note as it originally stood, although in your 
Lordship's telegraphic despatch that advice was tendered. On the other hand 
Count Buol remarked, while he admitted the ability with whieh the French note 
was drawn up, yet that it was not conformable to the statement in your Lord- 
ship's despatch upon the subject of the declarations and assurances to be given 
to the Turkish Government. Count Buol being therefore of opinion that he 
could not new associate himself to any collective action which would not 
correspond with the communications he had already transmitted to Constanti- 
nople, and which he hod believed were conformable to the intentions of the 
other Powers, he recomended that we should each of us report to our Govern- 
ments the urgency of instructing their Representatives to bring before the Porte 
their desire that the original note should be adopted by the Turkish Government, 
accompanying that recommendation with such guarantees and assurances as 
they should each of them deem it udvisable to offer.

| 


342 


In stating this Count Buol announced that he had received such informa- 
tion from Constantinople as made him most anxious that no time should be 
lost in bringing before the Porte the opinions of the allied Governments, so that 
the importance of the decision it was about to take might be clearly explained ; 
and he had transmitted to Count Colloredo a copy of his instructions to the 
Internuncio, to be communicated to your Lordship. You would see the 
earnestness with which he had pressed the Porte, by accepting the terms of a 
document which the allied Governments had agreed to in the perfect conviction 
that it contained nothing which could in any way compromise the honour or 
dignity of the Sultan or his Government, to put an end to the occupation of the 
Principalities, and to the dangers which must necessarily arise from its continua- 
tion. When Count Buol read this instruction to the Conference I remarked 
upon some of the expressions, as of a character too menacing to be justified 
while the Government of the Sultan was suffering from so great a grievance as the 
forcible occupation of two of its provinces , but he stated, that the dangerous 
posture of affairs required that they should be pointed out without reserve. 
Before the Conference closed Count Buol read a despatch from M. de Hiibner, 
in which he reports a conversation with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in which that 
Minister had stated his having instructed M. de la Cour to press upon Reshid 
Pasha, in the strongest manner, his advice that the unmodified note should he 
accepted, as the Government of the Sultan would otherwise render themselves 
responsible for the consequences which might ensue. Baron Bourqueney 
replied that he had no instructions which contained such a menace, although he 
was aware of the great anxiety of his Government that the note shou d be 
adopted; and with that view, after the Conference was ended, le wrote to 
M. de la Cour a despatch, the substance of which I transmitted to your Lordship 
on the evenings of the 16th-18th September. 

I had written the foregoing part of this despatch when I received, this 
morning, your Lordship’s telegraphic message of yesterday's date. I have to 
express my regret at having misunderstood the meaning of your IPEVIOUS 
telegraphic message of the 15th; I certainly thought that the words “J'ai tout 
lieu de eroire que M. de Bourqueney recevra une dépéche semblable a ce qui 
suit,” referred to the one which had just reached that Minister, and which jie 
brought with him to the Conference; more particularly ns it corresponded in 
part to the description your Lordship gave of it. IT imust add, that all the 
members of the Conference partook entirely of the same opinion. I very much 
regret this mistake, as it has led to a delay in bringing your Lordship’s views 
before the Conference. 

Upon the receipt, this morning, of your Lordships incasage | waited upon 
Count Buol, and placed it in his hands, “I have transmitted to you, by my two 
telegraphic despatches of this day, the result of my interview, Tan extremely 
sorry [ was not able, with every exertion that I made, anil in which M. de 
Bourqueney (who joined me during the discussion) assisted with the most 
anxious zeal, to obtain the object of your Lordship’s instructions. I have 
already informed you that Count Buol, at our former conferences, had stated, 


id 


that having sent his instructions to the Internuncio he could not take part in 
any collective communication upon the same subject to the Government oft the 
Sultan. Such a communication must now arrive too late to alter the impression 
made by his despatch, and therefore it would be better that each Government 
should separately forward their own instructions to their own Representatives, 
particularly as they would thus be enabled to direct them to give such 
unrantees and assurances as they conceived it would be advisuble to offer. 

I combatted this reasoning, which Count Buol immediately reproduced by 
pointing out the immense importance, in the present decisive crisis of this 
question, of the maintenance of that unity of counsel which had hitherto been 
attended with advantage, and which would still offer the most probable chance 
ofa favourable result, Count Buol expressed his anxious desire that the saine 
unity of action should continue amongst the allied Powers; bat that upon the 
present case it had been rendered impossible from the pressing neevssity of 
acting without delay, which had been thrown upon him in consequence of the 
absence of any previously concerted line of conduct amongst the Powers upon 

he emergency which had arisen, 

| recapitulated to Count Buol the great advantages which might be 
expected from the assurances and guarantees which your Lordship proposed to 


S43 


render to the Government of the Sultan, in inducing them to adopt the course 
which the Four Powers so strenuously recommended. and I expressed the most 
anxious hope that this opportunity of maintaining an attitude of impartiality 
between the conflicting parties wend not be thrown away. 

Count Buol replied that he felt himself obliged, under the circumstances 
which pressed upon him, to come to a decision, which he must maintain. He 
added that in no case could he agree to a pledge of “‘adhérence en toute occa- 
sion,”’ to the interpretation of any document, because he considered engagements 
binding for the future at all times as much as possible to be avoided; but he 
declared himself willing to take part with the other Powers in a declaration that 
the terms of the Vienna note could in no way be considered as menacing or 
derogatory to the independence or authority of the Sultan, 

M. de Bourqueney, who had taken an active part in this discussion, adhered, 
in conjunction with myself, to the acceptation of this proposal asa means of 
continuing the common action of the Four Powers, and of giving the Porte the 
benefit of their declared interpretation of the note and the security thereby 
afforded against any perversion of its terms to sanction pretensions prejudicial 
to the interests or independence of Turkey, 

It was under these circumstances that the project of the declaration which 
L forwarded to your Lordship in my first telegraphic message was drawn up; 
and as only Baron Bourqueney and myself had been present at this meeting 
with Count Buol, we repaired to Count Arnim’s to obtain his sanction to the 
declaration, and we fixed a conference for the evening, at which the amended 
document was agreed to, which I transmitted in my second despatch. 

I beg your Lordship to believe that with the zealous assistance of M. de 
Bourqueney, no exertion was spared on my part to secure the entire adoption of 
your Lordship's proposals, and that what we at last accepted only as a project 
to be submitted to your Lordship’s decision, has been the utmost which, unter 
the circumstances I have detailed, it was possible to obtain, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 23.) 


(No. 365. Confidential ) 
My Lord, Berlin, September 18, 1853. 

| HAD an opportunity yesterday at the review of taking leave of the King 
of Prussia and of the Princes, on the occasion of my approaching departure for 
England, was charged by His Majesty to convey to the Queen the expres- 
sions of his unalterable feelings of devotion and attachment to Her Majesty. 
The Prince of Prussia charged me also with the like assurances. 

In the course of the conversation which I had the honour of holding with 
the King, His Majesty alluded to Eastern atfairs. Lregretted to observe that he 
appeared extremely apprehensive that the Porte would refuse to adopt the 
original Vienna note, and that it consequently was impossible to foresee what 
calamities might not be entailed on Turkey in the event of their refusal. | 
availed myself of an opportunity which offered of inquiring if His Majesty 
thought that there was a chance of the immediate evacuation of the Principalittes, 
provided the Porte acceded to the recommendations which would be urged on 
her conjointly by the Four Powers; and he replied that notwithstanding the 
Emperor of Russia’s declaration that this would not tuke place until the ‘Turkish 
Ambassador had reached St. Petersburgh, it was his conviction that His 
Imperial Majesty would order the troops ta move from those Turkish provinces 
as soon as he learned that the note had been agreed to. The King’s conversa- 
tion turned on various points connected with this question, and one of his 
greatest apprehensions was that, even if the note was accepted, serous troubles 
might occur at Constantinople, and perhaps end in the deposition of the Sultan 
or some other disastrous event, ny ; 

Elis Majesty ended by requesting Er ta stute to your Lordship his anxious

of hoth countries to leave no means untried to preserve the peace of the world.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No, 378.) 
My Lord, 


Foreign Office, September 23, 1853, 
YOUR Excelleney’s report in your despatch No. 692 of your conversation 
with M. Drouyn de Lhuys on the proceedings of the Vienna Conference, subse- 
quently to the rejection by Russia of the Turkish modifications of the Vienna 
note, has been read with interest by Her Majesty’s Government, who, under the 
altered phase of affairs caused by the recent interpretation given by Russia to 
that note, do not think it expedient further to press the note on the acceptance 
of the Porte, nor to offer the British interpretation of it as an inducement to the 
Turkish Government to adopt it. 

The reagons which have induced Her Majesty's Government to come to 
this determination are fully explained in my despatch No. 308 to the Earl of 
Westmorland, of which, as well as of Count Nesselrode’s despatches to Baron 
Meyendortf detailing the Russian objections to the modifications of the Porte, 
copies were forwarded to you in my despatch No. 372. 

It will be a satisfaction to Her Majesty’s Government to find that the 
French Government concur in their views on this subject. 

lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON. 


No. 364. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 379.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, September 23, 1853. 

HER Majesty's Government entirely approve the language which you state 
in your despatch No, 693 that you held to M, Drouyn de Lhuys upon the sub- 
ject of the measures to be adopted by England and France in regard to the 
Eastern question, with reference to observations made by Count Buol to M. de 
Bourqueney urging that Turkey should be deterred by France from resorting to 
hostilities, while Austria would exert her influence to prevent further aggression 
by Russia, 

However much Her Majesty's Government will lament the commencement, 
of active hostilities, yet they will certainly offer no advice to the Turkish 
Government contrary to the interests of the Porte ; and those interests might be 
seriously affected by the maintenance of the actual status quo, which would leave 
Russia in peaceful possession of the Principalities during the winter. 

It isto be hoped that the Austrian proposal adverted to by M. de Bourqueney 
to call up the fleets to Constantinople under false pretences, and in order to make 
Russia believe that they were sent to the Bosphorus to overawe the Porte, has 
not been seriously contemplated, or at ull events that it will not be made, as Her 
Majesty's Government and that of France will not then be under the disagreeable 
necessity of treating such a proposal in the manner it deserves. 

lam, &e, 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(No. 205.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, September 23, 1859. 


BY a telegraphic despatch of the 11th instant from M. de la Cour to his 
Government, which has been communicated to me by Count Walewski, Her 
Majesty's Government have learnt the alarming state of affairs which then 
existed at Constantinople ; and that, upon the representations of Reshid Pasha 
and the Grand Vizier to your Excellency and M. de la Cour, you had each 
determined to send for two war-steamers trom Besika. 

The latest date of the despatches received from your Exeelleney at this 
office is the Sth instant, and Her Majesty's Government have, therefore, 10 
information of the events alluded to by M. de la Cour; but assuming, of course,

My Lord, Paris, September 26, 1853, 
* 1 HAVE communicated to M. Drouyn de Lhuys your Lordship's despateh 
No. 382, in which you inform me that Her Majesty's Government assents to the 
proposition made by the French Government, that the fleets should be ordered 


} 
, 
| 


48 


up to Constantinople ; and I have read to him also, the instructions which you 
have addressed in consequence to Viscount Stratford de Redeliffe, M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys has read me, in return, the despatches which were sent to M. de la 


Cour last night, to be forwarded by a special steamer from Marseilles. The 


French Ambassador at Constantinople is enjoined to spare no effort to obtain 


the acquiescence of the Ottoman Government in the contemplated advance of 


the fleets. The French Government justifies the act on the advantage of getting 
out of a false position, now that the real intentions of Russia are known; on the 
impossibility of the fleets wintering m Besika Bay; on the need of their presence 
at Constantinople to protect French subjects, the Christian population, and 
perhaps the Sultan himself; and on the necessity of letting it be seen that the 
voice of France is not silenced in the affairs of the East, 

M. de la Cour is desired to employ these arguments, should he find the 
Porte unwilling to take the step of declaring the status belli which would justify 
her in calling up the fleets; arguments which, M. Drouyn de Lhuys says, he 
has made use of towards the Turkish Ambassador in Paris. : 

Two dangers are signalized to M. de la Cour to avoid: cither discouraging 
hostilities on the part of Turkey by any show of apathy, or exciting the Porte by 
showing too great an enthusiasm in her course. 

Finally, he is instructed to act in complete concert with Her Majesty's 
Ambassador. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,— (Received September 27.) 


(No. 718.) 
My Lord, Paris, September 26, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has received despatches from Constantinople 
up tothe 15th instant. In them M. de la Cour relates the reasons which led 
the Ottoman Minister to ask for the presence of a few vessels from the combined 
flects, those reasons being an attempt made by the Ulemas, but which failed, to 
excite the Turkish population of Constantinople to dictate terms to the Sultan. 
The vessels sent for hod arrived, and together with those previously stationed or 
uecidentally at Constantinople, made « squadron of some nine or ten ships, 

M. de la Cour states further, that there was no longer the same hesitation 
in the Divan about admitting the two fleets within the Dardanelles; ond, indeed, 
that he had found, on applying for a firman to admit the vessels to which 
allusion has been made above, that a firman hod been dispatched some weeks 
ago to the Pasha of the Dardanelles, authorizing him to allow any French or 
English vessels, that might desire it, to pass up the Straits, 

The situation of the Turkish Ministry, M. de la Cour represents to be most 
deplorable—no two Ministers agreeing, and the Sultun at his wit's end. 

have, &e. 


(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received September 28.) 


(No, 272.) 
My Lord, Therapia, Seplember 15, 18.53. 

ALTHOUGH we have no messenger to go by the French steam-packet 
to-day, | avail myself of the opportunity to inform your Lordship of some 
important occurrences Which have taken place within the last week, 

1 stated on a former occasion that a placard Urging the Government to 
declare war had been posted on one of the mosques at situa Pa That 
demonstration of popular excitement was followed after aeverul divs by ii 
petition of the sume purpert presented to the Council and to the Sultan himself 


a49 


by a knot of individuals belonging to the class of muderris, or theological 
students. The paper was signed by thirty-five Pe of no individual distine- 
tion, but having the corporate importance of belonging to the “ Ulemab. 

Though free from menace, it was worded in serious and impressive terms, 
implying m strone bere of religious duty, and a very independent disregard of 
consequences. The Ministers took alarm, and conceived it to be the immediate 
forerunner of a revolution. Those who first communicated with me upon the 
subject suspected that one of their colleagues was the secret instigator of the 
movement, that his views were of a most ambitious character, and that sup- 
ported by partizans high in office, he might succeed in sacrificing his adversaries, 
dethroning the Sultan, and plunging the country into war. I was admonished 
of personal danger if the storm were to burst, and implored to take part in 
measures calculated to maintain the public tranquillity, Sk. 

The French Ambassador called upon me to compare his information with 
mine, and to consult as to the course which it would be most advisable to 
pursue, The Internuncio also, retained at home by business or indisposition, 
sent his principal bitecpresr to make me a similar communication. Both had 
been apprized by his Highness the Foreign Secretary of danger impending in 
the shape of a popular revolution, and both were ready to join with me in adopt- 
ing measures adequate to the occasion. S% 

I expressed in reply a cordial readiness to act in concert with them, but | 
declared at the same time that I was desirous of taking no step unwarranted by 
the necessities of the case, and that | wished to guard myself against mistake or 
exaggeration by a more precise knowledge of cireumstances. Any joint inter- 
ference on our parts, whether by note to the Minister or by direct application to 
the Sultan, would in my judgment be attended with serious inconvenience ; and 
I was still less inclined to join in bringing up the squadrons to Constantinople 
without more proofs of urgent peril than we had yet obtained. Tsuggested, as an 
opinion of my own, that we should do well, in the actual state of our informa- 
tion, to procure from our respective Admirals such an addition of steam force as 
might protect us from any immediate attack, and enable us to assist the Govern. 
ment in case of an outbreak threatening its existence, without attracting any 
unusual attention, or assuming an air of intimidation. This limited plan could 
easily be executed under cover of the steam communication continually plying 
between the squadrons and the capital, and it might be accompaniec with 
separate representations from us to such of the Ottoman Ministers as were most 
to be relie upon at so eritical a juncture. oe 

Reshid Pasha approved of this idea, and it has been carried into effect with 
much appearance of success by the French Ambassador and myself, The 
Admirals at Besika Bay have complied with our request ; and my private advice 
to the Sultan induced His Majesty to send for his principal Ministers, and by 
their agency to restrain the enthusiasts or instruments of intrigue, whose conduct 
had caused the prevailing alarm. evi 

I have sinee received, not only from the Secretary of State for Foreign 
Affairs, but also from the greater part of his colleagues, including the Grand 
Vizier and Sheik-ul-Islam, a strong assurance that the revolutionary movement 
ix checked for the present, and that its revival, though by no means impossible, 
is scarcely to be apprehended. La, 

In this state of things | should now feel myself ut liberty to release the 
extra steamers from their attendance here, did not the daily expectation of a 
final answer from Russia, and the impression likely to be made upon the fanatics 
at Constantinople by a pacific one, make it an object of prudence to postpone 
their departure, until an incident as near at hand as it may prove critical, shall 
have actually oceurred, . A oe i ee | 

Such are the principal features of the crisis, in so far as it affects the 
stability of the Government, the peace of the capital, and the safety of its 
Christian inhabitants. I have spared your Lordship a recital of particulars, us 
they have already lost much of their interest, and would require more time to 
relate than 1 can at present dispose of. 

I have, &e. ae
